frames.title: A real scenario.
frames.text: A real scenario. The problem in plain terms — something that could happen to a real product, described before any jargon.

frames.title: The concept, with a diagram.
frames.text: The concept, with a diagram. What the idea actually is, how the pieces relate, and a simple visual so you can picture it, not just recite it.

frames.title: A worked example.
frames.text: A worked example. Real numbers, a step-by-step walkthrough, or a concrete design decision — so the idea sticks as something you did, not something you read.

frames.title: Common mistakes and a knowledge check.
frames.text: Common mistakes and a knowledge check. The traps people fall into, and one question to test whether the idea actually landed.

frames.title: Finish Welcome and Introduction to System Design first.
frames.text: Finish Welcome and Introduction to System Design first. They set the vocabulary every later lesson assumes you already have.

frames.title: Go through Core Concepts in order.
frames.text: Go through Core Concepts in order. Scalability, Availability, Reliability, and the rest build on each other — skipping ahead usually means backtracking later.

frames.title: Treat Networking and Load Balancing as one unit.
frames.text: Treat Networking and Load Balancing as one unit. Together they explain how a single request actually reaches a server, which every later section assumes.

frames.title: Revisit, don't just reread.
frames.text: Revisit, don't just reread. Come back to a finished lesson a week later and try to redraw its diagram from memory before checking it.

diagrams.caption: You almost never do this once. Real designs loop through "add complexity → justify it" several times.

frames.title: Clarify requirements.
frames.text: Clarify requirements. Users can shorten a URL and share it; visiting the short link redirects to the original. Reads will vastly outnumber writes.

frames.title: Estimate the scale.
frames.text: Estimate the scale. Say 10M new links a month and 500M redirects a month — roughly 200 redirects/second on average, more at peak. That single number already rules out "one small server".

frames.title: Start simple.
frames.text: Start simple. One web server, one database table mapping short code → long URL. This works and is worth saying out loud — it is your baseline.

frames.title: Find the bottleneck.
frames.text: Find the bottleneck. At 200+ redirects/second, hitting the database on every single redirect is wasteful and risky if it goes down.

frames.title: Explain the trade-off.
frames.text: Explain the trade-off. Add a cache in front of the database for redirects. You gain speed and resilience; you give up instant consistency if a link's target is ever changed — a trade-off you can defend because you know the numbers behind it.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 640 200" role="img" aria-label="Networking, Load balancing, Caching, Data and storage, Communication, Reliability"><rect class="boxAccent" x="15" y="15" width="190" height="70" rx="8"/><text class="boxText" x="110" y="55">Networking</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="225" y="15" width="190" height="70" rx="8"/><text class="boxText" x="320" y="55">Load balancing</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="435" y="15" width="190" height="70" rx="8"/><text class="boxText" x="530" y="55">Caching</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="15" y="110" width="190" height="70" rx="8"/><text class="boxText" x="110" y="150">Data and storage</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="225" y="110" width="190" height="70" rx="8"/><text class="boxText" x="320" y="150">Communication</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="435" y="110" width="190" height="70" rx="8"/><text class="boxText" x="530" y="150">Reliability</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: The concepts work together: follow a request, find the bottleneck, and choose the right building blocks.

frames.title: You open the app.
frames.text: You open the app. DNS resolves the domain, HTTPS secures the connection, your request hits a load balancer.

frames.title: The load balancer
frames.text: The load balancer picks one of many app servers — that pool exists because of horizontal scaling.

frames.title: The app server calls an internal API
frames.text: The app server calls an internal API, checks a cache first, and only queries the database (indexed for speed) on a miss.

frames.title: Your uploaded photo
frames.text: Your uploaded photo goes to blob storage, and is served back to viewers through a CDN so it is fast worldwide.

frames.title: Behind the scenes,
frames.text: Behind the scenes, a like or comment might go through a message queue so the request returns instantly while a notification is sent later.

frames.title: An API gateway
frames.text: An API gateway in front of all of this enforces rate limiting so one bad client cannot take the app down for everyone.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 640 220" role="img" aria-labelledby="frTitle"><title id="frTitle">Functional requirements are the features; non-functional requirements wrap around them as quality constraints.</title><rect class="boxAccent" x="40" y="30" width="560" height="160" rx="8"></rect><text class="figLabel" x="320" y="52">NON-FUNCTIONAL: fast, available, secure, scalable</text><rect class="box" x="80" y="80" width="140" height="80"></rect><text class="boxText" x="150" y="125">Search</text><rect class="box" x="250" y="80" width="140" height="80"></rect><text class="boxText" x="320" y="125">Place order</text><rect class="box" x="420" y="80" width="140" height="80"></rect><text class="boxText" x="490" y="125">Track rider</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Features sit inside a box of quality constraints. Change a constraint (say, 10× the traffic) and the design inside the box changes too.

frames.title: List the features.
frames.text: List the features. Create a short link from a long URL; visiting the short link redirects to the long URL; optionally pick a custom alias; optionally see click counts.

frames.title: Find the actors.
frames.text: Find the actors. Anonymous visitor (redirect), signed-in user (create + analytics), admin (abuse takedowns).

frames.title: Attach numbers to each NFR.
frames.text: Attach numbers to each NFR. Redirects must be < 100 ms (p99). Reads are ~100× more common than writes. A created link must survive a server crash.

frames.title: Mark what is out of scope.
frames.text: Mark what is out of scope. No editing a link's target after creation, no team accounts in v1. Writing this down prevents scope creep.

frames.title: Derive scale.
frames.text: Derive scale. 100M new links/month and 10B redirects/month → ~4k redirects/s average, ~20k/s peak. That number decides caching and database choices.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 640 260" role="img" aria-labelledby="scaleTitle"><title id="scaleTitle">Vertical scaling makes one machine bigger; horizontal scaling adds more machines.</title><text class="figLabel" x="120" y="24">VERTICAL (scale up)</text><rect class="box" x="70" y="150" width="100" height="70"></rect><text class="boxText" x="120" y="190">1 server</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="255" y="70" width="120" height="150"></rect><text class="boxText" x="315" y="150">bigger server</text><text class="figHint" x="120" y="245">more CPU / RAM</text><line class="divider" x1="420" y1="30" x2="420" y2="235"></line><text class="figLabel" x="530" y="24">HORIZONTAL (scale out)</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="460" y="150" width="60" height="70"></rect><rect class="boxAccent" x="530" y="150" width="60" height="70"></rect><rect class="boxAccent" x="600" y="150" width="30" height="70"></rect><text class="figHint" x="535" y="245">more servers, same size</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Scalability: components and relationships.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 640 240" role="img" aria-labelledby="lbTitle"><title id="lbTitle">A load balancer spreads incoming traffic across several identical app servers, which share one database.</title><rect class="box" x="20" y="95" width="90" height="50"></rect><text class="boxText" x="65" y="125">Users</text><line class="flow" x1="110" y1="120" x2="180" y2="120"></line><rect class="boxAccent" x="180" y="90" width="110" height="60"></rect><text class="boxText" x="235" y="125">Load balancer</text><line class="flow" x1="290" y1="115" x2="370" y2="55"></line><line class="flow" x1="290" y1="120" x2="370" y2="120"></line><line class="flow" x1="290" y1="125" x2="370" y2="185"></line><rect class="box" x="370" y="35" width="90" height="40"></rect><text class="boxText" x="415" y="60">app #1</text><rect class="box" x="370" y="100" width="90" height="40"></rect><text class="boxText" x="415" y="125">app #2</text><rect class="box" x="370" y="165" width="90" height="40"></rect><text class="boxText" x="415" y="190">app #3…</text><line class="flow" x1="460" y1="55" x2="540" y2="115"></line><line class="flow" x1="460" y1="120" x2="540" y2="120"></line><line class="flow" x1="460" y1="185" x2="540" y2="125"></line><rect class="boxAccent" x="540" y="90" width="90" height="60"></rect><text class="boxText" x="585" y="125">Database</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Scalability: components and relationships.

frames.title: The idea
frames.text: Scalability is a system's ability to keep working well as the amount of work grows.

frames.title: The mechanism
frames.text: Every scaling decision is a mix of these two directions. Knowing which one you are reaching for—and why—is the core skill.

frames.title: In practice
frames.text: You launch a photo app. It becomes popular. Let's walk the numbers a fresher can reason about on paper.

frames.title: Remember
frames.text: Keeping a user's session or uploaded file on one machine breaks the moment the load balancer sends their next request elsewhere. Push state to a shared store.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 640 200" role="img" aria-labelledby="availTitle"><title id="availTitle">A single server is a point of failure; two servers with automatic failover keep serving when one dies.</title><text class="figLabel" x="150" y="24">SINGLE POINT OF FAILURE</text><rect class="box" x="40" y="80" width="80" height="45"></rect><text class="boxText" x="80" y="107">Users</text><line class="flow" x1="120" y1="102" x2="180" y2="102"></line><rect class="boxWarn" x="180" y="78" width="100" height="50"></rect><text class="boxText" x="230" y="108">1 server</text><text class="figHint" x="230" y="150">dies → everyone down</text><line class="divider" x1="330" y1="20" x2="330" y2="175"></line><text class="figLabel" x="480" y="24">REDUNDANT + FAILOVER</text><rect class="box" x="350" y="80" width="70" height="45"></rect><text class="boxText" x="385" y="107">Users</text><line class="flow" x1="420" y1="95" x2="470" y2="70"></line><line class="flowMuted" x1="420" y1="110" x2="470" y2="150"></line><rect class="boxAccent" x="470" y="48" width="110" height="44"></rect><text class="boxText" x="525" y="75">server A (live)</text><rect class="box" x="470" y="128" width="110" height="44"></rect><text class="boxText" x="525" y="155">server B (standby)</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: With redundancy, one machine failing drops capacity, not the whole service. Traffic shifts to the healthy node automatically.

frames.title: The idea
frames.text: Availability is the share of time a system is up and able to serve requests. It is usually written as a percentage, like 99.9%.

frames.title: The mechanism
frames.text: Each extra 9 cuts the allowed downtime by 10×. This is why people talk about "three nines" or "four nines" — it is a shorthand for a downtime budget.

frames.title: In practice
frames.text: Suppose one server is available 99% of the time (down ~3.65 days/year). What happens when we chain components versus duplicate them?

frames.title: Remember
frames.text: Chaining components multiplies their weaknesses; duplicating a component multiplies its strength. Redundancy on the weakest link buys the most availability.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 640 190" role="img" aria-labelledby="relTitle"><title id="relTitle">A request tries the primary path, retries once on failure, then falls back to a degraded response instead of erroring.</title><rect class="box" x="30" y="72" width="90" height="46"></rect><text class="boxText" x="75" y="99">Request</text><line class="flow" x1="120" y1="95" x2="180" y2="95"></line><rect class="boxAccent" x="180" y="70" width="120" height="50"></rect><text class="boxText" x="240" y="100">Call service</text><path class="flowMuted" d="M240 120 C 240 160, 300 160, 300 122"></path><text class="figHint" x="270" y="178">retry once</text><line class="flow" x1="300" y1="95" x2="360" y2="95"></line><rect class="boxWarn" x="360" y="70" width="110" height="50"></rect><text class="boxText" x="415" y="100">still failing?</text><line class="flow" x1="470" y1="95" x2="520" y2="95"></line><rect class="box" x="520" y="70" width="100" height="50"></rect><text class="boxText" x="570" y="93">cached /</text><text class="boxText" x="570" y="109">default</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Reliable systems have a plan for "what if this call fails?" at every hop, not just a try/catch that returns 500.

frames.title: The idea
frames.text: Reliability is the system doing the right thing — correct results, no lost data — continuously over time, even when parts fail.

frames.title: The mechanism
frames.text: Failures come from three places: hardware (disks, memory, power), software (bugs, bad deploys, memory leaks), and humans (wrong config, fat-fingered command). At scale, software and human errors cause most outages.

frames.title: In practice
frames.text: The two ideas connect through a simple formula. If a service fails on average every 30 days and takes 1 hour to fully recover:

frames.title: Remember
frames.text: You do not always need fewer failures — recovering faster (lower MTTR) is often the cheaper path to more nines.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 640 200" role="img" aria-labelledby="spofTitle"><title id="spofTitle">Redundant app servers still funnel through one load balancer and one database, each a single point of failure.</title><rect class="box" x="20" y="85" width="70" height="40"></rect><text class="boxText" x="55" y="110">Users</text><line class="flow" x1="90" y1="105" x2="130" y2="105"></line><rect class="boxWarn" x="130" y="82" width="90" height="46"></rect><text class="boxText" x="175" y="103">1 load</text><text class="boxText" x="175" y="119">balancer</text><line class="flow" x1="220" y1="90" x2="280" y2="55"></line><line class="flow" x1="220" y1="105" x2="280" y2="105"></line><line class="flow" x1="220" y1="120" x2="280" y2="155"></line><rect class="box" x="280" y="38" width="90" height="34"></rect><text class="boxText" x="325" y="60">app</text><rect class="box" x="280" y="88" width="90" height="34"></rect><text class="boxText" x="325" y="110">app</text><rect class="box" x="280" y="138" width="90" height="34"></rect><text class="boxText" x="325" y="160">app</text><line class="flow" x1="370" y1="55" x2="430" y2="100"></line><line class="flow" x1="370" y1="105" x2="430" y2="105"></line><line class="flow" x1="370" y1="155" x2="430" y2="110"></line><rect class="boxWarn" x="430" y="82" width="100" height="46"></rect><text class="boxText" x="480" y="103">1 database</text><text class="figHint" x="480" y="150">two SPOFs remain</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: The red boxes are single points of failure. The app tier is fine; the funnels on either side are not.

frames.title: Draw the request path
frames.text: Draw the request path end to end, including DNS, CDN, load balancer, app, cache, database, and any third-party call.

frames.title: Circle everything there is only one of.
frames.text: Circle everything there is only one of. Each circle is a candidate SPOF.

frames.title: Ask "what happens if this dies right now?"
frames.text: Ask "what happens if this dies right now?" If the answer is "total outage", it is confirmed.

frames.title: Add redundancy from the weakest link inward.
frames.text: Add redundancy from the weakest link inward. Two of the component, in different failure domains (racks / availability zones).

frames.title: Add detection + automatic failover.
frames.text: Add detection + automatic failover. Redundancy without fast, automated failover just means a human has to notice and react.

frames.title: Test it.
frames.text: Test it. Kill the primary on purpose in staging (or production game days) and confirm traffic moves with no outage.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 640 120" role="img" aria-labelledby="latTitle"><title id="latTitle">One request's latency is network time out, queue wait, app processing, database time, and network time back.</title><rect class="box" x="20" y="40" width="110" height="40"></rect><text class="boxText" x="75" y="57">network</text><text class="boxText" x="75" y="73">~20 ms</text><rect class="boxWarn" x="140" y="40" width="110" height="40"></rect><text class="boxText" x="195" y="57">queue wait</text><text class="boxText" x="195" y="73">0–? ms</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="260" y="40" width="110" height="40"></rect><text class="boxText" x="315" y="57">app work</text><text class="boxText" x="315" y="73">~15 ms</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="380" y="40" width="110" height="40"></rect><text class="boxText" x="435" y="57">database</text><text class="boxText" x="435" y="73">~30 ms</text><rect class="box" x="500" y="40" width="110" height="40"></rect><text class="boxText" x="555" y="57">network</text><text class="boxText" x="555" y="73">~20 ms</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Queue wait is the sneaky part: near capacity, requests sit in line and latency spikes even though the work itself did not slow down.

frames.title: Target throughput:
frames.text: Target throughput: 1,000 requests/second at peak.

frames.title: Measured latency:
frames.text: Measured latency: 200 ms (0.2 s) per request, mostly a database call.

frames.title: Concurrency needed:
frames.text: Concurrency needed: 1000 × 0.2 = 200 in flight at once.

frames.title: Servers:
frames.text: Servers: if one server handles 50 concurrent requests, you need 200 / 50 = 4 servers plus headroom.

frames.title: Check bandwidth:
frames.text: Check bandwidth: each response is 40 KB. 1000/s × 40 KB = 40 MB/s = 320 Mbps — fine on a 1 Gbps link, but a 10× traffic spike would saturate it, so plan a CDN.

frames.title: Attack latency:
frames.text: Attack latency: add a cache so 80% of reads skip the DB → latency ~60 ms → concurrency drops to 60 → 2 servers do the same work.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 640 260" role="img" aria-labelledby="ringTitle"><title id="ringTitle">Servers and keys are placed around a circle; each key is owned by the next server clockwise.</title><circle cx="200" cy="130" r="90" fill="none" stroke="var(--line)" stroke-width="2"></circle><circle class="ringNode" cx="200" cy="40" r="9"></circle><text class="figLabel" x="200" y="28">S1</text><circle class="ringNode" cx="278" cy="175" r="9"></circle><text class="figLabel" x="298" y="180">S2</text><circle class="ringNode" cx="122" cy="175" r="9"></circle><text class="figLabel" x="100" y="180">S3</text><circle class="ringKey" cx="243" cy="58" r="5"></circle><text class="figHint" x="255" y="52">key A</text><circle class="ringKey" cx="255" cy="205" r="5"></circle><text class="figHint" x="268" y="218">key B</text><circle class="ringKey" cx="140" cy="70" r="5"></circle><text class="figHint" x="120" y="60">key C</text><text class="boxText" x="470" y="80">key A → clockwise → S2</text><text class="boxText" x="470" y="120">key B → clockwise → S3</text><text class="boxText" x="470" y="160">key C → clockwise → S1</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Add S4 between S1 and S2 and only the keys in that arc move — to S4. Every other key stays put.

frames.title: Place the servers.
frames.text: Place the servers. hash("S1") = 12, hash("S2") = 48, hash("S3") = 90 (on a 0–99 ring for simplicity).

frames.title: Hash the key.
frames.text: Hash the key. hash("user:42") = 55.

frames.title: Walk clockwise
frames.text: Walk clockwise from 55: the next server point is S3 at 90. user:42 lives on S3.

frames.title: Add S4 at 70.
frames.text: Add S4 at 70. Walk clockwise from 55 again → now you hit S4 first. Only keys between 48 and 70 moved (from S3 to S4). Keys elsewhere are untouched.

frames.title: Remove S2 (at 48).
frames.text: Remove S2 (at 48). Its keys (from 12 to 48) now walk clockwise to S3. No other server is affected.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 640 200" role="img" aria-labelledby="capTitle"><title id="capTitle">During a network partition, a CP system rejects requests to stay consistent; an AP system answers with possibly-stale data to stay available.</title><rect class="box" x="60" y="80" width="90" height="44"></rect><text class="boxText" x="105" y="107">Node A</text><line class="flowMuted" x1="150" y1="102" x2="260" y2="102"></line><text class="figHint" x="205" y="92">partition</text><text class="figHint" x="205" y="122">(link down)</text><rect class="box" x="260" y="80" width="90" height="44"></rect><text class="boxText" x="305" y="107">Node B</text><line class="divider" x1="390" y1="20" x2="390" y2="180"></line><text class="figLabel" x="480" y="34">CP: reject / wait</text><rect class="boxWarn" x="420" y="50" width="140" height="34"></rect><text class="boxText" x="490" y="72">error, stay correct</text><text class="figLabel" x="480" y="120">AP: answer anyway</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="420" y="136" width="140" height="34"></rect><text class="boxText" x="490" y="158">stale, stay up</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Outside a partition you can have both C and A. The trade-off only bites during the partition window.

frames.title: Bank account balance.
frames.text: Bank account balance. Showing stale money or allowing a double-spend is unacceptable → CP: refuse the operation during a partition.

frames.title: Shopping cart.
frames.text: Shopping cart. A user must always be able to add items; a briefly out-of-sync cart can be merged later → AP.

frames.title: Leader election / distributed lock.
frames.text: Leader election / distributed lock. Two leaders = disaster → CP: only the majority side may elect.

frames.title: View counter / like count.
frames.text: View counter / like count. Off by a few for a minute is invisible → AP, reconcile by summing later.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 640 180" role="img" aria-labelledby="consTitle"><title id="consTitle">A write goes to the primary, replicates to a follower after a short delay; a read from the follower during that delay sees the old value.</title><rect class="box" x="20" y="70" width="80" height="44"></rect><text class="boxText" x="60" y="97">Client</text><line class="flow" x1="100" y1="82" x2="170" y2="62"></line><text class="figHint" x="130" y="52">write x=5</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="170" y="40" width="120" height="46"></rect><text class="boxText" x="230" y="68">Primary x=5</text><line class="flowMuted" x1="290" y1="63" x2="400" y2="63"></line><text class="figHint" x="345" y="53">replication lag</text><rect class="boxWarn" x="400" y="40" width="120" height="46"></rect><text class="boxText" x="460" y="68">Follower x=4</text><line class="flow" x1="100" y1="100" x2="400" y2="120"></line><text class="figHint" x="250" y="140">read → still sees x=4</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: The window between "write accepted" and "every replica updated" is where consistency models differ.

frames.title: Follower count on a profile.
frames.text: Follower count on a profile. Off by 3 for a few seconds? Nobody cares → eventual.

frames.title: "Seats left" on a flight.
frames.text: "Seats left" on a flight. Selling the same seat twice is a real problem → strong for the final booking step.

frames.title: Your own draft post.
frames.text: Your own draft post. You must see your edits immediately even if others do not → read-your-writes.

frames.title: A chat conversation.
frames.text: A chat conversation. Messages must not appear, vanish, then reappear → monotonic reads at minimum.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 640 160" role="img" aria-labelledby="capTitle"><title id="capTitle">Users multiply into daily actions, which divide into a per-second rate, which divides into a server count.</title><rect class="boxAccent" x="20" y="60" width="120" height="44"></rect><text class="boxText" x="80" y="87">10M DAU</text><line class="flow" x1="140" y1="82" x2="190" y2="82"></line><rect class="boxAccent" x="190" y="60" width="130" height="44"></rect><text class="boxText" x="255" y="80">×20 actions</text><text class="boxText" x="255" y="96">= 200M/day</text><line class="flow" x1="320" y1="82" x2="370" y2="82"></line><rect class="boxAccent" x="370" y="60" width="120" height="44"></rect><text class="boxText" x="430" y="80">÷ 86,400</text><text class="boxText" x="430" y="96">≈ 2.3k/s</text><line class="flow" x1="490" y1="82" x2="540" y2="82"></line><rect class="box" x="540" y="60" width="90" height="44"></rect><text class="boxText" x="585" y="80">×5 peak</text><text class="boxText" x="585" y="96">≈ 12k/s</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Every capacity number is this same chain: multiply out, then divide down.

frames.title: The idea
frames.text: Capacity estimation is working out — before you build — roughly how many requests per second, how much storage, and how much bandwidth a system will need.

frames.title: The mechanism
frames.text: Start with users. Daily Active Users (DAU). If given monthly, assume DAU ≈ MAU / 3.

frames.title: In practice
frames.text: Two conclusions fell out for free: reads are ~50× writes so a cache + CDN is mandatory, and 33 PB means object storage (like S3), never a single database.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 640 150" role="img" aria-labelledby="ladderTitle"><title id="ladderTitle">Bar chart: RAM is 100 times slower than cache, SSD 1000 times slower than RAM, a cross-continent round trip a million times slower again.</title><text class="figHint" x="70" y="30">RAM</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="110" y="18" width="40" height="16"></rect><text class="figHint" x="70" y="60">SSD read</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="110" y="48" width="130" height="16"></rect><text class="figHint" x="70" y="90">DC round trip</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="110" y="78" width="240" height="16"></rect><text class="figHint" x="70" y="120">cross-continent</text><rect class="boxWarn" x="110" y="108" width="500" height="16"></rect></svg>
diagrams.caption: Each step down the storage/network stack is roughly 10–1000× slower. This is why "keep it in RAM" and "keep data near the user" are such common answers.

frames.title: "A year of tweets — how much storage?"
frames.text: "A year of tweets — how much storage?" 500M tweets/day × 300 bytes ≈ 150 GB/day. × 365 ≈ 55 TB/year. ×3 replication ≈ 165 TB. Verdict: fits on a modest cluster, not in memory.

frames.title: "Can we cache all product data in RAM?"
frames.text: "Can we cache all product data in RAM?" 2M products × 2 KB each = 4 GB. A single server has 64–256 GB RAM. Verdict: easily — do it.

frames.title: "QPS for a URL shortener?"
frames.text: "QPS for a URL shortener?" 10B redirects/month ÷ (30 × 10 5 ) ≈ 3,300/s average, ~10k/s peak. Verdict: needs a cache, but one region can handle it.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 640 170" role="img" aria-labelledby="netTitle"><title id="netTitle">A request travels from your device through your router and ISP, across the internet backbone, to the destination server, then back.</title><rect class="box" x="15" y="65" width="80" height="42"></rect><text class="boxText" x="55" y="90">You</text><line class="flow" x1="95" y1="86" x2="140" y2="86"></line><rect class="box" x="140" y="65" width="80" height="42"></rect><text class="boxText" x="180" y="90">Router</text><line class="flow" x1="220" y1="86" x2="265" y2="86"></line><rect class="box" x="265" y="65" width="70" height="42"></rect><text class="boxText" x="300" y="90">ISP</text><line class="flow" x1="335" y1="86" x2="380" y2="86"></line><rect class="boxAccent" x="380" y="55" width="120" height="62"></rect><text class="boxText" x="440" y="82">Internet</text><text class="boxText" x="440" y="98">(many routers)</text><line class="flow" x1="500" y1="86" x2="545" y2="86"></line><rect class="box" x="545" y="65" width="80" height="42"></rect><text class="boxText" x="585" y="90">Server</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Every hop only knows "which neighbour gets this packet next?" — no single router knows the whole path.

frames.title: Name → address (DNS).
frames.text: Name → address (DNS). Your device asks a DNS resolver for the IP of engineering-decoded.com and gets back something like 76.76.21.21.

frames.title: Open a connection (TCP).
frames.text: Open a connection (TCP). Your device and the server exchange a 3-message handshake (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK) to agree to talk.

frames.title: Secure it (TLS).
frames.text: Secure it (TLS). For HTTPS, they swap certificates and keys so the rest of the conversation is encrypted.

frames.title: Send the request (HTTP).
frames.text: Send the request (HTTP). Your device sends GET / HTTP/1.1 plus headers.

frames.title: Route the packets (IP).
frames.text: Route the packets (IP). Each packet hops router-to-router. Routers read the destination IP and forward toward it; TTL stops loops.

frames.title: Server responds.
frames.text: Server responds. It sends back the HTML, then the browser requests CSS, JS, and images the same way.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 640 130" role="img" aria-labelledby="cidrTitle"><title id="cidrTitle">In a /24, the first three octets are the network prefix and the last octet is the host number.</title><rect class="boxAccent" x="30" y="45" width="330" height="44"></rect><text class="boxText" x="195" y="64">192 . 168 . 1</text><text class="boxText" x="195" y="80">network (24 bits)</text><rect class="box" x="370" y="45" width="150" height="44"></rect><text class="boxText" x="445" y="64">. 23</text><text class="boxText" x="445" y="80">host (8 bits)</text><text class="figHint" x="280" y="115">/24 → 256 addresses, 254 usable</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Smaller number after the slash = bigger network. /16 holds 65,536 addresses; /30 holds just 4 (handy for a point-to-point link).

frames.title: /22 = 22 network bits
frames.text: /22 = 22 network bits → the mask is 255.255.252.0. The third octet's top 6 bits are fixed, bottom 2 are host space.

frames.title: Network of A:
frames.text: Network of A: 10.1.4.0 (4 in binary is 000001|00; masked → block starts at 4).

frames.title: Network of B:
frames.text: Network of B: 10.1.4.0 as well — the /22 block covers third octets 4, 5, 6, 7.

frames.title: Same network →
frames.text: Same network → A and B talk directly, no router needed. If B were 10.1.8.5 it would be in the next block and need routing.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 640 180" role="img" aria-labelledby="dnsTitle"><title id="dnsTitle">The resolver asks the root, then the TLD server, then the authoritative server, then returns the IP to your device.</title><rect class="box" x="15" y="70" width="80" height="40"></rect><text class="boxText" x="55" y="94">You</text><line class="flow" x1="95" y1="90" x2="135" y2="90"></line><rect class="boxAccent" x="135" y="66" width="100" height="48"></rect><text class="boxText" x="185" y="86">Recursive</text><text class="boxText" x="185" y="102">resolver</text><line class="flow" x1="235" y1="80" x2="300" y2="45"></line><rect class="box" x="300" y="25" width="90" height="34"></rect><text class="boxText" x="345" y="47">Root</text><line class="flow" x1="235" y1="90" x2="300" y2="90"></line><rect class="box" x="300" y="73" width="90" height="34"></rect><text class="boxText" x="345" y="95">.com TLD</text><line class="flow" x1="235" y1="100" x2="300" y2="135"></line><rect class="box" x="300" y="120" width="90" height="34"></rect><text class="boxText" x="345" y="142">Authoritative</text><line class="flow" x1="390" y1="137" x2="470" y2="110"></line><rect class="boxAccent" x="470" y="90" width="120" height="40"></rect><text class="boxText" x="530" y="114">A = 76.76.21.21</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Each step narrows the search: root knows .com, .com knows the domain, the domain knows the host.

frames.title: Check caches.
frames.text: Check caches. Browser cache → OS cache → recursive resolver cache. A hit here ends the story in < 1 ms.

frames.title: Ask a root server:
frames.text: Ask a root server: "where is .com?" It replies with the .com TLD server addresses.

frames.title: Ask the .com TLD server:
frames.text: Ask the .com TLD server: "where is example.com?" It replies with example.com 's authoritative name servers (NS records).

frames.title: Ask the authoritative server:
frames.text: Ask the authoritative server: "what is blog.example.com?" It returns the A record, say 93.184.216.34, with a TTL (e.g. 300s).

frames.title: Cache and use.
frames.text: Cache and use. The resolver caches the answer for the TTL and hands the IP to your device, which now opens a TCP connection.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 640 170" role="img" aria-labelledby="tcpTitle"><title id="tcpTitle">TCP opens with SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK before any data, and closes with FIN and ACK.</title><text class="figLabel" x="90" y="24">CLIENT</text><text class="figLabel" x="550" y="24">SERVER</text><line class="divider" x1="90" y1="30" x2="90" y2="150"></line><line class="divider" x1="550" y1="30" x2="550" y2="150"></line><line class="flow" x1="90" y1="45" x2="550" y2="60"></line><text class="figHint" x="320" y="40">SYN (let's talk)</text><line class="flow" x1="550" y1="75" x2="90" y2="90"></line><text class="figHint" x="320" y="70">SYN-ACK (ok, you too)</text><line class="flow" x1="90" y1="105" x2="550" y2="120"></line><text class="figHint" x="320" y="100">ACK (confirmed) + data flows</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: That is one full round trip before the first byte of your request — the cost of reliability. Keep-alive connections avoid paying it repeatedly.

frames.title: Is every byte essential?
frames.text: Is every byte essential? File transfer, API call, payment → TCP.

frames.title: Is fresh data more valuable than complete data?
frames.text: Is fresh data more valuable than complete data? Live audio, sensor telemetry, game position → UDP.

frames.title: Do you need many short request/replies with low latency?
frames.text: Do you need many short request/replies with low latency? DNS uses UDP (one packet each way) and only falls back to TCP for large answers.

frames.title: Want UDP's speed but TCP's reliability?
frames.text: Want UDP's speed but TCP's reliability? Use QUIC (the basis of HTTP/3): runs on UDP but adds ordering, retransmission, and encryption in user space.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 640 160" role="img" aria-labelledby="httpsTitle"><title id="httpsTitle">After the TCP handshake, TLS exchanges a certificate and keys, then all HTTP data is encrypted.</title><rect class="box" x="20" y="60" width="90" height="44"></rect><text class="boxText" x="65" y="86">Browser</text><line class="flow" x1="110" y1="70" x2="520" y2="70"></line><text class="figHint" x="315" y="60">TCP handshake</text><line class="flow" x1="110" y1="95" x2="520" y2="95"></line><text class="figHint" x="315" y="88">TLS: cert + key exchange</text><line class="flow" x1="110" y1="120" x2="520" y2="120"></line><text class="figHint" x="315" y="135">encrypted HTTP (GET / POST ...)</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="520" y="60" width="90" height="44"></rect><text class="boxText" x="565" y="86">Server</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: The certificate proves the server really is shop.example.com (signed by a Certificate Authority the browser trusts). Then a shared secret encrypts everything.

frames.title: First request:
frames.text: First request: browser sends GET /logo.png. Server replies 200 OK with ETag: "abc123" and Cache-Control: max-age=3600.

frames.title: Within the hour:
frames.text: Within the hour: the browser serves logo.png straight from disk — zero network.

frames.title: After an hour:
frames.text: After an hour: browser revalidates with If-None-Match: "abc123".

frames.title: Unchanged:
frames.text: Unchanged: server replies 304 Not Modified with an empty body — a few bytes instead of re-downloading the image.

frames.title: Changed:
frames.text: Changed: server replies 200 OK with the new bytes and a new ETag.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 640 160" role="img" aria-labelledby="wsTitle"><title id="wsTitle">An HTTP upgrade request becomes a persistent two-way WebSocket connection.</title><rect class="box" x="20" y="60" width="90" height="44"></rect><text class="boxText" x="65" y="86">Browser</text><line class="flow" x1="110" y1="70" x2="520" y2="70"></line><text class="figHint" x="315" y="60">GET /chat  Upgrade: websocket</text><line class="flow" x1="520" y1="90" x2="110" y2="90"></line><text class="figHint" x="315" y="105">101 Switching Protocols</text><line class="flow" x1="110" y1="125" x2="520" y2="125"></line><line class="flow" x1="520" y1="132" x2="110" y2="132"></line><text class="figHint" x="315" y="150">messages flow both ways, anytime</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="520" y="60" width="90" height="44"></rect><text class="boxText" x="565" y="86">Server</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: One TCP + TLS setup, then the connection stays open for minutes or hours. Each message is a tiny frame (2–14 bytes of header) instead of a full HTTP request.

frames.title: Connect:
frames.text: Connect: browser opens new WebSocket("wss://app.example.com/doc/42"). Handshake completes, connection is open.

frames.title: Join:
frames.text: Join: client sends {"type":"join","user":"amy"}. Server adds this socket to the room for doc 42.

frames.title: Move:
frames.text: Move: as Amy moves her cursor, the client sends {"type":"cursor","pos":128} a few times a second.

frames.title: Fan out:
frames.text: Fan out: the server forwards each message to every other socket in room 42 — no polling, sub-50 ms.

frames.title: Heartbeat:
frames.text: Heartbeat: every 30s each side sends a ping/pong frame so dead connections are detected and cleaned up.

frames.title: Reconnect:
frames.text: Reconnect: on network drop the client retries with backoff and re-sends join to restore state.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 640 190" role="img" aria-labelledby="cdnTitle"><title id="cdnTitle">Users hit a nearby edge server; on a cache miss the edge fetches once from the distant origin and stores it.</title><rect class="box" x="20" y="30" width="80" height="36"></rect><text class="boxText" x="60" y="52">User EU</text><rect class="box" x="20" y="80" width="80" height="36"></rect><text class="boxText" x="60" y="102">User US</text><rect class="box" x="20" y="130" width="80" height="36"></rect><text class="boxText" x="60" y="152">User Asia</text><line class="flow" x1="100" y1="48" x2="170" y2="60"></line><line class="flow" x1="100" y1="98" x2="170" y2="98"></line><line class="flow" x1="100" y1="148" x2="170" y2="135"></line><rect class="boxAccent" x="170" y="45" width="110" height="34"></rect><text class="boxText" x="225" y="67">Edge EU</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="170" y="82" width="110" height="34"></rect><text class="boxText" x="225" y="104">Edge US</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="170" y="119" width="110" height="34"></rect><text class="boxText" x="225" y="141">Edge Asia</text><line class="flowMuted" x1="280" y1="62" x2="470" y2="95"></line><line class="flowMuted" x1="280" y1="99" x2="470" y2="99"></line><line class="flowMuted" x1="280" y1="136" x2="470" y2="103"></line><text class="figHint" x="380" y="80">only on cache miss</text><rect class="box" x="470" y="80" width="110" height="40"></rect><text class="boxText" x="525" y="104">Origin</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Each edge location (Point of Presence) serves its region. A cache miss is a one-time cost; every hit after that skips the origin entirely.

frames.title: DNS points to the CDN.
frames.text: DNS points to the CDN. cdn.example.com resolves to the CDN, which returns the IP of the nearest edge (anycast / geo-DNS).

frames.title: Edge checks its cache.
frames.text: Edge checks its cache. Cache key = host + path + selected headers.

frames.title: Hit:
frames.text: Hit: the edge returns the file in ~10 ms. Origin is untouched. Response carries X-Cache: HIT.

frames.title: Miss:
frames.text: Miss: the edge fetches from origin once, stores it per the Cache-Control TTL, and serves it. Later users in that region get hits.

frames.title: Purge on deploy:
frames.text: Purge on deploy: your pipeline calls the CDN's purge API (or you rely on hashed filenames) so stale files are dropped.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 640 300" role="img" aria-labelledby="osiTitle"><title id="osiTitle">Layers 7 to 1: Application, Presentation, Session, Transport, Network, Data Link, Physical.</title><rect class="boxAccent" x="60" y="15" width="520" height="34"></rect><text class="boxText" x="320" y="37">7 Application — HTTP, DNS, SMTP (the data you care about)</text><rect class="box" x="60" y="53" width="520" height="34"></rect><text class="boxText" x="320" y="75">6 Presentation — TLS encryption, compression, encoding</text><rect class="box" x="60" y="91" width="520" height="34"></rect><text class="boxText" x="320" y="113">5 Session — open / keep / close a conversation</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="60" y="129" width="520" height="34"></rect><text class="boxText" x="320" y="151">4 Transport — TCP / UDP, ports, reliability</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="60" y="167" width="520" height="34"></rect><text class="boxText" x="320" y="189">3 Network — IP addresses, routing between networks</text><rect class="box" x="60" y="205" width="520" height="34"></rect><text class="boxText" x="320" y="227">2 Data Link — MAC addresses, switches, one local hop</text><rect class="box" x="60" y="243" width="520" height="34"></rect><text class="boxText" x="320" y="265">1 Physical — cables, radio, voltages, bits on a wire</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Mnemonic (top to bottom): A ll P eople S eem T o N eed D ata P rocessing.

frames.title: L7:
frames.text: L7: your app builds GET /orders.

frames.title: L6:
frames.text: L6: TLS encrypts it.

frames.title: L4:
frames.text: L4: TCP wraps it in a segment, adds source/destination ports, sequence numbers.

frames.title: L3:
frames.text: L3: IP wraps that in a packet, adds source/destination IP addresses.

frames.title: L2:
frames.text: L2: the NIC wraps it in a frame with the next hop's MAC address.

frames.title: L1:
frames.text: L1: the frame becomes electrical / optical / radio signals on the wire.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 640 150" role="img" aria-labelledby="ckTitle"><title id="ckTitle">Sender computes a checksum over the data and appends it; receiver recomputes and compares.</title><rect class="box" x="20" y="55" width="150" height="40"></rect><text class="boxText" x="95" y="72">data</text><text class="boxText" x="95" y="88">[12, 44, 7, 91]</text><line class="flow" x1="170" y1="75" x2="230" y2="75"></line><rect class="boxAccent" x="230" y="55" width="120" height="40"></rect><text class="boxText" x="290" y="72">sum mod 256</text><text class="boxText" x="290" y="88">= 154</text><line class="flow" x1="350" y1="75" x2="410" y2="75"></line><rect class="box" x="410" y="55" width="210" height="40"></rect><text class="boxText" x="515" y="72">send: [12, 44, 7, 91] + 154</text><text class="figHint" x="320" y="125">receiver re-sums → 154? keep. 153? reject.</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Real checksums (CRC, Adler-32) use polynomial math so that common errors — burst flips, reordering, dropped bytes — are almost always caught.

frames.title: Publisher
frames.text: Publisher computes sha256(app-1.2.0.zip) and publishes it next to the file.

frames.title: You download
frames.text: You download the zip. Somewhere in transit, byte 900,001 flips from 0x41 to 0x40.

frames.title: You run
frames.text: You run sha256sum app-1.2.0.zip locally.

frames.title: Compare.
frames.text: Compare. One flipped bit changes about half the hash's bits — the values are obviously different.

frames.title: Act.
frames.text: Act. Re-download. If it still mismatches, suspect your disk or RAM, or a man-in-the-middle.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 640 210" role="img" aria-labelledby="proxyTitle"><title id="proxyTitle">A forward proxy sits next to the clients; a reverse proxy sits next to the servers.</title><text class="figLabel" x="160" y="20">FORWARD PROXY</text><rect class="box" x="30" y="35" width="60" height="28"></rect><text class="boxText" x="60" y="54">client</text><rect class="box" x="30" y="70" width="60" height="28"></rect><text class="boxText" x="60" y="89">client</text><line class="flow" x1="90" y1="66" x2="140" y2="66"></line><rect class="boxAccent" x="140" y="48" width="80" height="36"></rect><text class="boxText" x="180" y="70">proxy</text><line class="flow" x1="220" y1="66" x2="280" y2="66"></line><rect class="box" x="280" y="48" width="70" height="36"></rect><text class="boxText" x="315" y="70">internet</text><text class="figLabel" x="470" y="20">REVERSE PROXY</text><rect class="box" x="370" y="120" width="70" height="30"></rect><text class="boxText" x="405" y="140">visitor</text><line class="flow" x1="440" y1="135" x2="480" y2="135"></line><rect class="boxAccent" x="480" y="118" width="70" height="34"></rect><text class="boxText" x="515" y="139">proxy</text><line class="flow" x1="550" y1="128" x2="595" y2="105"></line><line class="flow" x1="550" y1="135" x2="595" y2="135"></line><line class="flow" x1="550" y1="142" x2="595" y2="165"></line><rect class="box" x="595" y="92" width="40" height="24"></rect><rect class="box" x="595" y="123" width="40" height="24"></rect><rect class="box" x="595" y="154" width="40" height="24"></rect><text class="figHint" x="615" y="192">backends</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Same box in the middle, opposite purpose. Forward: many known clients → the whole internet. Reverse: the whole internet → a few hidden servers.

frames.title: DNS
frames.text: DNS for shop.example.com points at the reverse proxy's IP, not any backend.

frames.title: TLS ends at the proxy.
frames.text: TLS ends at the proxy. It holds the certificate and private key; traffic to backends can be plain HTTP inside the private network.

frames.title: Security checks.
frames.text: Security checks. The proxy / WAF drops obvious attacks and rate-limits abusive IPs.

frames.title: Cache check.
frames.text: Cache check. If the page is cacheable and fresh, return it now — backends never see the request.

frames.title: Route + balance.
frames.text: Route + balance. /api/* goes to the API pool, everything else to the web pool; pick a healthy instance (round-robin / least-connections).

frames.title: Add headers.
frames.text: Add headers. The proxy sets X-Forwarded-For so the backend still knows the real client IP, then relays the response back.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 640 200" role="img" aria-labelledby="lbTitle"><title id="lbTitle">Users send every request to the load balancer, which forwards each one to a healthy backend server.</title><rect class="box" x="20" y="80" width="80" height="44"></rect><text class="boxText" x="60" y="106">Users</text><line class="flow" x1="100" y1="102" x2="160" y2="102"></line><rect class="boxAccent" x="160" y="78" width="110" height="48"></rect><text class="boxText" x="215" y="98">Load</text><text class="boxText" x="215" y="114">balancer</text><line class="flow" x1="270" y1="90" x2="340" y2="45"></line><line class="flow" x1="270" y1="102" x2="340" y2="102"></line><line class="flow" x1="270" y1="114" x2="340" y2="159"></line><rect class="box" x="340" y="28" width="110" height="36"></rect><text class="boxText" x="395" y="50">server 1 (ok)</text><rect class="boxWarn" x="340" y="84" width="110" height="36"></rect><text class="boxText" x="395" y="106">server 2 (down)</text><rect class="box" x="340" y="140" width="110" height="36"></rect><text class="boxText" x="395" y="162">server 3 (ok)</text><text class="figHint" x="520" y="106">server 2 skipped</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: The load balancer is the single stable front door. Behind it the set of servers is fluid.

frames.title: DNS resolves
frames.text: DNS resolves app.example.com to the load balancer's IP.

frames.title: The LB accepts the connection
frames.text: The LB accepts the connection and (for HTTPS) terminates TLS.

frames.title: It picks a backend
frames.text: It picks a backend using its algorithm (round robin, least connections, …) from the pool of servers currently passing health checks.

frames.title: It forwards the request
frames.text: It forwards the request, adding X-Forwarded-For so the backend still sees the real client IP.

frames.title: The backend responds
frames.text: The backend responds; the LB relays it to the user and may log latency / status for metrics.

frames.title: If that backend fails a health check
frames.text: If that backend fails a health check moments later, the LB stops routing to it — the next user never notices.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 640 170" role="img" aria-labelledby="algoTitle"><title id="algoTitle">Round robin cycles through servers in order; least connections sends to whichever server currently has the fewest active requests.</title><text class="figLabel" x="150" y="20">ROUND ROBIN</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="60" y="40" width="60" height="30"></rect><text class="boxText" x="90" y="60">S1</text><rect class="box" x="130" y="40" width="60" height="30"></rect><text class="boxText" x="160" y="60">S2</text><rect class="box" x="200" y="40" width="60" height="30"></rect><text class="boxText" x="230" y="60">S3</text><text class="figHint" x="160" y="95">1 → 2 → 3 → 1 (ignores load)</text><line class="divider" x1="330" y1="15" x2="330" y2="150"></line><text class="figLabel" x="480" y="20">LEAST CONNECTIONS</text><rect class="box" x="390" y="40" width="60" height="30"></rect><text class="boxText" x="420" y="60">S1: 5</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="460" y="40" width="60" height="30"></rect><text class="boxText" x="490" y="60">S2: 1</text><rect class="box" x="530" y="40" width="60" height="30"></rect><text class="boxText" x="560" y="60">S3: 4</text><text class="figHint" x="480" y="95">next request → S2 (fewest active)</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Static algorithms are simple and predictable; dynamic algorithms adapt but need the LB to track per-server state.

frames.title: Are all requests roughly equal in cost?
frames.text: Are all requests roughly equal in cost? Yes → round robin is fine and cheapest.

frames.title: Are servers different sizes?
frames.text: Are servers different sizes? Yes → add weights (a 2× server gets weight 2).

frames.title: Do some requests take much longer than others?
frames.text: Do some requests take much longer than others? Yes → least connections or least response time.

frames.title: Do you have thousands of backends?
frames.text: Do you have thousands of backends? Use power of two choices — global "least" tracking gets expensive at that scale.

frames.title: Must a user keep hitting the same server?
frames.text: Must a user keep hitting the same server? Only if you truly cannot share state → IP hash or cookie affinity, and accept the trade-offs.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 640 190" role="img" aria-labelledby="l4l7Title"><title id="l4l7Title">A Layer 4 balancer forwards by port only; a Layer 7 balancer reads the URL path and routes /api and /static to different pools.</title><text class="figLabel" x="150" y="18">LAYER 4</text><rect class="box" x="40" y="70" width="70" height="34"></rect><text class="boxText" x="75" y="91">client</text><line class="flow" x1="110" y1="87" x2="160" y2="87"></line><rect class="boxAccent" x="160" y="66" width="70" height="42"></rect><text class="boxText" x="195" y="83">L4 LB</text><text class="boxText" x="195" y="99">:443</text><line class="flow" x1="230" y1="87" x2="280" y2="87"></line><rect class="box" x="280" y="66" width="70" height="42"></rect><text class="boxText" x="315" y="91">any server</text><line class="divider" x1="380" y1="20" x2="380" y2="170"></line><text class="figLabel" x="510" y="18">LAYER 7</text><rect class="box" x="400" y="70" width="60" height="32"></rect><text class="boxText" x="430" y="90">client</text><line class="flow" x1="460" y1="86" x2="500" y2="86"></line><rect class="boxAccent" x="500" y="66" width="60" height="42"></rect><text class="boxText" x="530" y="90">L7 LB</text><line class="flow" x1="560" y1="78" x2="600" y2="55"></line><line class="flow" x1="560" y1="96" x2="600" y2="125"></line><rect class="box" x="595" y="40" width="45" height="26"></rect><text class="boxText" x="617" y="57">/api</text><rect class="box" x="595" y="118" width="45" height="26"></rect><text class="boxText" x="617" y="135">/static</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Layer 4 is a fast pipe. Layer 7 is a smart router that understands what is flowing through it.

frames.title: Just spreading raw TCP traffic
frames.text: Just spreading raw TCP traffic (a database proxy, a game server, gRPC streams where you do not need routing) → Layer 4. Lowest latency, handles any protocol.

frames.title: Routing HTTP by path or host
frames.text: Routing HTTP by path or host ( api. vs www., /v1 vs /v2 ) → Layer 7.

frames.title: Want TLS certificates managed in one place
frames.text: Want TLS certificates managed in one place → Layer 7 terminates TLS at the edge.

frames.title: Need retries, canary releases, header-based A/B, or a WAF
frames.text: Need retries, canary releases, header-based A/B, or a WAF → Layer 7.

frames.title: Both?
frames.text: Both? Common pattern: an L4 balancer spreads traffic across several L7 balancers, which then do the smart routing.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 640 180" role="img" aria-labelledby="dnslbTitle"><title id="dnslbTitle">The DNS resolver returns a region-appropriate IP: EU users get the Frankfurt load balancer, Asia users get the Mumbai one.</title><rect class="box" x="20" y="35" width="90" height="34"></rect><text class="boxText" x="65" y="57">EU user</text><rect class="box" x="20" y="110" width="90" height="34"></rect><text class="boxText" x="65" y="132">Asia user</text><line class="flow" x1="110" y1="52" x2="170" y2="80"></line><line class="flow" x1="110" y1="127" x2="170" y2="100"></line><rect class="boxAccent" x="170" y="70" width="110" height="40"></rect><text class="boxText" x="225" y="94">Geo DNS</text><line class="flow" x1="280" y1="82" x2="360" y2="52"></line><line class="flow" x1="280" y1="100" x2="360" y2="130"></line><rect class="box" x="360" y="35" width="120" height="34"></rect><text class="boxText" x="420" y="57">Frankfurt LB</text><rect class="box" x="360" y="115" width="120" height="34"></rect><text class="boxText" x="420" y="137">Mumbai LB</text><text class="figHint" x="420" y="95">answer depends on where you ask from</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: DNS load balancing is coarse (per-lookup, then cached) but it is the only way to steer traffic between data centres.

frames.title: Setup:
frames.text: Setup: example.com has two A records — 1.1.1.1 (US, primary) and 2.2.2.2 (EU, standby) — with a health-checked failover policy and a 60s TTL.

frames.title: Normal:
frames.text: Normal: the DNS provider health-checks 1.1.1.1 every 30s and returns it to everyone.

frames.title: The US region goes down.
frames.text: The US region goes down. Two checks fail; the provider marks 1.1.1.1 unhealthy.

frames.title: New lookups get 2.2.2.2.
frames.text: New lookups get 2.2.2.2. Within one TTL (≤ 60s) most clients have switched to the EU region.

frames.title: Recovery:
frames.text: Recovery: when 1.1.1.1 passes checks again, the provider resumes returning it and traffic drifts back.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 640 190" role="img" aria-labelledby="anycastTitle"><title id="anycastTitle">Three locations all announce the same IP; each user is routed to the closest one by internet routing.</title><rect class="box" x="20" y="30" width="90" height="30"></rect><text class="boxText" x="65" y="50">user US</text><rect class="box" x="20" y="80" width="90" height="30"></rect><text class="boxText" x="65" y="100">user EU</text><rect class="box" x="20" y="130" width="90" height="30"></rect><text class="boxText" x="65" y="150">user Asia</text><line class="flow" x1="110" y1="45" x2="300" y2="45"></line><line class="flow" x1="110" y1="95" x2="300" y2="95"></line><line class="flow" x1="110" y1="145" x2="300" y2="145"></line><rect class="boxAccent" x="300" y="28" width="150" height="34"></rect><text class="boxText" x="375" y="49">203.0.113.5 (US)</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="300" y="78" width="150" height="34"></rect><text class="boxText" x="375" y="99">203.0.113.5 (EU)</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="300" y="128" width="150" height="34"></rect><text class="boxText" x="375" y="149">203.0.113.5 (Asia)</text><text class="figHint" x="530" y="98">same IP everywhere</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Because every location announces the identical prefix, routers just forward toward "the closest 203.0.113.5" — the user and their app never negotiate a region.

frames.title: Every resolver site
frames.text: Every resolver site announces the prefix containing 1.1.1.1 to its local internet providers via BGP.

frames.title: Your router
frames.text: Your router has learned many paths to that prefix and keeps the one with the lowest cost — usually the geographically nearest site.

frames.title: You send
frames.text: You send a UDP DNS query to 1.1.1.1. It follows that path to, say, the Mumbai site.

frames.title: Mumbai answers
frames.text: Mumbai answers in ~5 ms. Because DNS over UDP is a single request/response, path stability does not matter.

frames.title: Mumbai has an outage.
frames.text: Mumbai has an outage. It stops announcing the route; within seconds your router switches to the next-best site (say Singapore) with no config change on your side.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 640 170" role="img" aria-labelledby="hcTitle"><title id="hcTitle">The load balancer probes each backend; after 3 consecutive failures it removes that server and sends its share of traffic to the healthy ones.</title><rect class="boxAccent" x="40" y="65" width="110" height="44"></rect><text class="boxText" x="95" y="85">Load</text><text class="boxText" x="95" y="101">balancer</text><line class="flowMuted" x1="150" y1="75" x2="260" y2="45"></line><text class="figHint" x="205" y="35">GET /health</text><line class="flowMuted" x1="150" y1="90" x2="260" y2="90"></line><line class="flowMuted" x1="150" y1="105" x2="260" y2="135"></line><rect class="box" x="260" y="28" width="120" height="34"></rect><text class="boxText" x="320" y="50">200 — healthy</text><rect class="box" x="260" y="73" width="120" height="34"></rect><text class="boxText" x="320" y="95">200 — healthy</text><rect class="boxWarn" x="260" y="118" width="120" height="34"></rect><text class="boxText" x="320" y="140">timeout x3 — out</text><text class="figHint" x="500" y="95">traffic → the 2 healthy</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Thresholds trade speed against stability: react in 3 checks, not 1, so a single dropped packet does not evict a good server.

frames.title: Steady state:
frames.text: Steady state: 3 servers, each passing /health every 5s. Traffic split evenly.

frames.title: Server 2's disk fills.
frames.text: Server 2's disk fills. /health starts returning 503.

frames.title: 3 fails in a row (~15s):
frames.text: 3 fails in a row (~15s): the LB marks server 2 unhealthy and stops routing to it. Existing requests are allowed to finish (connection draining).

frames.title: Servers 1 and 3 absorb the load.
frames.text: Servers 1 and 3 absorb the load. This is why you size for N+1 — two servers must handle 100% while one is out.

frames.title: Ops clears the disk.
frames.text: Ops clears the disk. /health returns 200 again.

frames.title: 2 passes in a row:
frames.text: 2 passes in a row: the LB slowly ramps traffic back to server 2 (slow start) so it is not hit with a full third of load on a cold cache.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 640 150" role="img" aria-labelledby="apiTitle"><title id="apiTitle">The client is a diner, the API is the waiter and menu, the server is the kitchen.</title><rect class="box" x="30" y="55" width="120" height="44"></rect><text class="boxText" x="90" y="75">Client</text><text class="boxText" x="90" y="91">(diner)</text><line class="flow" x1="150" y1="70" x2="250" y2="70"></line><text class="figHint" x="200" y="60">request (order)</text><line class="flow" x1="250" y1="88" x2="150" y2="88"></line><text class="figHint" x="200" y="108">response (food)</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="250" y="50" width="130" height="54"></rect><text class="boxText" x="315" y="73">API</text><text class="boxText" x="315" y="89">(waiter + menu)</text><line class="flow" x1="380" y1="77" x2="470" y2="77"></line><rect class="box" x="470" y="50" width="130" height="54"></rect><text class="boxText" x="535" y="73">Server</text><text class="boxText" x="535" y="89">(kitchen)</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: You order from the menu (the documented endpoints), the waiter carries the request, the kitchen does the work. You never walk into the kitchen.

frames.title: Name the resource, not the action.
frames.text: Name the resource, not the action. /orders, not /createOrder. The HTTP method is the verb.

frames.title: Pick the method.
frames.text: Pick the method. Create → POST /orders. Read one → GET /orders/{id}. Read many → GET /orders.

frames.title: Define the request body.
frames.text: Define the request body. {"items": [{"sku": "A1", "qty": 2}], "address_id": 9}.

frames.title: Define the response.
frames.text: Define the response. 201 Created, body = {"id": 501, "status": "pending", "total": 780}, header Location: /orders/501.

frames.title: Define the errors.
frames.text: Define the errors. 400 for bad input, 401 if not logged in, 422 if the item is out of stock — each with a consistent error body.

frames.title: Write it down.
frames.text: Write it down. An OpenAPI / Swagger spec so clients can build against it before the code exists.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 640 170" role="img" aria-labelledby="idemTitle"><title id="idemTitle">First request with a key does the work and stores the result; a retry with the same key returns the stored result without repeating the work.</title><rect class="box" x="20" y="30" width="90" height="34"></rect><text class="boxText" x="65" y="51">request 1</text><line class="flow" x1="110" y1="47" x2="200" y2="47"></line><text class="figHint" x="155" y="37">key=abc</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="200" y="55" width="150" height="44"></rect><text class="boxText" x="275" y="72">key seen before?</text><text class="boxText" x="275" y="88">no → charge, store</text><line class="flow" x1="350" y1="77" x2="440" y2="77"></line><rect class="box" x="440" y="55" width="120" height="44"></rect><text class="boxText" x="500" y="81">200 + result</text><rect class="boxWarn" x="20" y="115" width="90" height="34"></rect><text class="boxText" x="65" y="136">retry</text><line class="flowMuted" x1="110" y1="132" x2="200" y2="110"></line><text class="figHint" x="330" y="140">key=abc seen → return stored 200, no second charge</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: The key ties "this intent" to "this result" so retries are free of side effects.

frames.title: Client
frames.text: Client creates key = uuid() once, before the first attempt, and keeps it for all retries of this order.

frames.title: POST /orders
frames.text: POST /orders with header Idempotency-Key: {key} and the order body.

frames.title: Server checks a key store
frames.text: Server checks a key store (Redis, a DB table) inside a transaction. Not found → lock the key, create the order, save {key -> orderId, response} with a 24h TTL.

frames.title: Server responds
frames.text: Server responds 201 with the order.

frames.title: Timeout, client retries
frames.text: Timeout, client retries with the same key. Server finds the key → returns the stored 201 and the same order. No duplicate.

frames.title: Edge case:
frames.text: Edge case: same key, different body → return 422 — the client is confused, do not silently pick one.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 640 130" role="img" aria-labelledby="fmtTitle"><title id="fmtTitle">The same record is verbose in XML, medium in JSON, and tiny in Protocol Buffers.</title><text class="figHint" x="70" y="35">XML</text><rect class="box" x="120" y="22" width="470" height="18"></rect><text class="figHint" x="70" y="70">JSON</text><rect class="box" x="120" y="57" width="300" height="18"></rect><text class="figHint" x="70" y="105">Protobuf</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="120" y="92" width="90" height="18"></rect></svg>
diagrams.caption: Bar length = bytes on the wire for one small object. Binary formats also skip the parse-the-text step entirely.

frames.title: Who calls it?
frames.text: Who calls it? External developers / browsers → JSON. It is the default expectation and debuggable with curl.

frames.title: Is it a hot internal path?
frames.text: Is it a hot internal path? Millions of calls between your own services → consider Protobuf over gRPC for the size and speed win.

frames.title: Is it an event stream?
frames.text: Is it an event stream? Kafka topic feeding analytics → Avro, so each message carries or references its schema and consumers can evolve independently.

frames.title: Must you support an old client?
frames.text: Must you support an old client? They may only speak XML — use content negotiation ( Accept: application/xml ) rather than forcing a rewrite.

frames.title: Set the headers.
frames.text: Set the headers. Send Content-Type, honour Accept, and document exactly which formats the endpoint supports.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 640 170" role="img" aria-labelledby="stylesTitle"><title id="stylesTitle">REST uses many resource URLs; GraphQL uses one endpoint with a query; gRPC calls typed methods.</title><text class="figLabel" x="105" y="20">REST</text><rect class="box" x="30" y="30" width="150" height="22"></rect><text class="boxText" x="105" y="46">GET /users/1</text><rect class="box" x="30" y="58" width="150" height="22"></rect><text class="boxText" x="105" y="74">GET /users/1/orders</text><rect class="box" x="30" y="86" width="150" height="22"></rect><text class="boxText" x="105" y="102">GET /orders/9/items</text><text class="figLabel" x="320" y="20">GRAPHQL</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="230" y="30" width="180" height="78"></rect><text class="boxText" x="320" y="52">POST /graphql</text><text class="boxText" x="320" y="72">{ user(id:1){ name</text><text class="boxText" x="320" y="90">orders{ items }}}</text><text class="figLabel" x="530" y="20">GRPC</text><rect class="box" x="450" y="30" width="160" height="22"></rect><text class="boxText" x="530" y="46">GetUser(id:1)</text><rect class="box" x="450" y="58" width="160" height="22"></rect><text class="boxText" x="530" y="74">ListOrders(userId:1)</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: REST: three trips. GraphQL: one trip, exact fields. gRPC: typed method calls, tiny binary payloads.

frames.title: Public API for outside developers?
frames.text: Public API for outside developers? → REST. Lowest learning curve, works with every HTTP tool, cache-friendly.

frames.title: A mobile / SPA front-end with many screens needing different slices of data?
frames.text: A mobile / SPA front-end with many screens needing different slices of data? → GraphQL cuts round trips and over-fetching.

frames.title: Internal service-to-service, latency-sensitive, same company?
frames.text: Internal service-to-service, latency-sensitive, same company? → gRPC for speed, streaming, and generated typed clients.

frames.title: Need to notify another system when something happens?
frames.text: Need to notify another system when something happens? → webhooks (or a message queue) instead of making them poll.

frames.title: Integrating with a bank / government system?
frames.text: Integrating with a bank / government system? → you may be handed SOAP and a WSDL — wrap it, do not fight it.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 640 130" role="img" aria-labelledby="restTitle"><title id="restTitle">One base URL, resources as paths, methods as the verbs acting on them.</title><rect class="boxAccent" x="40" y="50" width="180" height="34"></rect><text class="boxText" x="130" y="71">api.shop.com/v1</text><line class="flow" x1="220" y1="67" x2="270" y2="67"></line><rect class="box" x="270" y="30" width="150" height="24"></rect><text class="boxText" x="345" y="47">GET /products</text><rect class="box" x="270" y="59" width="150" height="24"></rect><text class="boxText" x="345" y="76">POST /orders</text><rect class="box" x="270" y="88" width="150" height="24"></rect><text class="boxText" x="345" y="105">DELETE /cart/9</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: The URL locates the thing; the method says what to do to it.

frames.title: Identify the resource:
frames.text: Identify the resource: a comment belongs to a post → base is /posts/{postId}/comments.

frames.title: List:
frames.text: List: GET /posts/12/comments?sort=-created_at&limit=20&cursor=abc → 200 with an array and a next_cursor.

frames.title: Create:
frames.text: Create: POST /posts/12/comments body {"body": "Nice!"} → 201, Location: /comments/501.

frames.title: Edit:
frames.text: Edit: PATCH /comments/501 body {"body": "Edited"} → 200. Return 403 if it is not the author.

frames.title: Delete:
frames.text: Delete: DELETE /comments/501 → 204. A repeat call also returns 204 (idempotent).

frames.title: Errors:
frames.text: Errors: post not found → 404; empty body → 422 with the field that failed.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 640 150" role="img" aria-labelledby="gqlTitle"><title id="gqlTitle">One GraphQL request fans out to resolvers that pull from several data sources and comes back as one response.</title><rect class="box" x="20" y="55" width="90" height="40"></rect><text class="boxText" x="65" y="79">Client</text><line class="flow" x1="110" y1="75" x2="170" y2="75"></line><rect class="boxAccent" x="170" y="50" width="120" height="50"></rect><text class="boxText" x="230" y="72">GraphQL</text><text class="boxText" x="230" y="88">server</text><line class="flow" x1="290" y1="62" x2="360" y2="40"></line><line class="flow" x1="290" y1="75" x2="360" y2="75"></line><line class="flow" x1="290" y1="88" x2="360" y2="110"></line><rect class="box" x="360" y="25" width="120" height="28"></rect><text class="boxText" x="420" y="43">users DB</text><rect class="box" x="360" y="61" width="120" height="28"></rect><text class="boxText" x="420" y="79">orders service</text><rect class="box" x="360" y="97" width="120" height="28"></rect><text class="boxText" x="420" y="115">reviews API</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: The client sees one endpoint and one response; the server stitches together many sources behind the schema.

frames.title: Client sends
frames.text: Client sends the query string to POST /graphql.

frames.title: Server parses and validates
frames.text: Server parses and validates it against the schema — unknown field or wrong type is rejected before any data is touched.

frames.title: Resolvers run,
frames.text: Resolvers run, field by field. user hits the users DB; user.orders calls the orders service.

frames.title: The N+1 trap:
frames.text: The N+1 trap: asking for 50 users and each user's orders naively fires 51 queries. A DataLoader batches them into 2.

frames.title: Server assembles
frames.text: Server assembles the response in the exact shape of the query and returns it, with any partial errors in an errors array alongside data.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 640 130" role="img" aria-labelledby="grpcTitle"><title id="grpcTitle">A .proto file generates both the client stub and the server skeleton, which talk Protobuf over one reused HTTP/2 connection.</title><rect class="boxAccent" x="240" y="15" width="160" height="26"></rect><text class="boxText" x="320" y="32">catalog.proto</text><line class="flow" x1="300" y1="41" x2="150" y2="65"></line><line class="flow" x1="340" y1="41" x2="490" y2="65"></line><rect class="box" x="60" y="65" width="180" height="30"></rect><text class="boxText" x="150" y="84">generated client</text><rect class="box" x="400" y="65" width="180" height="30"></rect><text class="boxText" x="490" y="84">generated server</text><line class="flow" x1="240" y1="105" x2="400" y2="105"></line><text class="figHint" x="320" y="122">HTTP/2 + Protobuf (binary)</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Both sides are generated from the same file, so a type mismatch is a compile error, not a production surprise.

frames.title: Edit the .proto:
frames.text: Edit the .proto: add rpc GetItems(ItemRequest) returns (ItemList); and the messages, each field with a fresh number.

frames.title: Regenerate
frames.text: Regenerate client and server code for every language that uses it.

frames.title: Implement the server method
frames.text: Implement the server method — just fill in the generated stub with the real catalog lookup.

frames.title: Call it from the client
frames.text: Call it from the client like a function: client.GetItems({ids}). gRPC handles connection reuse, serialization, and retries.

frames.title: Evolve safely:
frames.text: Evolve safely: to add a field later, give it a new number; old clients ignore unknown fields, new clients get a default for missing ones.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 640 180" role="img" aria-labelledby="gwTitle"><title id="gwTitle">Web, mobile, and partner clients all hit one gateway, which authenticates, limits, and routes to the right internal service.</title><rect class="box" x="20" y="20" width="90" height="28"></rect><text class="boxText" x="65" y="39">web</text><rect class="box" x="20" y="76" width="90" height="28"></rect><text class="boxText" x="65" y="95">mobile</text><rect class="box" x="20" y="132" width="90" height="28"></rect><text class="boxText" x="65" y="151">partner</text><line class="flow" x1="110" y1="34" x2="200" y2="85"></line><line class="flow" x1="110" y1="90" x2="200" y2="90"></line><line class="flow" x1="110" y1="146" x2="200" y2="95"></line><rect class="boxAccent" x="200" y="65" width="120" height="50"></rect><text class="boxText" x="260" y="86">API gateway</text><text class="boxText" x="260" y="102">auth · limit · route</text><line class="flow" x1="320" y1="78" x2="410" y2="40"></line><line class="flow" x1="320" y1="90" x2="410" y2="90"></line><line class="flow" x1="320" y1="102" x2="410" y2="140"></line><rect class="box" x="410" y="25" width="150" height="28"></rect><text class="boxText" x="485" y="44">order service</text><rect class="box" x="410" y="76" width="150" height="28"></rect><text class="boxText" x="485" y="95">user service</text><rect class="box" x="410" y="127" width="150" height="28"></rect><text class="boxText" x="485" y="146">catalog service</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: One public front door; the services behind it are private and focused on business logic.

frames.title: Client sends
frames.text: Client sends GET /v1/orders/42 with Authorization: Bearer … to api.example.com.

frames.title: TLS terminates
frames.text: TLS terminates at the gateway.

frames.title: Auth:
frames.text: Auth: the gateway verifies the JWT signature and expiry. Invalid → 401, the order service is never touched.

frames.title: Rate limit:
frames.text: Rate limit: check this client's counter. Over quota → 429 with Retry-After.

frames.title: Route + enrich:
frames.text: Route + enrich: match /v1/orders/* → order service; add X-User-Id and X-Correlation-Id headers.

frames.title: Forward, then respond:
frames.text: Forward, then respond: relay the service's response, record latency and status for metrics.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 640 150" role="img" aria-labelledby="tbTitle"><title id="tbTitle">A token bucket refills at a steady rate; each request removes a token, and requests are rejected when the bucket is empty.</title><text class="figHint" x="90" y="30">refill 10/sec</text><line class="flow" x1="90" y1="38" x2="90" y2="60"></line><rect class="boxAccent" x="40" y="60" width="100" height="60"></rect><text class="boxText" x="90" y="95">tokens: 6</text><line class="flow" x1="140" y1="90" x2="210" y2="90"></line><text class="figHint" x="175" y="80">request</text><text class="figHint" x="175" y="108">spends 1</text><rect class="box" x="210" y="72" width="120" height="36"></rect><text class="boxText" x="270" y="94">allowed (200)</text><rect class="boxWarn" x="360" y="72" width="180" height="36"></rect><text class="boxText" x="450" y="94">bucket empty → 429</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Bucket size sets the burst you tolerate; refill rate sets the sustained limit.

frames.title: Store per-key state in Redis:
frames.text: Store per-key state in Redis: tokens and last_refill time.

frames.title: On each request,
frames.text: On each request, compute how many tokens to add since last_refill ( elapsed × rate ), capped at bucket size.

frames.title: If tokens ≥ 1:
frames.text: If tokens ≥ 1: subtract one, update state, allow the request.

frames.title: If tokens < 1:
frames.text: If tokens < 1: return 429 with Retry-After = seconds until one token refills.

frames.title: Make the check atomic
frames.text: Make the check atomic — a Redis Lua script — so two servers handling the same client cannot both pass on the last token.

frames.title: Fail open or closed?
frames.text: Fail open or closed? If Redis is down, decide deliberately: allow traffic (open, risk overload) or reject (closed, risk false 429s).

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 640 130" role="img" aria-labelledby="authTitle"><title id="authTitle">A request is first authenticated to an identity, then that identity is checked against the permission needed for the action.</title><rect class="box" x="20" y="50" width="90" height="36"></rect><text class="boxText" x="65" y="72">request</text><line class="flow" x1="110" y1="68" x2="160" y2="68"></line><rect class="boxAccent" x="160" y="46" width="130" height="44"></rect><text class="boxText" x="225" y="63">authn: verify</text><text class="boxText" x="225" y="79">→ user 7</text><line class="flow" x1="290" y1="68" x2="340" y2="68"></line><rect class="boxAccent" x="340" y="46" width="150" height="44"></rect><text class="boxText" x="415" y="63">authz: user 7 may</text><text class="boxText" x="415" y="79">DELETE /docs/9?</text><line class="flow" x1="490" y1="68" x2="540" y2="68"></line><rect class="box" x="540" y="50" width="90" height="36"></rect><text class="boxText" x="585" y="72">allow / 403</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Authentication produces an identity once; authorization uses that identity to gate each action.

frames.title: Client sends
frames.text: Client sends DELETE /projects/12 with Authorization: Bearer ….

frames.title: Authn:
frames.text: Authn: the gateway verifies the token. Bad or missing → 401 ("log in first").

frames.title: Identity established:
frames.text: Identity established: the token says sub = user_7, roles = [member].

frames.title: Authz:
frames.text: Authz: the project service checks — is user 7 an owner or admin of project 12? They are only a member → 403 ("you are known, but not allowed").

frames.title: If allowed:
frames.text: If allowed: perform the delete, return 204.

frames.title: Log both outcomes
frames.text: Log both outcomes — repeated 403s from one user can signal an attack or a broken client.
