diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 640 190" role="img" aria-labelledby="svtTitle"><title id="svtTitle">Session auth stores state on the server and looks it up per request; token auth carries signed state in the request and just verifies the signature.</title><text class="figLabel" x="160" y="18">SESSION</text><rect class="box" x="30" y="35" width="80" height="30"></rect><text class="boxText" x="70" y="54">client</text><line class="flow" x1="110" y1="50" x2="180" y2="50"></line><text class="figHint" x="145" y="40">cookie: sid=abc</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="180" y="30" width="90" height="40"></rect><text class="boxText" x="225" y="54">server</text><line class="flow" x1="270" y1="50" x2="320" y2="50"></line><rect class="box" x="320" y="30" width="110" height="40"></rect><text class="boxText" x="375" y="49">session store</text><text class="boxText" x="375" y="64">abc → user 7</text><line class="divider" x1="30" y1="90" x2="610" y2="90"></line><text class="figLabel" x="160" y="112">TOKEN</text><rect class="box" x="30" y="128" width="80" height="30"></rect><text class="boxText" x="70" y="147">client</text><line class="flow" x1="110" y1="143" x2="200" y2="143"></line><text class="figHint" x="155" y="133">Bearer eyJ... (user 7, exp)</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="200" y="123" width="120" height="40"></rect><text class="boxText" x="260" y="142">server: verify</text><text class="boxText" x="260" y="157">signature only</text><text class="figHint" x="430" y="147">no lookup needed</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Session = server remembers, small ID travels. Token = client remembers, signed payload travels.

frames.title: Session — login:
frames.text: Session — login: verify credentials, create a session row {sid: abc, userId: 7, expires}, send Set-Cookie: sid=abc; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite.

frames.title: Session — each request:
frames.text: Session — each request: browser auto-sends the cookie; server looks up abc in the store to get user 7.

frames.title: Session — logout:
frames.text: Session — logout: delete the row. The cookie is now useless immediately.

frames.title: Token — login:
frames.text: Token — login: verify credentials, sign a short-lived access token (15 min) and a longer refresh token. Return both.

frames.title: Token — each request:
frames.text: Token — each request: client sends Authorization: Bearer <access>; server verifies the signature and expiry — no lookup.

frames.title: Token — expiry:
frames.text: Token — expiry: when the access token dies, the client exchanges the refresh token for a new one. Logout = delete the refresh token server-side and drop the access token client-side.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 640 120" role="img" aria-labelledby="jwtTitle"><title id="jwtTitle">A JWT is header, payload, and signature joined by dots; the server recomputes the signature to check it.</title><rect class="box" x="30" y="45" width="130" height="30"></rect><text class="boxText" x="95" y="64">header</text><rect class="box" x="175" y="45" width="200" height="30"></rect><text class="boxText" x="275" y="64">payload (claims)</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="390" y="45" width="200" height="30"></rect><text class="boxText" x="490" y="64">signature</text><text class="figHint" x="320" y="100">verify: re-sign header + payload, compare to signature, check exp</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Verification is a hash/signature check plus an expiry check — fast, and needs no database.

frames.title: Login:
frames.text: Login: the auth server checks the password, then builds a payload {sub, role, iss, aud, exp: now+15m}.

frames.title: Sign:
frames.text: Sign: with RS256 it signs using a private key; services verify with the matching public key (so only the auth server can mint tokens).

frames.title: Client stores it
frames.text: Client stores it (cookie or memory) and sends it as Authorization: Bearer ….

frames.title: Each service verifies:
frames.text: Each service verifies: signature valid? exp in the future? aud matches this service? iss is trusted? All yes → trust the claims.

frames.title: Access expires in 15 min.
frames.text: Access expires in 15 min. The client uses a refresh token to get a fresh JWT without re-entering the password.

frames.title: Need instant revoke?
frames.text: Need instant revoke? Keep a short deny-list of token IDs ( jti ) that services check — a small compromise on the "no lookup" ideal.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 640 200" role="img" aria-labelledby="oauthTitle"><title id="oauthTitle">The client redirects the user to the auth server, gets back a short code, then swaps the code for an access token on a back channel.</title><rect class="box" x="20" y="30" width="90" height="34"></rect><text class="boxText" x="65" y="51">user</text><rect class="box" x="20" y="120" width="90" height="34"></rect><text class="boxText" x="65" y="141">client app</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="270" y="75" width="120" height="44"></rect><text class="boxText" x="330" y="93">auth server</text><text class="boxText" x="330" y="109">(Google)</text><rect class="box" x="520" y="120" width="100" height="34"></rect><text class="boxText" x="570" y="141">calendar API</text><line class="flow" x1="110" y1="47" x2="270" y2="85"></line><text class="figHint" x="180" y="40">1 redirect to log in + consent</text><line class="flow" x1="270" y1="110" x2="110" y2="135"></line><text class="figHint" x="180" y="128">2 redirect back with a code</text><line class="flow" x1="110" y1="140" x2="270" y2="110"></line><text class="figHint" x="185" y="165">3 code + verifier → access token</text><line class="flow" x1="115" y1="150" x2="520" y2="140"></line><text class="figHint" x="360" y="185">4 call API with the access token</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: The token is fetched on a server-to-server call (step 3), so it never appears in a URL or the browser history. PKCE stops a stolen code from being used by anyone else.

frames.title: Client redirects
frames.text: Client redirects you to Google's /authorize with its client_id, the scope, a redirect_uri, and a PKCE code_challenge.

frames.title: You authenticate to Google
frames.text: You authenticate to Google (not to the app) and approve the consent screen.

frames.title: Google redirects back
frames.text: Google redirects back to the app's redirect_uri with a one-time code.

frames.title: The app's server
frames.text: The app's server calls Google's /token with the code, its client_secret, and the PKCE code_verifier.

frames.title: Google returns
frames.text: Google returns an access token (1 hour) and a refresh token.

frames.title: The app calls the Calendar API
frames.text: The app calls the Calendar API with Authorization: Bearer <access>; when it expires, it uses the refresh token silently. You can revoke access in your Google account at any time.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 640 170" role="img" aria-labelledby="ssoTitle"><title id="ssoTitle">The user logs in once at the identity provider; each app redirects there and receives a signed identity assertion.</title><rect class="boxAccent" x="250" y="20" width="140" height="40"></rect><text class="boxText" x="320" y="38">Identity Provider</text><text class="boxText" x="320" y="53">(one login)</text><line class="flow" x1="270" y1="60" x2="120" y2="120"></line><line class="flow" x1="320" y1="60" x2="320" y2="120"></line><line class="flow" x1="370" y1="60" x2="520" y2="120"></line><rect class="box" x="60" y="120" width="110" height="34"></rect><text class="boxText" x="115" y="141">Slack</text><rect class="box" x="265" y="120" width="110" height="34"></rect><text class="boxText" x="320" y="141">Jira</text><rect class="box" x="470" y="120" width="110" height="34"></rect><text class="boxText" x="525" y="141">Wiki</text><text class="figHint" x="320" y="95">each app trusts the IdP's signed assertion</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: The apps never see your password. They only see a signed statement from an IdP they were configured to trust.

frames.title: You visit Jira.
frames.text: You visit Jira. It has no session for you, so it redirects your browser to the company IdP with an authentication request.

frames.title: The IdP checks its own session.
frames.text: The IdP checks its own session. You logged in this morning, so it already knows you — no password prompt.

frames.title: The IdP builds a signed assertion / ID token
frames.text: The IdP builds a signed assertion / ID token: sub, name, email, groups, expiry.

frames.title: Browser posts it back to Jira.
frames.text: Browser posts it back to Jira. Jira verifies the signature against the IdP's public key and checks it has not expired.

frames.title: Jira creates a local session
frames.text: Jira creates a local session for you and maps your IdP groups to Jira roles.

frames.title: Single logout:
frames.text: Single logout: logging out at the IdP can notify each app to end its session too, so one click signs you out everywhere.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 640 130" role="img" aria-labelledby="syncTitle"><title id="syncTitle">The client sends a request and sits idle until the server responds, then continues.</title><rect class="box" x="20" y="45" width="100" height="40"></rect><text class="boxText" x="70" y="69">client</text><line class="flow" x1="120" y1="55" x2="260" y2="55"></line><text class="figHint" x="190" y="45">request</text><rect class="boxWarn" x="260" y="35" width="140" height="60"></rect><text class="boxText" x="330" y="60">client waits</text><text class="boxText" x="330" y="78">(blocked)</text><line class="flow" x1="400" y1="80" x2="540" y2="80"></line><text class="figHint" x="470" y="70">response</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="540" y="45" width="80" height="40"></rect><text class="boxText" x="580" y="69">server</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: The client cannot do anything else useful for that flow until the response arrives — it is committed to waiting.

frames.title: Client calls
frames.text: Client calls POST /checkout and stops — the UI shows a spinner.

frames.title: The checkout service calls
frames.text: The checkout service calls the payment service synchronously and waits for it.

frames.title: The payment service calls
frames.text: The payment service calls the bank's API synchronously and waits.

frames.title: The bank is slow today
frames.text: The bank is slow today (3 seconds). That delay now sits inside every layer above it — the user waits 3+ seconds, and the checkout service's thread was tied up the whole time.

frames.title: The fix isn't "never use sync"
frames.text: The fix isn't "never use sync" — it is choosing which calls truly need an immediate answer (charge the card: yes) versus which can be handed off (send a receipt email: no, that can be asynchronous).

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 640 150" role="img" aria-labelledby="asyncTitle"><title id="asyncTitle">The client sends a request, gets an immediate acknowledgement, and continues; the real work finishes later in the background.</title><rect class="box" x="20" y="55" width="100" height="40"></rect><text class="boxText" x="70" y="79">client</text><line class="flow" x1="120" y1="65" x2="240" y2="65"></line><text class="figHint" x="180" y="55">submit job</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="240" y="45" width="120" height="40"></rect><text class="boxText" x="300" y="69">202 accepted</text><line class="flow" x1="120" y1="80" x2="640" y2="80"></line><text class="figHint" x="380" y="100">client keeps working immediately, no waiting</text><rect class="box" x="360" y="45" width="140" height="40"></rect><text class="boxText" x="430" y="69">worker processes</text><line class="flowMuted" x1="240" y1="55" x2="360" y2="55"></line></svg>
diagrams.caption: The client gets a fast "got it", not the final result — the result shows up later through polling, a callback, or a notification.

frames.title: Client uploads
frames.text: Client uploads the video file to POST /videos.

frames.title: Server stores the raw file,
frames.text: Server stores the raw file, creates a job record {status: "queued"}, and immediately returns 202 Accepted with a job ID.

frames.title: The request pushes a message
frames.text: The request pushes a message onto a queue: "transcode video 501." The HTTP request is now done.

frames.title: A worker picks up the job
frames.text: A worker picks up the job whenever it has capacity, transcodes the video, and updates the job to {status: "done", url: "..."}.

frames.title: The client finds out
frames.text: The client finds out by polling GET /videos/501, or the server sends a push notification / websocket event when it flips to done.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 640 110" role="img" aria-labelledby="rrTitle"><title id="rrTitle">A client sends one request, the server sends back one response, and the interaction is complete.</title><rect class="box" x="20" y="35" width="100" height="40"></rect><text class="boxText" x="70" y="59">client</text><line class="flow" x1="120" y1="45" x2="520" y2="45"></line><text class="figHint" x="320" y="35">1 request</text><line class="flow" x1="520" y1="65" x2="120" y2="65"></line><text class="figHint" x="320" y="90">1 response — then the exchange is over</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="520" y="35" width="100" height="40"></rect><text class="boxText" x="570" y="59">server</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: No memory of the exchange is kept by default (stateless) — each request stands on its own.

frames.title: Client builds a request:
frames.text: Client builds a request: method, URL, headers, optional body — GET /product/42.

frames.title: Client opens a connection
frames.text: Client opens a connection to the server (or reuses one via keep-alive).

frames.title: Server reads the request,
frames.text: Server reads the request, does the work (a database lookup), and builds a response: status code, headers, body.

frames.title: Server sends the response
frames.text: Server sends the response and considers this exchange finished — it keeps no record that this particular request happened.

frames.title: Client reads the response
frames.text: Client reads the response and uses it. If it wants fresher data later, it simply repeats the whole exchange.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 640 140" role="img" aria-labelledby="pollTitle"><title id="pollTitle">The client repeatedly asks on a fixed interval; most checks return nothing new until one finally does.</title><rect class="box" x="20" y="55" width="90" height="34"></rect><text class="boxText" x="65" y="76">client</text><line class="flow" x1="110" y1="60" x2="240" y2="40"></line><text class="figHint" x="175" y="30">t=0s: check → no</text><line class="flow" x1="110" y1="70" x2="240" y2="70"></line><text class="figHint" x="175" y="90">t=5s: check → no</text><line class="flow" x1="110" y1="80" x2="240" y2="105"></line><text class="figHint" x="175" y="120">t=10s: check → no</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="240" y="50" width="140" height="34"></rect><text class="boxText" x="310" y="71">server</text><line class="flow" x1="380" y1="55" x2="520" y2="40"></line><text class="figHint" x="470" y="30">t=15s: yes!</text><rect class="box" x="520" y="25" width="90" height="30"></rect><text class="boxText" x="565" y="45">new data</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Most requests are wasted work — the trade-off you accept for simplicity and no special infrastructure.

frames.title: Client submits
frames.text: Client submits a video-processing job and gets back {jobId: 501, status: "queued"}.

frames.title: Client starts polling
frames.text: Client starts polling GET /jobs/501 every 3 seconds.

frames.title: Each response
frames.text: Each response returns the current status: queued → processing → eventually done.

frames.title: Client stops polling
frames.text: Client stops polling the moment it sees done (or failed ), and shows the result.

frames.title: To be kind to the server,
frames.text: To be kind to the server, the client backs off the interval the longer it waits (3s, then 5s, then 10s) instead of hammering forever.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 640 170" role="img" aria-labelledby="lpTitle"><title id="lpTitle">Short polling gets an instant empty reply repeatedly; long polling holds the request open until data is ready, then the client immediately reopens it.</title><text class="figLabel" x="150" y="18">SHORT POLLING</text><line class="flow" x1="30" y1="35" x2="230" y2="35"></line><text class="figHint" x="130" y="28">ask → instant "no"</text><line class="flow" x1="30" y1="55" x2="230" y2="55"></line><text class="figHint" x="130" y="48">ask → instant "no"</text><line class="flow" x1="30" y1="75" x2="230" y2="75"></line><text class="figHint" x="130" y="68">ask → instant "yes"</text><line class="divider" x1="290" y1="10" x2="290" y2="160"></line><text class="figLabel" x="470" y="18">LONG POLLING</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="330" y="35" width="280" height="34"></rect><text class="boxText" x="470" y="57">ask → server HOLDS the request…</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="330" y="75" width="280" height="34"></rect><text class="boxText" x="470" y="97">…18s later, data ready → reply now</text><line class="flow" x1="330" y1="120" x2="610" y2="120"></line><text class="figHint" x="470" y="140">client immediately reopens the request</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Long polling replaces many empty round trips with one held-open request that answers the moment something happens.

frames.title: Client calls
frames.text: Client calls GET /notifications/poll?since=1000.

frames.title: Server checks
frames.text: Server checks if anything is newer than since=1000. Nothing yet — instead of replying, it holds the connection open and waits.

frames.title: A new notification arrives
frames.text: A new notification arrives 12 seconds later. The server immediately writes the response and closes this request.

frames.title: Client receives it,
frames.text: Client receives it, processes the notification, and immediately opens a new long-poll request with the updated since value.

frames.title: Timeout safety net:
frames.text: Timeout safety net: if nothing happens for, say, 30 seconds, the server responds with an empty result anyway so the connection does not hang forever — the client just reopens it.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 640 140" role="img" aria-labelledby="sseTitle"><title id="sseTitle">The client opens one connection; the server sends a sequence of events down it over time without the client asking again.</title><rect class="box" x="20" y="50" width="90" height="40"></rect><text class="boxText" x="65" y="74">client</text><line class="flow" x1="110" y1="60" x2="270" y2="60"></line><text class="figHint" x="190" y="50">GET /events (opens once)</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="270" y="45" width="120" height="34"></rect><text class="boxText" x="330" y="66">server keeps</text><line class="flow" x1="390" y1="55" x2="600" y2="30"></line><text class="figHint" x="520" y="20">event: score 1-0</text><line class="flow" x1="390" y1="65" x2="600" y2="70"></line><text class="figHint" x="520" y="82">event: score 1-1</text><line class="flow" x1="390" y1="75" x2="600" y2="105"></line><text class="figHint" x="520" y="118">event: score 2-1</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: The connection stays open indefinitely; the server just keeps writing new events onto it whenever it has something to say.

frames.title: Browser creates
frames.text: Browser creates new EventSource("/api/stats/stream").

frames.title: Server responds
frames.text: Server responds with Content-Type: text/event-stream and keeps the connection open instead of closing it.

frames.title: Whenever a new stat is ready
frames.text: Whenever a new stat is ready (every few seconds), the server writes a data: {...} block and flushes it — the browser fires an onmessage event immediately.

frames.title: If the connection drops
frames.text: If the connection drops (network blip), EventSource automatically reconnects on its own — no code required.

frames.title: The server can resume where it left off
frames.text: The server can resume where it left off using the Last-Event-ID header the browser sends on reconnect, so no updates are missed.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 640 140" role="img" aria-labelledby="wsPatternTitle"><title id="wsPatternTitle">Over one open connection, the client and server both send messages whenever they have something to say, in no fixed order.</title><rect class="box" x="20" y="52" width="100" height="36"></rect><text class="boxText" x="70" y="74">client</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="520" y="52" width="100" height="36"></rect><text class="boxText" x="570" y="74">server</text><line class="flow" x1="120" y1="45" x2="520" y2="35"></line><text class="figHint" x="320" y="25">client → cursor moved</text><line class="flow" x1="520" y1="60" x2="120" y2="60"></line><text class="figHint" x="320" y="75">server → teammate typed</text><line class="flow" x1="120" y1="95" x2="520" y2="105"></line><text class="figHint" x="320" y="122">client → new keystroke</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: No request/response turn-taking — messages flow in whichever direction has something new, whenever it happens.

frames.title: Both clients open a WebSocket
frames.text: Both clients open a WebSocket to /doc/42 and join "room 42" on the server.

frames.title: Client A moves its cursor.
frames.text: Client A moves its cursor. It sends {"type": "cursor", "pos": 120} — no request/response, just a message.

frames.title: The server receives it
frames.text: The server receives it and immediately relays it to every other client in room 42, including client B — the server is now routing, not just answering.

frames.title: Client B sends a keystroke
frames.text: Client B sends a keystroke the very next instant, on the same connection, with no need to wait for anything from A.

frames.title: If a client disconnects,
frames.text: If a client disconnects, the server removes it from the room; reconnecting means rejoining and re-syncing state, since the socket itself carries no history.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 640 140" role="img" aria-labelledby="mqTitle"><title id="mqTitle">A producer pushes messages onto a queue; one or more consumers pull messages off it at their own pace.</title><rect class="box" x="20" y="50" width="110" height="40"></rect><text class="boxText" x="75" y="74">producer</text><line class="flow" x1="130" y1="70" x2="220" y2="70"></line><rect class="boxAccent" x="220" y="35" width="200" height="70"></rect><text class="boxText" x="320" y="60">queue</text><text class="boxText" x="320" y="78">[m1][m2][m3][m4]</text><line class="flow" x1="420" y1="55" x2="500" y2="45"></line><line class="flow" x1="420" y1="85" x2="500" y2="95"></line><rect class="box" x="500" y="25" width="120" height="34"></rect><text class="boxText" x="560" y="47">consumer A</text><rect class="box" x="500" y="80" width="120" height="34"></rect><text class="boxText" x="560" y="102">consumer B</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: The producer is free the instant the message is queued. Consumers pull at their own speed, and you can add more of them to drain the queue faster.

frames.title: Checkout service
frames.text: Checkout service validates the order and pushes {type: "order.placed", orderId: 501} onto the orders queue, then returns 201 to the user — instantly.

frames.title: An inventory worker
frames.text: An inventory worker pulls the message, reserves stock, and acknowledges it (the queue then removes it).

frames.title: If the worker crashes
frames.text: If the worker crashes before acknowledging, the message becomes visible again after a timeout and another worker picks it up — that is at-least-once delivery.

frames.title: Because a retry can redeliver the same message,
frames.text: Because a retry can redeliver the same message, the worker checks "have I already reserved stock for order 501?" before acting — making the handler idempotent.

frames.title: Repeated failures
frames.text: Repeated failures (say, 5 retries) move the message to a dead-letter queue instead of retrying forever, so a poison message does not block the rest.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 640 160" role="img" aria-labelledby="pubsubTitle"><title id="pubsubTitle">A queue message goes to exactly one consumer; a pub/sub message on a topic goes to every subscriber of that topic.</title><text class="figLabel" x="120" y="18">QUEUE (one wins)</text><rect class="box" x="20" y="35" width="90" height="30"></rect><text class="boxText" x="65" y="54">message</text><line class="flow" x1="110" y1="50" x2="180" y2="50"></line><rect class="boxAccent" x="180" y="35" width="70" height="30"></rect><text class="boxText" x="215" y="54">worker A</text><text class="figHint" x="215" y="80">worker B gets nothing</text><line class="divider" x1="290" y1="10" x2="290" y2="150"></line><text class="figLabel" x="470" y="18">PUB/SUB (all get it)</text><rect class="box" x="330" y="60" width="100" height="30"></rect><text class="boxText" x="380" y="79">topic</text><line class="flow" x1="430" y1="65" x2="520" y2="30"></line><line class="flow" x1="430" y1="75" x2="520" y2="75"></line><line class="flow" x1="430" y1="85" x2="520" y2="120"></line><rect class="box" x="520" y="15" width="100" height="26"></rect><text class="boxText" x="570" y="33">inventory</text><rect class="box" x="520" y="62" width="100" height="26"></rect><text class="boxText" x="570" y="80">email</text><rect class="box" x="520" y="107" width="100" height="26"></rect><text class="boxText" x="570" y="125">analytics</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Same "drop a message and move on" feel as a queue, but the fan-out is the whole point.

frames.title: Checkout service publishes
frames.text: Checkout service publishes {topic: "order.placed", orderId: 501, total: 780} and is done — no idea who, if anyone, is listening.

frames.title: The message broker fans it out
frames.text: The message broker fans it out to every current subscriber of order.placed: inventory, email, analytics, fraud-check.

frames.title: Each subscriber processes its own copy independently.
frames.text: Each subscriber processes its own copy independently. Email being slow does not delay inventory reserving stock.

frames.title: Months later, a new "loyalty points" service is added.
frames.text: Months later, a new "loyalty points" service is added. It subscribes to the same topic — the checkout service is never modified.

frames.title: Each subscriber tracks its own progress
frames.text: Each subscriber tracks its own progress (which messages it has processed), so a slow subscriber does not block a fast one.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 640 160" role="img" aria-labelledby="edaTitle"><title id="edaTitle">Instead of services calling each other directly, they all publish and subscribe to events through a shared event bus.</title><rect class="boxAccent" x="240" y="60" width="160" height="40"></rect><text class="boxText" x="320" y="84">event bus</text><rect class="box" x="30" y="20" width="120" height="30"></rect><text class="boxText" x="90" y="39">order service</text><line class="flow" x1="150" y1="35" x2="240" y2="70"></line><text class="figHint" x="190" y="55">publishes</text><rect class="box" x="490" y="10" width="120" height="28"></rect><text class="boxText" x="550" y="28">inventory</text><rect class="box" x="490" y="66" width="120" height="28"></rect><text class="boxText" x="550" y="84">email</text><rect class="box" x="490" y="122" width="120" height="28"></rect><text class="boxText" x="550" y="140">loyalty</text><line class="flow" x1="400" y1="70" x2="490" y2="25"></line><line class="flow" x1="400" y1="80" x2="490" y2="80"></line><line class="flow" x1="400" y1="90" x2="490" y2="135"></line><text class="figHint" x="440" y="145">subscribes</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: No service calls another by name. Everything routes through events on a shared bus (Kafka, EventBridge, or a pub/sub broker).

frames.title: Order service
frames.text: Order service saves the order and publishes OrderPlaced {orderId: 501} to the event bus.

frames.title: Inventory service
frames.text: Inventory service (subscribed to OrderPlaced ) reserves stock and, if successful, publishes its own event: StockReserved {orderId: 501}.

frames.title: Shipping service
frames.text: Shipping service (subscribed to StockReserved, not OrderPlaced ) only starts once stock is actually confirmed — events can chain.

frames.title: Email and analytics
frames.text: Email and analytics both independently subscribed to OrderPlaced react in parallel, on their own time.

frames.title: If inventory fails
frames.text: If inventory fails (out of stock), it publishes StockReservationFailed, and a saga-style handler reacts by cancelling the order — no single service orchestrated the whole flow up front.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 640 140" role="img" aria-labelledby="whTitle"><title id="whTitle">You register a callback URL once; later, when an event happens on the other system, it calls that URL instead of you having to ask.</title><rect class="box" x="20" y="20" width="120" height="34"></rect><text class="boxText" x="80" y="42">your server</text><line class="flow" x1="140" y1="37" x2="330" y2="37"></line><text class="figHint" x="235" y="27">1. register callback URL</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="330" y="20" width="130" height="34"></rect><text class="boxText" x="395" y="42">Stripe</text><text class="figHint" x="395" y="70">…time passes, payment clears…</text><line class="flow" x1="330" y1="95" x2="140" y2="95"></line><text class="figHint" x="235" y="115">2. POST /webhooks/stripe {event}</text><rect class="box" x="20" y="80" width="120" height="34"></rect><text class="boxText" x="80" y="102">your server</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: You are now the server for this exchange — Stripe is the client calling you.

frames.title: Earlier, in your dashboard,
frames.text: Earlier, in your dashboard, you registered https://yourapp.com/webhooks/stripe as your payments callback URL.

frames.title: A payment clears.
frames.text: A payment clears. Stripe sends POST /webhooks/stripe with a JSON event body and a Stripe-Signature header.

frames.title: Your endpoint verifies the signature
frames.text: Your endpoint verifies the signature using your webhook secret — reject anything that does not match, since the URL is public and anyone could try to call it.

frames.title: Check the event ID
frames.text: Check the event ID against what you have already processed; if seen before, return 200 and do nothing further — this handles Stripe's retries safely.

frames.title: Queue the real work
frames.text: Queue the real work (mark the order paid, send a receipt) and return 200 immediately, well within Stripe's timeout.

frames.title: If your endpoint is down
frames.text: If your endpoint is down when the event fires, Stripe retries with backoff for a while — but you should still be able to reconcile via their API as a backup.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 640 140" role="img" aria-labelledby="cacheTitle"><title id="cacheTitle">A request checks the cache first; a hit returns instantly, a miss goes to the slower source and then fills the cache for next time.</title><rect class="box" x="20" y="50" width="90" height="40"></rect><text class="boxText" x="65" y="74">request</text><line class="flow" x1="110" y1="70" x2="190" y2="70"></line><rect class="boxAccent" x="190" y="50" width="110" height="40"></rect><text class="boxText" x="245" y="74">cache</text><line class="flow" x1="300" y1="60" x2="380" y2="30"></line><text class="figHint" x="340" y="20">hit → instant</text><rect class="box" x="380" y="15" width="90" height="30"></rect><text class="boxText" x="425" y="35">return</text><line class="flow" x1="300" y1="80" x2="380" y2="110"></line><text class="figHint" x="340" y="125">miss → go further</text><rect class="boxWarn" x="380" y="95" width="120" height="30"></rect><text class="boxText" x="440" y="115">database</text><line class="flowMuted" x1="500" y1="105" x2="300" y2="70"></line><text class="figHint" x="440" y="145">result is stored back in the cache</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: After a miss fills the cache, the next request for the same thing is a hit.

frames.title: Measure first.
frames.text: Measure first. GET /bestsellers takes 220 ms, almost all of it one expensive database query, and the result barely changes minute to minute.

frames.title: Pick a key.
frames.text: Pick a key. bestsellers:v1 — something that uniquely identifies this exact result.

frames.title: On each request,
frames.text: On each request, check the cache for that key first.

frames.title: Miss:
frames.text: Miss: run the query, store the result under the key with a TTL (say 60s), then return it.

frames.title: Hit:
frames.text: Hit: return the cached value directly — no database call at all.

frames.title: Result:
frames.text: Result: p99 latency drops from 220 ms to under 2 ms for the ~99% of requests that now hit the cache.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 640 140" role="img" aria-labelledby="clientCacheTitle"><title id="clientCacheTitle">Within max-age the browser serves the file with zero network calls; after it expires, a lightweight check confirms whether the cached copy is still valid.</title><rect class="box" x="20" y="30" width="180" height="36"></rect><text class="boxText" x="110" y="53">within max-age</text><text class="figHint" x="110" y="85">served from disk, 0 network calls</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="260" y="30" width="180" height="36"></rect><text class="boxText" x="350" y="53">after max-age</text><line class="flow" x1="440" y1="48" x2="540" y2="48"></line><text class="figHint" x="490" y="38">If-None-Match</text><rect class="box" x="540" y="30" width="80" height="36"></rect><text class="boxText" x="580" y="53">304?</text><text class="figHint" x="490" y="80">unchanged → keep using cached copy, no re-download</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Revalidation costs a tiny request-response, not the whole file — far cheaper than downloading it again.

frames.title: Build step
frames.text: Build step outputs app.9f2a1c.js — the hash changes whenever the content changes.

frames.title: Server responds
frames.text: Server responds with Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable — cache this for a year, it will never change under this exact name.

frames.title: Browser stores it.
frames.text: Browser stores it. Every later visit uses the local copy — zero requests for this file until the app is redeployed.

frames.title: You ship a new version:
frames.text: You ship a new version: the build produces app.7bd310.js — a brand-new filename, so it is guaranteed to be a fresh download, not a stale cache hit.

frames.title: The HTML file itself
frames.text: The HTML file itself is served with a short or no cache time, so the browser always finds out about the new filename promptly.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 640 140" role="img" aria-labelledby="cdnCacheTitle"><title id="cdnCacheTitle">A request checks the browser cache, then the CDN edge, then finally the origin server — each layer with its own, usually shorter, TTL.</title><rect class="box" x="20" y="50" width="130" height="40"></rect><text class="boxText" x="85" y="74">browser cache</text><line class="flow" x1="150" y1="70" x2="220" y2="70"></line><rect class="boxAccent" x="220" y="50" width="130" height="40"></rect><text class="boxText" x="285" y="74">CDN edge</text><line class="flow" x1="350" y1="70" x2="420" y2="70"></line><rect class="boxWarn" x="420" y="50" width="130" height="40"></rect><text class="boxText" x="485" y="74">origin server</text><text class="figHint" x="85" y="105">max-age=300</text><text class="figHint" x="285" y="105">s-maxage=3600</text><text class="figHint" x="485" y="105">source of truth</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: s-maxage lets you tell shared caches (CDNs) to hold something longer than an individual browser would — the two audiences often want different freshness.

frames.title: Origin serves
frames.text: Origin serves /images/shoe-42.jpg with Cache-Control: public, s-maxage=86400.

frames.title: First request from Tokyo:
frames.text: First request from Tokyo: the Tokyo edge has no copy — a miss. It fetches from origin once, stores it, and returns it (slower, one-time cost).

frames.title: Every later Tokyo visitor,
frames.text: Every later Tokyo visitor, for the next 24 hours, gets a hit straight from the Tokyo edge — origin sees nothing.

frames.title: A visitor from Berlin
frames.text: A visitor from Berlin hits a different edge, which is also a miss the first time — each region builds up its own cached copy independently.

frames.title: You update the image
frames.text: You update the image the next day. Because the filename did not change, you call the CDN's purge API for that path so every edge drops its stale copy right away, instead of waiting up to 24 hours.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 640 150" role="img" aria-labelledby="appCacheTitle"><title id="appCacheTitle">With in-process caches, each app server has its own separate, inconsistent copy; a shared Redis cache gives every server the same view.</title><text class="figLabel" x="150" y="18">IN-PROCESS: 3 different copies</text><rect class="box" x="20" y="35" width="90" height="30"></rect><text class="boxText" x="65" y="54">server 1</text><rect class="box" x="130" y="35" width="90" height="30"></rect><text class="boxText" x="175" y="54">server 2</text><rect class="box" x="240" y="35" width="90" height="30"></rect><text class="boxText" x="285" y="54">server 3</text><text class="figHint" x="175" y="80">each caches its own copy — can disagree</text><line class="divider" x1="360" y1="10" x2="360" y2="140"></line><text class="figLabel" x="500" y="18">DISTRIBUTED: one shared copy</text><rect class="box" x="390" y="35" width="70" height="26"></rect><rect class="box" x="470" y="35" width="70" height="26"></rect><rect class="box" x="550" y="35" width="70" height="26"></rect><line class="flow" x1="425" y1="61" x2="480" y2="100"></line><line class="flow" x1="505" y1="61" x2="480" y2="100"></line><line class="flow" x1="585" y1="61" x2="480" y2="100"></line><rect class="boxAccent" x="420" y="100" width="120" height="34"></rect><text class="boxText" x="480" y="122">Redis</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: An in-process cache can go stale differently on every server. A shared cache keeps one answer, everywhere.

frames.title: Request comes in
frames.text: Request comes in for user 42's recommendations.

frames.title: App checks Redis
frames.text: App checks Redis for key recs:42.

frames.title: Miss:
frames.text: Miss: run the expensive scoring logic (300 ms), then SET recs:42 <result> EX 600 — cache it for 10 minutes.

frames.title: Any app server
frames.text: Any app server serving user 42's next request in that window gets a hit — even a different server than the one that computed it.

frames.title: After 10 minutes,
frames.text: After 10 minutes, the key expires automatically and the next request recomputes a fresh result.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 640 130" role="img" aria-labelledby="dbCacheTitle"><title id="dbCacheTitle">Even a fast in-memory database read still costs a network round trip and query execution; an application-level cache skips both entirely.</title><rect class="box" x="20" y="45" width="120" height="40"></rect><text class="boxText" x="80" y="69">app server</text><line class="flow" x1="140" y1="55" x2="260" y2="35"></line><text class="figHint" x="200" y="25">query → ~5–40ms</text><rect class="box" x="260" y="18" width="150" height="34"></rect><text class="boxText" x="335" y="40">DB (buffer pool hit)</text><line class="flow" x1="140" y1="70" x2="260" y2="90"></line><text class="figHint" x="200" y="105">cache → ~0.5–1ms</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="260" y="75" width="150" height="34"></rect><text class="boxText" x="335" y="97">app cache hit</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Even a well-tuned database still has to parse, plan, and execute a query. An application cache in front skips all of that for repeat reads.

frames.title: A dashboard query
frames.text: A dashboard query aggregates last month's sales — expensive, called often, changes only a few times a day.

frames.title: Application checks Redis
frames.text: Application checks Redis for sales-summary:2026-09 first.

frames.title: Miss:
frames.text: Miss: the query runs against the database. If the relevant pages are already in the buffer pool, this is fast; if not, the database reads from disk once.

frames.title: The application stores
frames.text: The application stores the result in Redis with a several-hour TTL, then returns it.

frames.title: Every request for the rest of the day
frames.text: Every request for the rest of the day is a Redis hit — the database, and even its own buffer pool, are never touched again for this query.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 640 150" role="img" aria-labelledby="caTitle"><title id="caTitle">On a read, the application checks the cache; on a miss it queries the database itself and then writes the result into the cache.</title><rect class="box" x="20" y="55" width="90" height="40"></rect><text class="boxText" x="65" y="79">app</text><line class="flow" x1="110" y1="70" x2="190" y2="45"></line><text class="figHint" x="150" y="35">1. check</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="190" y="25" width="110" height="40"></rect><text class="boxText" x="245" y="49">cache: miss</text><line class="flow" x1="110" y1="80" x2="190" y2="105"></line><text class="figHint" x="150" y="120">2. query</text><rect class="boxWarn" x="190" y="90" width="110" height="34"></rect><text class="boxText" x="245" y="111">database</text><line class="flowMuted" x1="300" y1="105" x2="470" y2="45"></line><text class="figHint" x="400" y="130">3. app writes result into cache</text><rect class="box" x="470" y="25" width="110" height="40"></rect><text class="boxText" x="525" y="49">cache: filled</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Every arrow is driven by the application — that is the defining trait of cache-aside.

frames.title: Read:
frames.text: Read: GET /products/42 — app checks cache.get("product:42").

frames.title: Miss:
frames.text: Miss: app runs db.query("SELECT * FROM products WHERE id=42").

frames.title: App fills the cache:
frames.text: App fills the cache: cache.set("product:42", result, ttl=300), then returns the product.

frames.title: Write:
frames.text: Write: PATCH /products/42 updates the price in the database.

frames.title: Critical step:
frames.text: Critical step: the app also runs cache.delete("product:42") right after the write, so the next read is forced to be a miss and pulls the fresh price.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 640 140" role="img" aria-labelledby="rtTitle"><title id="rtTitle">With cache-aside the application handles the miss and fills the cache; with read-through the cache handles the miss itself using a configured loader.</title><text class="figLabel" x="150" y="18">CACHE-ASIDE</text><rect class="box" x="20" y="30" width="80" height="30"></rect><text class="boxText" x="60" y="49">app</text><line class="flow" x1="100" y1="40" x2="170" y2="40"></line><line class="flow" x1="170" y1="55" x2="100" y2="55"></line><rect class="boxAccent" x="170" y="30" width="80" height="30"></rect><text class="boxText" x="210" y="49">cache</text><text class="figHint" x="60" y="80">app also queries</text><line class="flow" x1="60" y1="60" x2="60" y2="95"></line><rect class="boxWarn" x="20" y="95" width="80" height="26"></rect><text class="boxText" x="60" y="113">database</text><line class="divider" x1="330" y1="10" x2="330" y2="130"></line><text class="figLabel" x="480" y="18">READ-THROUGH</text><rect class="box" x="380" y="30" width="80" height="30"></rect><text class="boxText" x="420" y="49">app</text><line class="flow" x1="460" y1="40" x2="530" y2="40"></line><line class="flow" x1="530" y1="55" x2="460" y2="55"></line><rect class="boxAccent" x="530" y="30" width="80" height="30"></rect><text class="boxText" x="570" y="49">cache</text><line class="flow" x1="570" y1="60" x2="570" y2="95"></line><text class="figHint" x="570" y="78">cache queries</text><rect class="boxWarn" x="530" y="95" width="80" height="26"></rect><text class="boxText" x="570" y="113">database</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Same end result, different owner of the "go fetch it" logic. The app talks to one thing in read-through: the cache.

frames.title: Set up the cache once
frames.text: Set up the cache once with a loader: cache.configure(loader: id => db.getProduct(id)).

frames.title: Any code, anywhere,
frames.text: Any code, anywhere, just calls cache.get("product:42").

frames.title: Hit:
frames.text: Hit: the cache returns the stored value directly.

frames.title: Miss:
frames.text: Miss: the cache itself calls the loader, gets the product from the database, stores it, and returns it — the calling code never wrote any of that logic.

frames.title: A second service
frames.text: A second service that also needs products just calls cache.get("product:42") too — it automatically benefits from the same loader and the same cached entry, with zero duplicated logic.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 640 130" role="img" aria-labelledby="wtTitle"><title id="wtTitle">A write goes through the cache, which writes to the database first and then updates itself, only confirming success once both are done.</title><rect class="box" x="20" y="45" width="90" height="40"></rect><text class="boxText" x="65" y="69">app</text><line class="flow" x1="110" y1="65" x2="230" y2="65"></line><text class="figHint" x="170" y="55">write</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="230" y="45" width="120" height="40"></rect><text class="boxText" x="290" y="69">cache</text><line class="flow" x1="350" y1="65" x2="480" y2="65"></line><text class="figHint" x="415" y="55">1. write DB</text><rect class="boxWarn" x="480" y="45" width="120" height="40"></rect><text class="boxText" x="540" y="69">database</text><text class="figHint" x="290" y="100">2. cache updates its own copy, then confirms "done" to the app</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Both writes happen before the app is told the write succeeded — the cache is never momentarily behind the database.

frames.title: App calls
frames.text: App calls cache.set("balance:42", 5200) through a write-through cache client.

frames.title: The cache client writes to the database first:
frames.text: The cache client writes to the database first: UPDATE accounts SET balance=5200 WHERE id=42.

frames.title: Only after the database confirms,
frames.text: Only after the database confirms, the cache updates its own stored value for balance:42.

frames.title: The write call returns success
frames.text: The write call returns success to the app only now — both stores agree.

frames.title: A read from a different server
frames.text: A read from a different server a moment later hits the cache and sees 5200 — never the stale 5000.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 640 140" role="img" aria-labelledby="wbTitle"><title id="wbTitle">A write is confirmed the instant it lands in the cache; a background process flushes it to the database a moment later.</title><rect class="box" x="20" y="45" width="90" height="40"></rect><text class="boxText" x="65" y="69">app</text><line class="flow" x1="110" y1="60" x2="220" y2="60"></line><text class="figHint" x="165" y="50">write</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="220" y="45" width="120" height="40"></rect><text class="boxText" x="280" y="69">cache</text><line class="flow" x1="340" y1="55" x2="200" y2="90"></line><text class="figHint" x="270" y="100">confirmed — instantly</text><line class="flowMuted" x1="340" y1="70" x2="480" y2="70"></line><text class="figHint" x="410" y="60">flushed later</text><rect class="boxWarn" x="480" y="45" width="130" height="40"></rect><text class="boxText" x="545" y="69">database</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: The app is told "done" before the database has seen the write at all.

frames.title: Player finishes a level.
frames.text: Player finishes a level. App writes cache.set("score:player7", 4200) and returns instantly — no database call in this request.

frames.title: The same player finishes another level
frames.text: The same player finishes another level 4 seconds later, overwriting the cached score to 5100 before the first value was ever flushed.

frames.title: Every 5 seconds,
frames.text: Every 5 seconds, a background flusher reads all "dirty" (unsaved) keys and writes them to the database in one batch — here, just the final 5100, not two separate writes.

frames.title: If the cache crashes
frames.text: If the cache crashes right before a flush, that unsaved score is gone — a real risk this pattern accepts in exchange for its speed.

frames.title: To reduce that risk,
frames.text: To reduce that risk, some systems also write the change to a durable log first (so it can be replayed), while still batching the actual database writes.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 640 130" role="img" aria-labelledby="lruTitle"><title id="lruTitle">Accessing an item moves it to the front; when the cache is full, the item at the back (least recently used) is evicted to make room.</title><text class="figHint" x="70" y="25">most recent</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="20" y="35" width="70" height="34"></rect><text class="boxText" x="55" y="57">D</text><rect class="box" x="100" y="35" width="70" height="34"></rect><text class="boxText" x="135" y="57">C</text><rect class="box" x="180" y="35" width="70" height="34"></rect><text class="boxText" x="215" y="57">A</text><rect class="boxWarn" x="260" y="35" width="70" height="34"></rect><text class="boxText" x="295" y="57">B</text><text class="figHint" x="295" y="25">least recent</text><line class="flow" x1="330" y1="52" x2="400" y2="52"></line><text class="figHint" x="480" y="42">cache full, new item E arrives</text><text class="figHint" x="480" y="90">B is evicted — it was used longest ago</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Each access reshuffles the order; eviction always removes from the "used longest ago" end.

frames.title: Default to LRU.
frames.text: Default to LRU. Most real traffic follows recency — what was used a moment ago is likely to be used again soon.

frames.title: Watch for one-time scans.
frames.text: Watch for one-time scans. A background job reading every row once can flush truly hot data out of an LRU cache — some caches offer a scan-resistant variant for this.

frames.title: Consider LFU
frames.text: Consider LFU if a small set of items (a homepage, top-selling products) are reliably hot for a long time, regardless of momentary bursts elsewhere.

frames.title: Layer on TTL regardless of policy.
frames.text: Layer on TTL regardless of policy. Even the "best" eviction choice should not keep genuinely stale data around just because it is popular.

frames.title: Measure the actual hit rate
frames.text: Measure the actual hit rate after choosing — the right policy is the one that empirically performs best for your traffic, not the theoretically fanciest one.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 640 130" role="img" aria-labelledby="invTitle"><title id="invTitle">On a write, you can either delete the cached key so the next read fetches fresh data, or update the cache with the new value directly.</title><rect class="box" x="20" y="50" width="100" height="34"></rect><text class="boxText" x="70" y="71">write happens</text><line class="flow" x1="120" y1="60" x2="220" y2="30"></line><rect class="boxAccent" x="220" y="12" width="150" height="34"></rect><text class="boxText" x="295" y="34">DELETE the key</text><text class="figHint" x="295" y="60">next read is a clean miss</text><line class="flow" x1="120" y1="75" x2="220" y2="100"></line><rect class="box" x="220" y="83" width="150" height="34"></rect><text class="boxText" x="295" y="105">UPDATE the value</text><text class="figHint" x="295" y="125">next read is a hit with fresh data</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Deleting is simpler and safer (nothing to get wrong about the new value); updating avoids a miss but risks writing the wrong thing if two writes race.

frames.title: An admin updates a product's price.
frames.text: An admin updates a product's price. The write path updates the database and deletes product:42 from the app cache — the direct copy is now fresh.

frames.title: But a "category:shoes" list
frames.text: But a "category:shoes" list that embeds this product's price is still cached with the old value — deleting one key did not touch it.

frames.title: The write path also publishes
frames.text: The write path also publishes a ProductUpdated {id: 42} event (from the Communication Patterns section).

frames.title: Any cache that embeds product 42
frames.text: Any cache that embeds product 42 — category lists, search results, related- items — subscribes to that event and invalidates its own affected keys.

frames.title: The CDN and browser caches
frames.text: The CDN and browser caches are handled separately: a short TTL plus, if urgent, an explicit purge call at the edge.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 460 150" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of one application talking to three different database types, each chosen for a different kind of data it stores."><rect class="boxAccent" x="180" y="10" width="100" height="34" rx="6"></rect><text x="230" y="32" class="boxText">application</text><line class="flow" x1="200" y1="44" x2="100" y2="90"></line><line class="flow" x1="230" y1="44" x2="230" y2="90"></line><line class="flow" x1="260" y1="44" x2="360" y2="90"></line><rect class="box" x="50" y="95" width="100" height="34" rx="6"></rect><text x="100" y="117" class="boxText">Postgres — orders</text><rect class="box" x="180" y="95" width="100" height="34" rx="6"></rect><text x="230" y="117" class="boxText">Redis — sessions</text><rect class="box" x="310" y="95" width="100" height="34" rx="6"></rect><text x="360" y="117" class="boxText">Search — catalog</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Different data shapes, different databases, one application.

frames.title: Start from the query, not the tool.
frames.text: Start from the query, not the tool. "Show me this user's order history" needs joins and consistency → relational.

frames.title: Check the shape.
frames.text: Check the shape. "Store this user's arbitrary settings object" is naturally nested and schema-flexible → document.

frames.title: Check the access pattern.
frames.text: Check the access pattern. "Look up a session by token in under a millisecond" is a pure key lookup → key-value store.

frames.title: Accept multiple databases.
frames.text: Accept multiple databases. One product ends up using Postgres for orders, Redis for sessions, and Elasticsearch for search — each doing what it's best at.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 460 140" role="img" aria-label="Diagram contrasting a fixed-schema SQL table of rows against a flexible NoSQL collection of documents with differing fields."><text x="110" y="18" class="figLabel" text-anchor="middle">SQL — FIXED SCHEMA</text><rect class="box" x="30" y="30" width="160" height="70" rx="6"></rect><line class="divider" x1="30" y1="53" x2="190" y2="53"></line><line class="divider" x1="30" y1="76" x2="190" y2="76"></line><line class="divider" x1="110" y1="30" x2="110" y2="100"></line><text x="70" y="45" class="boxText">id</text><text x="150" y="45" class="boxText">name</text><text x="70" y="68" class="boxText">1</text><text x="150" y="68" class="boxText">Ann</text><text x="70" y="91" class="boxText">2</text><text x="150" y="91" class="boxText">Bo</text><line class="divider" x1="230" y1="10" x2="230" y2="120"></line><text x="350" y="18" class="figLabel" text-anchor="middle">NOSQL — FLEXIBLE</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="270" y="30" width="160" height="28" rx="5"></rect><text x="350" y="48" class="boxText">{ id, name }</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="270" y="65" width="160" height="28" rx="5"></rect><text x="350" y="83" class="boxText">{ id, name, tags[] }</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Every SQL row shares the same columns; NoSQL documents can differ from each other.

frames.title: Payments → SQL.
frames.text: Payments → SQL. Debiting one account and crediting another must happen atomically — exactly what ACID transactions guarantee.

frames.title: Content metadata → NoSQL (document).
frames.text: Content metadata → NoSQL (document). Each article's fields change over time and vary by content type; a rigid schema would mean constant migrations.

frames.title: Both ship in the same product
frames.text: Both ship in the same product — the choice is per data set, not company-wide.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 460 140" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of a two-step transaction that either commits both the debit and credit together or rolls back both if anything fails before commit."><rect class="box" x="20" y="20" width="110" height="30" rx="5"></rect><text x="75" y="40" class="boxText">debit A</text><line class="flow" x1="130" y1="35" x2="180" y2="35"></line><rect class="box" x="190" y="20" width="110" height="30" rx="5"></rect><text x="245" y="40" class="boxText">credit B</text><line class="flow" x1="300" y1="35" x2="350" y2="35"></line><rect class="boxAccent" x="360" y="20" width="90" height="30" rx="5"></rect><text x="405" y="40" class="boxText">COMMIT</text><line class="flowMuted" x1="75" y1="55" x2="405" y2="55"></line><rect class="boxWarn" x="330" y="70" width="120" height="30" rx="5"></rect><text x="390" y="90" class="boxText">crash → rollback</text><text x="230" y="115" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">anything short of COMMIT undoes both steps</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Atomicity means partial completion isn't an option — it's all or nothing.

frames.title: Begin the transaction.
frames.text: Begin the transaction. BEGIN;

frames.title: Debit A.
frames.text: Debit A. UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 50 WHERE id = 'A';

frames.title: Credit B.
frames.text: Credit B. UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 50 WHERE id = 'B';

frames.title: Commit.
frames.text: Commit. COMMIT; — both writes become permanent together.

frames.title: If the server crashes after step 2
frames.text: If the server crashes after step 2 but before commit, the whole transaction rolls back on restart — A is never left debited without B being credited.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 420 140" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of three linked tables: customers, orders, and order items, connected by foreign keys."><rect class="box" x="20" y="50" width="100" height="34" rx="5"></rect><text x="70" y="72" class="boxText">customers</text><line class="flow" x1="120" y1="67" x2="170" y2="67"></line><rect class="boxAccent" x="180" y="50" width="100" height="34" rx="5"></rect><text x="230" y="72" class="boxText">orders</text><line class="flow" x1="280" y1="67" x2="330" y2="67"></line><rect class="box" x="300" y="50" width="100" height="34" rx="5"></rect><text x="350" y="72" class="boxText">order_items</text><text x="145" y="55" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">FK</text><text x="305" y="55" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">FK</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Each fact lives once; foreign keys let queries reassemble the relationships.

frames.title: Model the entities.
frames.text: Model the entities. customers, orders, order_items as separate tables.

frames.title: Link them.
frames.text: Link them. orders.customer_id references customers.id; order_items.order_id references orders.id.

frames.title: Query across them.
frames.text: Query across them. SELECT * FROM orders JOIN customers ON ... reassembles the full picture on demand.

frames.title: Rely on constraints.
frames.text: Rely on constraints. The database itself refuses an order for a non-existent customer — no application code has to check.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 460 140" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of two product documents in the same collection with different attribute fields, versus a relational model that would need separate attribute tables per product type."><rect class="boxAccent" x="30" y="20" width="180" height="45" rx="6"></rect><text x="120" y="38" class="boxText">{ name: 'Shirt',</text><text x="120" y="55" class="boxText">  size, color }</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="30" y="75" width="180" height="45" rx="6"></rect><text x="120" y="93" class="boxText">{ name: 'Laptop',</text><text x="120" y="110" class="boxText">  ram, cpu }</text><text x="120" y="128" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">same collection, different shapes</text><line class="divider" x1="250" y1="10" x2="250" y2="135"></line><text x="360" y="18" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">relational would need a</text><text x="360" y="32" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">separate attributes table</text><text x="360" y="46" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">joined per product type</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Variable shape, one collection — no schema migration needed to add a new product type.

frames.title: Model each product as one document.
frames.text: Model each product as one document. { id, name, price, attributes: {...} } — attributes vary freely.

frames.title: No migration for new categories.
frames.text: No migration for new categories. Adding "headphones" with its own attribute shape needs zero schema change.

frames.title: Read in one lookup.
frames.text: Read in one lookup. Rendering a product page fetches one document — no joins across an attributes table.

frames.title: Accept the trade.
frames.text: Accept the trade. "Find all products where any attribute equals X" needs a secondary index, since attributes aren't a fixed column.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 420 130" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of a key mapping directly to a value in a hash table, with constant time lookup regardless of how many keys are stored."><rect class="box" x="20" y="20" width="120" height="26" rx="4"></rect><text x="80" y="38" class="boxText">session:abc123</text><line class="flow" x1="140" y1="33" x2="200" y2="33"></line><rect class="boxAccent" x="210" y="20" width="160" height="26" rx="4"></rect><text x="290" y="38" class="boxText">{ userId: 42 }</text><text x="195" y="80" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">O(1) lookup — same speed whether the store holds 100 keys or 100 million</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: No schema, no joins — just a direct map from key to value.

frames.title: Pick the key.
frames.text: Pick the key. session:{sessionId} as the key.

frames.title: Store the value.
frames.text: Store the value. SET session:abc123 "{ userId: 42 }" EX 3600 — the value plus a 1-hour expiry.

frames.title: Read it back.
frames.text: Read it back. GET session:abc123 — one lookup, no query planning.

frames.title: Let it expire.
frames.text: Let it expire. The store automatically removes the key after the TTL — no cleanup job needed.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 460 140" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of sensor readings distributed across three nodes by device id partition key, with each node's readings sorted by timestamp."><g><rect class="box" x="30" y="20" width="120" height="90" rx="6"></rect><text x="90" y="15" class="figLabel" text-anchor="middle">NODE 1</text><text x="90" y="45" class="boxText">device: …</text><text x="90" y="65" class="boxText">t=09:02</text><text x="90" y="82" class="boxText">t=09:01</text><text x="90" y="99" class="boxText">t=09:00</text></g><g><rect class="boxAccent" x="175" y="20" width="120" height="90" rx="6"></rect><text x="235" y="15" class="figLabel" text-anchor="middle">NODE 2</text><text x="235" y="45" class="boxText">device: X</text><text x="235" y="65" class="boxText">t=09:02</text><text x="235" y="82" class="boxText">t=09:01</text><text x="235" y="99" class="boxText">t=09:00</text></g><g><rect class="box" x="320" y="20" width="120" height="90" rx="6"></rect><text x="380" y="15" class="figLabel" text-anchor="middle">NODE 3</text><text x="380" y="45" class="boxText">device: …</text><text x="380" y="65" class="boxText">t=09:02</text><text x="380" y="82" class="boxText">t=09:01</text><text x="380" y="99" class="boxText">t=09:00</text></g></svg>
diagrams.caption: Device X's partition sits on one node, pre-sorted by time — a fast read for its recent history.

frames.title: Pick the partition key.
frames.text: Pick the partition key. device_id — spreads write load evenly across nodes.

frames.title: Pick the clustering key.
frames.text: Pick the clustering key. timestamp DESC — readings for one device are stored pre-sorted, newest first.

frames.title: Write at scale.
frames.text: Write at scale. Each node only owns a slice of devices, so ingest scales by adding nodes.

frames.title: Read the common query.
frames.text: Read the common query. "Last 100 readings for device X" is a fast, sequential read within one partition — no scatter-gather needed.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 420 160" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of a small social graph, showing a two-hop traversal from one person through a mutual friend to a recommended new connection."><circle class="boxAccent" cx="60" cy="80" r="24"></circle><text x="60" y="85" class="boxText">You</text><line class="flow" x1="84" y1="80" x2="176" y2="80"></line><circle class="box" cx="200" cy="80" r="24"></circle><text x="200" y="85" class="boxText">Ann</text><line class="flow" x1="224" y1="80" x2="316" y2="80"></line><circle class="box" cx="340" cy="80" r="24"></circle><text x="340" y="85" class="boxText">Bo</text><text x="130" y="65" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">FOLLOWS</text><text x="270" y="65" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">FOLLOWS</text><text x="340" y="130" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">2 hops → recommend Bo</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Each hop is a direct pointer walk, not a re-join of the whole table.

frames.title: Model the domain as nodes and edges.
frames.text: Model the domain as nodes and edges. People are nodes; FOLLOWS and FRIENDS_WITH are edges between them.

frames.title: Ask a relationship question.
frames.text: Ask a relationship question. "Recommend people two hops away that I don't already follow."

frames.title: Traverse, don't join.
frames.text: Traverse, don't join. The database walks outward from your node, hop by hop, following edges directly.

frames.title: Get a result in milliseconds
frames.text: Get a result in milliseconds even on a graph with hundreds of millions of edges, because each hop is a pointer lookup, not a table scan.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 440 130" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of a time series stored in sequential time-bucketed chunks, with recent chunks kept at full resolution and older chunks downsampled."><line x1="20" y1="80" x2="420" y2="80" stroke="var(--muted)"></line><rect class="box" x="30" y="55" width="38" height="25" rx="3"></rect><rect class="box" x="78" y="55" width="38" height="25" rx="3"></rect><rect class="box" x="126" y="55" width="38" height="25" rx="3"></rect><rect class="box" x="174" y="55" width="38" height="25" rx="3"></rect><rect class="box" x="222" y="55" width="38" height="25" rx="3"></rect><rect class="boxAccent" x="270" y="55" width="38" height="25" rx="3"></rect><rect class="boxAccent" x="318" y="55" width="38" height="25" rx="3"></rect><rect class="boxAccent" x="366" y="55" width="38" height="25" rx="3"></rect><text x="70" y="105" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">downsampled, old</text><text x="370" y="105" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">full resolution, recent</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Storage shrinks as data ages — recent points stay precise, old points get summarized.

frames.title: Ingest continuously.
frames.text: Ingest continuously. Every server reports CPU usage once per second, tagged with a hostname.

frames.title: Store by time.
frames.text: Store by time. Data lands in the current time-bucketed chunk, compressed as it's written.

frames.title: Query a window.
frames.text: Query a window. "Average CPU per host over the last 15 minutes" touches only recent chunks.

frames.title: Downsample automatically.
frames.text: Downsample automatically. After 30 days, per-second data is rolled up into per-minute averages to save space, since nobody needs second-level detail from a month ago.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 460 140" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of an inverted index mapping words to the document ids that contain them, then intersecting two word lookups to find documents matching both search terms."><rect class="box" x="20" y="20" width="90" height="24" rx="4"></rect><text x="65" y="37" class="boxText">"distributed"</text><text x="130" y="37" class="figHint">→ docs 4, 9, 12</text><rect class="box" x="20" y="55" width="90" height="24" rx="4"></rect><text x="65" y="72" class="boxText">"systems"</text><text x="130" y="72" class="figHint">→ docs 2, 4, 9, 20</text><line class="flow" x1="65" y1="79" x2="65" y2="100"></line><line class="flow" x1="65" y1="44" x2="65" y2="100"></line><rect class="boxAccent" x="20" y="100" width="150" height="26" rx="4"></rect><text x="95" y="118" class="boxText">intersect → docs 4, 9</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Two word lookups and a set intersection — no document text scanned at query time.

frames.title: Index documents as they're created.
frames.text: Index documents as they're created. Each blog post is tokenized into words and added to the inverted index.

frames.title: User searches "distributed systems."
frames.text: User searches "distributed systems." The engine looks up both terms in the inverted index.

frames.title: Intersect and rank.
frames.text: Intersect and rank. Documents containing both terms are ranked higher than documents with just one, factoring in term frequency and field weight (title beats body).

frames.title: Return in milliseconds
frames.text: Return in milliseconds, even across millions of documents, because the lookup is by word, not a scan of every document's text.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 380 220" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of vectors plotted in a 2D space, with a new query vector and its three nearest neighbors highlighted as similar items."><circle class="box" cx="80" cy="60" r="6"></circle><circle class="box" cx="120" cy="100" r="6"></circle><circle class="box" cx="280" cy="50" r="6"></circle><circle class="box" cx="300" cy="170" r="6"></circle><circle class="boxAccent" cx="150" cy="150" r="7"></circle><circle class="boxAccent" cx="170" cy="120" r="7"></circle><circle class="boxAccent" cx="130" cy="170" r="7"></circle><circle cx="150" cy="145" r="9" fill="none" style="stroke:var(--course-accent);stroke-width:2;stroke-dasharray:3 3"></circle><circle cx="150" cy="145" r="55" fill="none" style="stroke:var(--course-accent);stroke-width:1.5;stroke-dasharray:4 4"></circle><text x="150" y="200" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">3 nearest neighbors highlighted around the query</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Similar meaning lands close together in vector space, regardless of exact wording.

frames.title: Embed every ticket.
frames.text: Embed every ticket. Run each ticket's text through an embedding model, producing a vector.

frames.title: Store the vectors.
frames.text: Store the vectors. Each vector is indexed in the vector database alongside the ticket ID.

frames.title: Embed the new query.
frames.text: Embed the new query. The new ticket's text is embedded the same way.

frames.title: Search by nearness.
frames.text: Search by nearness. The database returns the closest stored vectors — tickets that mean something similar, even with completely different wording.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 460 190" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of a B+ Tree with a root node, internal nodes, and leaf nodes linked together in a chain for fast range scans."><rect class="boxAccent" x="190" y="15" width="80" height="30" rx="5"></rect><text x="230" y="35" class="boxText">root</text><line class="flow" x1="210" y1="45" x2="110" y2="80"></line><line class="flow" x1="250" y1="45" x2="350" y2="80"></line><rect class="box" x="70" y="85" width="80" height="28" rx="5"></rect><text x="110" y="103" class="boxText">internal</text><rect class="box" x="310" y="85" width="80" height="28" rx="5"></rect><text x="350" y="103" class="boxText">internal</text><g><line class="flow" x1="110" y1="113" x2="40" y2="150"></line><rect class="box" x="20" y="155" width="90" height="26" rx="4"></rect><text x="65" y="172" class="boxText">leaf 1</text></g><g><line class="flow" x1="110" y1="113" x2="170" y2="150"></line><rect class="box" x="150" y="155" width="90" height="26" rx="4"></rect><text x="195" y="172" class="boxText">leaf 2</text></g><g><line class="flow" x1="350" y1="113" x2="300" y2="150"></line><rect class="box" x="280" y="155" width="90" height="26" rx="4"></rect><text x="325" y="172" class="boxText">leaf 3</text></g><g><line class="flow" x1="350" y1="113" x2="430" y2="150"></line><rect class="box" x="410" y="155" width="90" height="26" rx="4"></rect><text x="455" y="172" class="boxText">leaf 4</text></g><line class="flowMuted" x1="110" y1="168" x2="440" y2="168"></line><text x="230" y="188" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">leaves linked → fast range scans without revisiting the root</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Shallow tree for fast point lookups; linked leaves for fast range scans.

frames.title: Index a column.
frames.text: Index a column. CREATE INDEX ON orders(customer_id) builds a B+ Tree keyed on customer_id.

frames.title: Point lookup.
frames.text: Point lookup. Finding customer 42's orders starts at the root, and each node tells you which child to follow next — 3-4 hops reach the right leaf even with millions of rows.

frames.title: Range scan.
frames.text: Range scan. "All orders for customers 100-200" finds the first match, then walks the linked leaves forward — no repeated root-to-leaf traversals.

frames.title: Stays balanced.
frames.text: Stays balanced. As rows are inserted, nodes split automatically to keep every path from root to leaf the same length — lookups never degrade to a slow path.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 460 160" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of writes landing in an in-memory memtable, flushing to disk as sorted SSTable files, and being merged by background compaction."><rect class="boxAccent" x="20" y="20" width="110" height="34" rx="6"></rect><text x="75" y="42" class="boxText">memtable (RAM)</text><line class="flow" x1="75" y1="54" x2="75" y2="85"></line><text x="95" y="72" class="figHint">flush</text><rect class="box" x="20" y="90" width="70" height="28" rx="4"></rect><text x="55" y="108" class="boxText">SSTable</text><rect class="box" x="100" y="90" width="70" height="28" rx="4"></rect><text x="135" y="108" class="boxText">SSTable</text><rect class="box" x="180" y="90" width="70" height="28" rx="4"></rect><text x="215" y="108" class="boxText">SSTable</text><line class="flow" x1="135" y1="118" x2="135" y2="140"></line><text x="230" y="132" class="figHint">compaction merges</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="60" y="140" width="150" height="28" rx="4"></rect><text x="135" y="158" class="boxText">1 merged SSTable</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Sequential writes and flushes now, background merging later — the LSM trade for write speed.

frames.title: Write arrives.
frames.text: Write arrives. A new key-value pair is appended to the write-ahead log and inserted into the in-memory memtable.

frames.title: Memtable fills up.
frames.text: Memtable fills up. Its contents are flushed to disk as a new immutable, sorted SSTable file.

frames.title: More flushes happen.
frames.text: More flushes happen. Over time, several SSTables pile up on disk.

frames.title: Compaction runs in the background.
frames.text: Compaction runs in the background. Overlapping SSTables are merged into fewer, larger ones, dropping any values a later write overwrote.

frames.title: A read checks multiple places
frames.text: A read checks multiple places — the memtable, then SSTables from newest to oldest — which is why LSM Trees are optimized for writes at some cost to read speed.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 460 150" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of a transaction being written to a write-ahead log and fsynced to disk before the client is told success, with the main data file updated later in the background."><rect class="boxAccent" x="20" y="20" width="110" height="30" rx="5"></rect><text x="75" y="40" class="boxText">transaction</text><line class="flow" x1="130" y1="35" x2="180" y2="35"></line><rect class="box" x="190" y="20" width="120" height="30" rx="5"></rect><text x="250" y="40" class="boxText">WAL + fsync</text><line class="flow" x1="310" y1="35" x2="360" y2="35"></line><rect class="boxAccent" x="370" y="20" width="70" height="30" rx="5"></rect><text x="405" y="40" class="boxText">"OK"</text><line class="flowMuted" x1="250" y1="50" x2="250" y2="90"></line><rect class="box" x="190" y="95" width="120" height="30" rx="5"></rect><text x="250" y="115" class="boxText">data files</text><text x="250" y="135" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">updated later, replayed from WAL if crash happens first</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Success is reported only once the log entry is durably on disk — the data file can catch up afterward.

frames.title: Transaction commits.
frames.text: Transaction commits. The change is appended to the WAL first, and that write is fsynced to disk.

frames.title: Client is told "success."
frames.text: Client is told "success." Only after the WAL write is durably on disk — not when the in-memory change happens.

frames.title: Main data files update later,
frames.text: Main data files update later, in the background, batched for efficiency — this lag is safe because the WAL already has the record.

frames.title: Power fails
frames.text: Power fails before the main data file is updated.

frames.title: On restart, replay the WAL.
frames.text: On restart, replay the WAL. The database reads the log from the last checkpoint forward and reapplies any committed change the data files are missing.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 520 180" role="img" aria-label="Diagram comparing a full table scan that checks every row against an index lookup that walks a small tree to the matching row."><text x="120" y="20" class="figLabel" text-anchor="middle">NO INDEX</text><g><rect class="box" x="20" y="35" width="18" height="18" rx="3"></rect><rect class="box" x="42" y="35" width="18" height="18" rx="3"></rect><rect class="box" x="64" y="35" width="18" height="18" rx="3"></rect><rect class="box" x="86" y="35" width="18" height="18" rx="3"></rect><rect class="box" x="108" y="35" width="18" height="18" rx="3"></rect><rect class="box" x="130" y="35" width="18" height="18" rx="3"></rect><rect class="box" x="152" y="35" width="18" height="18" rx="3"></rect><rect class="boxAccent" x="174" y="35" width="18" height="18" rx="3"></rect><rect class="box" x="196" y="35" width="18" height="18" rx="3"></rect><rect class="box" x="218" y="35" width="18" height="18" rx="3"></rect></g><text x="120" y="70" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">checks every row until it finds a match</text><line x1="240" y1="90" x2="240" y2="90"></line><text x="400" y="20" class="figLabel" text-anchor="middle">WITH INDEX</text><g><rect class="box" x="370" y="35" width="60" height="20" rx="4"></rect><text x="400" y="49" class="boxText">root</text><line class="flow" x1="385" y1="55" x2="360" y2="80"></line><line class="flow" x1="415" y1="55" x2="440" y2="80"></line><rect class="box" x="330" y="80" width="60" height="20" rx="4"></rect><text x="360" y="94" class="boxText">a–m</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="410" y="80" width="60" height="20" rx="4"></rect><text x="440" y="94" class="boxText">n–z</text></g><text x="400" y="120" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">walks ~log(n) nodes straight to the row</text><line class="divider" x1="260" y1="10" x2="260" y2="150"></line></svg>
diagrams.caption: Same lookup, two strategies: linear scan vs a tree that skips most of the data.

frames.title: Confirm the scan.
