frames.text: Confirm the scan. Run EXPLAIN on the query — it shows a sequential scan touching all 20M rows.

frames.title: Add the index.
frames.text: Add the index. CREATE INDEX idx_orders_customer ON orders(customer_id);

frames.title: Re-run EXPLAIN.
frames.text: Re-run EXPLAIN. The plan now shows an index scan touching a few hundred rows.

frames.title: Measure again.
frames.text: Measure again. The query drops from 4s to 8ms.

frames.title: Watch write cost.
frames.text: Watch write cost. Bulk order inserts get ~5% slower — an acceptable trade for a query that runs on every checkout page view.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 480 160" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of one wide users table splitting into a small core table and a larger profile table, both keyed by the same user id."><rect class="box" x="20" y="20" width="140" height="100" rx="6"></rect><text x="90" y="15" class="figLabel" text-anchor="middle">USERS (WIDE)</text><text x="90" y="45" class="boxText">id</text><text x="90" y="63" class="boxText">name, email</text><text x="90" y="81" class="boxText">bio, avatar</text><text x="90" y="99" class="boxText">preferences</text><line class="flow" x1="165" y1="70" x2="220" y2="70"></line><rect class="boxAccent" x="230" y="20" width="110" height="45" rx="6"></rect><text x="285" y="15" class="figLabel" text-anchor="middle">users_core</text><text x="285" y="42" class="boxText">id, name, email</text><rect class="box" x="230" y="80" width="110" height="45" rx="6"></rect><text x="285" y="75" class="figLabel" text-anchor="middle">users_profile</text><text x="285" y="102" class="boxText">id, bio, avatar</text><text x="400" y="50" class="figHint">read on</text><text x="400" y="62" class="figHint">every request</text><text x="400" y="105" class="figHint">read on</text><text x="400" y="117" class="figHint">profile page</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Splitting by column keeps the frequently-read row small.

frames.title: Identify hot vs. cold columns.
frames.text: Identify hot vs. cold columns. Log which columns are actually selected by your busiest queries.

frames.title: Group them.
frames.text: Group them. Frequently-together, small columns go in one table; large or rarely-read columns (bios, JSON blobs, images) go in another.

frames.title: Split the table.
frames.text: Split the table. Create users_core and users_profile, both keyed by the same user_id.

frames.title: Update queries.
frames.text: Update queries. The auth path now reads a much smaller row; profile pages join in the second table only when needed.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 480 150" role="img" aria-label="Diagram comparing 50 separate per-row queries against one batched query returning the same data."><text x="110" y="18" class="figLabel" text-anchor="middle">N+1 PATTERN</text><g><rect class="box" x="20" y="30" width="20" height="16" rx="3"></rect></g><g><rect class="box" x="50" y="30" width="20" height="16" rx="3"></rect></g><g><rect class="box" x="80" y="30" width="20" height="16" rx="3"></rect></g><g><rect class="box" x="110" y="30" width="20" height="16" rx="3"></rect></g><g><rect class="boxWarn" x="140" y="30" width="20" height="16" rx="3"></rect></g><g><rect class="boxWarn" x="170" y="30" width="20" height="16" rx="3"></rect></g><text x="110" y="65" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">…50 queries, one per row</text><line class="divider" x1="230" y1="10" x2="230" y2="120"></line><text x="360" y="18" class="figLabel" text-anchor="middle">BATCHED</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="320" y="30" width="90" height="24" rx="4"></rect><text x="365" y="47" class="boxText">1 IN (...) query</text><line class="flow" x1="365" y1="54" x2="365" y2="80"></line><rect class="box" x="320" y="84" width="90" height="20" rx="4"></rect><text x="365" y="98" class="boxText">grouped in app</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Same data, one round trip instead of fifty.

frames.title: Spot the pattern.
frames.text: Spot the pattern. Request logs show 51 near-identical queries per page load.

frames.title: Rewrite as one query.
frames.text: Rewrite as one query. Fetch all reviews with a single WHERE product_id IN (...) query instead of one per product.

frames.title: Group in application code.
frames.text: Group in application code. Bucket the single result set by product_id.

frames.title: Measure.
frames.text: Measure. Page load query count drops from 51 to 2; response time drops from 900ms to 60ms.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 460 170" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of a primary database streaming writes to two replicas, while client reads are load balanced across the replicas and writes go only to the primary."><rect class="boxAccent" x="180" y="15" width="100" height="36" rx="6"></rect><text x="230" y="38" class="boxText">PRIMARY</text><line class="flow" x1="210" y1="51" x2="120" y2="90"></line><line class="flow" x1="250" y1="51" x2="340" y2="90"></line><text x="150" y="75" class="figHint">replication</text><rect class="box" x="70" y="95" width="100" height="36" rx="6"></rect><text x="120" y="118" class="boxText">REPLICA A</text><rect class="box" x="290" y="95" width="100" height="36" rx="6"></rect><text x="340" y="118" class="boxText">REPLICA B</text><line class="flowMuted" x1="230" y1="155" x2="230" y2="51"></line><text x="235" y="150" class="figHint">writes →</text><line class="flow" x1="120" y1="155" x2="120" y2="131"></line><line class="flow" x1="340" y1="155" x2="340" y2="131"></line><text x="120" y="167" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">reads</text><text x="340" y="167" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">reads</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Writes always go to one primary; reads spread across replicas that trail it slightly.

frames.title: Provision replicas.
frames.text: Provision replicas. Stand up two read replicas of the orders database.

frames.title: Split traffic at the connection layer.
frames.text: Split traffic at the connection layer. Writes ( INSERT, UPDATE ) go to the primary; reads go to a round-robin pool of replicas.

frames.title: Route carefully.
frames.text: Route carefully. A "view my order confirmation" page right after checkout reads from the primary to avoid showing a not-yet-replicated order as missing.

frames.title: Monitor lag.
frames.text: Monitor lag. Alert if replication lag exceeds a threshold, and temporarily pull a lagging replica out of the read pool.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 460 150" role="img" aria-label="Diagram showing a posts table and comments table joined on every read versus a posts table that carries its own comment_count column updated on write."><text x="110" y="18" class="figLabel" text-anchor="middle">NORMALIZED — READ TIME</text><rect class="box" x="30" y="35" width="90" height="30" rx="5"></rect><text x="75" y="55" class="boxText">posts</text><rect class="box" x="150" y="35" width="90" height="30" rx="5"></rect><text x="195" y="55" class="boxText">comments</text><line class="flowMuted" x1="120" y1="50" x2="150" y2="50"></line><text x="135" y="42" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">join</text><text x="130" y="90" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">counted fresh, every request</text><line class="divider" x1="270" y1="10" x2="270" y2="120"></line><text x="365" y="18" class="figLabel" text-anchor="middle">DENORMALIZED</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="310" y="35" width="110" height="40" rx="5"></rect><text x="365" y="52" class="boxText">posts</text><text x="365" y="68" class="boxText">comment_count: 42</text><text x="365" y="95" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">one row read, no join</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: The count moves from being computed at read time to being maintained at write time.

frames.title: Identify the expensive read.
frames.text: Identify the expensive read. Rendering the feed runs a COUNT(*) join per post to show comment counts.

frames.title: Add a denormalized column.
frames.text: Add a denormalized column. ALTER TABLE posts ADD comment_count INT DEFAULT 0;

frames.title: Keep it in sync.
frames.text: Keep it in sync. Increment it inside the same transaction that inserts a comment; decrement on delete.

frames.title: Backfill once.
frames.text: Backfill once. Run a one-time job to populate existing rows from the real count.

frames.title: Read the fast path.
frames.text: Read the fast path. The feed now reads comment_count directly — no join.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 480 150" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of an expensive five-table join being run once into a materialized view, which dashboard reads then hit directly instead of re-running the join."><rect class="box" x="20" y="20" width="150" height="40" rx="6"></rect><text x="95" y="45" class="boxText">5-table join, 50M rows</text><line class="flow" x1="170" y1="40" x2="230" y2="40"></line><text x="200" y="32" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">refresh</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="240" y="20" width="150" height="40" rx="6"></rect><text x="315" y="45" class="boxText">materialized view</text><line class="flow" x1="315" y1="60" x2="315" y2="100"></line><line class="flow" x1="315" y1="100" x2="220" y2="100"></line><line class="flow" x1="315" y1="100" x2="410" y2="100"></line><rect class="box" x="160" y="105" width="120" height="24" rx="4"></rect><text x="220" y="121" class="boxText">dashboard read</text><rect class="box" x="350" y="105" width="120" height="24" rx="4"></rect><text x="410" y="121" class="boxText">dashboard read</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: The expensive query runs once per refresh; every read after that is cheap.

frames.title: Define the view.
frames.text: Define the view. CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW daily_revenue AS SELECT ... — the same expensive query, saved as a view.

frames.title: Populate it.
frames.text: Populate it. The first REFRESH runs the full 12-second query once.

frames.title: Point the dashboard at the view.
frames.text: Point the dashboard at the view. Reads now hit the precomputed table: ~20ms.

frames.title: Schedule refreshes.
frames.text: Schedule refreshes. A nightly job re-runs REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW, accepting up-to-24-hours staleness for a dashboard that's reviewed each morning.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 480 170" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of many application requests sharing a small fixed pool of database connections instead of each opening its own connection."><rect class="box" x="20" y="10" width="40" height="20" rx="4"></rect><rect class="box" x="75" y="10" width="40" height="20" rx="4"></rect><rect class="box" x="130" y="10" width="40" height="20" rx="4"></rect><rect class="box" x="185" y="10" width="40" height="20" rx="4"></rect><rect class="box" x="20" y="40" width="40" height="20" rx="4"></rect><rect class="box" x="75" y="40" width="40" height="20" rx="4"></rect><rect class="box" x="130" y="40" width="40" height="20" rx="4"></rect><rect class="box" x="185" y="40" width="40" height="20" rx="4"></rect><text x="130" y="80" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">8 concurrent requests</text><line class="flow" x1="130" y1="90" x2="130" y2="110"></line><rect class="boxAccent" x="60" y="115" width="140" height="40" rx="6"></rect><text x="130" y="132" class="boxText">connection pool</text><text x="130" y="148" class="boxText">4 live connections</text><line class="flow" x1="200" y1="135" x2="260" y2="135"></line><rect class="box" x="270" y="115" width="100" height="40" rx="6"></rect><text x="320" y="139" class="boxText">database</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Requests queue briefly for a connection rather than each opening its own.

frames.title: Size the pool.
frames.text: Size the pool. 20 app instances, each configured with a pool of 10 → up to 200 concurrent DB connections, checked against the database's max_connections limit.

frames.title: Checkout.
frames.text: Checkout. A request comes in; the app borrows a free connection from its local pool (fast — no handshake).

frames.title: Use and release.
frames.text: Use and release. The query runs, the connection is returned to the pool for the next request.

frames.title: Handle exhaustion.
frames.text: Handle exhaustion. If all 10 local connections are busy, the next request waits briefly (with a timeout) rather than opening an 11th connection.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 320 300" role="img" aria-label="Hash ring diagram with four database shards placed around a circle, and a new fifth shard inserted, with only the small arc of keys between the neighboring shards moving to it."><circle cx="160" cy="150" r="110" fill="none" stroke="var(--muted)" opacity="0.4"></circle><circle class="ringNode" cx="160" cy="40" r="16"></circle><text x="160" y="45" class="ringKey" text-anchor="middle">S1</text><circle class="ringNode" cx="270" cy="150" r="16"></circle><text x="270" y="155" class="ringKey" text-anchor="middle">S2</text><circle class="ringNode" cx="160" cy="260" r="16"></circle><text x="160" y="265" class="ringKey" text-anchor="middle">S3</text><circle class="ringNode" cx="50" cy="150" r="16"></circle><text x="50" y="155" class="ringKey" text-anchor="middle">S4</text><circle class="boxAccent" cx="105" cy="212" r="17"></circle><text x="105" y="217" class="ringKey" text-anchor="middle">S5</text><path d="M160,260 A110,110 0 0,1 105,212" fill="none" stroke="var(--course-accent)" stroke-width="5"></path><text x="95" y="284" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">only this arc of keys</text><text x="95" y="296" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">moves to the new shard S5</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Adding shard S5 remaps only the keys between S3 and S5 — S1, S2, and S4 are untouched.

frames.title: Pick the shard key.
frames.text: Pick the shard key. user_id — most queries already filter by user, so most reads stay on one shard.

frames.title: Choose a strategy.
frames.text: Choose a strategy. Consistent hashing across 8 shards, to make future rebalancing cheap.

frames.title: Add a routing layer.
frames.text: Add a routing layer. The application (or a proxy) hashes user_id and sends the query to the right shard.

frames.title: Handle cross-shard queries as a special case.
frames.text: Handle cross-shard queries as a special case. "Total events this week across all users" now has to fan out to all 8 shards and merge results — slower, and used sparingly.

frames.title: Plan for growth.
frames.text: Plan for growth. When shard 8 approaches capacity, add shard 9; consistent hashing means only ~1/9 of keys move.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 480 160" role="img" aria-label="Diagram comparing one database server internally divided into partitions against three separate, independent database servers each holding one shard."><text x="110" y="18" class="figLabel" text-anchor="middle">PARTITIONING</text><rect class="box" x="30" y="30" width="160" height="90" rx="8"></rect><line class="divider" x1="30" y1="60" x2="190" y2="60"></line><line class="divider" x1="30" y1="90" x2="190" y2="90"></line><text x="110" y="48" class="boxText">Jan partition</text><text x="110" y="78" class="boxText">Feb partition</text><text x="110" y="108" class="boxText">Mar partition</text><text x="110" y="135" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">one server, one disk</text><line class="divider" x1="230" y1="10" x2="230" y2="150"></line><text x="360" y="18" class="figLabel" text-anchor="middle">SHARDING</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="250" y="30" width="60" height="90" rx="6"></rect><text x="280" y="78" class="boxText">shard 1</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="320" y="30" width="60" height="90" rx="6"></rect><text x="350" y="78" class="boxText">shard 2</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="390" y="30" width="60" height="90" rx="6"></rect><text x="420" y="78" class="boxText">shard 3</text><text x="360" y="135" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">three independent servers</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Partitioning reorganizes data on one machine; sharding spreads it across many.

frames.title: Start with partitioning.
frames.text: Start with partitioning. A 500GB events table on one Postgres server is partitioned by month, so old partitions can be archived and queries on recent data skip scanning old months.

frames.title: Hit a real ceiling.
frames.text: Hit a real ceiling. Even partitioned, one server's disk and write throughput max out at 3TB and 20K writes/sec.

frames.title: Move to sharding.
frames.text: Move to sharding. The same table is split across 6 independent Postgres servers by user_id — now there are 6x the disks and 6x the write capacity.

frames.title: Combine them.
frames.text: Combine them. Each of those 6 shards can still be internally partitioned by month — the two techniques stack.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 420 140" role="img" aria-label="Diagram showing an 800 gigabyte table shrinking to 140 gigabytes after compression, with a small CPU cost added and a larger disk I/O saving."><text x="90" y="18" class="figLabel" text-anchor="middle">BEFORE</text><rect class="box" x="20" y="30" width="140" height="60" rx="6"></rect><text x="90" y="65" class="boxText">800 GB on disk</text><line class="flow" x1="170" y1="60" x2="230" y2="60"></line><text x="200" y="50" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">compress</text><text x="330" y="18" class="figLabel" text-anchor="middle">AFTER</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="260" y="45" width="70" height="30" rx="6"></rect><text x="295" y="64" class="boxText">140 GB</text><text x="295" y="100" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">+ small CPU cost to read</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Less to move off disk, a little more to decode on the way out.

frames.title: Identify a cold, large table.
frames.text: Identify a cold, large table. A 2-year archive of application logs, rarely queried but taking up 800GB.

frames.title: Pick a compression scheme.
frames.text: Pick a compression scheme. Enable columnar compression for the archive table (many databases and storage engines support this per-table).

frames.title: Measure the trade.
frames.text: Measure the trade. Storage drops from 800GB to 140GB; a full scan takes slightly more CPU per row but far less disk I/O overall, so it's still faster end to end.

frames.title: Leave hot tables alone.
frames.text: Leave hot tables alone. The live "current_sessions" table stays uncompressed — it's small and read/written constantly, where compression's CPU cost isn't worth it.

system-design-fundamentals/storage-syste.title: Block vs File vs Object Storage

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 460 150" role="img" aria-label="Diagram contrasting block storage as numbered blocks, file storage as a folder hierarchy, and object storage as a flat namespace of keyed objects with metadata."><text x="70" y="18" class="figLabel" text-anchor="middle">BLOCK</text><rect class="box" x="20" y="30" width="28" height="28" rx="3"></rect><rect class="box" x="54" y="30" width="28" height="28" rx="3"></rect><rect class="box" x="88" y="30" width="28" height="28" rx="3"></rect><text x="230" y="18" class="figLabel" text-anchor="middle">FILE</text><rect class="box" x="190" y="30" width="80" height="28" rx="4"></rect><text x="230" y="48" class="boxText">/docs/a.txt</text><text x="380" y="18" class="figLabel" text-anchor="middle">OBJECT</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="330" y="30" width="110" height="28" rx="4"></rect><text x="385" y="48" class="boxText">key: img-42.jpg</text><text x="230" y="90" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">same data, three different access models</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Block is raw and low-level; file adds hierarchy; object trades hierarchy for flat, metadata-rich scale.

frames.title: Database needs fast, low-level disk access.
frames.text: Database needs fast, low-level disk access. It attaches a block volume (like AWS EBS) and manages its own file layout on top.

frames.title: Team needs a shared drive.
frames.text: Team needs a shared drive. A file share (like NFS) gives them familiar folders and file paths, mounted like a local disk.

frames.title: App needs to store millions of user-uploaded images.
frames.text: App needs to store millions of user-uploaded images. Object storage (like S3) handles that natively — each image is one object, retrieved by key, with no folder depth limits or file-count ceilings to worry about.

frames.title: Match the model to the access pattern
frames.text: Match the model to the access pattern — trying to run a high-transaction database directly on object storage, for instance, fights its design instead of using it.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 420 130" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of a client uploading an object which is then replicated across three separate disks for durability."><rect class="boxAccent" x="20" y="45" width="90" height="30" rx="5"></rect><text x="65" y="65" class="boxText">PUT object</text><line class="flow" x1="110" y1="60" x2="160" y2="60"></line><rect class="box" x="170" y="15" width="80" height="26" rx="4"></rect><text x="210" y="33" class="boxText">disk / AZ 1</text><rect class="box" x="170" y="47" width="80" height="26" rx="4"></rect><text x="210" y="65" class="boxText">disk / AZ 2</text><rect class="box" x="170" y="79" width="80" height="26" rx="4"></rect><text x="210" y="97" class="boxText">disk / AZ 3</text><text x="330" y="60" class="figHint">replicated for durability</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: One upload, replicated behind the scenes — the client never manages the copies directly.

frames.title: Upload.
frames.text: Upload. Each photo is PUT to a bucket with a unique key, like users/42/photo-9183.jpg.

frames.title: Replicate automatically.
frames.text: Replicate automatically. The storage service copies the object across multiple disks and availability zones behind the scenes.

frames.title: Serve directly.
frames.text: Serve directly. Photos are fetched straight from object storage (often via a CDN in front of it) — the application server doesn't sit in the data path.

frames.title: Update means replace.
frames.text: Update means replace. Editing a photo's caption in its metadata doesn't rewrite the image bytes; changing the image itself uploads a new object.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 460 160" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of a metadata service directing a client to the machines holding replicated chunks of a large file split across storage nodes."><rect class="boxAccent" x="190" y="10" width="90" height="30" rx="5"></rect><text x="235" y="30" class="boxText">metadata svc</text><line class="flow" x1="235" y1="40" x2="235" y2="65"></line><text x="255" y="55" class="figHint">"chunk 1 → A,B,C"</text><rect class="box" x="60" y="75" width="90" height="30" rx="5"></rect><text x="105" y="95" class="boxText">node A: chunk1</text><rect class="box" x="185" y="75" width="90" height="30" rx="5"></rect><text x="230" y="95" class="boxText">node B: chunk1</text><rect class="box" x="310" y="75" width="90" height="30" rx="5"></rect><text x="355" y="95" class="boxText">node C: chunk1</text><text x="230" y="135" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">same chunk lives on 3 machines — any one can fail without data loss</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: A metadata service tracks chunk locations; storage nodes hold the replicated data itself.

frames.title: Split a large file.
frames.text: Split a large file. A 3GB log file is split into 128MB chunks — roughly 24 chunks.

frames.title: Replicate each chunk.
frames.text: Replicate each chunk. Each chunk is written to 3 different machines, so losing any one machine loses no data.

frames.title: Record the map.
frames.text: Record the map. The metadata service stores "file X = chunks 1-24, chunk 1 is on machines A, B, C."

frames.title: Read in parallel.
frames.text: Read in parallel. A client reading the whole file fetches different chunks from different machines simultaneously — much faster than one machine serving it all.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 460 150" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of six data fragments and two parity fragments distributed across eight machines, with two machines lost but the original data still reconstructible from the remaining six fragments."><g><rect class="box" x="20" y="30" width="45" height="40" rx="5"></rect><text x="42" y="53" class="boxText">D1</text></g><g><rect class="boxWarn" x="75" y="30" width="45" height="40" rx="5"></rect><text x="97" y="53" class="boxText">D2</text></g><g><rect class="box" x="130" y="30" width="45" height="40" rx="5"></rect><text x="152" y="53" class="boxText">D3</text></g><g><rect class="box" x="185" y="30" width="45" height="40" rx="5"></rect><text x="207" y="53" class="boxText">D4</text></g><g><rect class="box" x="240" y="30" width="45" height="40" rx="5"></rect><text x="262" y="53" class="boxText">D5</text></g><g><rect class="boxWarn" x="295" y="30" width="45" height="40" rx="5"></rect><text x="317" y="53" class="boxText">D6</text></g><g><rect class="boxAccent" x="350" y="30" width="45" height="40" rx="5"></rect><text x="372" y="53" class="boxText">P1</text></g><g><rect class="boxAccent" x="405" y="30" width="45" height="40" rx="5"></rect><text x="427" y="53" class="boxText">P2</text></g><text x="230" y="95" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">2 fragments lost (marked) — still reconstructible from the remaining 6 of 8</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: 6 data + 2 parity fragments: any 6 of the 8 reconstruct the original — for far less overhead than 3x replication.

frames.title: Split the data.
frames.text: Split the data. A file is split into, say, 6 data fragments.

frames.title: Compute parity.
frames.text: Compute parity. 2 parity fragments are calculated from the 6 data fragments using an erasure code.

frames.title: Distribute all 8.
frames.text: Distribute all 8. Each of the 8 fragments (6 data + 2 parity) is stored on a different machine.

frames.title: Lose 2 machines.
frames.text: Lose 2 machines. Any 6 of the remaining fragments are enough to fully reconstruct the original file — including if the 2 lost fragments were both data.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 440 140" role="img" aria-label="Diagram contrasting vertical scaling as one machine growing larger versus horizontal scaling as more machines added side by side."><text x="100" y="18" class="figLabel" text-anchor="middle">VERTICAL</text><rect class="box" x="70" y="70" width="30" height="30" rx="4"></rect><rect class="boxAccent" x="55" y="40" width="60" height="60" rx="5"></rect><text x="180" y="60" class="figHint">bigger machine</text><line class="divider" x1="220" y1="10" x2="220" y2="130"></line><text x="330" y="18" class="figLabel" text-anchor="middle">HORIZONTAL</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="260" y="75" width="30" height="30" rx="4"></rect><rect class="boxAccent" x="300" y="75" width="30" height="30" rx="4"></rect><rect class="boxAccent" x="340" y="75" width="30" height="30" rx="4"></rect><rect class="boxAccent" x="380" y="75" width="30" height="30" rx="4"></rect><text x="330" y="120" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">more machines, same size</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Vertical grows one machine; horizontal grows the count of machines.

frames.title: Start small, scale vertically.
frames.text: Start small, scale vertically. A new product's database runs on a modest server; traffic grows, so the team upgrades to a bigger instance — quick, no code changes.

frames.title: Hit the ceiling.
frames.text: Hit the ceiling. Eventually no bigger single machine is available, or the cost curve gets steep.

frames.title: Switch strategy.
frames.text: Switch strategy. The team adds read replicas and, later, shards the database across multiple machines — horizontal scaling.

frames.title: Pay the complexity cost.
frames.text: Pay the complexity cost. Now the application must route queries to the right shard and handle a replica occasionally lagging behind.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 440 150" role="img" aria-label="Diagram contrasting concurrency as one core rapidly switching between three tasks versus parallelism as three cores executing three tasks at the same instant."><text x="100" y="18" class="figLabel" text-anchor="middle">CONCURRENCY (1 core)</text><rect class="box" x="30" y="35" width="30" height="24" rx="3"></rect><rect class="boxAccent" x="65" y="35" width="30" height="24" rx="3"></rect><rect class="box" x="100" y="35" width="30" height="24" rx="3"></rect><text x="80" y="75" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">interleaved on one core over time</text><line class="divider" x1="200" y1="10" x2="200" y2="140"></line><text x="330" y="18" class="figLabel" text-anchor="middle">PARALLELISM (3 cores)</text><rect class="box" x="240" y="35" width="50" height="24" rx="3"></rect><rect class="boxAccent" x="240" y="65" width="50" height="24" rx="3"></rect><rect class="box" x="240" y="95" width="50" height="24" rx="3"></rect><text x="360" y="47" class="figHint">core 1</text><text x="360" y="77" class="figHint">core 2</text><text x="360" y="107" class="figHint">core 3</text><text x="330" y="130" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">all running at the same instant</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Concurrency is about structure over time; parallelism is about simultaneous execution.

frames.title: Concurrent, not parallel.
frames.text: Concurrent, not parallel. A single-threaded web server uses an event loop to juggle thousands of open connections, switching between them while waiting on I/O — one core, many things "in flight."

frames.title: Parallel, not concurrent.
frames.text: Parallel, not concurrent. A single large matrix multiplication is split across 8 CPU cores, each computing a different chunk simultaneously, with no coordination needed between chunks until the end.

frames.title: Both together.
frames.text: Both together. A web server handles thousands of concurrent requests, and each request's image-resizing work is parallelized across multiple cores.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 440 130" role="img" aria-label="Diagram contrasting a push model where the source sends data to the consumer versus a pull model where the consumer requests data from the source."><text x="100" y="18" class="figLabel" text-anchor="middle">PUSH</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="30" y="35" width="80" height="30" rx="5"></rect><text x="70" y="55" class="boxText">source</text><line class="flow" x1="110" y1="50" x2="160" y2="50"></line><rect class="box" x="170" y="35" width="80" height="30" rx="5"></rect><text x="210" y="55" class="boxText">consumer</text><line class="divider" x1="220" y1="10" x2="220" y2="120"></line><text x="340" y="18" class="figLabel" text-anchor="middle">PULL</text><rect class="box" x="270" y="80" width="80" height="30" rx="5"></rect><text x="310" y="100" class="boxText">source</text><line class="flow" x1="410" y1="95" x2="360" y2="95"></line><rect class="boxAccent" x="360" y="80" width="80" height="30" rx="5"></rect><text x="400" y="100" class="boxText">consumer</text><text x="400" y="65" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">consumer asks, on its own schedule</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Push sends immediately; pull lets the consumer set the pace.

frames.title: Metrics → pull.
frames.text: Metrics → pull. A central collector (like Prometheus) scrapes each server every 15 seconds — the collector controls its own load and a slow server just returns slightly stale data.

frames.title: Alerts → push.
frames.text: Alerts → push. The moment an event fires, it's pushed to the user's device — waiting for the user to "check" would defeat the purpose of an alert.

frames.title: Mixing both
frames.text: Mixing both is common: a message queue lets producers push messages in, while consumers pull messages off at whatever rate they can handle.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 440 150" role="img" aria-label="Diagram contrasting a stateful server holding session data in memory requiring sticky routing versus stateless servers reading shared state from an external store so any server can handle any request."><text x="100" y="18" class="figLabel" text-anchor="middle">STATEFUL</text><rect class="box" x="40" y="35" width="120" height="40" rx="5"></rect><text x="100" y="58" class="boxText">server (has cart in RAM)</text><text x="100" y="95" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">this user must always return here</text><line class="divider" x1="210" y1="10" x2="210" y2="140"></line><text x="330" y="18" class="figLabel" text-anchor="middle">STATELESS</text><rect class="box" x="240" y="35" width="60" height="30" rx="5"></rect><text x="270" y="55" class="boxText">server A</text><rect class="box" x="320" y="35" width="60" height="30" rx="5"></rect><text x="350" y="55" class="boxText">server B</text><line class="flow" x1="270" y1="65" x2="310" y2="100"></line><line class="flow" x1="350" y1="65" x2="310" y2="100"></line><rect class="boxAccent" x="270" y="100" width="80" height="30" rx="5"></rect><text x="310" y="120" class="boxText">shared store</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Moving state to a shared store frees any server to handle any request.

frames.title: Start stateful.
frames.text: Start stateful. A server stores each user's shopping cart in its own memory — simple, but that user must always hit the same server.

frames.title: Add a second server for scale.
frames.text: Add a second server for scale. Now a user's requests need "sticky" routing to the server holding their cart — the load balancer can't freely distribute load.

frames.title: Move state out.
frames.text: Move state out. The cart moves to a shared Redis store; any server can read or write it.

frames.title: Now stateless.
frames.text: Now stateless. Requests can be load-balanced freely across any number of servers — none of them hold client-specific memory anymore.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 440 150" role="img" aria-label="Diagram contrasting long polling as repeated request-response cycles versus WebSockets as one persistent bidirectional connection."><text x="100" y="18" class="figLabel" text-anchor="middle">LONG POLLING</text><g><line class="flow" x1="40" y1="35" x2="160" y2="35"></line><line class="flowMuted" x1="160" y1="43" x2="40" y2="43"></line></g><g><line class="flow" x1="40" y1="57" x2="160" y2="57"></line><line class="flowMuted" x1="160" y1="65" x2="40" y2="65"></line></g><g><line class="flow" x1="40" y1="79" x2="160" y2="79"></line><line class="flowMuted" x1="160" y1="87" x2="40" y2="87"></line></g><text x="100" y="115" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">request, hold, respond, repeat</text><line class="divider" x1="210" y1="10" x2="210" y2="140"></line><text x="330" y="18" class="figLabel" text-anchor="middle">WEBSOCKETS</text><rect class="box" x="250" y="55" width="60" height="26" rx="4"></rect><text x="280" y="72" class="boxText">client</text><line class="flow" x1="310" y1="60" x2="360" y2="60"></line><line class="flow" x1="360" y1="76" x2="310" y2="76"></line><rect class="boxAccent" x="360" y="55" width="60" height="26" rx="4"></rect><text x="390" y="72" class="boxText">server</text><text x="335" y="105" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">one open connection, both directions</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Long polling repeats request/response cycles; WebSockets keep one connection open both ways.

frames.title: Start with long polling.
frames.text: Start with long polling. A chat app's client sends a request; the server holds it until a new message arrives, responds, and the client re-requests immediately.

frames.title: Traffic grows.
frames.text: Traffic grows. Each idle-but-open long-poll request still consumes a server thread/connection, and message-heavy chats mean constant round trips.

frames.title: Switch to WebSockets.
frames.text: Switch to WebSockets. The client upgrades the HTTP connection once; the server can now push each new message down the same open socket instantly.

frames.title: Trade-off shows up in infra.
frames.text: Trade-off shows up in infra. The load balancer now needs to keep each client pinned to the same server instance for the life of that connection.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 440 150" role="img" aria-label="Diagram contrasting strong consistency where all replicas confirm a write before it succeeds versus eventual consistency where a write succeeds immediately and propagates to replicas afterward."><text x="110" y="18" class="figLabel" text-anchor="middle">STRONG</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="30" y="35" width="80" height="26" rx="4"></rect><text x="70" y="52" class="boxText">write</text><line class="flow" x1="110" y1="48" x2="150" y2="48"></line><rect class="box" x="160" y="30" width="60" height="20" rx="3"></rect><rect class="box" x="160" y="55" width="60" height="20" rx="3"></rect><text x="190" y="85" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">must ack before "success"</text><line class="divider" x1="240" y1="10" x2="240" y2="140"></line><text x="340" y="18" class="figLabel" text-anchor="middle">EVENTUAL</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="260" y="35" width="80" height="26" rx="4"></rect><text x="300" y="52" class="boxText">write → OK</text><line class="flowMuted" x1="340" y1="48" x2="400" y2="48"></line><rect class="box" x="330" y="75" width="60" height="20" rx="3"></rect><rect class="box" x="330" y="100" width="60" height="20" rx="3"></rect><text x="360" y="125" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">replicas catch up after</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Strong consistency waits for agreement; eventual consistency confirms immediately and syncs later.

frames.title: Bank balance → strong consistency.
frames.text: Bank balance → strong consistency. Reading a balance must reflect every confirmed transaction — showing a stale, too-high balance could let someone overdraw.

frames.title: Like count → eventual consistency.
frames.text: Like count → eventual consistency. If a like count is off by a few for a few seconds while it propagates across replicas, nobody's harmed, and the system stays fast and available even under partition.

frames.title: Pick per use case,
frames.text: Pick per use case, not globally — many real systems use strong consistency for money and state-changing operations, eventual consistency for high-volume, low-stakes counters and feeds.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 120" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of multiple clients sending requests to a server which holds the data and business logic and returns responses."><rect class="box" x="20" y="15" width="70" height="26" rx="4"></rect><text x="55" y="32" class="boxText">client A</text><rect class="box" x="20" y="50" width="70" height="26" rx="4"></rect><text x="55" y="67" class="boxText">client B</text><rect class="box" x="20" y="85" width="70" height="26" rx="4"></rect><text x="55" y="102" class="boxText">client C</text><line class="flow" x1="90" y1="28" x2="230" y2="55"></line><line class="flow" x1="90" y1="63" x2="230" y2="60"></line><line class="flow" x1="90" y1="98" x2="230" y2="65"></line><rect class="boxAccent" x="240" y="35" width="120" height="50" rx="6"></rect><text x="300" y="65" class="boxText">server + data</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Many clients, one shared server holding the logic and data.

frames.title: Client sends a request.
frames.text: Client sends a request. A mobile app requests GET /api/orders/42.

frames.title: Server authenticates and authorizes.
frames.text: Server authenticates and authorizes. It checks the request is from a logged-in user allowed to view that order.

frames.title: Server fetches and returns data.
frames.text: Server fetches and returns data. It queries the database and responds with JSON — the client never touches the database directly.

frames.title: Client renders.
frames.text: Client renders. The app is responsible only for displaying the data nicely — no business rules duplicated on the client.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 130" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of a single deployable application containing catalog, cart, orders, and users modules all within one process talking to one database."><rect class="boxAccent" x="40" y="15" width="320" height="70" rx="8"></rect><g><rect class="box" x="55" y="30" width="65" height="40" rx="4"></rect><text x="87" y="53" class="boxText">catalog</text></g><g><rect class="box" x="133" y="30" width="65" height="40" rx="4"></rect><text x="165" y="53" class="boxText">cart</text></g><g><rect class="box" x="211" y="30" width="65" height="40" rx="4"></rect><text x="243" y="53" class="boxText">orders</text></g><g><rect class="box" x="289" y="30" width="65" height="40" rx="4"></rect><text x="321" y="53" class="boxText">users</text></g><text x="200" y="100" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">one process, one deploy</text><line class="flow" x1="200" y1="85" x2="200" y2="110"></line><rect class="box" x="150" y="110" width="100" height="20" rx="3"></rect><text x="200" y="124" class="boxText">one database</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: All modules live and deploy together as a single unit.

frames.title: Start as a monolith.
frames.text: Start as a monolith. A new e-commerce app has one codebase with modules for catalog, cart, orders, and users, all calling each other as regular function calls.

frames.title: Deploy as one unit.
frames.text: Deploy as one unit. One build artifact, one deployment pipeline — simple to reason about.

frames.title: Scale it.
frames.text: Scale it. Under load, you run more copies of the whole application behind a load balancer — even if only the catalog module actually needs more capacity.

frames.title: Feel the seams later.
frames.text: Feel the seams later. As the team and codebase grow, module boundaries blur and deploys get riskier — this is usually the point teams consider splitting out services.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 440 140" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of four independent microservices, each with its own database, communicating with each other over the network via APIs."><g><rect class="boxAccent" x="20" y="20" width="85" height="34" rx="5"></rect><text x="62" y="42" class="boxText">catalog</text><rect class="box" x="35" y="70" width="55" height="24" rx="4"></rect><text x="62" y="86" class="boxText">DB</text><line class="flowMuted" x1="62" y1="54" x2="62" y2="70"></line></g><g><rect class="boxAccent" x="125" y="20" width="85" height="34" rx="5"></rect><text x="167" y="42" class="boxText">cart</text><rect class="box" x="140" y="70" width="55" height="24" rx="4"></rect><text x="167" y="86" class="boxText">DB</text><line class="flowMuted" x1="167" y1="54" x2="167" y2="70"></line></g><g><rect class="boxAccent" x="230" y="20" width="85" height="34" rx="5"></rect><text x="272" y="42" class="boxText">orders</text><rect class="box" x="245" y="70" width="55" height="24" rx="4"></rect><text x="272" y="86" class="boxText">DB</text><line class="flowMuted" x1="272" y1="54" x2="272" y2="70"></line></g><g><rect class="boxAccent" x="335" y="20" width="85" height="34" rx="5"></rect><text x="377" y="42" class="boxText">users</text><rect class="box" x="350" y="70" width="55" height="24" rx="4"></rect><text x="377" y="86" class="boxText">DB</text><line class="flowMuted" x1="377" y1="54" x2="377" y2="70"></line></g><line class="flow" x1="105" y1="37" x2="125" y2="37"></line><line class="flow" x1="210" y1="37" x2="230" y2="37"></line><line class="flow" x1="315" y1="37" x2="335" y2="37"></line><text x="220" y="120" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">each service: own deploy, own database, talks over the network</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Independent services, independent data, network calls where a monolith had function calls.

frames.title: Split by business capability.
frames.text: Split by business capability. The e-commerce monolith becomes separate catalog, cart, orders, and users services.

frames.title: Each owns its data.
frames.text: Each owns its data. The orders service has its own database; the catalog service can't query it directly — it calls the orders API.

frames.title: Deploy independently.
frames.text: Deploy independently. The catalog team ships three times a day; the orders team ships weekly — neither blocks the other.

frames.title: Handle the network.
frames.text: Handle the network. A call from cart to catalog can now time out or fail outright — code has to handle that, where an in-process function call never could.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 420 130" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of an upload event triggering a serverless function, with the platform automatically running as many concurrent instances as needed and scaling back to zero when idle."><rect class="box" x="20" y="45" width="90" height="30" rx="5"></rect><text x="65" y="65" class="boxText">upload event</text><line class="flow" x1="110" y1="60" x2="160" y2="60"></line><rect class="boxAccent" x="170" y="20" width="70" height="26" rx="4"></rect><text x="205" y="38" class="boxText">fn #1</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="170" y="52" width="70" height="26" rx="4"></rect><text x="205" y="70" class="boxText">fn #2</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="170" y="84" width="70" height="26" rx="4"></rect><text x="205" y="102" class="boxText">fn #3</text><text x="330" y="60" class="figHint">scales to match load, then to zero</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Instances spin up per event and scale back to zero — no idle server to pay for.

frames.title: User uploads an image.
frames.text: User uploads an image. It lands in object storage, which triggers an event.

frames.title: A function runs.
frames.text: A function runs. The platform spins up a resize function instance just for this event — no server was sitting idle waiting for it.

frames.title: It scales with bursts.
frames.text: It scales with bursts. If 500 images upload at once, the platform runs up to 500 concurrent instances automatically.

frames.title: It scales back to zero.
frames.text: It scales back to zero. When uploads stop, no instances run and nothing is billed for idle time.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 440 150" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of a producer publishing an event to a broker, with three independent consumers subscribing and reacting to the same event without the producer knowing about them."><rect class="boxAccent" x="20" y="55" width="90" height="30" rx="5"></rect><text x="65" y="75" class="boxText">orders svc</text><line class="flow" x1="110" y1="70" x2="160" y2="70"></line><rect class="box" x="170" y="55" width="80" height="30" rx="5"></rect><text x="210" y="75" class="boxText">broker</text><line class="flow" x1="250" y1="60" x2="330" y2="25"></line><line class="flow" x1="250" y1="70" x2="330" y2="70"></line><line class="flow" x1="250" y1="80" x2="330" y2="115"></line><rect class="box" x="335" y="12" width="90" height="26" rx="4"></rect><text x="380" y="30" class="boxText">inventory</text><rect class="box" x="335" y="57" width="90" height="26" rx="4"></rect><text x="380" y="75" class="boxText">email</text><rect class="box" x="335" y="102" width="90" height="26" rx="4"></rect><text x="380" y="120" class="boxText">analytics</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: One event, many independent consumers — none known to the producer in advance.

frames.title: An order is placed.
frames.text: An order is placed. The orders service publishes an OrderPlaced event to a broker — it doesn't call anyone directly.

frames.title: Multiple services react.
frames.text: Multiple services react. The inventory service decrements stock; the email service sends a confirmation; the analytics service logs it — all independently, all subscribed to the same event.

frames.title: Add a new consumer later.
frames.text: Add a new consumer later. A fraud-detection service starts subscribing to the same event stream, with zero changes needed in the orders service.

frames.title: A consumer goes down.
frames.text: A consumer goes down. Events queue up in the broker and the consumer catches up once it's back — no events lost.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 160" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of five peers connected directly to each other in a mesh, exchanging data without a central server."><circle class="boxAccent" cx="200" cy="20" r="22"></circle><circle class="box" cx="80" cy="70" r="22"></circle><circle class="box" cx="320" cy="70" r="22"></circle><circle class="box" cx="120" cy="140" r="22"></circle><circle class="box" cx="280" cy="140" r="22"></circle><line class="flowMuted" x1="200" y1="20" x2="80" y2="70"></line><line class="flowMuted" x1="200" y1="20" x2="320" y2="70"></line><line class="flowMuted" x1="80" y1="70" x2="120" y2="140"></line><line class="flowMuted" x1="320" y1="70" x2="280" y2="140"></line><line class="flowMuted" x1="120" y1="140" x2="280" y2="140"></line><line class="flowMuted" x1="80" y1="70" x2="320" y2="70"></line><text x="200" y="26" class="boxText" text-anchor="middle">peer</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Every peer connects to others directly — no central server in the data path.

frames.title: A file is split into pieces.
frames.text: A file is split into pieces. A large file is broken into chunks, each identified by a hash.

frames.title: Peers discover each other.
frames.text: Peers discover each other. A tracker or DHT tells a new peer which other peers already have pieces of the file.

frames.title: Peers exchange pieces directly.
frames.text: Peers exchange pieces directly. Downloaders fetch different pieces from different peers simultaneously, and also upload pieces they already have to others.

frames.title: Capacity grows with demand.
frames.text: Capacity grows with demand. More downloaders means more upload sources too — unlike a central server that gets more overloaded as more clients connect.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 420 150" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of core business logic in the center connected through ports to swappable adapters for the database, web framework, and message queue on the outside."><rect class="boxAccent" x="150" y="55" width="120" height="45" rx="8"></rect><text x="210" y="82" class="boxText">core logic</text><line class="flow" x1="150" y1="70" x2="90" y2="35"></line><line class="flow" x1="150" y1="90" x2="90" y2="115"></line><line class="flow" x1="270" y1="77" x2="340" y2="77"></line><rect class="box" x="20" y="15" width="90" height="26" rx="4"></rect><text x="65" y="33" class="boxText">DB adapter</text><rect class="box" x="20" y="105" width="90" height="26" rx="4"></rect><text x="65" y="123" class="boxText">queue adapter</text><rect class="box" x="340" y="64" width="90" height="26" rx="4"></rect><text x="385" y="82" class="boxText">HTTP adapter</text><text x="120" y="75" class="figHint">ports</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Core logic depends only on ports; adapters plug in the real, swappable implementations.

frames.title: Define a port.
frames.text: Define a port. The order-placing logic depends on an OrderRepository interface with save(order) — nothing about SQL or Postgres.

frames.title: Write an adapter.
frames.text: Write an adapter. A PostgresOrderRepository class implements that interface using real SQL queries.

frames.title: Wire it up.
frames.text: Wire it up. At startup, the concrete Postgres adapter is injected wherever the port is needed.

frames.title: Swap it later.
frames.text: Swap it later. Migrating to DynamoDB means writing a DynamoOrderRepository adapter — the order-placing business logic is untouched.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 440 140" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of a command going through a write model, publishing an event that updates a separate denormalized read model used to serve fast queries."><rect class="boxAccent" x="20" y="20" width="100" height="30" rx="5"></rect><text x="70" y="40" class="boxText">command</text><line class="flow" x1="120" y1="35" x2="170" y2="35"></line><rect class="box" x="180" y="20" width="100" height="30" rx="5"></rect><text x="230" y="40" class="boxText">write model</text><line class="flow" x1="230" y1="50" x2="230" y2="80"></line><rect class="box" x="180" y="85" width="100" height="26" rx="4"></rect><text x="230" y="102" class="boxText">event</text><line class="flow" x1="280" y1="98" x2="330" y2="98"></line><rect class="boxAccent" x="340" y="85" width="90" height="26" rx="4"></rect><text x="385" y="102" class="boxText">read model</text><line class="flow" x1="385" y1="85" x2="385" y2="50"></line><text x="385" y="35" class="boxText">query</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Writes go through a validated write model; reads are served from a separately-updated, query-optimized model.

frames.title: Command side.
frames.text: Command side. Placing an order goes through a normalized write model with strict validation — checking inventory, pricing rules, etc.

frames.title: Write triggers an update.
frames.text: Write triggers an update. The change is published as an event after the command succeeds.

frames.title: Read model updates.
frames.text: Read model updates. A separate process consumes that event and updates a denormalized "orders dashboard" table, pre-joined and pre-aggregated for fast reads.

frames.title: Dashboard reads the read model.
frames.text: Dashboard reads the read model. Loading the dashboard is a single fast query against data shaped exactly for that screen — no joins at read time.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 440 130" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of an append-only sequence of events being folded in order to produce the current derived state."><g><rect class="box" x="20" y="20" width="115" height="30" rx="5"></rect><text x="77" y="40" class="boxText">Opened</text><line class="flow" x1="135" y1="35" x2="150" y2="35"></line></g><g><rect class="box" x="150" y="20" width="115" height="30" rx="5"></rect><text x="207" y="40" class="boxText">Deposit 100</text><line class="flow" x1="265" y1="35" x2="280" y2="35"></line></g><g><rect class="box" x="280" y="20" width="115" height="30" rx="5"></rect><text x="337" y="40" class="boxText">Withdraw 30</text></g><line class="flow" x1="220" y1="50" x2="220" y2="80"></line><text x="240" y="70" class="figHint">fold in order</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="160" y="85" width="120" height="30" rx="5"></rect><text x="220" y="105" class="boxText">balance = 70</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Events are the source of truth; current state is always a derived, replayable value.

frames.title: Store events, not state.
frames.text: Store events, not state. An account's history is AccountOpened, Deposited(100), Withdrew(30) — each appended, never modified.

frames.title: Derive current balance.
frames.text: Derive current balance. Replaying the events: 0 → 100 → 70. That's the current state, computed, not stored directly.

frames.title: Need history?
frames.text: Need history? "What was the balance last Tuesday" replays events only up to that point — trivial, because the full history already exists.

frames.title: Speed it up with a snapshot.
frames.text: Speed it up with a snapshot. For a long history, periodically cache the computed state so you don't replay from the very beginning every time.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 440 140" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of service instances registering themselves with a registry, and a caller looking up a healthy instance location from that registry before calling it directly."><rect class="boxAccent" x="180" y="15" width="100" height="30" rx="5"></rect><text x="230" y="35" class="boxText">registry</text><line class="flowMuted" x1="200" y1="45" x2="100" y2="80"></line><line class="flowMuted" x1="260" y1="45" x2="360" y2="80"></line><rect class="box" x="60" y="85" width="90" height="28" rx="4"></rect><text x="105" y="103" class="boxText">instance A</text><rect class="box" x="310" y="85" width="90" height="28" rx="4"></rect><text x="355" y="103" class="boxText">instance B</text><text x="140" y="65" class="figHint">register/heartbeat</text><line class="flow" x1="230" y1="45" x2="230" y2="100"></line><rect class="box" x="185" y="87" width="90" height="26" rx="4"></rect><text x="230" y="104" class="boxText">caller</text><text x="230" y="128" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">"where is orders-service?" → lookup, then call directly</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Instances register and heartbeat; callers look up current, healthy locations instead of hardcoding them.

frames.title: Instance starts.
frames.text: Instance starts. A new orders-service instance boots and registers itself with the registry, including its IP and port.

frames.title: Heartbeats keep it listed.
frames.text: Heartbeats keep it listed. It periodically pings the registry to prove it's still healthy.

frames.title: Caller looks it up.
frames.text: Caller looks it up. The cart service asks the registry "where is orders-service" instead of using a hardcoded address.

frames.title: Instance crashes.
frames.text: Instance crashes. Heartbeats stop, the registry removes it after a timeout, and new lookups no longer return the dead instance.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 440 140" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of a client calling an API gateway which handles authentication and routing before forwarding requests to the appropriate backend microservice."><rect class="box" x="20" y="50" width="80" height="30" rx="5"></rect><text x="60" y="70" class="boxText">client</text><line class="flow" x1="100" y1="65" x2="150" y2="65"></line><rect class="boxAccent" x="160" y="40" width="110" height="50" rx="6"></rect><text x="215" y="60" class="boxText">API gateway</text><text x="215" y="76" class="figHint">auth, rate limit</text><line class="flow" x1="270" y1="55" x2="330" y2="25"></line><line class="flow" x1="270" y1="65" x2="330" y2="65"></line><line class="flow" x1="270" y1="75" x2="330" y2="105"></line><rect class="box" x="335" y="12" width="90" height="26" rx="4"></rect><text x="380" y="30" class="boxText">orders svc</text><rect class="box" x="335" y="52" width="90" height="26" rx="4"></rect><text x="380" y="70" class="boxText">users svc</text><rect class="box" x="335" y="92" width="90" height="26" rx="4"></rect><text x="380" y="110" class="boxText">catalog svc</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: One entry point handles cross-cutting concerns once, then routes to the right internal service.

frames.title: Client calls the gateway.
frames.text: Client calls the gateway. A single request goes to api.example.com/orders/42 — the client doesn't know or care which internal service handles it.

frames.title: Gateway authenticates.
frames.text: Gateway authenticates. It validates the request's auth token once, centrally.

frames.title: Gateway routes.
frames.text: Gateway routes. Based on the path, it forwards the request to the internal orders service.

frames.title: Gateway can also aggregate.
frames.text: Gateway can also aggregate. A "dashboard" endpoint might have the gateway call three internal services and combine their responses into one payload for the client.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 440 140" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of a mobile client and a web client each calling their own dedicated BFF, both of which call the same shared backend services underneath."><rect class="box" x="20" y="15" width="80" height="26" rx="4"></rect><text x="60" y="33" class="boxText">mobile app</text><rect class="box" x="20" y="90" width="80" height="26" rx="4"></rect><text x="60" y="108" class="boxText">web app</text><line class="flow" x1="100" y1="28" x2="150" y2="28"></line><line class="flow" x1="100" y1="103" x2="150" y2="103"></line><rect class="boxAccent" x="155" y="15" width="80" height="26" rx="4"></rect><text x="195" y="33" class="boxText">mobile BFF</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="155" y="90" width="80" height="26" rx="4"></rect><text x="195" y="108" class="boxText">web BFF</text><line class="flow" x1="235" y1="30" x2="320" y2="65"></line><line class="flow" x1="235" y1="100" x2="320" y2="70"></line><rect class="box" x="325" y="55" width="90" height="26" rx="4"></rect><text x="370" y="73" class="boxText">shared services</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Each client type gets a BFF shaped for its needs; backend services stay shared and generic.

frames.title: Mobile BFF.
frames.text: Mobile BFF. Calls the catalog and pricing services, returns just the name, price, and thumbnail — minimal payload for a slow connection.

frames.title: Web BFF.
frames.text: Web BFF. Calls catalog, pricing, reviews, and recommendations services, combining them into one larger response tailored for the richer web UI.

frames.title: Each BFF evolves independently.
frames.text: Each BFF evolves independently. Adding a new mobile screen doesn't require touching the web BFF, and vice versa.

frames.title: Backend services stay generic.
frames.text: Backend services stay generic. Catalog and pricing services don't need to know anything about mobile vs. web — that shaping logic lives in the BFFs.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 130" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of an application container and a sidecar proxy container running together in the same pod, with the application routing outbound traffic through the sidecar."><rect class="box" x="30" y="30" width="340" height="70" rx="8"></rect><text x="200" y="20" class="figLabel" text-anchor="middle">SAME POD</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="50" y="45" width="140" height="40" rx="5"></rect><text x="120" y="69" class="boxText">application</text><line class="flow" x1="190" y1="65" x2="230" y2="65"></line><rect class="box" x="240" y="45" width="110" height="40" rx="5"></rect><text x="295" y="69" class="boxText">sidecar proxy</text><text x="205" y="115" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">app talks to "localhost" — sidecar handles the network</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: The sidecar shares the app's lifecycle and handles cross-cutting concerns outside its code.

frames.title: Deploy app + sidecar together.
frames.text: Deploy app + sidecar together. A Java service and an Envoy proxy sidecar are deployed in the same Kubernetes pod, sharing the pod's network namespace.

frames.title: App calls "localhost."
frames.text: App calls "localhost." The Java service sends its outbound calls to the sidecar on localhost, not directly to other services.

frames.title: Sidecar handles the hard part.
frames.text: Sidecar handles the hard part. It manages retries, TLS, load balancing across instances of the destination service, and reports metrics — all outside the application's code.

frames.title: Upgrade the sidecar independently.
frames.text: Upgrade the sidecar independently. Rolling out a new retry policy means updating the sidecar, with zero changes to the Java application itself.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 460 150" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of a circuit breaker's three states: closed allowing calls through, open blocking calls immediately after too many failures, and half-open testing recovery with a trickle of requests."><rect class="box" x="20" y="55" width="110" height="34" rx="6"></rect><text x="75" y="76" class="boxText">CLOSED</text><line class="flow" x1="130" y1="72" x2="180" y2="72"></line><text x="155" y="60" class="figHint">too many fails</text><rect class="boxWarn" x="190" y="55" width="110" height="34" rx="6"></rect><text x="245" y="76" class="boxText">OPEN</text><line class="flow" x1="300" y1="72" x2="350" y2="72"></line><text x="325" y="60" class="figHint">cooldown</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="360" y="55" width="90" height="34" rx="6"></rect><text x="405" y="76" class="boxText">HALF-OPEN</text><line class="flowMuted" x1="405" y1="89" x2="245" y2="120"></line><line class="flowMuted" x1="245" y1="120" x2="75" y2="89"></line><text x="245" y="135" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">success → closed again · failure → open again</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: The breaker moves between three states so a failing dependency gets room to recover.

frames.title: Dependency starts failing.
frames.text: Dependency starts failing. The payments service starts timing out under load.

frames.title: Breaker trips open.
frames.text: Breaker trips open. After, say, 10 consecutive failures, the calling service's breaker opens — further calls fail instantly with a fallback, no network call attempted.

frames.title: Payments service recovers.
frames.text: Payments service recovers. With the flood of retries stopped, it has room to catch up.

frames.title: Breaker tests recovery.
frames.text: Breaker tests recovery. After a cooldown, it goes half-open, letting a few real requests through — if they succeed, it closes fully again.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 420 140" role="img" aria-label="Diagram contrasting one shared thread pool where a slow dependency exhausts all threads versus separate bulkheaded pools where a slow dependency only exhausts its own pool."><text x="100" y="18" class="figLabel" text-anchor="middle">SHARED POOL</text><rect class="boxWarn" x="30" y="30" width="140" height="50" rx="6"></rect><text x="100" y="60" class="boxText">all threads blocked</text><line class="divider" x1="200" y1="10" x2="200" y2="130"></line><text x="330" y="18" class="figLabel" text-anchor="middle">BULKHEADED</text><rect class="boxWarn" x="230" y="30" width="80" height="45" rx="5"></rect><text x="270" y="55" class="boxText">shipping pool</text><rect class="box" x="320" y="30" width="80" height="45" rx="5"></rect><text x="360" y="55" class="boxText">DB pool (fine)</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Separate pools contain a slow dependency's impact to only the requests that need it.

frames.title: Without bulkheads.
frames.text: Without bulkheads. The shipping API slows down; all threads in the shared pool end up blocked waiting on it — even requests that only needed the fast database now can't get a thread.

frames.title: Add a bulkhead.
frames.text: Add a bulkhead. Give the shipping API calls their own pool of, say, 10 threads, separate from the database calls' pool.

frames.title: Shipping API slows down again.
frames.text: Shipping API slows down again. Only its 10 dedicated threads fill up and back up — database calls keep flowing through their own separate pool, completely unaffected.

frames.title: Blast radius is contained
frames.text: Blast radius is contained — one slow dependency degrades only the functionality that depends on it.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 440 140" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of a router sending some traffic to a new search service and the remaining traffic to the legacy monolith, illustrating a gradual migration in progress."><rect class="box" x="20" y="50" width="70" height="30" rx="5"></rect><text x="55" y="70" class="boxText">traffic</text><line class="flow" x1="90" y1="65" x2="140" y2="65"></line><rect class="boxAccent" x="150" y="50" width="90" height="30" rx="5"></rect><text x="195" y="70" class="boxText">router</text><line class="flow" x1="240" y1="58" x2="300" y2="25"></line><line class="flow" x1="240" y1="72" x2="300" y2="100"></line><rect class="box" x="305" y="10" width="110" height="30" rx="5"></rect><text x="360" y="30" class="boxText">new: search</text><rect class="box" x="305" y="85" width="110" height="30" rx="5"></rect><text x="360" y="105" class="boxText">legacy monolith</text><text x="360" y="60" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">split, and shifts over time</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: The router splits traffic between new and legacy — the split shifts fully to new over time.

frames.title: Start with 100% legacy.
frames.text: Start with 100% legacy. All traffic hits the old monolith.

frames.title: Build one piece new.
frames.text: Build one piece new. The team rebuilds just the "search" functionality as a new service.

frames.title: Route incrementally.
frames.text: Route incrementally. The router sends search requests to the new service; everything else still goes to the legacy monolith.

frames.title: Repeat for each piece.
frames.text: Repeat for each piece. Checkout, then user accounts, then catalog — each migrated and routed over, one at a time.

frames.title: Retire the legacy system
frames.text: Retire the legacy system once nothing routes to it anymore — with each step having been small and independently reversible.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 440 150" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of a control plane configuring sidecar proxies attached to three services, with all inter-service traffic flowing through the sidecars rather than directly between services."><rect class="boxAccent" x="170" y="10" width="100" height="28" rx="5"></rect><text x="220" y="29" class="boxText">control plane</text><line class="flowMuted" x1="190" y1="38" x2="90" y2="65"></line><line class="flowMuted" x1="220" y1="38" x2="220" y2="65"></line><line class="flowMuted" x1="250" y1="38" x2="350" y2="65"></line><g><rect class="box" x="45" y="65" width="90" height="26" rx="4"></rect><text x="90" y="82" class="boxText">sidecar</text><rect class="box" x="55" y="100" width="70" height="24" rx="4"></rect><text x="90" y="116" class="boxText">svc A</text></g><g><rect class="box" x="175" y="65" width="90" height="26" rx="4"></rect><text x="220" y="82" class="boxText">sidecar</text><rect class="box" x="185" y="100" width="70" height="24" rx="4"></rect><text x="220" y="116" class="boxText">svc B</text></g><g><rect class="box" x="305" y="65" width="90" height="26" rx="4"></rect><text x="350" y="82" class="boxText">sidecar</text><rect class="box" x="315" y="100" width="70" height="24" rx="4"></rect><text x="350" y="116" class="boxText">svc C</text></g><line class="flow" x1="135" y1="78" x2="175" y2="78"></line><line class="flow" x1="265" y1="78" x2="305" y2="78"></line></svg>
diagrams.caption: A central control plane configures every sidecar, which then enforces routing and security uniformly.

frames.title: Every service gets a sidecar.
frames.text: Every service gets a sidecar. Deploying with the mesh automatically attaches a proxy sidecar to each service instance.

frames.title: Control plane pushes policy.
frames.text: Control plane pushes policy. An operator sets "all traffic between services must use mTLS" once, centrally.

frames.title: Sidecars enforce it.
frames.text: Sidecars enforce it. Every sidecar picks up that policy and encrypts traffic automatically — no service's code changed.

frames.title: Observe uniformly.
frames.text: Observe uniformly. The mesh reports consistent request metrics and traces for every service-to-service call, even across services written in different languages.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 420 130" role="img" aria-label="Diagram contrasting a single-process function call that is fast and reliable against a network call between two machines that can succeed, fail, or hang ambiguously."><text x="100" y="18" class="figLabel" text-anchor="middle">ONE PROCESS</text><rect class="box" x="40" y="35" width="60" height="30" rx="5"></rect><text x="70" y="55" class="boxText">A</text><line class="flow" x1="100" y1="50" x2="140" y2="50"></line><rect class="box" x="150" y="35" width="60" height="30" rx="5"></rect><text x="180" y="55" class="boxText">B</text><text x="125" y="90" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">always fast, always reliable</text><line class="divider" x1="240" y1="10" x2="240" y2="120"></line><text x="335" y="18" class="figLabel" text-anchor="middle">TWO MACHINES</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="270" y="35" width="60" height="30" rx="5"></rect><text x="300" y="55" class="boxText">A</text><line class="flowMuted" x1="330" y1="50" x2="370" y2="50"></line><rect class="boxAccent" x="380" y="35" width="30" height="30" rx="5"></rect><text x="395" y="55" class="boxText">?</text><text x="340" y="90" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">slow? lost? crashed after receiving?</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: A local call fails cleanly or succeeds; a network call can hang in genuine ambiguity.

frames.title: A single-machine app "just works."
frames.text: A single-machine app "just works." A function call either returns a result or throws immediately — there's no in-between.

frames.title: Split it across two machines.
frames.text: Split it across two machines. Now that same call goes over a network — it can succeed, fail, or hang with no way for the caller to tell "it failed" from "it's just slow."

frames.title: A message is lost.
frames.text: A message is lost. Did the recipient never receive it, or receive it and crash before replying? From the sender's side, these look identical.

frames.title: Design around it.
frames.text: Design around it. Real systems use timeouts, retries with idempotency, and replication specifically because these failure modes are unavoidable, not because of sloppy code.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 420 140" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of a six node cluster split by a broken network link into two groups of three nodes, each internally connected but unable to reach the other group."><circle class="box" cx="70" cy="30" r="18"></circle><circle class="box" cx="110" cy="60" r="18"></circle><circle class="box" cx="70" cy="90" r="18"></circle><circle class="box" cx="350" cy="30" r="18"></circle><circle class="box" cx="310" cy="60" r="18"></circle><circle class="box" cx="350" cy="90" r="18"></circle><line class="flowMuted" x1="70" y1="30" x2="110" y2="60"></line><line class="flowMuted" x1="110" y1="60" x2="70" y2="90"></line><line class="flowMuted" x1="70" y1="30" x2="70" y2="90"></line><line class="flowMuted" x1="350" y1="30" x2="310" y2="60"></line><line class="flowMuted" x1="310" y1="60" x2="350" y2="90"></line><line class="flowMuted" x1="350" y1="30" x2="350" y2="90"></line><line x1="150" y1="60" x2="270" y2="60" style="stroke:var(--course-accent);stroke-width:2;stroke-dasharray:4 4"></line><text x="210" y="45" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">✕ link down</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Two internally-healthy groups, unable to reach each other — the defining shape of a partition.

frames.title: Normal operation.
frames.text: Normal operation. A 6-node cluster split across two data centers replicates writes between all nodes.

frames.title: The link between data centers fails.
frames.text: The link between data centers fails. Now there are two groups of 3 nodes each, unable to reach each other, though each group is internally healthy.

frames.title: Choose CP.
frames.text: Choose CP. The system could refuse writes on the minority side (or even both sides) until the partition heals, keeping data consistent at the cost of availability.

frames.title: Or choose AP.
frames.text: Or choose AP. Both sides could keep accepting writes independently, staying available, and reconcile the diverging data once the partition heals.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 420 140" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of a five node cluster split by a partition, where the isolated single node cannot reach a majority quorum and steps down, while the remaining four nodes can and safely elect a new leader."><circle class="boxWarn" cx="70" cy="60" r="24"></circle><text x="70" y="65" class="boxText">N1</text><text x="70" y="105" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">alone, no quorum → steps down</text><line x1="140" y1="60" x2="200" y2="60" style="stroke:var(--course-accent);stroke-width:2;stroke-dasharray:4 4"></line><circle class="boxAccent" cx="280" cy="30" r="20"></circle><circle class="box" cx="340" cy="30" r="20"></circle><circle class="box" cx="280" cy="90" r="20"></circle><circle class="box" cx="340" cy="90" r="20"></circle><text x="310" y="120" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">4 of 5 = majority → safely elects new leader</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: A quorum requirement ensures at most one side of any partition can proceed.

frames.title: 5-node cluster, one leader.
frames.text: 5-node cluster, one leader. Node 1 is the leader; nodes 2-5 are followers.

frames.title: Partition isolates the leader.
frames.text: Partition isolates the leader. Node 1 ends up alone on one side; nodes 2-5 are together on the other.

frames.title: Without quorum:
frames.text: Without quorum: both sides might elect/keep a leader — node 1 keeps accepting writes on its side, nodes 2-5 elect node 3 and accept writes on theirs. Data diverges.

frames.title: With quorum (3 of 5 needed):
frames.text: With quorum (3 of 5 needed): node 1 alone can't reach a majority and steps down or refuses writes; nodes 2-5 can reach a majority and safely elect a new leader. Only one leader ever accepts writes.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 440 130" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of a node sending periodic heartbeat pulses to a peer, then the heartbeats stopping after a crash, with the peer detecting the failure once the timeout window elapses."><line x1="20" y1="60" x2="420" y2="60" stroke="var(--muted)"></line><circle class="box" cx="60" cy="60" r="6"></circle><circle class="box" cx="130" cy="60" r="6"></circle><circle class="box" cx="200" cy="60" r="6"></circle><text x="130" y="40" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">heartbeats every 2s</text><rect class="boxWarn" x="280" y="45" width="120" height="30" rx="5"></rect><text x="340" y="65" class="boxText">silence → timeout</text><text x="340" y="95" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">after 6s with no pulse, peer marks it failed</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Regular pulses signal life; their absence past a timeout signals failure.

frames.title: Set the interval.
frames.text: Set the interval. Each node sends a heartbeat every 2 seconds.

frames.title: Set the timeout.
frames.text: Set the timeout. A node is considered failed if no heartbeat arrives within 6 seconds — a few missed intervals, to absorb normal jitter.

frames.title: A node crashes.
frames.text: A node crashes. Its heartbeats stop.

frames.title: Peers notice within the timeout window.
frames.text: Peers notice within the timeout window. After 6 seconds of silence, peers mark it as failed and react — removing it from routing, starting a leader election, or alerting an operator.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 440 140" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of a client retrying a timed-out request with the same idempotency key, so the server can safely detect and ignore the duplicate instead of applying the payment twice."><rect class="box" x="20" y="20" width="100" height="28" rx="4"></rect><text x="70" y="38" class="boxText">request #1</text><line class="flowMuted" x1="120" y1="34" x2="170" y2="34"></line><text x="145" y="24" class="figHint">✕ lost</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="20" y="60" width="140" height="28" rx="4"></rect><text x="90" y="78" class="boxText">retry, same key</text><line class="flow" x1="160" y1="74" x2="220" y2="74"></line><rect class="box" x="230" y="60" width="180" height="28" rx="4"></rect><text x="320" y="78" class="boxText">server: "seen this key" → same result</text><text x="220" y="115" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">idempotency turns "retry after ambiguous failure" into a safe no-op</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: An idempotency key lets a safe retry stand in for an operation that may have already happened.

frames.title: Client sends a request with an idempotency key.
frames.text: Client sends a request with an idempotency key. A unique ID accompanies the payment request.

frames.title: Request times out.
frames.text: Request times out. The client doesn't know if the payment succeeded.

frames.title: Client retries with the same idempotency key.
frames.text: Client retries with the same idempotency key. The server checks: "have I seen this key before?" If the original request actually succeeded, the server returns that same result instead of charging twice.

frames.title: Combine with backoff.
frames.text: Combine with backoff. The retry waits a bit (and longer on each subsequent failure) so retries from many clients don't all hit the server at once and make things worse.
