diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 440 130" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of two machines with clocks offset from each other, showing how comparing their raw timestamps can misjudge which event actually happened first in real time."><line x1="20" y1="35" x2="420" y2="35" stroke="var(--muted)"></line><text x="20" y="25" class="figHint">machine A clock</text><circle class="boxAccent" cx="260" cy="35" r="6"></circle><text x="260" y="55" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">writes at 10:00:00.070</text><line x1="20" y1="85" x2="420" y2="85" stroke="var(--muted)"></line><text x="20" y="75" class="figHint">machine B clock</text><circle class="box" cx="210" cy="85" r="6"></circle><text x="210" y="105" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">writes at 10:00:00.000</text><text x="220" y="122" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">real order needs more than raw timestamps to trust</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Clock drift between machines can make raw timestamp comparison unreliable for true event order.

frames.title: Two machines, slightly different clocks.
frames.text: Two machines, slightly different clocks. Machine A's clock is 50ms ahead of machine B's.

frames.title: B writes first, in real time.
frames.text: B writes first, in real time. B updates a record at its local time 10:00:00.000.

frames.title: A writes second, in real time,
frames.text: A writes second, in real time, just 20ms later, at its local time 10:00:00.070 (50ms ahead + 20ms elapsed).

frames.title: Compare timestamps naively:
frames.text: Compare timestamps naively: both look like A came after B, which happens to be correct here — but flip the drift direction or the timing slightly and a "last-write-wins" system using raw timestamps can easily pick the wrong write as newest.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 420 140" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of two nodes exchanging a message, with the receiving node updating its logical clock to be greater than the sender's, preserving the causal happened-before relationship regardless of physical clock time."><text x="90" y="20" class="figLabel" text-anchor="middle">NODE A</text><line x1="90" y1="35" x2="90" y2="120" stroke="var(--muted)"></line><circle class="box" cx="90" cy="55" r="5"></circle><text x="115" y="59" class="figHint">t=1</text><circle class="boxAccent" cx="90" cy="90" r="5"></circle><text x="115" y="94" class="figHint">t=2, sends msg</text><text x="330" y="20" class="figLabel" text-anchor="middle">NODE B</text><line x1="330" y1="35" x2="330" y2="120" stroke="var(--muted)"></line><circle class="box" cx="330" cy="55" r="5"></circle><text x="300" y="59" class="figHint" text-anchor="end">t=1</text><line class="flow" x1="95" y1="90" x2="325" y2="90"></line><circle class="boxAccent" cx="330" cy="90" r="5"></circle><text x="300" y="94" class="figHint" text-anchor="end">receives → t=max(1,2)+1=3</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: The receiver's logical clock jumps ahead of the sender's, preserving causal order.

frames.title: Local event.
frames.text: Local event. A node increments its own logical counter for every local event.

frames.title: Send a message.
frames.text: Send a message. The current counter value is attached to any outgoing message.

frames.title: Receive a message.
frames.text: Receive a message. The receiving node updates its own counter to be at least one more than the received value — guaranteeing the "receive" event is ordered after the "send" event it depended on.

frames.title: Order is now derivable.
frames.text: Order is now derivable. Even though the two nodes' physical clocks may disagree entirely, the logical counters correctly reflect that the send caused the receive.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 420 130" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of a Lamport timestamp counter incrementing on a local event and jumping to max of local and received plus one when a message arrives, keeping causally related events correctly ordered."><rect class="box" x="20" y="20" width="90" height="28" rx="4"></rect><text x="65" y="38" class="boxText">local: 0→1</text><line class="flow" x1="110" y1="34" x2="170" y2="34"></line><rect class="boxAccent" x="180" y="20" width="90" height="28" rx="4"></rect><text x="225" y="38" class="boxText">send: ts=1</text><line class="flow" x1="270" y1="34" x2="330" y2="34"></line><rect class="box" x="340" y="20" width="70" height="28" rx="4"></rect><text x="375" y="38" class="boxText">recv</text><text x="375" y="70" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">B: max(0,1)+1 = 2</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: A single incrementing counter, bumped past any received value, keeps causal order intact.

frames.title: Node A: local event.
frames.text: Node A: local event. Counter goes from 0 to 1.

frames.title: Node A sends a message
frames.text: Node A sends a message tagged with timestamp 1.

frames.title: Node B receives it.
frames.text: Node B receives it. Node B's own counter was at 0; it becomes max(0, 1) + 1 = 2.

frames.title: Compare timestamps.
frames.text: Compare timestamps. A's send (1) is less than B's receive (2) — correctly reflecting that the send happened-before the receive.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 420 130" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of two nodes each independently writing without seeing the other's write, producing vector clocks that neither dominates the other, proving the writes are concurrent rather than causally ordered."><rect class="boxAccent" x="30" y="30" width="130" height="34" rx="5"></rect><text x="95" y="52" class="boxText">A: [1, 0]</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="260" y="30" width="130" height="34" rx="5"></rect><text x="325" y="52" class="boxText">B: [0, 1]</text><text x="210" y="50" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">neither dominates</text><text x="210" y="95" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">→ provably concurrent, not causally ordered</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Neither vector is fully ≤ the other — proof the two writes were genuinely concurrent.

frames.title: Node A writes.
frames.text: Node A writes. Its vector becomes [A:1, B:0].

frames.title: Node B writes independently,
frames.text: Node B writes independently, having never seen A's write. Its vector becomes [A:0, B:1].

frames.title: Compare the vectors.
frames.text: Compare the vectors. Neither [1,0] nor [0,1] dominates the other — the database now knows for certain these are concurrent, conflicting writes, not one superseding the other.

frames.title: Resolve the conflict explicitly
frames.text: Resolve the conflict explicitly — merge, prompt the application, or use a deterministic tiebreaker — because the vector clock proved a simple "keep the newer one" rule doesn't apply here.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 420 140" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of five nodes where any two possible majority groups of three must share at least one common node, which is what prevents two conflicting decisions from both being finalized."><circle class="boxAccent" cx="80" cy="30" r="20"></circle><circle class="boxAccent" cx="150" cy="20" r="20"></circle><circle class="boxAccent" cx="220" cy="30" r="20"></circle><circle class="box" cx="160" cy="90" r="20"></circle><circle class="box" cx="100" cy="100" r="20"></circle><text x="150" y="10" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">majority A (nodes 1,2,3)</text><circle class="box" cx="360" cy="60" r="20" style="opacity:0.001"></circle><text x="150" y="130" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">any other majority must overlap with this one</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Any two majorities among 5 nodes must share at least one node — the basis of safe consensus.

frames.title: Five database replicas must agree
frames.text: Five database replicas must agree on which one is the primary, accepting writes.

frames.title: Propose a value.
frames.text: Propose a value. One node proposes itself as leader.

frames.title: Gather a majority.
frames.text: Gather a majority. It needs agreement from at least 3 of 5 nodes — a quorum — before the decision is final.

frames.title: Decision is safe.
frames.text: Decision is safe. Because any two majorities out of 5 must overlap by at least one node, it's impossible for two different nodes to both gather a majority for conflicting proposals at the same time.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 440 140" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of the two-phase Paxos protocol: a prepare phase gathering promises from a majority of acceptors, followed by an accept phase where that majority accepts the proposed value."><text x="110" y="18" class="figLabel" text-anchor="middle">PHASE 1: PREPARE</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="30" y="30" width="90" height="28" rx="4"></rect><text x="75" y="48" class="boxText">proposer</text><line class="flow" x1="120" y1="44" x2="170" y2="30"></line><line class="flow" x1="120" y1="44" x2="170" y2="58"></line><rect class="box" x="180" y="15" width="70" height="24" rx="4"></rect><text x="215" y="31" class="boxText">acceptor</text><rect class="box" x="180" y="50" width="70" height="24" rx="4"></rect><text x="215" y="66" class="boxText">acceptor</text><text x="330" y="18" class="figLabel" text-anchor="middle">PHASE 2: ACCEPT</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="280" y="90" width="90" height="28" rx="4"></rect><text x="325" y="108" class="boxText">proposer</text><line class="flow" x1="370" y1="104" x2="410" y2="90" style="opacity:0"></line><text x="325" y="135" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">same majority accepts the value → chosen</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Prepare gathers promises from a majority; accept commits the value with that same majority.

frames.title: Proposer picks a proposal number
frames.text: Proposer picks a proposal number higher than any it's seen, and sends "prepare" to all acceptors.

frames.title: Acceptors promise.
frames.text: Acceptors promise. A majority reply "promise — we won't accept anything numbered lower than yours."

frames.title: Proposer sends "accept"
frames.text: Proposer sends "accept" with its value to that same majority.

frames.title: Majority accepts.
frames.text: Majority accepts. Once a majority has accepted the value, it's permanently chosen — any future proposal, even from a different proposer, is required to discover and preserve that already-chosen value.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 440 140" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of a Raft leader appending a log entry and replicating it to followers, committing the entry once a majority of followers acknowledge it."><rect class="boxAccent" x="170" y="15" width="100" height="30" rx="5"></rect><text x="220" y="35" class="boxText">leader</text><line class="flow" x1="190" y1="45" x2="100" y2="75"></line><line class="flow" x1="220" y1="45" x2="220" y2="75"></line><line class="flow" x1="250" y1="45" x2="340" y2="75"></line><rect class="box" x="55" y="80" width="90" height="26" rx="4"></rect><text x="100" y="97" class="boxText">follower ✓</text><rect class="box" x="175" y="80" width="90" height="26" rx="4"></rect><text x="220" y="97" class="boxText">follower ✓</text><rect class="box" x="295" y="80" width="90" height="26" rx="4"></rect><text x="340" y="97" class="boxText">follower</text><text x="220" y="125" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">2 of 3 followers ack'd → majority → entry committed</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: The leader replicates each entry and commits it once a majority of followers acknowledge.

frames.title: Election.
frames.text: Election. The current leader stops sending heartbeats (it crashed); a follower's randomized election timeout fires first, and it becomes a candidate, requesting votes.

frames.title: Majority votes.
frames.text: Majority votes. It wins a majority and becomes the new leader.

frames.title: Log replication.
frames.text: Log replication. A client write is appended to the new leader's log and sent to all followers.

frames.title: Commit on majority.
frames.text: Commit on majority. Once a majority of followers acknowledge the entry, it's committed and safely applied — the client gets a success response.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 420 130" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of three candidate nodes racing to claim a leadership key in a coordination service, with only one succeeding and becoming leader while renewing a lease to stay leader."><rect class="box" x="30" y="15" width="80" height="26" rx="4"></rect><rect class="box" x="30" y="55" width="80" height="26" rx="4"></rect><rect class="box" x="30" y="95" width="80" height="26" rx="4"></rect><text x="70" y="35" class="boxText" text-anchor="middle">node A</text><text x="70" y="75" class="boxText" text-anchor="middle">node B</text><text x="70" y="115" class="boxText" text-anchor="middle">node C</text><line class="flow" x1="110" y1="30" x2="180" y2="65"></line><line class="flow" x1="110" y1="70" x2="180" y2="65"></line><line class="flow" x1="110" y1="110" x2="180" y2="65"></line><rect class="boxAccent" x="190" y="50" width="110" height="30" rx="5"></rect><text x="245" y="70" class="boxText">lock key (1 wins)</text><text x="245" y="100" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">winner = leader, renews lease</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Only one candidate can claim the leadership key; it stays leader by renewing its lease.

frames.title: Nodes race to claim leadership.
frames.text: Nodes race to claim leadership. Each candidate tries to create the same uniquely-named lock/key in a coordination service (like etcd) — only one can succeed.

frames.title: Winner becomes leader.
frames.text: Winner becomes leader. The node that created the key is the leader; it attaches a lease that must be periodically renewed.

frames.title: Leader does its job
frames.text: Leader does its job — e.g., assigning work to other nodes — while periodically renewing its lease to prove it's still alive.

frames.title: Leader crashes.
frames.text: Leader crashes. It stops renewing the lease; the lease expires, the key is removed, and the remaining nodes race again to claim it.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 440 140" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of a worker acquiring a lock with a fencing token, pausing past the lock's expiry, and a second worker acquiring the lock with a higher token, so the first worker's stale write is rejected."><rect class="box" x="20" y="20" width="120" height="30" rx="5"></rect><text x="80" y="40" class="boxText">worker 1: token=5</text><rect class="boxWarn" x="20" y="60" width="120" height="24" rx="4"></rect><text x="80" y="76" class="boxText">long pause...</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="180" y="20" width="130" height="30" rx="5"></rect><text x="245" y="40" class="boxText">worker 2: token=6</text><line class="flow" x1="20" y1="100" x2="140" y2="100"></line><text x="80" y="115" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">worker 1 writes with token=5 → rejected (stale)</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: A fencing token lets the storage layer reject a stale write from a worker that lost its lock.

frames.title: Acquire the lock.
frames.text: Acquire the lock. A worker sets a key lock:job-42 in Redis with a 10-second TTL, and receives a fencing token (a monotonically increasing number).

frames.title: Do the work.
frames.text: Do the work. The worker processes job 42.

frames.title: A long pause happens
frames.text: A long pause happens (GC, scheduling delay) that exceeds 10 seconds — the lock expires and a second worker acquires it with a higher fencing token.

frames.title: First worker resumes
frames.text: First worker resumes and tries to write its result, presenting its (now stale) fencing token — the storage layer rejects it because a higher token has already been seen, preventing the two workers from corrupting each other's work.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 440 140" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of gossip spreading information exponentially across rounds, starting from one informed node and roughly doubling the number of informed nodes each round."><circle class="boxAccent" cx="60" cy="70" r="18"></circle><text x="60" y="30" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">round 0: 1 knows</text><line class="flow" x1="78" y1="60" x2="140" y2="35"></line><line class="flow" x1="78" y1="80" x2="140" y2="105"></line><circle class="boxAccent" cx="160" cy="30" r="16"></circle><circle class="boxAccent" cx="160" cy="110" r="16"></circle><text x="160" y="150" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">round 1: 3 know</text><circle class="boxAccent" cx="260" cy="15" r="13"></circle><circle class="boxAccent" cx="260" cy="45" r="13"></circle><circle class="boxAccent" cx="260" cy="95" r="13"></circle><circle class="boxAccent" cx="260" cy="125" r="13"></circle><text x="340" y="70" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">round 2: ~7 know...</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Each round roughly doubles how many nodes know — fast, decentralized convergence.

frames.title: Node A learns node X is unhealthy.
frames.text: Node A learns node X is unhealthy. It marks that in its local state.

frames.title: Round 1.
frames.text: Round 1. A gossips with 2 random peers, B and C, who now also know X is unhealthy.

frames.title: Round 2.
frames.text: Round 2. A, B, and C each gossip with 2 more random peers — the number of informed nodes roughly doubles each round.

frames.title: Convergence.
frames.text: Convergence. Within a handful of rounds, the whole cluster knows about X — with no node ever having to talk to more than a few others per round.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 420 130" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of two replicas independently incrementing their own counters during a partition, then merging by summing both counters once reconnected, with no conflict resolution needed."><rect class="box" x="30" y="20" width="100" height="30" rx="5"></rect><text x="80" y="40" class="boxText">A: count=7</text><rect class="box" x="290" y="20" width="100" height="30" rx="5"></rect><text x="340" y="40" class="boxText">B: count=4</text><line class="flow" x1="130" y1="35" x2="290" y2="35" style="stroke-dasharray:3 3"></line><line class="flow" x1="130" y1="60" x2="190" y2="90"></line><line class="flow" x1="290" y1="60" x2="230" y2="90"></line><rect class="boxAccent" x="150" y="90" width="120" height="30" rx="5"></rect><text x="210" y="110" class="boxText">merged = 11</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Merging is just addition — order and timing don't affect the converged result.

frames.title: Each replica tracks its own count.
frames.text: Each replica tracks its own count. Data center A tracks likes it received; data center B tracks likes it received — independently, with no coordination.

frames.title: Partition happens.
frames.text: Partition happens. A and B can't talk, but both keep accepting likes locally.

frames.title: Partition heals.
frames.text: Partition heals. The replicas exchange their per-replica counts.

frames.title: Merge by summing.
frames.text: Merge by summing. The total is simply the sum of every replica's count — no conflict to resolve, and the merge gives the same total no matter which replica initiates it.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 440 140" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of two users concurrently editing the same document, with one user's operation transformed to account for the position shift caused by the other user's earlier concurrent insert."><rect class="box" x="20" y="20" width="160" height="28" rx="4"></rect><text x="100" y="38" class="boxText">A: insert "cruel " @6</text><rect class="box" x="20" y="60" width="160" height="28" rx="4"></rect><text x="100" y="78" class="boxText">B: insert "!" @11</text><line class="flow" x1="180" y1="74" x2="230" y2="74"></line><rect class="boxAccent" x="240" y="60" width="180" height="28" rx="4"></rect><text x="330" y="78" class="boxText">transformed: insert "!" @17</text><text x="220" y="115" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">B's position shifts to account for A's earlier insert</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: OT adjusts each operation's position so concurrent edits still land correctly together.

frames.title: Starting text:
frames.text: Starting text: "Hello world" — both users see this.

frames.title: User A inserts
frames.text: User A inserts "cruel " at position 6: "Hello cruel world", and sends that operation to the server.

frames.title: User B, concurrently, inserts
frames.text: User B, concurrently, inserts "!" at position 11 (the end), based on the original text — before seeing A's edit.

frames.title: Transform B's operation.
frames.text: Transform B's operation. Since A's insert added 6 characters before position 11, B's operation is transformed to insert at position 17 instead — landing correctly at the new end of the combined text: "Hello cruel world!".

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 420 130" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of an order committing successfully in the inventory database but failing in the payments database, leaving the two databases in an inconsistent state with no single transaction spanning both."><rect class="box" x="20" y="30" width="150" height="34" rx="6"></rect><text x="95" y="52" class="boxText">inventory DB: ✓ committed</text><rect class="boxWarn" x="240" y="30" width="160" height="34" rx="6"></rect><text x="320" y="52" class="boxText">payments DB: ✕ failed</text><text x="210" y="95" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">no single transaction covers both — they can disagree</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Two independent local commits, no atomic guarantee spanning both.

frames.title: Deduct inventory.
frames.text: Deduct inventory. The inventory service commits its local transaction successfully.

frames.title: Charge the card.
frames.text: Charge the card. The payments service call fails or times out.

frames.title: Now what?
frames.text: Now what? Inventory has been deducted but payment never succeeded — the two databases disagree about whether this order actually happened.

frames.title: No single transaction covers both
frames.text: No single transaction covers both — some explicit strategy (2PC, saga with compensation, or the outbox pattern) is required to avoid this inconsistency, it doesn't happen automatically.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 440 140" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of a two-phase commit coordinator asking two participants to prepare, receiving yes votes from both, and then sending a commit instruction to both participants."><rect class="boxAccent" x="180" y="10" width="90" height="28" rx="5"></rect><text x="225" y="29" class="boxText">coordinator</text><line class="flow" x1="200" y1="38" x2="110" y2="65"></line><line class="flow" x1="250" y1="38" x2="340" y2="65"></line><rect class="box" x="60" y="70" width="100" height="26" rx="4"></rect><text x="110" y="87" class="boxText">participant A</text><rect class="box" x="290" y="70" width="100" height="26" rx="4"></rect><text x="340" y="87" class="boxText">participant B</text><text x="110" y="55" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">prepare</text><text x="340" y="55" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">prepare</text><text x="225" y="120" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">both vote yes → coordinator sends commit to both</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Every participant must vote yes before the coordinator commits any of them.

frames.title: Coordinator sends "prepare."
frames.text: Coordinator sends "prepare." Both the inventory and payments services are asked if they can commit.

frames.title: Both vote yes,
frames.text: Both vote yes, locking their relevant rows and writing their intent to a log, but not committing yet.

frames.title: Coordinator decides.
frames.text: Coordinator decides. Since both voted yes, it logs the decision and sends "commit" to both.

frames.title: Both commit
frames.text: Both commit and release their locks — the operation is now atomically complete across both databases.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 440 130" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of the three phases of 3PC: vote, pre-commit, and commit, with the extra pre-commit phase letting participants safely proceed on their own if the coordinator crashes afterward."><rect class="box" x="20" y="45" width="110" height="30" rx="5"></rect><text x="75" y="65" class="boxText">1. vote</text><line class="flow" x1="130" y1="60" x2="170" y2="60"></line><rect class="boxAccent" x="180" y="45" width="110" height="30" rx="5"></rect><text x="235" y="65" class="boxText">2. pre-commit</text><line class="flow" x1="290" y1="60" x2="330" y2="60"></line><rect class="box" x="340" y="45" width="90" height="30" rx="5"></rect><text x="385" y="65" class="boxText">3. commit</text><text x="235" y="100" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">crash after pre-commit → participants can safely proceed alone</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: The added pre-commit step lets participants recover independently, unlike in 2PC.

frames.title: Phase 1: vote.
frames.text: Phase 1: vote. Coordinator asks to prepare; all participants vote yes.

frames.title: Phase 2: pre-commit.
frames.text: Phase 2: pre-commit. Coordinator tells everyone "we're going to commit" — participants acknowledge but still don't apply the change yet.

frames.title: Coordinator crashes
frames.text: Coordinator crashes before sending the final commit.

frames.title: Participants recover independently.
frames.text: Participants recover independently. Since they already received pre-commit, they know every participant voted yes, so they can safely commit on their own without waiting for the coordinator to come back — the key improvement over 2PC.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 460 140" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of three saga steps executing in sequence, the third step failing, and compensating actions running in reverse order to undo the first two steps' effects."><rect class="box" x="20" y="20" width="110" height="28" rx="4"></rect><text x="75" y="38" class="boxText">1. reserve ✓</text><line class="flow" x1="130" y1="34" x2="170" y2="34"></line><rect class="box" x="180" y="20" width="110" height="28" rx="4"></rect><text x="235" y="38" class="boxText">2. charge ✓</text><line class="flow" x1="290" y1="34" x2="330" y2="34"></line><rect class="boxWarn" x="340" y="20" width="100" height="28" rx="4"></rect><text x="390" y="38" class="boxText">3. ship ✕</text><line class="flowMuted" x1="340" y1="55" x2="130" y2="90"></line><rect class="boxAccent" x="180" y="85" width="110" height="28" rx="4"></rect><text x="235" y="103" class="boxText">compensate: refund</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="20" y="85" width="110" height="28" rx="4"></rect><text x="75" y="103" class="boxText">compensate: release</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Each step commits locally; a failure triggers compensations for every completed step, in reverse.

frames.title: Step 1: reserve inventory.
frames.text: Step 1: reserve inventory. Commits immediately, locally.

frames.title: Step 2: charge payment.
frames.text: Step 2: charge payment. Commits immediately, locally.

frames.title: Step 3: schedule shipping — fails.
frames.text: Step 3: schedule shipping — fails. No shipping slot is available.

frames.title: Run compensations in reverse.
frames.text: Run compensations in reverse. Refund the payment (compensates step 2), then release the reserved inventory (compensates step 1) — each a real, explicit operation, not a database rollback.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 440 140" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of an order row and an outbox event row being inserted together in one atomic local transaction, with a separate relay process later reading the outbox and publishing the event to a message broker."><rect class="boxAccent" x="30" y="20" width="180" height="50" rx="6"></rect><text x="120" y="40" class="boxText" text-anchor="middle">one local transaction</text><rect class="box" x="45" y="48" width="70" height="16" rx="3"></rect><text x="80" y="60" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">order row</text><rect class="box" x="125" y="48" width="70" height="16" rx="3"></rect><text x="160" y="60" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">outbox row</text><line class="flow" x1="195" y1="70" x2="280" y2="100"></line><rect class="box" x="290" y="90" width="100" height="26" rx="4"></rect><text x="340" y="107" class="boxText">relay process</text><line class="flow" x1="390" y1="103" x2="420" y2="103" style="opacity:0"></line><text x="340" y="130" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">polls outbox, publishes to broker, marks sent</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: The data change and the event both commit atomically in one local transaction; publishing happens reliably afterward.

frames.title: Single local transaction.
frames.text: Single local transaction. The orders service inserts the new order row and an OrderPlaced row into its outbox table — both commit together, atomically, since they're in the same database.

frames.title: A relay process polls the outbox table
frames.text: A relay process polls the outbox table for unpublished rows.

frames.title: It publishes each row
frames.text: It publishes each row to the message broker.

frames.title: It marks the row published
frames.text: It marks the row published only after the broker confirms — if the relay crashes before marking it, the row is simply republished later; consumers handle occasional duplicates using an idempotency key.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 420 120" role="img" aria-label="Diagram contrasting exact data structures that need memory proportional to data size against probabilistic structures that use small, fixed memory in exchange for a bounded error rate."><text x="100" y="18" class="figLabel" text-anchor="middle">EXACT</text><rect class="box" x="20" y="30" width="160" height="26" rx="4"></rect><text x="100" y="48" class="boxText">memory grows with data</text><line class="divider" x1="210" y1="10" x2="210" y2="100"></line><text x="320" y="18" class="figLabel" text-anchor="middle">PROBABILISTIC</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="240" y="30" width="160" height="26" rx="4"></rect><text x="320" y="48" class="boxText">fixed, tiny memory</text><text x="320" y="75" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">small, bounded error accepted</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Specialized structures trade a controlled amount of accuracy or generality for massive space or speed savings.

frames.title: Exact tracking doesn't scale.
frames.text: Exact tracking doesn't scale. Counting unique visitors to a website exactly means storing every unique ID seen — potentially gigabytes of memory for a billion-visitor site.

frames.title: Trade accuracy for space.
frames.text: Trade accuracy for space. HyperLogLog estimates that same count within about 2% error, using just a few kilobytes — a difference of many orders of magnitude.

frames.title: The pattern repeats.
frames.text: The pattern repeats. Checking "has this URL been seen before" across billions of URLs, or "what are nearby restaurants," all have a specialized structure in this section built for exactly that shape of question at scale.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 420 140" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of a map area recursively divided into smaller rectangular grid cells, with each subdivision adding another character to the geohash string identifying that region."><rect class="box" x="30" y="20" width="360" height="100" rx="4"></rect><line class="divider" x1="210" y1="20" x2="210" y2="120"></line><line class="divider" x1="30" y1="70" x2="390" y2="70"></line><rect class="boxAccent" x="210" y="20" width="90" height="50" rx="3"></rect><text x="255" y="48" class="boxText">9q8y</text><line class="divider" x1="255" y1="20" x2="255" y2="70"></line><text x="345" y="140" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">each extra character narrows the region further</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Each character of a geohash narrows the bounding box — nearby points tend to share a prefix.

frames.title: Encode a location.
frames.text: Encode a location. San Francisco (37.77, -122.42) encodes to a geohash like "9q8yy".

frames.title: Store it as an indexed column.
frames.text: Store it as an indexed column. Every point of interest is stored with its geohash string.

frames.title: Query nearby points.
frames.text: Query nearby points. "Find restaurants near me" becomes a prefix query: WHERE geohash LIKE '9q8yy%' — a fast, indexable operation.

frames.title: Handle the edge case.
frames.text: Handle the edge case. Two points can be geographically close but fall just across a grid boundary, ending up with different prefixes — real implementations check a few neighboring cells too, not just an exact prefix match.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 160" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of a square region recursively subdivided into four quadrants, with a dense quadrant further subdivided into four smaller quadrants while sparse quadrants remain undivided."><rect class="box" x="30" y="20" width="340" height="120" rx="4"></rect><line class="divider" x1="200" y1="20" x2="200" y2="140"></line><line class="divider" x1="30" y1="80" x2="370" y2="80"></line><line class="divider" x1="30" y1="50" x2="200" y2="50"></line><line class="divider" x1="115" y1="20" x2="115" y2="80"></line><circle class="boxAccent" cx="55" cy="30" r="4"></circle><circle class="boxAccent" cx="165" cy="30" r="4"></circle><circle class="boxAccent" cx="55" cy="60" r="4"></circle><circle class="boxAccent" cx="160" cy="65" r="4"></circle><text x="115" y="15" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">dense → subdivided further</text><text x="285" y="85" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">sparse → left as one node</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Subdivision follows point density — fine detail where it's crowded, coarse elsewhere.

frames.title: Start with one region.
frames.text: Start with one region. The whole map is a single quad tree node.

frames.title: Points arrive, region fills up.
frames.text: Points arrive, region fills up. Once a node exceeds its capacity, it splits into four child quadrants: NW, NE, SW, SE.

frames.title: Recurse where it's crowded.
frames.text: Recurse where it's crowded. A busy downtown quadrant keeps splitting further; a quiet suburban quadrant stays as one node.

frames.title: Query a region.
frames.text: Query a region. "Points within this rectangle" walks only the nodes whose bounding box overlaps the query rectangle — sparse regions are skipped as whole subtrees in one check.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 420 150" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of small object bounding boxes grouped into a medium bounding box, which is itself grouped with another region into a large root bounding box, forming a hierarchical spatial index."><rect class="box" x="30" y="80" width="30" height="24" rx="3"></rect><rect class="box" x="70" y="70" width="26" height="20" rx="3"></rect><rect class="box" x="60" y="105" width="24" height="20" rx="3"></rect><rect x="25" y="60" width="80" height="75" rx="4" fill="none" style="stroke:var(--course-accent);stroke-width:2;stroke-dasharray:4 3"></rect><text x="65" y="150" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">grouped into a parent box</text><rect class="box" x="280" y="30" width="26" height="20" rx="3"></rect><rect class="box" x="320" y="45" width="24" height="20" rx="3"></rect><rect x="270" y="20" width="90" height="60" rx="4" fill="none" style="stroke:var(--course-accent);stroke-width:2;stroke-dasharray:4 3"></rect><rect x="10" y="10" width="400" height="130" rx="6" fill="none" style="stroke:var(--muted);stroke-width:1.5;stroke-dasharray:2 4"></rect><text x="210" y="12" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">root bounding box covers everything</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Objects group into tighter parent boxes bottom-up, forming a searchable hierarchy of bounding boxes.

frames.title: Insert building footprints.
frames.text: Insert building footprints. Each building's rectangular bounding box is inserted as a leaf entry.

frames.title: Group into parent boxes.
frames.text: Group into parent boxes. Nearby buildings' entries share a parent node whose bounding box tightly covers all of them.

frames.title: Grow the tree upward.
frames.text: Grow the tree upward. Parent boxes group further into a small number of top-level regions, up to the root.

frames.title: Query "buildings overlapping this map view."
frames.text: Query "buildings overlapping this map view." Starting at the root, only descend into child boxes that overlap the view — most of the tree, covering the rest of the world, is skipped without ever being examined.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 420 150" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of a hexagonal grid where a center cell has six equally-distant neighbors, contrasted with a square grid where diagonal neighbors are farther away than edge neighbors."><text x="100" y="18" class="figLabel" text-anchor="middle">HEXAGONAL (H3)</text><circle class="box" cx="100" cy="60" r="16"></circle><circle class="box" cx="135" cy="80" r="16"></circle><circle class="box" cx="135" cy="120" r="16"></circle><circle class="box" cx="100" cy="140" r="16"></circle><circle class="box" cx="65" cy="120" r="16"></circle><circle class="box" cx="65" cy="80" r="16"></circle><circle class="boxAccent" cx="100" cy="100" r="18"></circle><text x="100" y="105" class="boxText" text-anchor="middle">·</text><text x="100" y="8" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle" style="opacity:0">-</text><line class="divider" x1="220" y1="10" x2="220" y2="150"></line><text x="330" y="18" class="figLabel" text-anchor="middle">SQUARE GRID</text><rect class="box" x="286" y="46" width="28" height="28" rx="3"></rect><rect class="box" x="316" y="46" width="28" height="28" rx="3"></rect><rect class="box" x="346" y="46" width="28" height="28" rx="3"></rect><rect class="box" x="286" y="86" width="28" height="28" rx="3"></rect><rect class="box" x="346" y="86" width="28" height="28" rx="3"></rect><rect class="box" x="286" y="126" width="28" height="28" rx="3"></rect><rect class="box" x="316" y="126" width="28" height="28" rx="3"></rect><rect class="box" x="346" y="126" width="28" height="28" rx="3"></rect><rect class="boxAccent" x="316" y="86" width="28" height="28" rx="3"></rect></svg>
diagrams.caption: Hexagons keep every neighbor equidistant; a square grid's diagonal neighbors sit farther away.

frames.title: Uber needs uniform "nearby driver" zones.
frames.text: Uber needs uniform "nearby driver" zones. Hexagonal H3 cells give every driver's cell the same set of equally-spaced neighbors, unlike a square grid.

frames.title: Index each driver's location
frames.text: Index each driver's location as an H3 cell ID at an appropriate resolution (H3 supports multiple zoom levels, like Geohash's string length).

frames.title: Query "drivers near this rider."
frames.text: Query "drivers near this rider." Look up the rider's cell and its immediate hexagonal neighbors — a small, well-defined ring around the query point.

frames.title: Aggregate at coarser resolution
frames.text: Aggregate at coarser resolution for city-wide dashboards, using the same hexagonal grid at a lower zoom level — the same indexing scheme serves both fine-grained queries and broad aggregation.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 440 130" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of a bit array where adding an item sets three bit positions from three hash functions, and checking membership fails only if the item hashes to at least one zero bit."><rect class="box" x="20" y="30" width="20" height="26" rx="3"></rect><rect class="box" x="46" y="30" width="20" height="26" rx="3"></rect><rect class="box" x="72" y="30" width="20" height="26" rx="3"></rect><rect class="boxAccent" x="98" y="30" width="20" height="26" rx="3"></rect><rect class="box" x="124" y="30" width="20" height="26" rx="3"></rect><rect class="box" x="150" y="30" width="20" height="26" rx="3"></rect><rect class="box" x="176" y="30" width="20" height="26" rx="3"></rect><rect class="boxAccent" x="202" y="30" width="20" height="26" rx="3"></rect><rect class="box" x="228" y="30" width="20" height="26" rx="3"></rect><rect class="box" x="254" y="30" width="20" height="26" rx="3"></rect><rect class="box" x="280" y="30" width="20" height="26" rx="3"></rect><rect class="box" x="306" y="30" width="20" height="26" rx="3"></rect><rect class="boxAccent" x="332" y="30" width="20" height="26" rx="3"></rect><rect class="box" x="358" y="30" width="20" height="26" rx="3"></rect><rect class="box" x="384" y="30" width="20" height="26" rx="3"></rect><rect class="box" x="410" y="30" width="20" height="26" rx="3"></rect><text x="220" y="20" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">bit array — 3 bits set by 3 hash functions</text><text x="220" y="90" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">query: all 3 of its bits = 1 → "maybe seen" · any = 0 → "definitely not"</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: A handful of set bits per item is enough to answer membership with a small, bounded false-positive rate.

frames.title: Initialize a bit array
frames.text: Initialize a bit array of, say, 1 billion bits — all zeros.

frames.title: Crawl a URL, add it.
frames.text: Crawl a URL, add it. Hash it 3 ways, set those 3 bit positions to 1.

frames.title: See a new URL, check it first.
frames.text: See a new URL, check it first. Hash it the same 3 ways and check those bits.

frames.title: All 3 bits are 1 → skip it
frames.text: All 3 bits are 1 → skip it (probably already crawled — accept the small chance this is a false positive). Any bit is 0 → crawl it (definitely new).

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 440 130" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of a new item being inserted into a full bucket by evicting an existing fingerprint, which then relocates to its own alternate bucket."><rect class="box" x="30" y="35" width="90" height="50" rx="5"></rect><text x="75" y="55" class="boxText" text-anchor="middle">bucket 1</text><text x="75" y="72" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">[A][B]</text><line class="flow" x1="120" y1="60" x2="170" y2="60"></line><text x="145" y="50" class="figHint">insert X → evict A</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="30" y="35" width="90" height="50" rx="5" style="opacity:0"></rect><rect class="box" x="300" y="35" width="90" height="50" rx="5"></rect><text x="345" y="55" class="boxText" text-anchor="middle">bucket 2</text><text x="345" y="72" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">[C][A]</text><line class="flow" x1="180" y1="60" x2="290" y2="60"></line><text x="235" y="50" class="figHint">A relocates here</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: A full bucket evicts an existing fingerprint to its alternate location, making room for the new item.

frames.title: Insert item X.
frames.text: Insert item X. Hash it to find 2 candidate buckets; if either has space, store X's fingerprint there.

frames.title: Both candidate buckets are full.
frames.text: Both candidate buckets are full. Pick one, evict its existing fingerprint, place X there instead.

frames.title: Relocate the evicted fingerprint
frames.text: Relocate the evicted fingerprint to its own alternate bucket — possibly triggering another eviction, cascading a few times until everything settles.

frames.title: Delete an item later.
frames.text: Delete an item later. Hash it to find its fingerprint's bucket, and simply remove it — a straightforward operation a Bloom filter can't safely offer.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 420 120" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of hashed values shown as binary strings, with longer runs of leading zeros being rarer and therefore indicating a larger number of distinct items have been seen."><text x="20" y="30" class="boxText">0110...</text><text x="150" y="30" class="figHint">short run — common</text><text x="20" y="60" class="boxText">0001...</text><text x="150" y="60" class="figHint">longer run — less common</text><text x="20" y="90" class="boxText">00001...</text><text x="150" y="90" class="figHint">longest seen → estimates distinct count</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: The rarest leading-zero run observed is a statistical clue to how many distinct items were hashed.

frames.title: Hash each visitor ID
frames.text: Hash each visitor ID as it arrives, and look at the binary representation.

frames.title: Track the longest run of leading zeros
frames.text: Track the longest run of leading zeros seen so far, split across, say, 1024 small buckets for accuracy (each item routes to one bucket based on part of its hash).

frames.title: More unique visitors → longer runs become likely.
frames.text: More unique visitors → longer runs become likely. Seeing a run of 20 leading zeros suggests roughly a million distinct items have been hashed.

frames.title: Estimate the count
frames.text: Estimate the count from the pattern of longest runs across all buckets — accurate to within about 2%, using only a few KB total, whether a thousand or a billion visitors have been counted.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 420 140" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of a grid of counters with four rows, where an item hashes to one column per row, and its estimated count is the minimum value across its four row positions."><g><rect class="box" x="30" y="20" width="60" height="20" rx="3"></rect><rect class="boxAccent" x="100" y="20" width="60" height="20" rx="3"></rect><rect class="box" x="170" y="20" width="60" height="20" rx="3"></rect><rect class="box" x="240" y="20" width="60" height="20" rx="3"></rect><rect class="box" x="310" y="20" width="60" height="20" rx="3"></rect></g><g><rect class="box" x="30" y="46" width="60" height="20" rx="3"></rect><rect class="box" x="100" y="46" width="60" height="20" rx="3"></rect><rect class="box" x="170" y="46" width="60" height="20" rx="3"></rect><rect class="boxAccent" x="240" y="46" width="60" height="20" rx="3"></rect><rect class="box" x="310" y="46" width="60" height="20" rx="3"></rect></g><g><rect class="boxAccent" x="30" y="72" width="60" height="20" rx="3"></rect><rect class="box" x="100" y="72" width="60" height="20" rx="3"></rect><rect class="box" x="170" y="72" width="60" height="20" rx="3"></rect><rect class="box" x="240" y="72" width="60" height="20" rx="3"></rect><rect class="box" x="310" y="72" width="60" height="20" rx="3"></rect></g><g><rect class="box" x="30" y="98" width="60" height="20" rx="3"></rect><rect class="box" x="100" y="98" width="60" height="20" rx="3"></rect><rect class="boxAccent" x="170" y="98" width="60" height="20" rx="3"></rect><rect class="box" x="240" y="98" width="60" height="20" rx="3"></rect><rect class="box" x="310" y="98" width="60" height="20" rx="3"></rect></g><text x="210" y="130" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">item's 4 positions (highlighted) — estimate = min of the 4 values</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Each item touches one cell per row; the minimum across rows is the count estimate.

frames.title: Product X is viewed.
frames.text: Product X is viewed. Hash "X" with 4 different hash functions, incrementing one counter in each of the 4 rows.

frames.title: This repeats for every view
frames.text: This repeats for every view of every product, sharing the same fixed-size grid — other products' hashes sometimes collide into the same cells.

frames.title: Estimate X's count later.
frames.text: Estimate X's count later. Hash "X" the same 4 ways, look up the 4 corresponding counters, and take the minimum of the 4.

frames.title: The minimum filters out collisions
frames.text: The minimum filters out collisions — any single row might be inflated by a colliding popular product, but it's unlikely all 4 rows are inflated by the same amount, so the smallest value is the closest to the truth.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 420 130" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of two large sets each reduced to a small signature of minimum hash values, with the fraction of matching signature slots estimating how similar the original sets are."><rect class="box" x="20" y="20" width="140" height="30" rx="5"></rect><text x="90" y="40" class="boxText">set A (huge)</text><line class="flow" x1="90" y1="50" x2="90" y2="75"></line><rect class="boxAccent" x="30" y="80" width="120" height="26" rx="4"></rect><text x="90" y="97" class="boxText">signature A</text><rect class="box" x="260" y="20" width="140" height="30" rx="5"></rect><text x="330" y="40" class="boxText">set B (huge)</text><line class="flow" x1="330" y1="50" x2="330" y2="75"></line><rect class="boxAccent" x="270" y="80" width="120" height="26" rx="4"></rect><text x="330" y="97" class="boxText">signature B</text><text x="210" y="93" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">compare</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Small fixed-size signatures stand in for huge sets when estimating similarity.

frames.title: Two documents, as word sets.
frames.text: Two documents, as word sets. Document A and Document B each become a large set of words (or shingles of a few words).

frames.title: Compute MinHash signatures.
frames.text: Compute MinHash signatures. Apply, say, 100 different hash functions to each set, keeping the minimum hash value from each — producing a 100-number signature per document, regardless of how many words each document actually has.

frames.title: Compare signatures, not documents.
frames.text: Compare signatures, not documents. Count how many of the 100 corresponding hash-function slots match between the two signatures.

frames.title: That fraction estimates Jaccard similarity
frames.text: That fraction estimates Jaccard similarity — e.g., 78 of 100 matching suggests the documents are about 78% similar by this measure, without ever directly comparing the (possibly huge) original word sets.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 440 140" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of a skip list with three layers, where the top sparse layer allows large jumps forward before dropping down to denser layers to pinpoint the exact search target."><g><line x1="30" y1="30" x2="410" y2="30" stroke="var(--muted)"></line></g><g><line x1="30" y1="65" x2="410" y2="65" stroke="var(--muted)"></line></g><g><line x1="30" y1="100" x2="410" y2="100" stroke="var(--muted)"></line></g><circle class="box" cx="30" cy="100" r="6"></circle><circle class="box" cx="130" cy="100" r="6"></circle><circle class="box" cx="230" cy="100" r="6"></circle><circle class="box" cx="330" cy="100" r="6"></circle><circle class="box" cx="30" cy="65" r="6"></circle><circle class="box" cx="130" cy="65" r="6"></circle><circle class="box" cx="330" cy="65" r="6"></circle><circle class="boxAccent" cx="30" cy="30" r="6"></circle><circle class="boxAccent" cx="230" cy="30" r="6"></circle><text x="220" y="125" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">base layer: every element</text><text x="220" y="15" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">top layer: sparse "express lane"</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Sparser upper layers let a search skip ahead quickly before dropping down to pinpoint the target.

frames.title: Search for value 47
frames.text: Search for value 47 in a skip list of a million sorted elements.

frames.title: Start at the top layer.
frames.text: Start at the top layer. Only a handful of elements exist here; jump forward until the next element would exceed 47.

frames.title: Drop down a layer
frames.text: Drop down a layer at that point and continue forward on the denser layer below, again until about to overshoot.

frames.title: Repeat down to the base layer,
frames.text: Repeat down to the base layer, where the exact element (or its correct insertion point) is found — having examined only a small fraction of the million elements, roughly proportional to log(n).

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 420 150" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of a Merkle tree where a mismatched root hash is narrowed down level by level to the exact differing leaf, without comparing the full underlying data."><rect class="boxWarn" x="180" y="10" width="60" height="26" rx="4"></rect><text x="210" y="27" class="boxText">root ✕</text><line class="flow" x1="200" y1="36" x2="130" y2="65"></line><line class="flow" x1="220" y1="36" x2="290" y2="65"></line><rect class="box" x="100" y="70" width="60" height="24" rx="4"></rect><text x="130" y="86" class="boxText">✓ match</text><rect class="boxWarn" x="260" y="70" width="60" height="24" rx="4"></rect><text x="290" y="86" class="boxText">✕ differs</text><line class="flow" x1="280" y1="94" x2="255" y2="120"></line><line class="flow" x1="300" y1="94" x2="330" y2="120"></line><rect class="box" x="220" y="125" width="70" height="22" rx="3"></rect><text x="255" y="140" class="boxText">leaf ✓</text><rect class="boxWarn" x="300" y="125" width="70" height="22" rx="3"></rect><text x="335" y="140" class="boxText">leaf ✕</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Each mismatch halves the search space — the exact differing chunk is found in O(log n) steps.

frames.title: Both build a Merkle tree
frames.text: Both build a Merkle tree over their data, chunked the same way.

frames.title: Compare root hashes.
frames.text: Compare root hashes. They differ — something is out of sync somewhere.

frames.title: Compare one level down.
frames.text: Compare one level down. The left subtree's hash matches; the right subtree's doesn't — the difference is narrowed to the right half.

frames.title: Recurse into just the right subtree,
frames.text: Recurse into just the right subtree, repeating until the exact mismatched chunk (a small handful of rows) is found — then only that chunk needs to be resynced, not the whole dataset.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 420 130" role="img" aria-label="Diagram contrasting batch processing running periodically over a large accumulated dataset versus stream processing handling each event continuously as it arrives."><text x="100" y="18" class="figLabel" text-anchor="middle">BATCH</text><rect class="box" x="20" y="30" width="160" height="40" rx="5"></rect><text x="100" y="54" class="boxText">accumulated data</text><line class="flow" x1="100" y1="70" x2="100" y2="95"></line><text x="100" y="112" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">runs once, on a schedule</text><line class="divider" x1="210" y1="10" x2="210" y2="120"></line><text x="330" y="18" class="figLabel" text-anchor="middle">STREAM</text><circle class="boxAccent" cx="250" cy="50" r="8"></circle><circle class="boxAccent" cx="295" cy="50" r="8"></circle><circle class="boxAccent" cx="340" cy="50" r="8"></circle><circle class="boxAccent" cx="385" cy="50" r="8"></circle><line class="flow" x1="230" y1="50" x2="420" y2="50"></line><text x="330" y="90" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">processed continuously, event by event</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Batch waits for a full dataset; streaming reacts to each event as it happens.

frames.title: Monthly billing report → batch.
frames.text: Monthly billing report → batch. Runs once a month over the complete month's data — no need for it to be real-time, and a complete dataset makes the logic simpler.

frames.title: Fraud detection → stream.
frames.text: Fraud detection → stream. Must flag a suspicious transaction within seconds, not wait for the next nightly batch run.

frames.title: Many systems use both.
frames.text: Many systems use both. A streaming layer gives fast, approximate real-time numbers; a nightly batch job recomputes the authoritative, fully accurate version — this hybrid is exactly what the Lambda architecture (later in this section) formalizes.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 440 140" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of the MapReduce flow: many machines mapping input records in parallel, the framework shuffling and grouping results by key, then reduce combining each key's values into a final result."><text x="80" y="18" class="figLabel" text-anchor="middle">MAP</text><rect class="box" x="20" y="30" width="90" height="22" rx="3"></rect><rect class="box" x="20" y="60" width="90" height="22" rx="3"></rect><rect class="box" x="20" y="90" width="90" height="22" rx="3"></rect><line class="flow" x1="110" y1="65" x2="170" y2="65"></line><text x="200" y="18" class="figLabel" text-anchor="middle">SHUFFLE</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="180" y="50" width="90" height="30" rx="4"></rect><text x="225" y="70" class="boxText">group by key</text><line class="flow" x1="270" y1="65" x2="330" y2="65"></line><text x="380" y="18" class="figLabel" text-anchor="middle">REDUCE</text><rect class="box" x="340" y="50" width="80" height="30" rx="4"></rect><text x="380" y="70" class="boxText">sum per key</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Independent parallel map, a grouping shuffle, then parallel reduce per group.

frames.title: Map (parallel, per document).
frames.text: Map (parallel, per document). Each machine processes a subset of documents, emitting (word, 1) for every word it finds.

frames.title: Shuffle.
frames.text: Shuffle. The framework groups all pairs by word — every ("system", 1) pair, from every machine, ends up together.

frames.title: Reduce (parallel, per word).
frames.text: Reduce (parallel, per word). For each word, sum up all its 1 values — ("system", 1) appearing 4,201 times becomes ("system", 4201).

frames.title: Result.
frames.text: Result. A complete word-count across a billion documents, computed by thousands of machines working on small, independent pieces.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 440 120" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of the ETL pipeline: extracting raw data from source systems, transforming and cleaning it, then loading the result into a data warehouse for analysis."><rect class="box" x="20" y="40" width="100" height="30" rx="5"></rect><text x="70" y="60" class="boxText">sources</text><line class="flow" x1="120" y1="55" x2="170" y2="55"></line><text x="145" y="45" class="figHint">extract</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="180" y="40" width="100" height="30" rx="5"></rect><text x="230" y="60" class="boxText">transform</text><line class="flow" x1="280" y1="55" x2="330" y2="55"></line><text x="305" y="45" class="figHint">load</text><rect class="box" x="340" y="40" width="100" height="30" rx="5" style="opacity:0"></rect><rect class="box" x="335" y="40" width="90" height="30" rx="5"></rect><text x="380" y="60" class="boxText">warehouse</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Raw data is extracted, cleaned and reshaped, then loaded into an analysis-ready destination.

frames.title: Extract.
frames.text: Extract. Pull yesterday's orders from the production database and yesterday's page views from an events log.

frames.title: Transform.
frames.text: Transform. Standardize timestamps to UTC, join orders with customer reference data, filter out known bot traffic, and aggregate page views into daily per-user counts.

frames.title: Load.
frames.text: Load. Write the cleaned, joined, aggregated tables into the data warehouse.

frames.title: Analysts query the warehouse,
frames.text: Analysts query the warehouse, never touching the messy, high-volume raw production data directly.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 420 130" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of varied raw data types flowing into a data lake in their native format, with structure applied later at query time rather than upfront."><rect class="box" x="20" y="20" width="80" height="26" rx="4"></rect><rect class="box" x="120" y="20" width="80" height="26" rx="4"></rect><rect class="box" x="220" y="20" width="80" height="26" rx="4"></rect><rect class="box" x="320" y="20" width="80" height="26" rx="4"></rect><text x="60" y="38" class="boxText" text-anchor="middle">JSON</text><text x="160" y="38" class="boxText" text-anchor="middle">CSV</text><text x="260" y="38" class="boxText" text-anchor="middle">images</text><text x="360" y="38" class="boxText" text-anchor="middle">logs</text><line class="flow" x1="60" y1="46" x2="210" y2="75"></line><line class="flow" x1="160" y1="46" x2="210" y2="75"></line><line class="flow" x1="260" y1="46" x2="210" y2="75"></line><line class="flow" x1="360" y1="46" x2="210" y2="75"></line><rect class="boxAccent" x="140" y="80" width="140" height="30" rx="5"></rect><text x="210" y="100" class="boxText">data lake (raw, as-is)</text><text x="210" y="125" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">structure applied later, at query/read time</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Varied raw data lands unchanged; structure is applied later, only when it's actually read.

frames.title: Dump raw data as it arrives.
frames.text: Dump raw data as it arrives. Clickstream JSON, server logs, and exported CSVs all land in the lake in their native format, with no transformation required first.

frames.title: Data scientists explore it later.
frames.text: Data scientists explore it later. A researcher reads the raw clickstream data for an exploratory analysis nobody had planned for at ingest time.

frames.title: A defined pipeline reads a subset,
frames.text: A defined pipeline reads a subset, applies structure, and loads a clean, modeled version into a data warehouse for regular business reporting.

frames.title: The lake keeps the raw originals
frames.text: The lake keeps the raw originals — if the pipeline's transformation logic needs to change later, it can be rerun from the untouched original data.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 420 130" role="img" aria-label="Diagram contrasting row-oriented storage where whole rows are read together versus columnar storage where only the needed columns are read across all rows, favoring analytical queries."><text x="100" y="18" class="figLabel" text-anchor="middle">ROW-ORIENTED</text><rect class="box" x="30" y="25" width="150" height="18" rx="3"></rect><rect class="box" x="30" y="49" width="150" height="18" rx="3"></rect><rect class="box" x="30" y="73" width="150" height="18" rx="3"></rect><text x="330" y="18" class="figLabel" text-anchor="middle">COLUMNAR</text><rect class="box" x="250" y="25" width="45" height="66" rx="3"></rect><rect class="boxAccent" x="305" y="25" width="45" height="66" rx="3"></rect><rect class="box" x="360" y="25" width="45" height="66" rx="3"></rect><text x="330" y="110" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">read only the needed column, across all rows</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Columnar layout matches the "few columns, many rows" shape of typical analytical queries.

frames.title: Operational database
frames.text: Operational database stores live order rows, optimized for fast individual inserts and lookups by order ID.

frames.title: ETL pipeline copies and reshapes
frames.text: ETL pipeline copies and reshapes that data nightly into the warehouse, in a columnar format organized around common analytical questions.

frames.title: Analyst runs a query:
frames.text: Analyst runs a query: "total revenue by region, last 12 months." Only the region, revenue, and date columns are read — not every column of every order row.

frames.title: The query returns in seconds
frames.text: The query returns in seconds across billions of historical rows — something the operational database, tuned for a different workload, would struggle to do without slowing down live traffic.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 420 130" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of a data lakehouse as one underlying object storage layer with a table format adding structure and transactions on top, serving both flexible raw access and fast structured queries."><rect class="box" x="60" y="70" width="300" height="30" rx="5"></rect><text x="210" y="90" class="boxText">object storage (raw files)</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="90" y="25" width="240" height="30" rx="5"></rect><text x="210" y="45" class="boxText">table format: schema + ACID</text><line class="flow" x1="210" y1="55" x2="210" y2="65"></line><text x="210" y="115" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">one storage layer serves both raw and structured access</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: A structured table format layered directly on object storage merges lake flexibility with warehouse capability.

frames.title: Old approach: lake + warehouse.
frames.text: Old approach: lake + warehouse. Raw data lands in the lake; a pipeline copies and reshapes a subset into the warehouse for analysts — two copies, two systems to keep in sync.

frames.title: Lakehouse approach.
frames.text: Lakehouse approach. Raw data lands in object storage, but a table format (like Iceberg) adds schema, versioning, and transaction guarantees directly on top.

frames.title: One copy, multiple uses.
frames.text: One copy, multiple uses. A data scientist reads the same underlying files for flexible exploration; an analyst runs fast structured SQL queries against the same files through the table format's query engine.

frames.title: No separate sync pipeline needed
frames.text: No separate sync pipeline needed between "the lake" and "the warehouse" — they're now the same underlying storage.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 440 140" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of data flowing into both a speed layer producing fast approximate results and a batch layer producing accurate results, merged together in a serving layer."><rect class="box" x="20" y="55" width="80" height="26" rx="4"></rect><text x="60" y="72" class="boxText">data</text><line class="flow" x1="100" y1="65" x2="150" y2="30"></line><line class="flow" x1="100" y1="65" x2="150" y2="100"></line><rect class="boxAccent" x="160" y="15" width="110" height="28" rx="4"></rect><text x="215" y="34" class="boxText">speed layer</text><rect class="box" x="160" y="90" width="110" height="28" rx="4"></rect><text x="215" y="109" class="boxText">batch layer</text><line class="flow" x1="270" y1="29" x2="320" y2="60"></line><line class="flow" x1="270" y1="104" x2="320" y2="70"></line><rect class="boxAccent" x="330" y="50" width="100" height="28" rx="4"></rect><text x="380" y="69" class="boxText">serving layer</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Fast approximate results and slower accurate results merge in the serving layer.

frames.title: Speed layer.
frames.text: Speed layer. A streaming job computes "views per video in the last hour," updating within seconds, but using simplified, approximate logic.

frames.title: Batch layer.
frames.text: Batch layer. A nightly job recomputes the exact, fully-accurate view counts over the complete historical data using the authoritative logic.

frames.title: Serving layer merges them.
frames.text: Serving layer merges them. For anything before last night's batch run, serve the accurate batch numbers; for the last few hours the batch hasn't covered yet, serve the speed layer's approximate numbers.

frames.title: Users see both freshness and eventual accuracy
frames.text: Users see both freshness and eventual accuracy — approximate now, exact once the batch layer catches up.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 420 130" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of a single retained event log being replayed from the beginning through a corrected streaming job to reprocess history, instead of maintaining a separate batch pipeline."><rect class="box" x="20" y="45" width="200" height="30" rx="5"></rect><text x="120" y="65" class="boxText">retained event log</text><line class="flow" x1="220" y1="60" x2="270" y2="60"></line><rect class="boxAccent" x="280" y="45" width="120" height="30" rx="5"></rect><text x="340" y="65" class="boxText">streaming job</text><text x="120" y="95" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">replay from the start to reprocess history</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: One pipeline, replayed from a retained log, replaces the need for a separate batch system.

frames.title: All events go through one stream.
frames.text: All events go through one stream. A single streaming job computes video view counts as events arrive, continuously.

frames.title: A bug is found
frames.text: A bug is found in the view-counting logic — some views were being double-counted.

frames.title: Fix the logic,
frames.text: Fix the logic, and deploy a new version of the same streaming job.

frames.title: Replay history.
frames.text: Replay history. The new job reads from the beginning of the retained event log, reprocessing everything with the corrected logic, until it catches up to live — at which point it becomes the new source of truth. No separate batch system was ever needed.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 440 130" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of a continuous event stream divided into fixed time windows by a streaming engine, with state checkpointed durably so a worker failure doesn't lose progress within a window."><line x1="20" y1="40" x2="420" y2="40" stroke="var(--muted)"></line><circle class="box" cx="40" cy="40" r="6"></circle><circle class="box" cx="105" cy="40" r="6"></circle><circle class="box" cx="170" cy="40" r="6"></circle><circle class="box" cx="235" cy="40" r="6"></circle><circle class="box" cx="300" cy="40" r="6"></circle><circle class="box" cx="365" cy="40" r="6"></circle><line class="divider" x1="150" y1="20" x2="150" y2="60"></line><line class="divider" x1="280" y1="20" x2="280" y2="60"></line><line class="divider" x1="410" y1="20" x2="410" y2="60"></line><text x="215" y="18" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">5-min window</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="150" y="80" width="130" height="26" rx="4"></rect><text x="215" y="98" class="boxText">checkpointed state</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: The engine buckets events into windows and durably checkpoints state, surviving failures transparently.

frames.title: Define a windowed aggregation.
frames.text: Define a windowed aggregation. "Count events per user, in 5-minute tumbling windows" — the engine handles bucketing events by time automatically.

frames.title: Engine manages state.
frames.text: Engine manages state. Running counts per user per window are checkpointed durably, so a worker crash doesn't lose progress.

frames.title: A worker crashes mid-window.
frames.text: A worker crashes mid-window. The engine restarts processing from the last checkpoint, guaranteeing events aren't silently dropped or double-counted.

frames.title: Window closes.
frames.text: Window closes. The engine emits the final count for that 5-minute window, having handled failure recovery and state transparently the whole time.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 420 120" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of a spectrum of deployment strategies from a big bang release exposing all traffic at once to a controlled, gradual rollout exposing traffic incrementally."><line x1="30" y1="60" x2="390" y2="60" stroke="var(--muted)"></line><circle class="boxWarn" cx="60" cy="60" r="10"></circle><text x="60" y="90" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">big-bang</text><circle class="box" cx="200" cy="60" r="10"></circle><text x="200" y="90" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">rolling / blue-green</text><circle class="boxAccent" cx="360" cy="60" r="10"></circle><text x="360" y="90" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">canary + flags</text><text x="200" y="25" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">more control, more gradual exposure →</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Deployment strategies sit on a spectrum from all-at-once to gradually and carefully controlled.

frames.title: Old approach: big-bang deploy.
frames.text: Old approach: big-bang deploy. Stop the old version, start the new one — simple, but every user hits the new code at once, and any bug affects everyone immediately.

frames.title: Modern approach: controlled exposure.
frames.text: Modern approach: controlled exposure. New code reaches a small fraction of traffic first, with monitoring watching for errors.

frames.title: Problem detected early,
frames.text: Problem detected early, affecting only that small fraction — the rollout is halted before most users are ever affected.

frames.title: Gradually increase exposure
frames.text: Gradually increase exposure once confidence is high, until the new version fully replaces the old one.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 440 120" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of a CI/CD pipeline flowing through build, test, security scan, and deploy stages, with a failure at any stage stopping the change from progressing further."><g><rect class="box" x="20" y="40" width="85" height="34" rx="5"></rect><text x="62" y="61" class="boxText">build</text><line class="flow" x1="105" y1="57" x2="125" y2="57"></line></g><g><rect class="box" x="125" y="40" width="85" height="34" rx="5"></rect><text x="167" y="61" class="boxText">test</text><line class="flow" x1="210" y1="57" x2="230" y2="57"></line></g><g><rect class="box" x="230" y="40" width="85" height="34" rx="5"></rect><text x="272" y="61" class="boxText">scan</text><line class="flow" x1="315" y1="57" x2="335" y2="57"></line></g><g><rect class="boxAccent" x="335" y="40" width="85" height="34" rx="5"></rect><text x="377" y="61" class="boxText">deploy</text></g><text x="220" y="95" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">a failure at any stage stops the pipeline there</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Each stage gates the next — a change only reaches deploy after passing everything before it.

frames.title: Developer pushes a code change.
frames.text: Developer pushes a code change. The pipeline triggers automatically.

frames.title: Build and unit tests run.
frames.text: Build and unit tests run. If anything fails, the developer is notified immediately — no waiting for a human reviewer to notice.

frames.title: Integration tests and security scans run
frames.text: Integration tests and security scans run against a real, deployed test environment.

frames.title: Deploy.
frames.text: Deploy. Under Continuous Delivery, the change waits for a person to click "release"; under Continuous Deployment, it goes live automatically once every stage passes.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 420 120" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of ten instances being replaced from the old version to the new version in small batches, with the service remaining available throughout the gradual rollout."><rect class="box" x="20" y="40" width="30" height="30" rx="4"></rect><rect class="box" x="58" y="40" width="30" height="30" rx="4"></rect><rect class="box" x="96" y="40" width="30" height="30" rx="4"></rect><rect class="box" x="134" y="40" width="30" height="30" rx="4"></rect><rect class="box" x="172" y="40" width="30" height="30" rx="4"></rect><rect class="box" x="210" y="40" width="30" height="30" rx="4"></rect><rect class="boxAccent" x="248" y="40" width="30" height="30" rx="4"></rect><rect class="boxAccent" x="286" y="40" width="30" height="30" rx="4"></rect><rect class="boxAccent" x="324" y="40" width="30" height="30" rx="4"></rect><rect class="boxAccent" x="362" y="40" width="30" height="30" rx="4"></rect><text x="220" y="90" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">6 old + 4 new, both serving traffic mid-rollout</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Instances flip to the new version in small batches, with old and new coexisting during the rollout.

frames.title: 10 instances running v1.
frames.text: 10 instances running v1. A rolling deployment begins with a batch size of 2.

frames.title: Take 2 instances out
frames.text: Take 2 instances out of the load balancer, deploy v2 to them, wait for health checks to pass.

frames.title: Add them back
frames.text: Add them back to the load balancer — now 8 instances run v1, 2 run v2, both serving live traffic.

frames.title: Repeat in batches of 2
frames.text: Repeat in batches of 2 until all 10 instances run v2 — the service was never fully down, but briefly served a mix of both versions.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 420 130" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of a router pointing to a live blue environment while an identical green environment runs the new version idle, ready for an instant traffic switch."><rect class="box" x="20" y="60" width="150" height="40" rx="6"></rect><text x="95" y="84" class="boxText">blue (live, v1)</text><rect class="box" x="250" y="60" width="150" height="40" rx="6"></rect><text x="325" y="84" class="boxText">green (idle, v2)</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="150" y="10" width="90" height="30" rx="5"></rect><text x="195" y="29" class="boxText">router</text><line class="flow" x1="180" y1="40" x2="110" y2="55"></line><line class="flowMuted" x1="210" y1="40" x2="300" y2="55"></line><text x="195" y="115" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">switching the router flips live traffic instantly</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Two complete environments; the router's switch is the entire release, and the entire rollback.

frames.title: Blue serves 100% of live traffic,
frames.text: Blue serves 100% of live traffic, running v1.

frames.title: Deploy v2 to green,
frames.text: Deploy v2 to green, completely idle from a traffic perspective — run full smoke tests against it directly.

frames.title: Switch the router
frames.text: Switch the router to send all traffic to green — the cutover happens in seconds, all at once.

frames.title: A critical bug appears.
frames.text: A critical bug appears. Switch the router back to blue immediately — an instant rollback, since blue was never torn down.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 420 120" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of traffic split mostly to a stable version with a small percentage routed to a canary version, whose metrics are monitored before gradually increasing its traffic share."><rect class="box" x="30" y="30" width="200" height="50" rx="6"></rect><text x="130" y="60" class="boxText">stable v1 — 99%</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="250" y="45" width="140" height="24" rx="4"></rect><text x="320" y="61" class="boxText">canary v2 — 1%</text><text x="210" y="100" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">canary's metrics decide whether its share grows or drops to zero</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: A small, closely-watched slice of traffic decides whether the rollout proceeds.

frames.title: Deploy v2 as the canary,
frames.text: Deploy v2 as the canary, receiving 1% of live traffic; 99% still goes to the stable v1.

frames.title: Monitor automatically.
frames.text: Monitor automatically. Error rates and latency for the canary are compared against the stable version in real time.

frames.title: Canary looks healthy.
frames.text: Canary looks healthy. Traffic is gradually increased — 5%, 25%, 50% — with monitoring at each step.

frames.title: Canary shows elevated errors instead.
frames.text: Canary shows elevated errors instead. The rollout is automatically halted and traffic reverted to 0% on the canary — only the small fraction of users on it were ever affected.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 420 120" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of application code checking a feature flag service at runtime to decide whether to show old or new functionality, without requiring a new deployment to change that decision."><rect class="box" x="20" y="40" width="140" height="34" rx="5"></rect><text x="90" y="62" class="boxText">app code</text><line class="flow" x1="160" y1="57" x2="200" y2="57"></line><text x="180" y="45" class="figHint">check flag</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="210" y="40" width="140" height="34" rx="5"></rect><text x="280" y="62" class="boxText">flag service</text><text x="185" y="95" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">flag value changes instantly, no redeploy needed</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: A runtime lookup decides feature behavior — changing that decision needs no new deployment.

frames.title: New checkout flow is built
frames.text: New checkout flow is built behind a flag, deployed to production, but the flag is off for everyone — the code exists but has zero effect.

frames.title: Enable for internal employees first,
frames.text: Enable for internal employees first, by targeting the flag at that user segment — real production testing with essentially zero external risk.

frames.title: Ramp to 10% of real users,
frames.text: Ramp to 10% of real users, monitoring conversion and error metrics.

frames.title: Problem detected.
frames.text: Problem detected. Flip the flag off instantly for everyone — no deployment, no rollback, the fix is live within seconds.
