diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 420 130" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of users being consistently hash-assigned to variant A or variant B, with each variant's outcome events tracked separately and compared for statistical significance."><rect class="box" x="20" y="45" width="90" height="30" rx="5"></rect><text x="65" y="65" class="boxText">user</text><line class="flow" x1="110" y1="55" x2="150" y2="30"></line><line class="flow" x1="110" y1="65" x2="150" y2="95"></line><rect class="box" x="160" y="15" width="90" height="28" rx="4"></rect><text x="205" y="33" class="boxText">variant A</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="160" y="85" width="90" height="28" rx="4"></rect><text x="205" y="103" class="boxText">variant B</text><text x="335" y="29" class="figHint">track outcomes →</text><text x="335" y="99" class="figHint">track outcomes →</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Consistent per-user assignment and separate outcome tracking are what make the comparison valid.

frames.title: Define the experiment.
frames.text: Define the experiment. Variant A: current checkout button; Variant B: a redesigned button. Success metric: click-through rate.

frames.title: Assign users consistently.
frames.text: Assign users consistently. Each user's ID is hashed into a bucket, determining which variant they see — and they keep seeing that same variant for the experiment's duration.

frames.title: Track events per variant
frames.text: Track events per variant as users interact, accumulating enough data over time to reach statistical significance.

frames.title: Analyze the result.
frames.text: Analyze the result. Variant B shows a statistically significant lift in click-through rate — it's rolled out to 100% of users, informed by real evidence rather than a guess.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 440 120" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of the expand-contract migration pattern: adding a new column alongside the old one, dual-writing to both, migrating reads to the new column, then removing the old column."><g><rect class="box" x="15" y="40" width="92" height="34" rx="5"></rect><text x="61" y="61" class="boxText">expand</text><line class="flow" x1="107" y1="57" x2="123" y2="57"></line></g><g><rect class="box" x="123" y="40" width="92" height="34" rx="5"></rect><text x="169" y="61" class="boxText">dual-write</text><line class="flow" x1="215" y1="57" x2="231" y2="57"></line></g><g><rect class="box" x="231" y="40" width="92" height="34" rx="5"></rect><text x="277" y="61" class="boxText">migrate reads</text><line class="flow" x1="323" y1="57" x2="339" y2="57"></line></g><g><rect class="boxAccent" x="339" y="40" width="92" height="34" rx="5"></rect><text x="385" y="61" class="boxText">contract</text></g><text x="220" y="95" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">both schema shapes stay valid at every stage</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Each stage keeps both old and new code working against the schema simultaneously.

frames.title: Expand:
frames.text: Expand: Add a new full_name column, alongside the existing user_name — both now exist.

frames.title: Dual-write:
frames.text: Dual-write: Deploy code that writes every update to both columns — old instances still reading/writing user_name keep working unaffected.

frames.title: Migrate and switch reads:
frames.text: Migrate and switch reads: Backfill full_name for existing rows, then roll out code that reads from full_name instead.

frames.title: Contract:
frames.text: Contract: Once every instance runs the new code, stop writing to user_name and drop it — the migration is complete with zero downtime.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 420 120" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of a sequence of versioned, immutable images where rolling back simply means deploying instances from a previous image instead of running undo logic on a live server."><rect class="box" x="40" y="30" width="90" height="34" rx="5"></rect><rect class="box" x="160" y="30" width="90" height="34" rx="5"></rect><rect class="boxWarn" x="280" y="30" width="90" height="34" rx="5"></rect><text x="85" y="51" class="boxText" text-anchor="middle">v41</text><text x="205" y="51" class="boxText" text-anchor="middle">v42</text><text x="325" y="51" class="boxText" text-anchor="middle">v43</text><line class="flowMuted" x1="325" y1="47" x2="175" y2="47"></line><text x="250" y="35" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">rollback = redeploy v42</text><text x="230" y="95" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">every past image is preserved, unmodified, ready to redeploy</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Immutable, versioned images make rollback identical in mechanism to a forward deploy.

frames.title: Build an immutable image
frames.text: Build an immutable image for every release — v41, v42, v43 — each a complete, versioned snapshot, never modified after being built.

frames.title: Deploy v43.
frames.text: Deploy v43. Old v42 instances are terminated and replaced by fresh instances booted from the v43 image.

frames.title: v43 has a critical bug.
frames.text: v43 has a critical bug. Roll back by simply redeploying instances from the v42 image — the exact same image that was running and working minutes earlier.

frames.title: No "undo" logic needed
frames.text: No "undo" logic needed — a rollback is just a forward deployment of an older, known-good, unmodified image.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 440 130" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of the three observability pillars: metrics showing an overall trend, traces narrowing down which service is slow, and logs providing the exact detail of what happened there."><rect class="box" x="20" y="20" width="110" height="30" rx="5"></rect><text x="75" y="40" class="boxText">metrics: trend</text><line class="flow" x1="130" y1="35" x2="170" y2="35"></line><rect class="box" x="180" y="20" width="110" height="30" rx="5"></rect><text x="235" y="40" class="boxText">traces: where</text><line class="flow" x1="290" y1="35" x2="330" y2="35"></line><rect class="boxAccent" x="340" y="20" width="90" height="30" rx="5"></rect><text x="385" y="40" class="boxText">logs: what</text><text x="225" y="90" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">broad signal narrows to exact detail across the three pillars</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Each pillar answers a different question; incident response typically moves through all three.

frames.title: A metric alerts:
frames.text: A metric alerts: "p99 latency for the checkout API has doubled in the last 10 minutes" — a trend, not a detail.

frames.title: Traces narrow it down.
frames.text: Traces narrow it down. Sampling slow requests' traces shows most of the extra time is spent in calls to the inventory service specifically.

frames.title: Logs give the detail.
frames.text: Logs give the detail. The inventory service's logs around that time period show repeated database connection timeouts.

frames.title: Root cause found
frames.text: Root cause found — a database connection pool exhaustion — by moving from broad trend (metric) to specific path (trace) to exact detail (log).

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 420 110" role="img" aria-label="Diagram contrasting an unstructured free-text log line that is hard to search against a structured JSON log line with consistent, filterable fields."><text x="100" y="20" class="figLabel" text-anchor="middle">UNSTRUCTURED</text><rect class="box" x="20" y="30" width="160" height="40" rx="5"></rect><text x="100" y="54" class="boxText" style="font-size:10px">"error processing order"</text><text x="320" y="20" class="figLabel" text-anchor="middle">STRUCTURED</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="240" y="30" width="160" height="40" rx="5"></rect><text x="320" y="48" class="boxText" style="font-size:9px">{level, msg, orderId,</text><text x="320" y="62" class="boxText" style="font-size:9px">  userId, service}</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Structured, context-rich logs are searchable by field instead of requiring fragile text matching.

frames.title: Log at the right level.
frames.text: Log at the right level. Routine operations at DEBUG/INFO, genuine problems at WARN/ERROR — so production log volume stays manageable and searchable.

frames.title: Always include request context
frames.text: Always include request context — a request ID at minimum — so every log line from one request can be found and grouped together.

frames.title: Avoid logging sensitive data
frames.text: Avoid logging sensitive data (passwords, full credit card numbers) even at DEBUG level — logs often have weaker access controls than the primary database.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 420 130" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of many service instances each shipping their local logs to a central aggregation pipeline, which indexes them into one searchable store."><rect class="box" x="20" y="20" width="80" height="26" rx="4"></rect><rect class="box" x="120" y="20" width="80" height="26" rx="4"></rect><rect class="box" x="220" y="20" width="80" height="26" rx="4"></rect><rect class="box" x="320" y="20" width="80" height="26" rx="4"></rect><line class="flow" x1="60" y1="46" x2="210" y2="80"></line><line class="flow" x1="160" y1="46" x2="210" y2="80"></line><line class="flow" x1="260" y1="46" x2="210" y2="80"></line><line class="flow" x1="360" y1="46" x2="210" y2="80"></line><rect class="boxAccent" x="150" y="85" width="120" height="30" rx="5"></rect><text x="210" y="105" class="boxText">central store</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Every instance ships logs to one central, searchable index — decoupled from any single instance's lifetime.

frames.title: Each of 200 service instances
frames.text: Each of 200 service instances writes logs locally and ships them continuously via a lightweight agent.

frames.title: A central pipeline ingests, parses,
frames.text: A central pipeline ingests, parses, and indexes every log line from every instance into one searchable store.

frames.title: An engineer searches
frames.text: An engineer searches "all ERROR logs for orderId=o-4471" — one query across all 200 instances at once, instead of 200 separate manual checks.

frames.title: An instance is later terminated
frames.text: An instance is later terminated (autoscaled down, or crashed) — its logs remain fully searchable in the central store, unaffected by the instance's own lifecycle.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 440 130" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of a single correlation ID being forwarded through a chain of service calls, letting logs from every service in the chain later be pulled together by that same id."><rect class="box" x="20" y="45" width="80" height="30" rx="5"></rect><text x="60" y="65" class="boxText">gateway</text><line class="flow" x1="100" y1="60" x2="150" y2="60"></line><text x="125" y="45" class="figHint">id: req-8871</text><rect class="box" x="160" y="45" width="80" height="30" rx="5"></rect><text x="200" y="65" class="boxText">orders</text><line class="flow" x1="240" y1="60" x2="290" y2="60"></line><text x="265" y="45" class="figHint">id: req-8871</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="300" y="45" width="90" height="30" rx="5"></rect><text x="345" y="65" class="boxText">payments</text><text x="220" y="105" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">same id, forwarded through every hop</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: The same ID travels through every downstream call, tying together the whole request's log trail.

frames.title: Request enters at the gateway.
frames.text: Request enters at the gateway. It's assigned correlationId: "req-8871".

frames.title: Gateway calls the orders service,
frames.text: Gateway calls the orders service, forwarding the ID in a header; orders service logs everything it does with that same ID.

frames.title: Orders service calls payments and inventory,
frames.text: Orders service calls payments and inventory, forwarding the same ID onward to each — every service in the chain logs with correlationId: "req-8871".

frames.title: A user reports an error.
frames.text: A user reports an error. Searching logs for correlationId: "req-8871" instantly pulls together every log line from every service that request touched, in order.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 420 120" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of three metric types: a counter that only increases, a gauge that moves up and down, and a histogram summarizing a distribution of values into percentiles."><text x="70" y="18" class="figLabel" text-anchor="middle">COUNTER</text><polyline points="20,80 40,70 60,65 80,50 100,30" fill="none" style="stroke:var(--course-accent);stroke-width:2"></polyline><text x="220" y="18" class="figLabel" text-anchor="middle">GAUGE</text><polyline points="160,55 180,40 200,60 220,35 240,50" fill="none" style="stroke:var(--course-accent);stroke-width:2"></polyline><text x="360" y="18" class="figLabel" text-anchor="middle">HISTOGRAM</text><rect class="box" x="310" y="70" width="14" height="20"></rect><rect class="box" x="330" y="45" width="14" height="45"></rect><rect class="box" x="350" y="25" width="14" height="65"></rect><rect class="box" x="370" y="55" width="14" height="35"></rect><rect class="box" x="390" y="75" width="14" height="15"></rect></svg>
diagrams.caption: Counters only rise, gauges move freely, and histograms summarize a distribution for percentiles.

frames.title: Instrument the checkout endpoint.
frames.text: Instrument the checkout endpoint. Increment a checkout_requests_total counter on every call, and record each request's duration into a checkout_duration_seconds histogram.

frames.title: A metrics system scrapes or receives
frames.text: A metrics system scrapes or receives these values continuously from every instance.

frames.title: Aggregate across instances.
frames.text: Aggregate across instances. Sum the counters and combine the histograms across all instances to get a fleet-wide view.

frames.title: Compute p99 latency
frames.text: Compute p99 latency from the histogram — "99% of checkout requests complete within 340ms" — a single, cheap-to-query number summarizing millions of requests.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 420 120" role="img" aria-label="Diagram contrasting a cause-based alert on CPU usage that may not reflect real user impact against a symptom-based alert on error rate that directly reflects what users experience."><text x="100" y="18" class="figLabel" text-anchor="middle">CAUSE-BASED</text><rect class="box" x="20" y="30" width="160" height="30" rx="5"></rect><text x="100" y="50" class="boxText">CPU > 80%</text><text x="100" y="80" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">may or may not matter to users</text><text x="320" y="18" class="figLabel" text-anchor="middle">SYMPTOM-BASED</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="240" y="30" width="160" height="30" rx="5"></rect><text x="320" y="50" class="boxText">error rate > 5%</text><text x="320" y="80" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">directly reflects real user impact</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Symptom-based alerts fire on what users actually feel; cause-based alerts can fire on harmless conditions.

frames.title: Cause-based alert (weaker):
frames.text: Cause-based alert (weaker): "CPU usage exceeded 80%" — might be totally fine (a scheduled batch job), or might not be — the alert alone can't tell you.

frames.title: Symptom-based alert (stronger):
frames.text: Symptom-based alert (stronger): "Error rate exceeded 5% for 5 minutes" — this directly reflects real user impact, regardless of the underlying cause.

frames.title: Add context to the alert.
frames.text: Add context to the alert. Include a link to the relevant dashboard and runbook directly in the notification, so the on-call engineer doesn't start from zero.

frames.title: Tune the threshold and duration
frames.text: Tune the threshold and duration (5 minutes, not 5 seconds) to avoid firing on brief, self-resolving blips that don't need a human response.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 420 120" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of an alert linking to both a dashboard showing current system state and a runbook providing concrete response steps, together enabling a fast guided incident response."><rect class="boxWarn" x="150" y="10" width="120" height="28" rx="5"></rect><text x="210" y="28" class="boxText">alert fires</text><line class="flow" x1="190" y1="38" x2="120" y2="65"></line><line class="flow" x1="230" y1="38" x2="300" y2="65"></line><rect class="box" x="40" y="70" width="140" height="30" rx="5"></rect><text x="110" y="90" class="boxText">dashboard: state</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="240" y="70" width="140" height="30" rx="5"></rect><text x="310" y="90" class="boxText">runbook: steps</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: An alert points to both what's happening now and exactly what to do about it.

frames.title: Alert fires:
frames.text: Alert fires: "checkout error rate > 5%," linking directly to both a dashboard and a runbook.

frames.title: Dashboard shows the picture.
frames.text: Dashboard shows the picture. Error rate spiked at 2:14 AM, correlated with a latency spike specifically in calls to the payments service.

frames.title: Runbook provides the steps.
frames.text: Runbook provides the steps. "If payments service latency is elevated: 1) check payments service's own dashboard, 2) check its upstream dependency (the card processor) status page, 3) if the processor is degraded, enable the fallback processor flag."

frames.title: On-call engineer follows the runbook
frames.text: On-call engineer follows the runbook and resolves the incident in minutes, instead of starting an investigation from zero.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 440 140" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of a trace timeline with nested spans, showing a gateway span containing an orders span, which contains a short inventory span and a much longer payments span that dominates the total request time."><rect class="box" x="20" y="15" width="400" height="24" rx="4"></rect><text x="30" y="31" class="boxText" style="font-size:10px">gateway — 1.2s</text><rect class="box" x="35" y="45" width="370" height="22" rx="4"></rect><text x="45" y="60" class="boxText" style="font-size:10px">orders — 1.1s</text><rect class="box" x="50" y="75" width="60" height="20" rx="3"></rect><text x="80" y="89" class="boxText" style="font-size:9px">inv 50ms</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="120" y="75" width="280" height="20" rx="3"></rect><text x="260" y="89" class="boxText" style="font-size:9px">payments — 980ms</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Nested spans render as a visual timeline — the dominant cost is immediately obvious.

frames.title: A slow checkout request
frames.text: A slow checkout request takes 1.2 seconds total — a metric flagged it, but not which part was slow.

frames.title: Pull up its trace.
frames.text: Pull up its trace. The root span (gateway) took 1.2s; its child span (orders service) took 1.1s of that.

frames.title: Drill into the orders span's children.
frames.text: Drill into the orders span's children. A call to the inventory service took just 50ms, but a call to the payments service took 980ms — clearly the dominant cost.

frames.title: Root cause is visually obvious
frames.text: Root cause is visually obvious from the timeline — payments service latency, not orders or inventory — without manually correlating separate log streams by hand.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 420 130" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of a TLS handshake where the client verifies the server's certificate and both agree on a shared secret using asymmetric cryptography, then switch to fast symmetric encryption for the rest of the connection."><rect class="box" x="20" y="20" width="90" height="28" rx="4"></rect><text x="65" y="38" class="boxText">client</text><rect class="box" x="310" y="20" width="90" height="28" rx="4"></rect><text x="355" y="38" class="boxText">server</text><line class="flow" x1="110" y1="34" x2="300" y2="34"></line><text x="210" y="24" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">handshake: verify cert, agree on secret</text><line class="flowMuted" x1="110" y1="80" x2="300" y2="80"></line><text x="210" y="70" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">encrypted traffic (fast, symmetric)</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: A brief asymmetric handshake establishes trust and a shared secret; fast symmetric encryption handles the rest.

frames.title: Client connects to https://bank.example.com.
frames.text: Client connects to https://bank.example.com. The server presents its TLS certificate.

frames.title: Client verifies the certificate
frames.text: Client verifies the certificate — is it signed by a trusted authority, is it unexpired, and does its domain name actually match bank.example.com?

frames.title: Handshake establishes a shared secret,
frames.text: Handshake establishes a shared secret, using asymmetric cryptography briefly for this one exchange.

frames.title: All further traffic is encrypted
frames.text: All further traffic is encrypted with fast symmetric encryption using that shared secret — safe from eavesdropping, and the client can trust it's really talking to the bank, not an impersonator.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 420 130" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of encrypted data on disk with the decryption key held separately in a key management service, so access to the raw storage alone is not enough to read the data."><rect class="box" x="30" y="45" width="150" height="40" rx="6"></rect><text x="105" y="70" class="boxText">encrypted data (disk)</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="250" y="45" width="140" height="40" rx="6"></rect><text x="320" y="70" class="boxText">key management svc</text><text x="210" y="30" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">held separately — one alone isn't enough</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Keeping keys separate from the data they protect means stolen storage alone isn't enough to read it.

frames.title: Database writes are encrypted
frames.text: Database writes are encrypted before being written to disk, using a key managed by a separate key management service (KMS) — not stored alongside the data.

frames.title: A backup of the database is taken
frames.text: A backup of the database is taken and stored in object storage — still encrypted, since the encryption happens at the storage layer, not per-backup.

frames.title: An attacker gains access to the raw storage
frames.text: An attacker gains access to the raw storage (a misconfigured bucket permission, say) — they get encrypted bytes, not usable data, without also compromising the separate KMS.

frames.title: An authorized application requests decryption
frames.text: An authorized application requests decryption through the KMS, which enforces its own access controls and audit logging on every key use.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 420 120" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of a service authenticating to a centralized secrets manager at runtime to retrieve a credential, instead of having that credential hardcoded or stored in a config file."><rect class="box" x="30" y="45" width="120" height="30" rx="5"></rect><text x="90" y="65" class="boxText">service</text><line class="flow" x1="150" y1="60" x2="250" y2="60"></line><text x="200" y="45" class="figHint">authenticated request</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="260" y="45" width="140" height="30" rx="5"></rect><text x="330" y="65" class="boxText">secrets manager</text><text x="200" y="95" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">no secret ever lives in source code or a config file</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Secrets are fetched at runtime through an authenticated, audited request — never hardcoded.

frames.title: A service needs a database password.
frames.text: A service needs a database password. Instead of it being hardcoded, the service authenticates to the secrets manager at startup and requests it.

frames.title: Secrets manager verifies the service's identity
frames.text: Secrets manager verifies the service's identity and returns the current password, logging the access.

frames.title: The password needs to rotate
frames.text: The password needs to rotate (routine security practice, or in response to a suspected leak). A new password is generated and the old one retired in the secrets manager.

frames.title: Services pick up the new value
frames.text: Services pick up the new value on their next request to the secrets manager — no code change or manual credential distribution needed.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 420 120" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of a password combined with a unique random salt and run through a deliberately slow hashing algorithm, with only the resulting salt and hash stored, never the original password."><rect class="box" x="20" y="45" width="90" height="28" rx="4"></rect><text x="65" y="63" class="boxText">password</text><rect class="box" x="20" y="80" width="90" height="24" rx="4"></rect><text x="65" y="96" class="boxText">salt</text><line class="flow" x1="110" y1="55" x2="170" y2="65"></line><line class="flow" x1="110" y1="90" x2="170" y2="70"></line><rect class="boxAccent" x="180" y="50" width="110" height="34" rx="5"></rect><text x="235" y="72" class="boxText">slow hash</text><line class="flow" x1="290" y1="67" x2="330" y2="67"></line><rect class="box" x="340" y="52" width="70" height="30" rx="4"></rect><text x="375" y="71" class="boxText">stored</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: A unique salt and a deliberately slow hash — the original password is never stored anywhere.

frames.title: User creates a password.
frames.text: User creates a password. A unique random salt is generated for this user.

frames.title: Hash with a slow algorithm.
frames.text: Hash with a slow algorithm. The password and salt are combined and hashed with bcrypt (or similar) — deliberately taking a noticeable fraction of a second.

frames.title: Store only the salt and hash
frames.text: Store only the salt and hash — never the original password.

frames.title: Login later:
frames.text: Login later: re-hash the entered password with the stored salt, and compare to the stored hash. If the database is later stolen, an attacker faces the same slow hashing cost for every single guess, against every single unique salt.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 420 130" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of users assigned to roles, with each role holding a defined set of permissions, so changing a role's permissions updates every user assigned to it at once."><rect class="box" x="20" y="20" width="80" height="26" rx="4"></rect><rect class="box" x="20" y="54" width="80" height="26" rx="4"></rect><rect class="box" x="20" y="88" width="80" height="26" rx="4"></rect><text x="60" y="38" class="boxText" text-anchor="middle">Alice</text><text x="60" y="72" class="boxText" text-anchor="middle">Bob</text><text x="60" y="106" class="boxText" text-anchor="middle">Carol</text><line class="flow" x1="100" y1="33" x2="170" y2="60"></line><line class="flow" x1="100" y1="67" x2="170" y2="90"></line><line class="flow" x1="100" y1="101" x2="170" y2="35"></line><rect class="boxAccent" x="180" y="20" width="90" height="26" rx="4"></rect><rect class="boxAccent" x="180" y="54" width="90" height="26" rx="4"></rect><rect class="boxAccent" x="180" y="88" width="90" height="26" rx="4"></rect><text x="225" y="38" class="boxText" text-anchor="middle">Editor</text><text x="225" y="72" class="boxText" text-anchor="middle">Viewer</text><text x="225" y="106" class="boxText" text-anchor="middle">Admin</text><text x="340" y="65" class="figHint">roles hold the actual permissions</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Permissions attach to roles, not individuals — changing a role updates everyone assigned to it.

frames.title: Define roles.
frames.text: Define roles. "Viewer" can read documents; "Editor" can read and write; "Admin" can read, write, and manage users.

frames.title: Assign users to roles.
frames.text: Assign users to roles. Alice is an Editor; Bob is a Viewer; Carol is an Admin.

frames.title: Alice gets promoted
frames.text: Alice gets promoted to a role needing admin access — she's reassigned from Editor to Admin. Her new permissions take effect immediately, with no per-permission editing required.

frames.title: Policy changes org-wide.
frames.text: Policy changes org-wide. "Editors should no longer be able to delete documents" — one change to the Editor role's permissions updates every Editor simultaneously.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 440 140" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of a user redirected from a service provider to an identity provider to log in, receiving a signed assertion that is carried back to the service provider, which verifies it and grants access."><rect class="box" x="20" y="50" width="80" height="30" rx="5"></rect><text x="60" y="70" class="boxText">user</text><line class="flow" x1="100" y1="60" x2="150" y2="35"></line><text x="125" y="30" class="figHint">redirect</text><rect class="box" x="160" y="15" width="110" height="30" rx="5"></rect><text x="215" y="35" class="boxText">identity provider</text><line class="flow" x1="270" y1="30" x2="330" y2="30" style="opacity:0"></line><line class="flow" x1="215" y1="45" x2="100" y2="90"></line><text x="150" y="90" class="figHint">signed assertion</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="160" y="95" width="140" height="30" rx="5"></rect><text x="230" y="115" class="boxText">service provider</text><line class="flow" x1="100" y1="70" x2="160" y2="105"></line></svg>
diagrams.caption: The identity provider authenticates once and vouches for the user via a signed assertion the application trusts.

frames.title: User opens a work application
frames.text: User opens a work application (the SP) and isn't logged in yet.

frames.title: SP redirects to the IdP
frames.text: SP redirects to the IdP (the company's central login system).

frames.title: User logs in at the IdP
frames.text: User logs in at the IdP — often with multi-factor authentication — and the IdP creates a signed SAML assertion confirming their identity.

frames.title: Browser carries the assertion back to the SP,
frames.text: Browser carries the assertion back to the SP, which verifies its signature and logs the user in — the application never saw or handled the user's actual password at any point.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 460 140" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of three layers: System Design Fundamentals providing building blocks, High Level Design combining them into an architecture, and Low Level Design detailing the inside of one component."><rect class="box" x="15" y="55" width="130" height="40" rx="6"></rect><text x="80" y="80" class="boxText">Fundamentals</text><line class="flow" x1="145" y1="75" x2="195" y2="75"></line><rect class="boxAccent" x="200" y="45" width="140" height="55" rx="6"></rect><text x="270" y="77" class="boxText">High Level Design</text><line class="flow" x1="340" y1="75" x2="390" y2="75"></line><rect class="box" x="395" y="55" width="55" height="40" rx="6"></rect><text x="422" y="80" class="boxText" style="font-size:9px">LLD</text><text x="270" y="30" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">this course lives here</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: HLD sits between the individual concepts you already know and the class-level detail of a single component.

frames.title: Clarified requirements.
frames.text: Clarified requirements. Reserve a spot ahead of time, pay on entry, support three garage sizes — explicitly out of scope: dynamic pricing.

frames.title: Rough capacity numbers.
frames.text: Rough capacity numbers. 50 garages, 2,000 spots each, peak 10 reservations/sec across the fleet — small enough that a single relational database is plausible.

frames.title: A handful of APIs and a data model.
frames.text: A handful of APIs and a data model. POST /reservations, GET /garages/{id}/availability, and a Garage / Spot / Reservation schema.

frames.title: A box diagram.
frames.text: A box diagram. API service, a Postgres database, and a cache for availability lookups — nothing more, because the numbers didn’t justify more.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 460 150" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of a pipeline of six sections: Foundations, Scalability, Data Layer, Distributed Systems, Reliability and Operations, converging into Case Studies."><rect class="box" x="10" y="20" width="78" height="34" rx="5"></rect><rect class="box" x="98" y="20" width="78" height="34" rx="5"></rect><rect class="box" x="186" y="20" width="78" height="34" rx="5"></rect><rect class="box" x="274" y="20" width="78" height="34" rx="5"></rect><rect class="box" x="362" y="20" width="78" height="34" rx="5"></rect><text x="49" y="41" class="boxText" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:8px">Foundations</text><text x="137" y="41" class="boxText" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:8px">Scalability</text><text x="225" y="41" class="boxText" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:8px">Data Layer</text><text x="313" y="41" class="boxText" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:8px">Dist. Systems</text><text x="401" y="41" class="boxText" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:8px">Reliability / Ops</text><line class="flow" x1="88" y1="37" x2="98" y2="37"></line><line class="flow" x1="176" y1="37" x2="186" y2="37"></line><line class="flow" x1="264" y1="37" x2="274" y2="37"></line><line class="flow" x1="352" y1="37" x2="362" y2="37"></line><line class="flow" x1="230" y1="54" x2="230" y2="90"></line><rect class="boxAccent" x="150" y="95" width="160" height="36" rx="6"></rect><text x="230" y="117" class="boxText">Case Studies</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Each section is a tool; Case Studies is where every tool gets used together.

frames.title: Asked to design something small and read-heavy?
frames.text: Asked to design something small and read-heavy? Lean hardest on Scalability (caching, CDNs) and Data Layer (replication).

frames.title: Asked to design something with heavy writes and coordination?
frames.text: Asked to design something with heavy writes and coordination? Lean hardest on Distributed Systems (consistent hashing, message queues, leader election).

frames.title: Asked “what happens if this component goes down”?
frames.text: Asked “what happens if this component goes down”? That’s Reliability — failover, circuit breakers, retries.

frames.title: Asked to walk through a full design end-to-end?
frames.text: Asked to walk through a full design end-to-end? That’s exactly the shape of the Case Studies section.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 420 130" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of a four-step loop: clarify, estimate, define, and build, arranged in a cycle with arrows connecting each step to the next."><g><rect class="box" x="15" y="7" width="90" height="36" rx="6"></rect><text x="60" y="30" class="boxText" text-anchor="middle">Clarify</text></g><g><rect class="box" x="255" y="7" width="90" height="36" rx="6"></rect><text x="300" y="30" class="boxText" text-anchor="middle">Estimate</text></g><g><rect class="box" x="255" y="72" width="90" height="36" rx="6"></rect><text x="300" y="95" class="boxText" text-anchor="middle">Define</text></g><g><rect class="boxAccent" x="15" y="72" width="90" height="36" rx="6"></rect><text x="60" y="95" class="boxText" text-anchor="middle">Build</text></g><line class="flow" x1="105" y1="25" x2="255" y2="25"></line><line class="flow" x1="300" y1="43" x2="300" y2="72"></line><line class="flow" x1="255" y1="90" x2="105" y2="90"></line></svg>
diagrams.caption: The same four-step loop applies whether the prompt is a URL shortener or a global chat platform.

frames.title: Clarify.
frames.text: Clarify. Custom aliases needed? Analytics needed? Assume: no custom aliases, basic click count is enough.

frames.title: Estimate.
frames.text: Estimate. 100M new URLs/month, 100:1 read-to-write ratio — reads dominate, so the design should optimize for fast redirects over write throughput.

frames.title: Define.
frames.text: Define. POST /urls, GET /{code}, and a single ShortUrl(code, longUrl, createdAt) record.

frames.title: Build.
frames.text: Build. Because reads dominate, add a cache in front of the database from the start — a decision justified by step 2, not assumed upfront.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 460 130" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of three concentric boxes: Fundamentals as isolated concepts, High Level Design as those concepts applied to one system's components, and Low Level Design as the detail inside one component."><rect class="box" x="20" y="20" width="420" height="95" rx="10"></rect><text x="40" y="38" class="figLabel" style="text-anchor:start">FUNDAMENTALS: isolated concepts</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="45" y="48" width="370" height="55" rx="8"></rect><text x="65" y="65" class="figLabel" style="text-anchor:start;fill:var(--text)">HLD: components + APIs for THIS system</text><rect class="box" x="70" y="75" width="150" height="20" rx="5"></rect><text x="145" y="89" class="boxText" style="font-size:8px">LLD: inside one box</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: HLD applies isolated concepts to one system's components; LLD zooms into just one of those boxes.

frames.title: The idea
frames.text: High Level Design answers “what are the major pieces, and how do they talk to each other” — nothing about exact classes, and nothing about isolated theory without a specific problem attached.

frames.title: The mechanism
frames.text: HLD output is a small number of components (services, databases, caches, queues), the APIs between them, and the data each one owns — typically drawn as boxes and arrows. It deliberately stops before class diagrams, method signatures, or specific concurrency handling inside one box — that detail is Low Level Design’s job. It also goes beyond naming a concept in isolation (that’s the Fundamentals course); HLD always answers for this specific system.

frames.title: In practice
frames.text: For the prompt “design a rate limiter,” contrast the three layers:

frames.title: Remember
frames.text: HLD is theory applied to one specific system, stopping at the boundary of components and their contracts — one level more concrete than Fundamentals, one level less detailed than LLD.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 420 130" role="img" aria-label="Funnel diagram narrowing a broad prompt through functional and non-functional clarifying questions down to a concrete, agreed scope."><path class="box" d="M20 20 L400 20 L280 60 L280 100 L140 100 L140 60 Z"></path><text x="210" y="15" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">broad prompt</text><text x="210" y="45" class="boxText" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:9px">+ functional questions</text><text x="210" y="80" class="boxText" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:9px">+ non-functional questions</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="140" y="105" width="140" height="20" rx="4"></rect><text x="210" y="119" class="boxText" style="font-size:8px">agreed scope</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Clarifying questions narrow an open-ended prompt down to a scope small enough to actually design.

frames.title: Start broad.
frames.text: Start broad. “Design Twitter” — too large to design directly.

frames.title: Ask functional questions.
frames.text: Ask functional questions. Does it need posting, following, and a timeline? Are retweets and likes in scope? Agree: posting, following, and a timeline; skip likes and retweets for now.

frames.title: Ask non-functional questions.
frames.text: Ask non-functional questions. How many users? Is the timeline allowed to be a few seconds stale? Agree: 50M users, timeline can be eventually consistent.

frames.title: State the narrowed scope back.
frames.text: State the narrowed scope back. “So we’re designing posting, following, and an eventually-consistent timeline for 50M users” — now there’s something concrete to design.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 640 200" role="img" aria-label="100M URLs / month, ≈ 40 writes / sec, 100:1 read/write, ≈ 4,000 reads / sec, 1.2B records / year, ≈ 600 GB raw / year"><rect class="boxAccent" x="15" y="15" width="190" height="70" rx="8"/><text class="boxText" x="110" y="55">100M URLs / month</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="225" y="15" width="190" height="70" rx="8"/><text class="boxText" x="320" y="55">≈ 40 writes / sec</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="435" y="15" width="190" height="70" rx="8"/><text class="boxText" x="530" y="55">100:1 read/write</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="15" y="110" width="190" height="70" rx="8"/><text class="boxText" x="110" y="150">≈ 4,000 reads / sec</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="225" y="110" width="190" height="70" rx="8"/><text class="boxText" x="320" y="150">1.2B records / year</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="435" y="110" width="190" height="70" rx="8"/><text class="boxText" x="530" y="150">≈ 600 GB raw / year</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Estimate requests, read/write ratio, and storage independently. These numbers exclude replica and index overhead.

frames.title: The idea
frames.text: Rough back-of-envelope math — how many requests per second, how much data per year — decides whether a single server is plenty or a distributed system is unavoidable, well before any component gets drawn.

frames.title: The mechanism
frames.text: Capacity estimation converts a user count into three numbers that actually drive design decisions: queries per second (does this need one server or a fleet behind a load balancer?), storage growth (does this fit on one disk, or does it need sharding within a year?), and bandwidth (is this text-sized or video-sized traffic?). The goal is the right order of magnitude — thousands vs. millions vs. billions — not a precise figure.

frames.title: In practice
frames.text: Estimating for a URL shortener with 100M new URLs created per month:

frames.title: Remember
frames.text: Capacity estimation turns “is this a big system?” into concrete numbers that justify — or rule out — specific architecture decisions later in the design.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 420 110" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of a client calling two coarse-grained APIs, POST /urls and GET /code, both operating on a single ShortUrl data model."><rect class="box" x="20" y="35" width="90" height="34" rx="6"></rect><text x="65" y="57" class="boxText">Client</text><line class="flow" x1="110" y1="45" x2="180" y2="45"></line><text x="145" y="35" class="figHint" style="font-size:8px">POST /urls</text><line class="flow" x1="110" y1="60" x2="180" y2="60"></line><text x="145" y="80" class="figHint" style="font-size:8px">GET /code</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="190" y="30" width="120" height="44" rx="6"></rect><text x="250" y="56" class="boxText">API service</text><line class="flow" x1="310" y1="52" x2="360" y2="52"></line><rect class="box" x="365" y="30" width="45" height="44" rx="6"></rect><text x="387" y="56" class="boxText" style="font-size:8px">ShortUrl</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Two coarse APIs and one entity are enough to satisfy the stated requirements.

frames.title: Start from the functional requirements.
frames.text: Start from the functional requirements. A URL shortener needs to create a short URL and resolve one back to its original.

frames.title: Write the APIs.
frames.text: Write the APIs. POST /urls { longUrl } → returns a code; GET /{code} → redirects to the original URL.

frames.title: Draft the data model.
frames.text: Draft the data model. A single ShortUrl entity: code, longUrl, createdAt, and a click count.

frames.title: Check it against requirements.
frames.text: Check it against requirements. Every functional requirement maps to exactly one API call and touches exactly this one entity — nothing is missing, nothing extra was added.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 440 110" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of a client calling an API service, which checks a cache before falling back to a database, each box justified by a specific requirement or estimate."><rect class="box" x="10" y="35" width="80" height="34" rx="6"></rect><text x="50" y="57" class="boxText">Client</text><line class="flow" x1="90" y1="52" x2="140" y2="52"></line><rect class="boxAccent" x="145" y="30" width="100" height="44" rx="6"></rect><text x="195" y="56" class="boxText">API service</text><line class="flow" x1="245" y1="45" x2="290" y2="45"></line><text x="267" y="38" class="figHint" style="font-size:8px">check</text><rect class="box" x="295" y="20" width="70" height="30" rx="5"></rect><text x="330" y="39" class="boxText" style="font-size:9px">Cache</text><line class="flow" x1="245" y1="65" x2="290" y2="65"></line><text x="267" y="80" class="figHint" style="font-size:8px">fallback</text><rect class="box" x="295" y="60" width="70" height="30" rx="5"></rect><text x="330" y="79" class="boxText" style="font-size:9px">DB</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Every box in the diagram is present because a requirement or an estimate specifically justified it.

frames.title: Start from the API service and data model
frames.text: Start from the API service and data model already defined — that’s always the first box.

frames.title: Check the estimate.
frames.text: Check the estimate. Earlier estimation showed reads far outnumber writes — that justifies adding a cache in front of the database.

frames.title: Check for anything else the estimate implies.
frames.text: Check for anything else the estimate implies. Write volume was low, so a message queue isn’t justified yet — it stays out of the diagram.

frames.title: Draw the final box diagram.
frames.text: Draw the final box diagram. Client → API service → cache → database, with each box present for a stated reason.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 440 130" role="img" aria-label="Diagram contrasting vertical scaling, one machine growing larger, against horizontal scaling, many identical machines behind a load balancer."><text x="100" y="18" class="figLabel" text-anchor="middle">VERTICAL</text><rect class="box" x="60" y="30" width="80" height="60" rx="8"></rect><text x="100" y="65" class="boxText">bigger box</text><text x="330" y="18" class="figLabel" text-anchor="middle">HORIZONTAL</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="290" y="25" width="80" height="24" rx="5"></rect><text x="330" y="41" class="boxText" style="font-size:9px">LB</text><line class="flow" x1="330" y1="49" x2="330" y2="60"></line><rect class="box" x="260" y="65" width="35" height="28" rx="5"></rect><rect class="box" x="305" y="65" width="35" height="28" rx="5"></rect><rect class="box" x="350" y="65" width="35" height="28" rx="5"></rect></svg>
diagrams.caption: Vertical scaling grows one machine; horizontal scaling adds more machines behind a load balancer.

frames.title: Estimate says 40 writes/sec, 4,000 reads/sec.
frames.text: Estimate says 40 writes/sec, 4,000 reads/sec. That’s well within a single well-specified server’s capacity — vertical scaling (a bigger box) is the simplest correct answer for now.

frames.title: Traffic grows 100×.
frames.text: Traffic grows 100×. No single machine, however large, comfortably serves 400,000 reads/sec — the design now needs horizontal scaling.

frames.title: Make the API service stateless.
frames.text: Make the API service stateless. Move session data out of the process (into a shared cache) so any instance can serve any request.

frames.title: Add a load balancer
frames.text: Add a load balancer in front of a fleet of identical instances, and the design now scales by adding more boxes rather than a bigger one.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 420 130" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of a load balancer distributing requests across three service instances, with a health check line to each and one instance marked unhealthy and removed from rotation."><rect class="box" x="20" y="45" width="70" height="34" rx="6"></rect><text x="55" y="67" class="boxText">Client</text><line class="flow" x1="90" y1="62" x2="140" y2="62"></line><rect class="boxAccent" x="150" y="47" width="70" height="30" rx="6"></rect><text x="185" y="66" class="boxText" style="font-size:9px">LB</text><line class="flow" x1="220" y1="55" x2="270" y2="25"></line><line class="flow" x1="220" y1="62" x2="270" y2="62"></line><line class="flowMuted" x1="220" y1="70" x2="270" y2="100"></line><rect class="box" x="275" y="10" width="60" height="26" rx="5"></rect><text x="305" y="27" class="boxText" style="font-size:8px">node A</text><rect class="box" x="275" y="49" width="60" height="26" rx="5"></rect><text x="305" y="66" class="boxText" style="font-size:8px">node B</text><rect class="boxWarn" x="275" y="88" width="60" height="26" rx="5"></rect><text x="305" y="105" class="boxText" style="font-size:8px">unhealthy</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: The load balancer stops routing to an unhealthy node as soon as its health checks start failing.

frames.title: Traffic outgrows one instance.
frames.text: Traffic outgrows one instance. Three identical API service instances are deployed to share the load.

frames.title: It health-checks each instance
frames.text: It health-checks each instance every few seconds, routing only to instances that respond successfully.

frames.title: One instance crashes.
frames.text: One instance crashes. The load balancer stops sending it traffic within one health-check interval — clients notice nothing beyond a brief blip.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 420 120" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of a read request checking a cache first, returning immediately on a hit, or falling through to the database and populating the cache on a miss."><rect class="box" x="20" y="45" width="70" height="30" rx="5"></rect><text x="55" y="64" class="boxText">Request</text><line class="flow" x1="90" y1="60" x2="150" y2="60"></line><rect class="boxAccent" x="160" y="45" width="70" height="30" rx="5"></rect><text x="195" y="64" class="boxText" style="font-size:9px">Cache</text><line class="flow" x1="230" y1="52" x2="200" y2="20"></line><text x="235" y="22" class="figHint" style="font-size:8px">hit → return</text><line class="flowMuted" x1="230" y1="68" x2="300" y2="68"></line><text x="265" y="85" class="figHint" style="font-size:8px">miss</text><rect class="box" x="305" y="53" width="70" height="30" rx="5"></rect><text x="340" y="72" class="boxText" style="font-size:9px">Database</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: A cache hit skips the database entirely; a miss falls through and refills the cache for next time.

frames.title: Estimate shows 4,000 reads/sec against 40 writes/sec
frames.text: Estimate shows 4,000 reads/sec against 40 writes/sec for URL redirects — a strong signal to cache.

frames.title: On a redirect request,
frames.text: On a redirect request, check the cache first for that short code.

frames.title: Cache hit:
frames.text: Cache hit: return the long URL immediately, without touching the database.

frames.title: Cache miss:
frames.text: Cache miss: read from the database, return the result, and populate the cache so the next request for that code is fast too.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 440 130" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of users in different regions being served by nearby CDN edge nodes, which fetch from a single origin server only on a cache miss."><rect class="boxAccent" x="180" y="50" width="80" height="30" rx="5"></rect><text x="220" y="69" class="boxText" style="font-size:9px">Origin</text><g><rect class="box" x="10" y="5" width="60" height="26" rx="5"></rect><text x="40" y="23" class="boxText" style="font-size:7px">edge 1</text><line class="flowMuted" x1="40" y1="31" x2="220" y2="65"></line></g><g><rect class="box" x="350" y="5" width="60" height="26" rx="5"></rect><text x="380" y="23" class="boxText" style="font-size:7px">edge 2</text><line class="flowMuted" x1="380" y1="31" x2="220" y2="65"></line></g><g><rect class="box" x="10" y="85" width="60" height="26" rx="5"></rect><text x="40" y="103" class="boxText" style="font-size:7px">edge 3</text><line class="flowMuted" x1="40" y1="85" x2="220" y2="65"></line></g><g><rect class="box" x="350" y="85" width="60" height="26" rx="5"></rect><text x="380" y="103" class="boxText" style="font-size:7px">edge 4</text><line class="flowMuted" x1="380" y1="85" x2="220" y2="65"></line></g></svg>
diagrams.caption: Edge nodes serve most requests locally, falling back to the origin only when their cache misses.

frames.title: A video platform serves thumbnails
frames.text: A video platform serves thumbnails to users worldwide from a single origin data center.

frames.title: Users far from that data center
frames.text: Users far from that data center experience noticeably higher latency loading thumbnails than users nearby.

frames.title: Put a CDN in front of thumbnail URLs.
frames.text: Put a CDN in front of thumbnail URLs. The first request in a region pulls from origin and caches at the nearby edge node.

frames.title: Every subsequent request in that region
frames.text: Every subsequent request in that region is served from the edge node directly — faster for users, and far less load reaching the origin.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 440 120" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of an API service responding immediately to the client while placing a slow job on a queue, which background workers process independently."><rect class="box" x="15" y="45" width="70" height="30" rx="5"></rect><text x="50" y="64" class="boxText">Client</text><line class="flow" x1="85" y1="55" x2="140" y2="55"></line><rect class="boxAccent" x="145" y="40" width="90" height="30" rx="5"></rect><text x="190" y="59" class="boxText" style="font-size:9px">API service</text><line class="flow" x1="235" y1="45" x2="85" y2="30"></line><text x="160" y="20" class="figHint" style="font-size:8px">immediate response</text><line class="flow" x1="235" y1="60" x2="290" y2="60"></line><text x="262" y="80" class="figHint" style="font-size:7px">enqueue</text><rect class="box" x="295" y="45" width="60" height="30" rx="5"></rect><text x="325" y="64" class="boxText" style="font-size:8px">Queue</text><line class="flow" x1="355" y1="60" x2="400" y2="60"></line><rect class="box" x="360" y="90" width="70" height="26" rx="5"></rect><text x="395" y="107" class="boxText" style="font-size:7px">Worker</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: The client gets an immediate response while a queue and background workers handle the slow work.

frames.title: A user uploads a video.
frames.text: A user uploads a video. The upload itself must be synchronous — the user is waiting for confirmation it succeeded.

frames.title: Thumbnail generation and transcoding are slow
frames.text: Thumbnail generation and transcoding are slow (seconds to minutes) and don’t need to block that confirmation.

frames.title: The API service enqueues a “process video” job
frames.text: The API service enqueues a “process video” job and immediately responds “upload received.”

frames.title: A pool of background workers
frames.text: A pool of background workers pulls jobs off the queue, transcodes the video, and updates its status when done — independently of the original request.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 420 110" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of a request pipeline where a scaled API layer feeds into a single unscaled database, with the database marked as the bottleneck limiting overall throughput."><text x="130" y="18" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle">scaled, plenty of capacity</text><rect class="box" x="20" y="25" width="65" height="26" rx="5"></rect><rect class="box" x="100" y="25" width="65" height="26" rx="5"></rect><rect class="box" x="180" y="25" width="65" height="26" rx="5"></rect><line class="flow" x1="130" y1="51" x2="250" y2="80"></line><line class="flow" x1="210" y1="51" x2="250" y2="80"></line><line class="flow" x1="290" y1="51" x2="270" y2="80"></line><rect class="boxWarn" x="230" y="82" width="100" height="26" rx="5"></rect><text x="280" y="99" class="boxText" style="font-size:8px">DB: bottleneck</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Scaling the layer above a bottleneck doesn't help until the bottleneck itself is fixed.

frames.title: API service is scaled to 20 instances,
frames.text: API service is scaled to 20 instances, but overall throughput hasn’t improved as expected.

frames.title: Trace a slow request end-to-end.
frames.text: Trace a slow request end-to-end. Nearly all of its time is spent waiting on a single database query.

frames.title: Inspect that query.
frames.text: Inspect that query. It’s scanning a full table because the column it filters on isn’t indexed.

frames.title: Add the index.
frames.text: Add the index. The database, the true bottleneck, speeds up dramatically — and only then does adding more API instances actually help.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 440 120" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of one application with three different access patterns, each routed to a different datastore chosen specifically for that pattern: relational for orders, key-value for cart counts, and search index for product search."><rect class="boxAccent" x="180" y="45" width="80" height="30" rx="5"></rect><text x="220" y="64" class="boxText" style="font-size:9px">App</text><line class="flow" x1="180" y1="55" x2="60" y2="25"></line><line class="flow" x1="260" y1="55" x2="380" y2="25"></line><line class="flow" x1="220" y1="75" x2="220" y2="95"></line><rect class="box" x="15" y="10" width="90" height="26" rx="5"></rect><text x="60" y="27" class="boxText" style="font-size:8px">Relational</text><rect class="box" x="335" y="10" width="90" height="26" rx="5"></rect><text x="380" y="27" class="boxText" style="font-size:8px">Search index</text><rect class="box" x="175" y="98" width="90" height="22" rx="5"></rect><text x="220" y="113" class="boxText" style="font-size:8px">Key-value</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Three access patterns, three datastores, each chosen specifically for the pattern it serves.

frames.title: An orders system
frames.text: An orders system needs orders, line items, and customers, with joins between them and strict correctness on totals — a relational database fits well.

frames.title: The same product also needs product search by keyword
frames.text: The same product also needs product search by keyword — a relational database is a poor fit for full-text ranking, so a dedicated search index is added alongside it.

frames.title: It also needs a live “items in cart” count per user,
frames.text: It also needs a live “items in cart” count per user, a simple, extremely high-volume key lookup — a key-value store fits better than routing that through the relational database.

frames.title: The result is three datastores,
frames.text: The result is three datastores, each chosen for one access pattern, not one database stretched to cover all three.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 420 100" role="img" aria-label="Diagram positioning SQL databases toward strong consistency and joins, and NoSQL databases toward flexible schema and horizontal scale, as two ends of one spectrum."><line class="divider" x1="30" y1="55" x2="390" y2="55"></line><rect class="boxAccent" x="20" y="25" width="110" height="30" rx="5"></rect><text x="75" y="44" class="boxText" style="font-size:8px">SQL: consistency, joins</text><rect class="box" x="290" y="25" width="110" height="30" rx="5"></rect><text x="345" y="44" class="boxText" style="font-size:8px">NoSQL: flexible, scale</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Most real designs sit closer to one end for a given piece of data, not at a single fixed point for the whole system.

frames.title: The idea
frames.text: “SQL or NoSQL” isn’t really one decision — it’s shorthand for a handful of narrower trade-offs around consistency, schema flexibility, and how the data will scale.

frames.title: The mechanism
frames.text: Relational (SQL) databases give strong consistency, transactions across multiple rows and tables, and a fixed schema that catches structural mistakes early — well suited to data where correctness and relationships matter (money, inventory, anything with joins). NoSQL databases (document, key-value, wide-column) trade some of that rigor for flexible schemas and horizontal scalability that’s often easier to reach — well suited to high-volume, loosely-structured data where a single entity is looked up on its own, not joined across many tables.

frames.title: In practice
frames.text: Debits and credits must balance exactly, across multiple rows, inside one transaction — a relational database’s guarantees are exactly what this needs.

frames.title: Remember
frames.text: Ask the SQL-vs-NoSQL question per entity, driven by whether that entity needs strong cross-row consistency or benefits more from flexible schema and easier horizontal scale.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 420 110" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of a primary database streaming writes to two replicas, with writes going only to the primary and reads spread across all three."><rect class="boxAccent" x="170" y="15" width="90" height="30" rx="5"></rect><text x="215" y="34" class="boxText" style="font-size:9px">Primary</text><line class="flow" x1="200" y1="45" x2="100" y2="75"></line><line class="flow" x1="240" y1="45" x2="330" y2="75"></line><rect class="box" x="55" y="78" width="90" height="28" rx="5"></rect><text x="100" y="96" class="boxText" style="font-size:8px">Replica A</text><rect class="box" x="285" y="78" width="90" height="28" rx="5"></rect><text x="330" y="96" class="boxText" style="font-size:8px">Replica B</text><text x="215" y="60" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:8px">writes replicate down</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Writes flow only to the primary; replicas take reads and stand ready to be promoted.

frames.title: Estimate shows heavy read traffic
frames.text: Estimate shows heavy read traffic against a single database instance already near its limit.

frames.title: Add two read replicas.
frames.text: Add two read replicas. All writes still go to the primary; reads are spread across the replicas.

frames.title: The primary fails.
frames.text: The primary fails. One replica is promoted to primary, and the design keeps serving writes within seconds instead of going fully down.

frames.title: A user updates their profile, then immediately reloads it
frames.text: A user updates their profile, then immediately reloads it from a replica that hasn’t caught up yet — they briefly see the old value, a direct consequence of replication lag.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 420 110" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of a router directing each user's data to one of three shards based on a hash of their user ID, with each shard holding only its own slice of the data."><rect class="box" x="20" y="40" width="70" height="30" rx="5"></rect><text x="55" y="59" class="boxText" style="font-size:9px">Request</text><line class="flow" x1="90" y1="55" x2="140" y2="55"></line><rect class="boxAccent" x="150" y="40" width="70" height="30" rx="5"></rect><text x="185" y="59" class="boxText" style="font-size:8px">hash(userId)</text><line class="flow" x1="220" y1="45" x2="270" y2="20"></line><line class="flow" x1="220" y1="55" x2="270" y2="55"></line><line class="flow" x1="220" y1="65" x2="270" y2="90"></line><rect class="box" x="275" y="5" width="70" height="26" rx="5"></rect><rect class="box" x="275" y="45" width="70" height="26" rx="5"></rect><rect class="box" x="275" y="85" width="70" height="26" rx="5"></rect><text x="310" y="22" class="boxText" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:8px">Shard 1</text><text x="310" y="62" class="boxText" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:8px">Shard 2</text><text x="310" y="102" class="boxText" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:8px">Shard 3</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Each record lives on exactly one shard, chosen by hashing the shard key.

frames.title: A single database can no longer hold
frames.text: A single database can no longer hold the full user dataset, even with read replicas absorbing read traffic.

frames.title: Pick a shard key.
frames.text: Pick a shard key. Almost every query in this design looks up data by user ID — user ID is the natural shard key.

frames.title: Route each user’s data
frames.text: Route each user’s data to one of N shards based on a hash of their user ID.

frames.title: A query for “this user’s data”
frames.text: A query for “this user’s data” now goes to exactly one shard — but a query like “all users in this city” now has to fan out across every shard, a direct cost of this shard key choice.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 420 100" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of one large table split into monthly partitions inside a single database, with a query for a recent date range touching only the relevant partition."><rect class="box" x="20" y="30" width="380" height="40" rx="6"></rect><line class="divider" x1="115" y1="30" x2="115" y2="70"></line><line class="divider" x1="210" y1="30" x2="210" y2="70"></line><line class="divider" x1="305" y1="30" x2="305" y2="70"></line><line class="divider" x1="400" y1="30" x2="400" y2="70"></line><text x="67" y="53" class="boxText" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:9px">Jan</text><text x="162" y="53" class="boxText" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:9px">Feb</text><text x="257" y="53" class="boxText" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:9px">Mar</text><text x="352" y="53" class="boxText" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:9px">Apr</text><text x="447" y="53" class="boxText" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:9px">May</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="20" y="30" width="95" height="40" rx="0" style="opacity:0.35"></rect><text x="67" y="20" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:8px">query touches only this partition</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: A query scoped to one month scans only that partition, not the whole table.

frames.title: An events table grows by millions of rows a day,
frames.text: An events table grows by millions of rows a day, and queries for “last week’s events” are getting slower as the table grows.

frames.title: Partition the table by month.
frames.text: Partition the table by month. Each month’s events live in their own partition, still inside the same database.

frames.title: A query for last week’s events
frames.text: A query for last week’s events now only scans this month’s partition, ignoring years of older data entirely.

frames.title: Old partitions (say, over a year old)
frames.text: Old partitions (say, over a year old) can be archived to cold storage or dropped, without touching the current, actively-queried partition at all.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 420 100" role="img" aria-label="Diagram positioning strong consistency toward correctness at the cost of latency, and eventual consistency toward availability and speed at the cost of a brief staleness window."><line class="divider" x1="30" y1="55" x2="390" y2="55"></line><rect class="boxAccent" x="20" y="25" width="130" height="30" rx="5"></rect><text x="85" y="44" class="boxText" style="font-size:8px">Strong: correct, slower</text><rect class="box" x="270" y="25" width="130" height="30" rx="5"></rect><text x="335" y="44" class="boxText" style="font-size:8px">Eventual: fast, briefly stale</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Every piece of data sits somewhere on this spectrum — the choice should be explicit, not accidental.

frames.title: The idea
frames.text: Once data lives in more than one place — a replica, a cache, a second data center — the design has to decide, deliberately, how quickly those copies are allowed to agree.

frames.title: The mechanism
frames.text: Strong consistency guarantees every read sees the latest write, immediately — simpler to reason about, but it usually costs latency or availability to guarantee. Eventual consistency allows a brief window where different copies disagree, in exchange for lower latency and higher availability. The right choice is per-piece-of-data: a bank balance almost always needs strong consistency; a like count on a post can usually tolerate a few seconds of eventual consistency.

frames.title: In practice
frames.text: A withdrawal must see the true, current balance — reading a stale value could let someone overdraw. Worth the extra latency.

frames.title: Remember
frames.text: Consistency is a per-data-type design decision, not a single system-wide setting — spend strong consistency’s cost only where being wrong is actually expensive.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 420 120" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of two data centers split by a network partition, where a consistency-leaning system refuses a request during the split and an availability-leaning system answers it anyway with possibly stale data."><rect class="box" x="20" y="40" width="100" height="34" rx="6"></rect><text x="70" y="62" class="boxText" style="font-size:9px">Region A</text><rect class="box" x="300" y="40" width="100" height="34" rx="6"></rect><text x="350" y="62" class="boxText" style="font-size:9px">Region B</text><line class="divider" x1="210" y1="10" x2="210" y2="110" style="stroke-dasharray:4 4"></line><text x="210" y="20" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:8px">partition</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: When the link between regions breaks, each side must decide: refuse requests, or answer with what it locally has.

frames.title: The idea
frames.text: CAP theorem is the reminder that once a system is split across a network that can fail, you cannot have perfect consistency and perfect availability at the same time — and every HLD design implicitly picks a side.

frames.title: The mechanism
frames.text: CAP says a distributed system, during a network partition, must choose between consistency (every node sees the same data, but some requests may be refused) and availability (every request gets a response, but it might be stale). Partitions are the trigger — when the network is healthy, a well-built system can usually give both. The practical use of CAP in HLD isn’t reciting the theorem; it’s explicitly stating which side a given piece of data falls on when a partition happens.

frames.title: In practice
frames.text: Selling the last unit of stock twice is a real business problem — during a partition, better to refuse the sale than risk overselling.

frames.title: Remember
frames.text: Use CAP as a prompt to state, out loud, which side each piece of data falls on during a partition — not as a single label for the whole system.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 300 300" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of a hash ring with four server nodes, showing keys assigned to the next node clockwise, with only a small arc of keys reassigned when a new node is added."><circle cx="150" cy="150" r="110" fill="none" stroke="var(--line)" stroke-width="1.5"></circle><circle class="box" cx="150" cy="40" r="14" style="fill:var(--surface-2);stroke:var(--muted)"></circle><circle class="ringNode" cx="260" cy="150" r="14"></circle><circle class="box" cx="150" cy="260" r="14" style="fill:var(--surface-2);stroke:var(--muted)"></circle><circle class="box" cx="40" cy="150" r="14" style="fill:var(--surface-2);stroke:var(--muted)"></circle><text x="150" y="35" class="boxText" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:9px">N1</text><text x="270" y="150" class="boxText" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:9px">new</text><text x="150" y="270" class="boxText" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:9px">N3</text><text x="30" y="150" class="boxText" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:9px">N4</text><path d="M 150 40 A 110 110 0 0 1 260 150" fill="none" stroke="var(--course-accent)" stroke-width="4"></path><text x="150" y="150" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:8px">only this arc moves</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Adding a node to the ring only reassigns the small arc of keys nearest to it.

frames.title: Three cache servers
frames.text: Three cache servers sit on a hash ring, each owning the keys between itself and the next server clockwise.

frames.title: A fourth server is added
frames.text: A fourth server is added to handle growing load, landing at one point on the ring.

frames.title: Only the keys between the new server and its counter-clockwise neighbor
frames.text: Only the keys between the new server and its counter-clockwise neighbor move to it — every other key-to-server mapping is untouched.

frames.title: Contrast with naive hashing:
frames.text: Contrast with naive hashing: going from 3 to 4 servers with hash(key) % N would have remapped roughly three-quarters of all keys at once.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 420 120" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of a leader sending heartbeats to two followers, then, after the leader fails, the followers electing a new leader among themselves."><rect class="boxAccent" x="170" y="15" width="80" height="30" rx="5"></rect><text x="210" y="34" class="boxText" style="font-size:9px">Leader</text><line class="flowMuted" x1="200" y1="45" x2="100" y2="75"></line><line class="flowMuted" x1="240" y1="45" x2="330" y2="75"></line><rect class="box" x="55" y="78" width="90" height="28" rx="5"></rect><text x="100" y="96" class="boxText" style="font-size:8px">Follower A</text><rect class="box" x="285" y="78" width="90" height="28" rx="5"></rect><text x="330" y="96" class="boxText" style="font-size:8px">Follower B</text><text x="210" y="65" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:8px">heartbeats stop → election</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: When heartbeats from the leader stop arriving, the remaining nodes elect a replacement among themselves.

frames.title: Three database nodes
frames.text: Three database nodes run a leader election protocol on startup; one becomes the primary, the other two become replicas.

frames.title: The primary sends heartbeats
frames.text: The primary sends heartbeats to the replicas at a regular interval.

frames.title: The primary crashes.
frames.text: The primary crashes. Replicas notice the missing heartbeats after a timeout and start an election.

frames.title: A new primary is chosen
frames.text: A new primary is chosen among the surviving replicas, and writes resume being accepted — without a person intervening.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 420 120" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of three instances racing to acquire a lock key in a shared store, with only one instance succeeding and proceeding while the others back off."><rect class="boxAccent" x="20" y="20" width="70" height="30" rx="5"></rect><rect class="box" x="110" y="20" width="70" height="30" rx="5"></rect><rect class="box" x="200" y="20" width="70" height="30" rx="5"></rect><text x="55" y="40" class="boxText" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:8px">wins</text><text x="145" y="40" class="boxText" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:8px">skips</text><text x="235" y="40" class="boxText" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:8px">skips</text><line class="flow" x1="55" y1="50" x2="210" y2="85"></line><line class="flow" x1="145" y1="50" x2="210" y2="85"></line><line class="flow" x1="235" y1="50" x2="210" y2="85"></line><rect class="box" x="170" y="88" width="80" height="26" rx="5"></rect><text x="210" y="105" class="boxText" style="font-size:8px">lock store</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Every instance races for the same lock key; only the winner proceeds, and the lock's TTL protects against it crashing mid-task.

frames.title: A nightly billing job
frames.text: A nightly billing job must run on exactly one instance, even though the job scheduler runs on every instance of the service.

frames.title: Each instance tries to acquire a lock key
frames.text: Each instance tries to acquire a lock key (e.g. lock:billing-job ) in Redis at the scheduled time.

frames.title: Only one instance’s write succeeds;
frames.text: Only one instance’s write succeeds; the rest see the key already exists and skip running the job.

frames.title: The lock has a TTL of, say, 10 minutes.
frames.text: The lock has a TTL of, say, 10 minutes. If the winning instance crashes mid-job, the lock expires and the job can be safely retried on the next run.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 440 120" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of a producer pushing one message onto a queue, which three independent consumers pull from at their own pace, one of them temporarily down without affecting the others."><rect class="box" x="15" y="45" width="80" height="30" rx="5"></rect><text x="55" y="64" class="boxText" style="font-size:9px">Producer</text><line class="flow" x1="95" y1="60" x2="150" y2="60"></line><rect class="boxAccent" x="155" y="45" width="70" height="30" rx="5"></rect><text x="190" y="64" class="boxText" style="font-size:9px">Queue</text><line class="flow" x1="225" y1="50" x2="290" y2="20"></line><line class="flow" x1="225" y1="60" x2="290" y2="60"></line><line class="flowMuted" x1="225" y1="70" x2="290" y2="100"></line><rect class="box" x="295" y="8" width="70" height="24" rx="5"></rect><text x="330" y="24" class="boxText" style="font-size:7px">Email</text><rect class="box" x="295" y="48" width="70" height="24" rx="5"></rect><text x="330" y="64" class="boxText" style="font-size:7px">Inventory</text><rect class="boxWarn" x="295" y="88" width="70" height="24" rx="5"></rect><text x="330" y="104" class="boxText" style="font-size:7px">Receipts (down)</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: One consumer being temporarily down doesn't affect the producer or the other consumers — its messages simply wait.

frames.title: An order is placed,
frames.text: An order is placed, triggering an email confirmation, a receipt PDF, and an inventory update — three unrelated pieces of downstream work.

frames.title: The order service publishes one “order placed” message
frames.text: The order service publishes one “order placed” message to a queue and returns to the user immediately.

frames.title: Three independent consumers
frames.text: Three independent consumers (email, receipts, inventory) each process that message at their own pace.

frames.title: The receipts service goes down for five minutes.
frames.text: The receipts service goes down for five minutes. Its messages simply wait in the queue and get processed once it’s back — the order and the other two consumers are entirely unaffected.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 440 120" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of an ordered event log being read independently by three consumer groups, each at its own position, including one reading from the beginning of retained history."><rect class="box" x="30" y="50" width="380" height="24" rx="4"></rect><line class="divider" x1="30" y1="50" x2="30" y2="74"></line><line class="divider" x1="93.3" y1="50" x2="93.3" y2="74"></line><line class="divider" x1="156.6" y1="50" x2="156.6" y2="74"></line><line class="divider" x1="219.89999999999998" y1="50" x2="219.89999999999998" y2="74"></line><line class="divider" x1="283.2" y1="50" x2="283.2" y2="74"></line><line class="divider" x1="346.5" y1="50" x2="346.5" y2="74"></line><text x="220" y="40" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:8px">ordered, retained event log</text><line class="flow" x1="60" y1="74" x2="60" y2="100"></line><text x="60" y="112" class="figHint" style="font-size:7px">analytics (replay)</text><line class="flow" x1="220" y1="74" x2="220" y2="100"></line><text x="220" y="112" class="figHint" style="font-size:7px">recommendations (live)</text><line class="flow" x1="380" y1="74" x2="380" y2="100"></line><text x="380" y="112" class="figHint" style="font-size:7px">fraud (new, replays all)</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Each consumer group reads the retained log independently, from whatever position it needs.

frames.title: Every “order placed” event
frames.text: Every “order placed” event is written to an orders stream, in the order it happened.

frames.title: The analytics service
frames.text: The analytics service reads the stream from the beginning to build historical reports, independent of any other consumer.

frames.title: The recommendation service
frames.text: The recommendation service reads the same stream, live, to update a user’s suggestions in near real time.

frames.title: A brand-new fraud-detection service is added months later.
