frames.text: A brand-new fraud-detection service is added months later. It can replay the entire retained history of the stream to build its initial model, something a traditional queue — which already discarded consumed messages — couldn’t offer.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 440 120" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of service instances registering themselves with a central registry, and a caller querying the registry for a current list of healthy instances instead of using a fixed address."><rect class="box" x="280" y="10" width="80" height="26" rx="5"></rect><rect class="box" x="280" y="45" width="80" height="26" rx="5"></rect><rect class="box" x="280" y="80" width="80" height="26" rx="5"></rect><text x="320" y="27" class="boxText" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:8px">instance 1</text><text x="320" y="62" class="boxText" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:8px">instance 2</text><text x="320" y="97" class="boxText" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:8px">instance 3</text><line class="flowMuted" x1="280" y1="23" x2="230" y2="60"></line><line class="flowMuted" x1="280" y1="58" x2="230" y2="60"></line><line class="flowMuted" x1="280" y1="93" x2="230" y2="60"></line><rect class="boxAccent" x="150" y="45" width="80" height="30" rx="6"></rect><text x="190" y="64" class="boxText" style="font-size:8px">Registry</text><line class="flow" x1="150" y1="60" x2="90" y2="60"></line><rect class="box" x="15" y="45" width="75" height="30" rx="6"></rect><text x="52" y="64" class="boxText" style="font-size:8px">Orders svc</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: The caller asks the registry for a current, healthy instance instead of relying on a fixed address.

frames.title: The orders service needs to call the inventory service,
frames.text: The orders service needs to call the inventory service, which runs as a fleet of instances that scales up and down with load.

frames.title: Each inventory instance registers itself
frames.text: Each inventory instance registers itself with the service registry on startup, including its address and a health-check endpoint.

frames.title: The orders service asks the registry
frames.text: The orders service asks the registry “give me healthy inventory instances” instead of using a fixed address.

frames.title: The inventory fleet scales from 3 to 8 instances
frames.text: The inventory fleet scales from 3 to 8 instances during a sale — the orders service picks this up automatically through the registry, with no reconfiguration or redeploy needed.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 420 110" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of a product page that continues to render its main content when a non-critical recommendations dependency fails, instead of failing the entire page."><rect class="box" x="20" y="20" width="380" height="75" rx="8"></rect><rect class="boxAccent" x="35" y="32" width="220" height="50" rx="6"></rect><text x="145" y="60" class="boxText" style="font-size:9px">Product page: still renders</text><rect class="boxWarn" x="270" y="32" width="115" height="50" rx="6"></rect><text x="327" y="55" class="boxText" style="font-size:8px">Recs:</text><text x="327" y="70" class="boxText" style="font-size:8px">down, omitted</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: A non-critical dependency failing degrades the page instead of breaking it entirely.

frames.title: Design review question:
frames.text: Design review question: “what happens if the recommendation service is completely down?”

frames.title: Without fault tolerance:
frames.text: Without fault tolerance: the product page itself fails to load, because it was written to require recommendations to succeed.

frames.title: With fault tolerance:
frames.text: With fault tolerance: the product page loads normally, simply omitting the recommendations section, because that dependency was explicitly made non-critical.

frames.title: The same question gets asked
frames.text: The same question gets asked of every dependency in the design, one at a time, until every failure mode has a defined, acceptable behavior.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 420 120" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of a primary database failing and a standby replica in a different zone being automatically promoted to take over traffic within seconds."><rect class="boxWarn" x="30" y="35" width="120" height="40" rx="6"></rect><text x="90" y="59" class="boxText" style="font-size:8px">Primary: down</text><line class="flow" x1="150" y1="55" x2="250" y2="55"></line><text x="200" y="42" class="figHint" style="font-size:8px">failover</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="260" y="35" width="130" height="40" rx="6"></rect><text x="325" y="59" class="boxText" style="font-size:8px">Standby: promoted</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Redundancy provides the standby; failover is what actually promotes it when the primary fails.

frames.title: A single database instance
frames.text: A single database instance is a single point of failure — its loss takes down every write in the system.

frames.title: Add a standby replica
frames.text: Add a standby replica in a different availability zone, continuously replicating from the primary.

frames.title: Health checks monitor the primary
frames.text: Health checks monitor the primary continuously for responsiveness.

frames.title: The primary’s zone has an outage.
frames.text: The primary’s zone has an outage. Failover promotes the standby automatically, and writes resume within seconds — the redundancy (the standby) was only useful because the failover (automatic promotion) existed alongside it.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 420 140" role="img" aria-label="State diagram of a circuit breaker moving from closed to open after too many failures, then to half-open after a cooldown, closing again on success or reopening on failure."><rect class="box" x="20" y="20" width="100" height="34" rx="6"></rect><text x="70" y="42" class="boxText" style="font-size:9px">Closed</text><line class="flow" x1="120" y1="37" x2="190" y2="37"></line><text x="155" y="27" class="figHint" style="font-size:7px">too many fails</text><rect class="boxWarn" x="195" y="20" width="100" height="34" rx="6"></rect><text x="245" y="42" class="boxText" style="font-size:9px">Open</text><line class="flow" x1="245" y1="54" x2="245" y2="90"></line><text x="290" y="75" class="figHint" style="font-size:7px">cooldown</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="195" y="95" width="100" height="34" rx="6"></rect><text x="245" y="117" class="boxText" style="font-size:8px">Half-open</text><line class="flow" x1="195" y1="105" x2="120" y2="50"></line><text x="140" y="85" class="figHint" style="font-size:7px">success → closed</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: The breaker cycles through closed, open, and half-open states based on the dependency's recent health.

frames.title: The payments service starts timing out
frames.text: The payments service starts timing out under load, and the checkout service keeps calling it anyway.

frames.title: Without a circuit breaker,
frames.text: Without a circuit breaker, checkout requests pile up waiting on timeouts, exhausting checkout’s own thread pool and taking it down too.

frames.title: With a circuit breaker,
frames.text: With a circuit breaker, after enough failures it opens: checkout immediately returns “payments temporarily unavailable” instead of waiting on a timeout every time.

frames.title: After the cooldown,
frames.text: After the cooldown, a few test requests go through; once payments is healthy again, the breaker closes and normal traffic resumes.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 420 100" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of retry attempts spaced with exponentially increasing delays plus jitter, ending in a capped final attempt before giving up."><rect class="box" x="20" y="30" width="26" height="26" rx="5"></rect><rect class="box" x="45" y="30" width="26" height="26" rx="5"></rect><rect class="box" x="80" y="30" width="26" height="26" rx="5"></rect><rect class="boxWarn" x="130" y="30" width="26" height="26" rx="5"></rect><text x="33" y="47" class="boxText" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:9px">1</text><text x="58" y="47" class="boxText" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:9px">2</text><text x="93" y="47" class="boxText" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:9px">3</text><text x="143" y="47" class="boxText" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:9px">4</text><text x="220" y="20" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:8px">gaps grow: ~1s, ~2s, ~4s, then give up</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Each retry waits longer than the last, with a hard cap before the caller gives up and surfaces the error.

frames.title: A call to the inventory service fails
frames.text: A call to the inventory service fails due to a brief network blip.

frames.title: Wait ~1 second (plus a small random jitter),
frames.text: Wait ~1 second (plus a small random jitter), then retry.

frames.title: It fails again
frames.text: It fails again — wait ~2 seconds, then retry; then ~4 seconds if needed.

frames.title: After 4 attempts,
frames.text: After 4 attempts, give up and surface a clear error, rather than retrying indefinitely and leaving the user staring at a spinner.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 420 110" role="img" aria-label="Timeline diagram showing the last backup point, the moment of failure, the recovery point objective window of acceptable data loss, and the recovery time objective window before service is restored."><line x1="20" y1="60" x2="400" y2="60" stroke="var(--line)" stroke-width="1.5"></line><circle class="ringNode" cx="150" cy="60" r="5"></circle><text x="150" y="45" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:7px">last backup</text><circle class="boxWarn" cx="220" cy="60" r="5" style="stroke:#e0574f"></circle><text x="220" y="80" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:7px">failure</text><line class="flow" x1="150" y1="60" x2="220" y2="60" style="stroke:#e0574f"></line><text x="185" y="95" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:7px">RPO: data at risk</text><circle class="ringNode" cx="320" cy="60" r="5"></circle><text x="320" y="45" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:7px">restored</text><line class="flow" x1="220" y1="60" x2="320" y2="60"></line><text x="270" y="95" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:7px">RTO: downtime</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: RPO bounds how much data can be lost; RTO bounds how long recovery is allowed to take.

frames.title: The business states its tolerance:
frames.text: The business states its tolerance: RPO of 15 minutes, RTO of 1 hour for the order database.

frames.title: RPO of 15 minutes
frames.text: RPO of 15 minutes rules out daily backups alone — it requires continuous replication to a secondary region, at minimum.

frames.title: RTO of 1 hour
frames.text: RTO of 1 hour rules out a fully manual, from-scratch rebuild — it requires a standby that can be promoted with mostly-automated steps.

frames.title: The region hosting the primary goes dark.
frames.text: The region hosting the primary goes dark. The team promotes the secondary region’s replica, following a tested runbook, and is back within the agreed hour, having lost at most the last few minutes of writes.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 420 120" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of authentication happening once at login to issue an identity token, and authorization being checked separately at the point where a specific action is attempted."><rect class="box" x="20" y="20" width="110" height="30" rx="5"></rect><text x="75" y="39" class="boxText" style="font-size:8px">Login (authN)</text><line class="flow" x1="130" y1="35" x2="290" y2="35"></line><text x="210" y="25" class="figHint" style="font-size:7px">identity token</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="295" y="20" width="110" height="30" rx="5"></rect><text x="350" y="39" class="boxText" style="font-size:8px">every request</text><line class="flow" x1="350" y1="50" x2="350" y2="75"></line><rect class="box" x="280" y="80" width="130" height="30" rx="5"></rect><text x="345" y="99" class="boxText" style="font-size:8px">Action check (authZ)</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Authentication happens once and travels with the request; authorization is checked at each specific action.

frames.title: A user logs in.
frames.text: A user logs in. The auth service verifies their credentials and issues a signed token identifying them — authentication, done once.

frames.title: The token is attached to every subsequent request
frames.text: The token is attached to every subsequent request so downstream services know who’s calling without re-checking credentials each time.

frames.title: The user tries to delete another user’s post.
frames.text: The user tries to delete another user’s post. The posts service checks: is this identity authorized to delete this specific resource? — authorization, checked at the point of the action.

frames.title: The check fails
frames.text: The check fails (they’re not the post’s author or an admin), and the request is rejected — independent of the fact that they were successfully authenticated.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 420 110" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of a token bucket per client, refilling steadily over time, with each request consuming one token and requests rejected once the bucket is empty."><rect class="box" x="150" y="20" width="120" height="50" rx="8"></rect><text x="210" y="50" class="boxText" style="font-size:9px">Token bucket</text><line class="flow" x1="210" y1="10" x2="210" y2="20"></line><text x="210" y="8" class="figHint" style="font-size:7px">refills steadily</text><line class="flow" x1="150" y1="45" x2="90" y2="45"></line><text x="120" y="35" class="figHint" style="font-size:7px">consume</text><rect class="box" x="20" y="30" width="65" height="30" rx="5"></rect><text x="52" y="49" class="boxText" style="font-size:8px">Request</text><line class="flow" x1="270" y1="45" x2="330" y2="45"></line><text x="300" y="35" class="figHint" style="font-size:7px">empty</text><rect class="boxWarn" x="335" y="30" width="65" height="30" rx="5"></rect><text x="367" y="49" class="boxText" style="font-size:7px">429</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Every request consumes a token; once the bucket is empty, further requests are rejected until it refills.

frames.title: Each API key gets a bucket of 100 tokens,
frames.text: Each API key gets a bucket of 100 tokens, refilling at 10 tokens per second.

frames.title: A well-behaved client
frames.text: A well-behaved client making a handful of requests per second never empties its bucket — it never notices the limiter exists.

frames.title: A buggy client retries in a tight loop,
frames.text: A buggy client retries in a tight loop, burning through 100 tokens in under a second.

frames.title: Further requests are rejected
frames.text: Further requests are rejected with a 429 status until the bucket refills — protecting the backend from the buggy client without needing a human to intervene.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 420 100" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of three observability pillars, metrics, traces, and logs, each answering a different question: something is wrong, where the time went, and exactly why it failed."><rect class="boxAccent" x="20" y="20" width="120" height="34" rx="6"></rect><rect class="boxAccent" x="160" y="20" width="120" height="34" rx="6"></rect><rect class="boxAccent" x="300" y="20" width="120" height="34" rx="6"></rect><text x="80" y="41" class="boxText" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:9px">Metrics</text><text x="220" y="41" class="boxText" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:9px">Traces</text><text x="360" y="41" class="boxText" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:9px">Logs</text><text x="80" y="70" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:7px">something's wrong</text><text x="220" y="70" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:7px">where time went</text><text x="360" y="70" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:7px">exactly why</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Each pillar answers a different part of a production incident; none alone tells the whole story.

frames.title: A metric dashboard shows checkout error rate spiking
frames.text: A metric dashboard shows checkout error rate spiking at 2 AM — the “something is wrong” signal.

frames.title: Traces for failing requests
frames.text: Traces for failing requests show nearly all their time is spent in a call to the payments service.

frames.title: Logs from the payments service,
frames.text: Logs from the payments service, filtered to that time window, show a specific downstream timeout error.

frames.title: Root cause is found in minutes,
frames.text: Root cause is found in minutes, because metrics, traces, and logs each answered a different part of “what, where, and why.”

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 420 110" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of structured logs from many service instances being aggregated centrally, alongside a monitoring system that watches error rate and pages an engineer when a threshold is crossed."><rect class="box" x="20" y="15" width="55" height="24" rx="4"></rect><rect class="box" x="90" y="15" width="55" height="24" rx="4"></rect><rect class="box" x="160" y="15" width="55" height="24" rx="4"></rect><line class="flow" x1="47" y1="39" x2="200" y2="65"></line><line class="flow" x1="117" y1="39" x2="200" y2="65"></line><line class="flow" x1="187" y1="39" x2="200" y2="65"></line><rect class="boxAccent" x="150" y="68" width="120" height="28" rx="5"></rect><text x="210" y="86" class="boxText" style="font-size:8px">Aggregated logs</text><rect class="box" x="300" y="15" width="100" height="26" rx="5"></rect><text x="350" y="32" class="boxText" style="font-size:8px">Monitoring</text><line class="flow" x1="350" y1="41" x2="350" y2="70"></line><text x="380" y="55" class="figHint" style="font-size:7px">alert</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Structured logs aggregate for searchability; monitoring watches metrics and pages someone when a threshold is crossed.

frames.title: Every service emits structured logs
frames.text: Every service emits structured logs with consistent fields: timestamp, request ID, service name, status.

frames.title: Logs from every instance
frames.text: Logs from every instance are aggregated centrally, searchable by request ID across the whole fleet, not one server at a time.

frames.title: A monitoring system tracks error rate
frames.text: A monitoring system tracks error rate continuously against a threshold agreed with the team.

frames.title: Error rate crosses 5% for five minutes.
frames.text: Error rate crosses 5% for five minutes. An alert pages the on-call engineer, who searches the aggregated logs by the affected request IDs to start investigating immediately.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 420 110" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of a canary release routing a small percentage of traffic to a new version while most traffic stays on the current version, with metrics compared before rolling out further."><rect class="box" x="20" y="20" width="90" height="30" rx="5"></rect><text x="65" y="39" class="boxText" style="font-size:8px">Load balancer</text><line class="flow" x1="110" y1="30" x2="200" y2="20"></line><text x="155" y="12" class="figHint" style="font-size:7px">95%</text><rect class="box" x="205" y="8" width="100" height="26" rx="5"></rect><text x="255" y="25" class="boxText" style="font-size:8px">current version</text><line class="flow" x1="110" y1="40" x2="200" y2="70"></line><text x="155" y="65" class="figHint" style="font-size:7px">5%</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="205" y="60" width="100" height="26" rx="5"></rect><text x="255" y="77" class="boxText" style="font-size:8px">canary (new)</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: A small slice of real traffic validates the new version before it takes over completely.

frames.title: A new version of the checkout service
frames.text: A new version of the checkout service is ready to deploy.

frames.title: Route 5% of real traffic
frames.text: Route 5% of real traffic to the new version (a canary), leaving 95% on the current, known-good version.

frames.title: Watch the canary’s error rate and latency
frames.text: Watch the canary’s error rate and latency against the existing version’s baseline for several minutes.

frames.title: Metrics look healthy
frames.text: Metrics look healthy — gradually shift more traffic to the new version until it serves 100%, or roll back instantly if the canary had shown a regression.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 460 150" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of the write path, where a server claims IDs from a local block before writing to the datastore, above the read path, where a visitor is served from a cache first and the datastore is touched only on a miss."><rect class="box" x="20" y="20" width="110" height="32" rx="6"></rect><text x="75" y="40" class="boxText" style="font-size:8px">New URL</text><line class="flow" x1="130" y1="36" x2="175" y2="36"></line><text x="152" y="26" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:6.5px">local ID block</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="180" y="20" width="120" height="32" rx="6"></rect><text x="240" y="40" class="boxText" style="font-size:8px">App server</text><line class="flow" x1="300" y1="36" x2="345" y2="36"></line><rect class="box" x="350" y="20" width="95" height="32" rx="6"></rect><text x="397" y="40" class="boxText" style="font-size:8px">Datastore</text><line class="divider" x1="20" y1="75" x2="445" y2="75"></line><rect class="box" x="20" y="95" width="140" height="32" rx="6"></rect><text x="90" y="115" class="boxText" style="font-size:8px">Short link visited</text><line class="flow" x1="160" y1="111" x2="205" y2="111"></line><text x="182" y="101" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:6.5px">check</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="210" y="95" width="90" height="32" rx="6"></rect><text x="255" y="115" class="boxText" style="font-size:8px">Cache</text><line class="flow" x1="255" y1="95" x2="255" y2="52"></line><text x="270" y="75" class="figHint" style="font-size:6.5px">hit → redirect</text><line class="flowMuted" x1="300" y1="111" x2="350" y2="111"></line><text x="325" y="101" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:6.5px">miss</text><line class="flowMuted" x1="397" y1="95" x2="397" y2="52"></line></svg>
diagrams.caption: Writes claim IDs from a local block before reaching the datastore; reads are served from cache first, touching the datastore only on a miss.

frames.title: A user submits a long URL.
frames.text: A user submits a long URL. The app server handling the request already holds a locally-claimed block of IDs, so it takes the next free one without talking to any other server.

frames.title: That ID is base62-encoded
frames.text: That ID is base62-encoded into a short code and written to the datastore as {code: longURL}, along with the owner and any expiry.

frames.title: A visitor opens the short link.
frames.text: A visitor opens the short link. The app checks a cache first, since reads so heavily outnumber writes — a cache hit returns the long URL immediately.

frames.title: On a cache miss,
frames.text: On a cache miss, the app looks up the datastore, backfills the cache with that mapping, and then redirects — using a 302, not a 301, so every visit still passes through the service and can be counted.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 460 150" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of an ordinary account's post fanning out to follower inboxes at write time, while a celebrity account's post skips fan-out and is merged into the feed at read time instead."><rect class="box" x="20" y="15" width="130" height="30" rx="6"></rect><text x="85" y="34" class="boxText" style="font-size:8px">Ordinary post</text><line class="flow" x1="150" y1="30" x2="195" y2="30"></line><text x="172" y="20" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:6.5px">fan-out now</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="200" y="5" width="90" height="22" rx="5"></rect><rect class="boxAccent" x="200" y="35" width="90" height="22" rx="5"></rect><rect class="boxAccent" x="200" y="65" width="90" height="22" rx="5"></rect><text x="245" y="19" class="boxText" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:7px">follower inbox</text><text x="245" y="49" class="boxText" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:7px">follower inbox</text><text x="245" y="79" class="boxText" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:7px">follower inbox</text><rect class="box" x="20" y="105" width="130" height="30" rx="6"></rect><text x="85" y="124" class="boxText" style="font-size:8px">Celebrity post</text><line class="flowMuted" x1="150" y1="120" x2="320" y2="70"></line><text x="260" y="100" class="figHint" style="font-size:6.5px">no fan-out</text><line class="flow" x1="290" y1="35" x2="330" y2="60"></line><rect class="boxAccent" x="325" y="60" width="115" height="34" rx="6"></rect><text x="382" y="82" class="boxText" style="font-size:7.5px">Feed, merged at read</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Ordinary accounts fan out at post time; a followed-by-millions account is merged in only when a viewer's feed is actually read.

frames.title: An ordinary account posts.
frames.text: An ordinary account posts. The post is saved, then a fan-out worker looks up its follower list and pushes the post’s ID into each follower’s precomputed feed.

frames.title: A celebrity account posts.
frames.text: A celebrity account posts. Fan-out is skipped entirely for this account — with millions of followers, pushing to every one of them at once is the write storm the design exists to avoid.

frames.title: A viewer opens their feed.
frames.text: A viewer opens their feed. The feed service reads their precomputed feed list (already built, so this is fast) and separately fetches recent posts from any celebrity accounts they follow.

frames.title: The two are merged by recency
frames.text: The two are merged by recency (and in most real feeds, re-ranked by predicted relevance) before being returned — the push/pull split happens underneath the ranking step, not instead of it.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 440 150" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of two chat servers, each holding one user's socket, both consulting a shared connection registry and exchanging messages over an internal bus, with everything also persisted to a message store."><rect class="box" x="20" y="20" width="110" height="32" rx="6"></rect><text x="75" y="40" class="boxText" style="font-size:8px">Alice's server</text><rect class="box" x="310" y="20" width="110" height="32" rx="6"></rect><text x="365" y="40" class="boxText" style="font-size:8px">Bob's server</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="165" y="20" width="110" height="32" rx="6"></rect><text x="220" y="40" class="boxText" style="font-size:7.5px">Connection registry</text><line class="flowMuted" x1="130" y1="36" x2="165" y2="36"></line><line class="flowMuted" x1="275" y1="36" x2="310" y2="36"></line><line class="flow" x1="130" y1="60" x2="310" y2="60"></line><text x="220" y="72" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:6.5px">internal bus</text><line class="flowMuted" x1="75" y1="52" x2="75" y2="105"></line><line class="flowMuted" x1="365" y1="52" x2="365" y2="105"></line><rect class="box" x="140" y="105" width="160" height="32" rx="6"></rect><text x="220" y="125" class="boxText" style="font-size:8px">Message store</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Two chat servers consult a shared registry to find each other and exchange messages over an internal bus, while every message is persisted regardless of whether the recipient is online.

frames.title: Alice's client opens a persistent connection
frames.text: Alice's client opens a persistent connection to whichever chat server the load balancer assigns her to; that server records “Alice → this server” in the connection registry.

frames.title: Alice sends a message to Bob.
frames.text: Alice sends a message to Bob. Her server persists the message first — so it’s never lost even if delivery stalls — then looks up Bob’s server in the registry.

frames.title: If Bob is online,
frames.text: If Bob is online, the message is handed to Bob’s server over the internal bus and pushed down his open socket right away.

frames.title: If Bob is offline,
frames.text: If Bob is offline, there's no entry for him in the registry, so the message simply waits in storage and a push notification is triggered instead.

frames.title: When Bob reconnects,
frames.text: When Bob reconnects, his client first asks for anything since its last sync — pulling the backlog from storage — before real-time delivery resumes.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 460 150" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of an upload triggering an asynchronous transcoding pipeline that produces multiple renditions, above a separate viewing path where the CDN edge serves viewers directly and only reaches the origin on a cache miss."><rect class="box" x="20" y="20" width="90" height="32" rx="6"></rect><text x="65" y="40" class="boxText" style="font-size:8px">Upload</text><line class="flow" x1="110" y1="36" x2="150" y2="36"></line><rect class="box" x="155" y="20" width="110" height="32" rx="6"></rect><text x="210" y="40" class="boxText" style="font-size:7.5px">Object storage</text><line class="flow" x1="265" y1="36" x2="305" y2="36"></line><text x="285" y="26" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:6.5px">event</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="310" y="20" width="130" height="32" rx="6"></rect><text x="375" y="40" class="boxText" style="font-size:7.5px">Transcode workers</text><line class="divider" x1="20" y1="75" x2="440" y2="75"></line><rect class="box" x="20" y="95" width="90" height="32" rx="6"></rect><text x="65" y="115" class="boxText" style="font-size:8px">Viewer</text><line class="flow" x1="110" y1="111" x2="150" y2="111"></line><rect class="boxAccent" x="155" y="95" width="110" height="32" rx="6"></rect><text x="210" y="115" class="boxText" style="font-size:8px">CDN edge</text><line class="flowMuted" x1="265" y1="111" x2="305" y2="111"></line><text x="285" y="101" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:6.5px">miss only</text><rect class="box" x="310" y="95" width="90" height="32" rx="6"></rect><text x="355" y="115" class="boxText" style="font-size:8px">Origin</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Upload and transcoding run asynchronously above; viewer traffic below is served from the CDN edge, reaching the origin only on a cache miss.

frames.title: A creator uploads the raw file.
frames.text: A creator uploads the raw file. It's written to object storage, and an event is emitted — the upload request itself doesn't do any processing.

frames.title: Transcoding workers consume that event,
frames.text: Transcoding workers consume that event, producing several renditions at different resolutions plus a manifest describing them, then mark the video “ready” in the metadata store.

frames.title: Only once marked ready
frames.text: Only once marked ready does the video appear as watchable; the creator sees a “processing” state in the meantime.

frames.title: A viewer opens the video.
frames.text: A viewer opens the video. The app fetches its metadata and manifest, and the player requests segments from the nearest CDN edge rather than the origin.

frames.title: The edge serves from its own cache
frames.text: The edge serves from its own cache if a nearby viewer has already requested that segment, or fetches it from the origin once and caches it for everyone after. The player also watches its own buffering health and switches renditions to match the viewer's actual bandwidth.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 440 140" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of drivers streaming location updates into grid cells of a geospatial index, and a rider's request being matched only against the drivers in the nearby cells, ranked and locked before acceptance."><rect class="box" x="20" y="20" width="76" height="40" rx="5"></rect><rect class="box" x="102" y="20" width="76" height="40" rx="5"></rect><rect class="box" x="184" y="20" width="76" height="40" rx="5"></rect><rect class="box" x="266" y="20" width="76" height="40" rx="5"></rect><rect class="box" x="348" y="20" width="76" height="40" rx="5"></rect><circle class="ringNode" cx="58" cy="40" r="4"></circle><circle class="ringNode" cx="222" cy="35" r="4"></circle><circle class="ringNode" cx="222" cy="48" r="4"></circle><circle class="ringNode" cx="386" cy="42" r="4"></circle><text x="222" y="16" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:6.5px">nearby cells hold the candidates</text><line class="flow" x1="222" y1="60" x2="222" y2="90"></line><rect class="boxAccent" x="140" y="95" width="165" height="32" rx="6"></rect><text x="222" y="115" class="boxText" style="font-size:7.5px">Ranked, locked, offered</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Drivers update a grid-indexed store; a match only ever looks at the rider's nearby cells, then locks one candidate before offering the trip.

frames.title: Every few seconds, each driver's app reports its coordinates,
frames.text: Every few seconds, each driver's app reports its coordinates, overwriting that driver's previous position in a geospatial index keyed by grid cell — there's no history to keep, only a current value.

frames.title: A rider requests a trip.
frames.text: A rider requests a trip. The matching service maps the rider's location to a cell and its immediate neighbors, and pulls the small set of available drivers indexed there.

frames.title: Candidates are ranked
frames.text: Candidates are ranked by distance and estimated arrival time, and the top one is offered the trip. A short-lived lock marks that driver as pending so a second, concurrent request can't also offer them a ride.

frames.title: The driver accepts.
frames.text: The driver accepts. The lock becomes final, the driver is marked unavailable, and the rider is notified; both apps then receive live position pushes over a persistent connection for the rest of the trip.

frames.title: If the driver doesn't respond in time,
frames.text: If the driver doesn't respond in time, the lock expires and the offer moves to the next-ranked candidate.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 460 130" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of an order-shipped event passing through a queue to a notification service, which fans out independent jobs to separate push, email, and SMS workers, each calling its own external provider."><rect class="box" x="15" y="35" width="100" height="32" rx="6"></rect><text x="65" y="55" class="boxText" style="font-size:7.5px">Order shipped</text><line class="flow" x1="115" y1="51" x2="155" y2="51"></line><rect class="boxAccent" x="160" y="35" width="80" height="32" rx="6"></rect><text x="200" y="55" class="boxText" style="font-size:8px">Queue</text><line class="flow" x1="240" y1="51" x2="280" y2="51"></line><rect class="box" x="285" y="35" width="130" height="32" rx="6"></rect><text x="350" y="55" class="boxText" style="font-size:7px">Notification service</text><line class="flowMuted" x1="350" y1="67" x2="290" y2="100"></line><line class="flowMuted" x1="350" y1="67" x2="350" y2="100"></line><line class="flowMuted" x1="350" y1="67" x2="410" y2="100"></line><rect class="box" x="260" y="100" width="50" height="24" rx="5"></rect><rect class="box" x="320" y="100" width="50" height="24" rx="5"></rect><rect class="box" x="380" y="100" width="50" height="24" rx="5"></rect><text x="285" y="116" class="boxText" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:7px">Push</text><text x="345" y="116" class="boxText" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:7px">Email</text><text x="405" y="116" class="boxText" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:7px">SMS</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: The triggering event only ever reaches a queue; notification fan-out and each channel's provider call happen entirely downstream of it.

frames.title: The orders service marks an order shipped
frames.text: The orders service marks an order shipped and publishes an “order.shipped” event to a queue — its own request finishes right away, regardless of what happens next.

frames.title: A notification service consumes the event,
frames.text: A notification service consumes the event, loads the user's channel preferences, and decides this user gets a push notification and an email, but is inside a quiet-hours window for text messages.

frames.title: One job per applicable channel
frames.text: One job per applicable channel lands on separate, channel-specific queues; a push worker and an email worker each call their own provider independently.

frames.title: The suppressed SMS job
frames.text: The suppressed SMS job is instead scheduled for once the quiet-hours window ends, rather than dropped.

frames.title: If the email provider is down,
frames.text: If the email provider is down, its worker retries with backoff on its own queue — the push notification still goes out immediately, and the orders service was never aware any of this was happening.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 440 130" role="img" aria-label="Diagram contrasting a high level design view, made of services and databases connected by network calls, with a low level design view of the same prompt, made of classes connected by relationships."><rect class="box" x="20" y="20" width="180" height="90" rx="8"></rect><text x="110" y="16" class="figLabel" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:8px">HLD view</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="35" y="35" width="70" height="24" rx="5"></rect><text x="70" y="51" class="boxText" style="font-size:7px">Service</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="115" y="35" width="65" height="24" rx="5"></rect><text x="147" y="51" class="boxText" style="font-size:7px">Service</text><rect class="box" x="70" y="80" width="90" height="22" rx="5"></rect><text x="115" y="95" class="boxText" style="font-size:7px">Database</text><line class="divider" x1="220" y1="15" x2="220" y2="115"></line><rect class="box" x="240" y="20" width="180" height="90" rx="8"></rect><text x="330" y="16" class="figLabel" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:8px">LLD view</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="255" y="35" width="65" height="22" rx="5"></rect><text x="287" y="50" class="boxText" style="font-size:7px">Vehicle</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="335" y="35" width="70" height="22" rx="5"></rect><text x="370" y="50" class="boxText" style="font-size:7px">ParkingSpot</text><rect class="box" x="290" y="80" width="70" height="22" rx="5"></rect><text x="325" y="95" class="boxText" style="font-size:7px">Ticket</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Two valid answers to the same prompt: one about services and data flow, the other about classes and relationships.

frames.title: An HLD answer to “design a parking lot”
frames.text: An HLD answer to “design a parking lot” might discuss a payments service, a notifications service, and a database that scales across multiple physical locations.

frames.title: An LLD answer to the same prompt
frames.text: An LLD answer to the same prompt instead defines a ParkingSpot class with a size and occupied flag, a Vehicle class with a size, and a ParkingLot class that matches one to the other — no servers in sight.

frames.title: Both are valid designs for the same system;
frames.text: Both are valid designs for the same system; they're just answering different questions about it.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 460 150" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of a pipeline of sections: Foundations, SOLID, UML, Patterns, and Practices, converging into Case Studies."><rect class="box" x="10" y="20" width="78" height="34" rx="5"></rect><rect class="box" x="98" y="20" width="78" height="34" rx="5"></rect><rect class="box" x="186" y="20" width="78" height="34" rx="5"></rect><rect class="box" x="274" y="20" width="78" height="34" rx="5"></rect><rect class="box" x="362" y="20" width="78" height="34" rx="5"></rect><text x="49" y="41" class="boxText" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:7.5px">Foundations</text><text x="137" y="41" class="boxText" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:7.5px">SOLID</text><text x="225" y="41" class="boxText" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:7.5px">UML</text><text x="313" y="41" class="boxText" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:7.5px">Patterns</text><text x="401" y="41" class="boxText" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:7.5px">Practices</text><line class="flow" x1="88" y1="37" x2="98" y2="37"></line><line class="flow" x1="176" y1="37" x2="186" y2="37"></line><line class="flow" x1="264" y1="37" x2="274" y2="37"></line><line class="flow" x1="352" y1="37" x2="362" y2="37"></line><line class="flow" x1="230" y1="54" x2="230" y2="90"></line><rect class="boxAccent" x="150" y="95" width="160" height="36" rx="6"></rect><text x="230" y="117" class="boxText">Case Studies</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Each section is a tool; Case Studies is where every tool gets used together.

frames.title: Asked to turn a paragraph of requirements into classes?
frames.text: Asked to turn a paragraph of requirements into classes? That’s LLD Foundations.

frames.title: Asked why a design “feels wrong” even though it works?
frames.text: Asked why a design “feels wrong” even though it works? That’s usually a SOLID principle being quietly violated.

frames.title: Asked to communicate a design without writing code?
frames.text: Asked to communicate a design without writing code? Reach for the UML and Modeling section’s diagrams.

frames.title: Recognize a recurring shape
frames.text: Recognize a recurring shape — swappable behavior, a family of related objects, a fixed algorithm with variable steps? That’s a Design Pattern from one of the three pattern sections.

frames.title: Asked to walk through a full design end-to-end?
frames.text: Asked to walk through a full design end-to-end? That’s exactly the shape of the Case Studies section.

diagrams.caption: A repeatable six-step process, applied the same way regardless of which system the prompt names.

frames.title: The idea
frames.text: A reliable process matters more than knowing every pattern by name — the same six steps apply whether the prompt is a parking lot or a chat application.

frames.title: The mechanism
frames.text: Clarify scope. What does the system actually need to do, and what’s explicitly out of scope? A vague prompt answered with a huge class hierarchy usually solved the wrong problem.

frames.title: In practice
frames.text: For “design a vending machine,” the first three steps might look like: scope is a single machine, one transaction at a time, no networked payment; candidate classes are VendingMachine, Product, and Coin; VendingMachine owns the transaction flow, Product owns its own price and stock count, Coin only represents a value. Only after that does it make sense to ask which relationships and patterns fit — jumping to “I’ll use the State pattern” before this groundwork is done tends to produce a design that fits the pattern better than it fits the problem.

frames.title: Remember
frames.text: Scope, classes, responsibilities, relationships, patterns, sketch — in that order, the same six steps carry you through almost any LLD prompt.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 420 100" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of a one-line requirement expanding into a small object model with a Book class and a checkOut method that checks availability first."><rect class="box" x="20" y="35" width="140" height="30" rx="6"></rect><text x="90" y="54" class="boxText" style="font-size:7.5px">"A member can check out a book"</text><line class="flow" x1="160" y1="50" x2="205" y2="50"></line><rect class="boxAccent" x="210" y="15" width="90" height="28" rx="5"></rect><text x="255" y="33" class="boxText" style="font-size:7.5px">Book</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="210" y="55" width="90" height="28" rx="5"></rect><text x="255" y="73" class="boxText" style="font-size:7px">Loan.checkOut()</text><line class="flow" x1="300" y1="69" x2="345" y2="69"></line><rect class="box" x="350" y="55" width="60" height="28" rx="5"></rect><text x="380" y="73" class="boxText" style="font-size:6.5px">availability check</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: A single requirement expands into specific classes, a specific method, and an explicit precondition once LLD is applied.

frames.title: The idea
frames.text: Low level design turns a component’s responsibilities into a concrete object model — the classes that exist, what each one knows and does, and how instances of those classes collaborate.

frames.title: The mechanism
frames.text: A good LLD is detailed enough that writing the actual code becomes close to transcription — the hard decisions (who's responsible for what, how objects relate) are already made. The usual artifacts are a class diagram (structure), sometimes a sequence diagram (behavior for one scenario), and clear interfaces between the pieces.

frames.title: In practice
frames.text: Take one requirement: “a member can check out a book.” Turning that into LLD means deciding there's a Book class (title, author), that “check out” is a method that probably lives on a Library or Loan class rather than on Book itself, and that the operation needs to check availability before it succeeds. None of that was visible in the one-line requirement — it's the product of doing the design work.

frames.title: Remember
frames.text: LLD is finished when writing the code is close to transcription — the classes, responsibilities, and relationships are already decided.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 440 120" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of a requirements sentence being parsed into nouns and verbs, which become candidate classes and methods, including one class the sentence never names directly."><rect class="box" x="20" y="15" width="400" height="28" rx="6"></rect><text x="220" y="33" class="boxText" style="font-size:7px">"A member can borrow up to 5 books; each book has a due date..."</text><line class="flow" x1="120" y1="43" x2="120" y2="65"></line><text x="120" y="60" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:6.5px">nouns</text><line class="flow" x1="320" y1="43" x2="320" y2="65"></line><text x="320" y="60" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:6.5px">verbs</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="30" y="70" width="180" height="30" rx="5"></rect><text x="120" y="89" class="boxText" style="font-size:7px">Member, Book, Librarian, Loan</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="230" y="70" width="180" height="30" rx="5"></rect><text x="320" y="89" class="boxText" style="font-size:7px">borrowBook(), addBook()</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Nouns and verbs give a first draft; the class the sentence never names (Loan) still has to be inferred.

frames.title: Nouns:
frames.text: Nouns: member, book, due date, librarian — candidates: Member, Book, Librarian.

frames.title: Verbs:
frames.text: Verbs: borrow, add — candidate methods: something like borrowBook() and addBook().

frames.title: “Due date” doesn’t need its own class
frames.text: “Due date” doesn’t need its own class — it's a field on whatever tracks an active borrow, which suggests a fourth class this sentence never named directly: a Loan linking a Member to a Book with a due date.

frames.title: “Up to 5 books”
frames.text: “Up to 5 books” is a rule, not a class — it belongs as a check inside borrowBook(), most naturally on Member or the system coordinating the loan.

diagrams.caption: Four relationships that all sound like "has-a" in English but differ in whether the parts share the whole's lifetime.

frames.title: The idea
frames.text: Once you have candidate classes, the next question is how their instances relate to each other — and “has-a” hides at least three genuinely different relationships that behave differently when an object is destroyed.

frames.title: The mechanism
frames.text: A Library going out of business doesn’t delete its Members — they existed before the library and continue to exist after (aggregation). A Car being scrapped does take its specific Engine instance with it — nobody reuses one car’s physical engine object as another car’s (composition). A Driver object simply calling car.start() is association — the Driver doesn’t own the Car’s lifetime at all. And a method signature like process(Logger logger) is a dependency — the class needs a Logger for this one call, not as a lasting part of its own structure.

frames.title: In practice
frames.text: "Has-a" isn't one relationship — whether the part shares the whole's lifetime is the detail that separates aggregation from composition, and getting it backwards causes real bugs.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 420 110" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of an object's private internal fields hidden behind a small public interface surface that callers depend on instead."><rect class="box" x="130" y="15" width="160" height="80" rx="8"></rect><text x="210" y="10" class="figLabel" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:8px">StripePaymentProcessor</text><rect class="boxWarn" x="145" y="30" width="60" height="22" rx="4"></rect><text x="175" y="45" class="boxText" style="font-size:6.5px">apiKey</text><rect class="boxWarn" x="215" y="30" width="60" height="22" rx="4"></rect><text x="245" y="45" class="boxText" style="font-size:6.5px">httpClient</text><text x="210" y="68" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:6.5px">private, hidden</text><line class="flow" x1="60" y1="55" x2="125" y2="55"></line><rect class="box" x="20" y="42" width="60" height="26" rx="5"></rect><text x="50" y="58" class="boxText" style="font-size:7px">Caller</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="120" y="88" width="180" height="20" rx="5"></rect><text x="210" y="102" class="boxText" style="font-size:7px">charge(amount)</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: The caller depends only on charge(amount); everything that makes it work is private and free to change.

frames.title: The idea
frames.text: Encapsulation and abstraction get used almost interchangeably in casual conversation, but they solve two different problems: one protects an object's state, the other hides a system's complexity behind a simpler contract.

frames.title: The mechanism
frames.text: Encapsulation bundles data with the methods that operate on it, and hides internal state behind a controlled interface — private fields, public methods — so the internals can change without breaking anything that depends on the class. Abstraction exposes only the essential behavior through an interface, hiding implementation details entirely — a caller depends on what a class does, never how it does it.

frames.title: In practice
frames.text: A PaymentProcessor interface exposing one method, charge(amount), is abstraction: calling code depends only on that contract, never on which payment provider is behind it. A concrete StripePaymentProcessor implementing that interface is where encapsulation applies: its API keys and HTTP client are private fields, never exposed as public getters, so swapping the HTTP library later doesn’t touch a single caller.

frames.title: Remember
frames.text: Encapsulation protects an object's state from the outside; abstraction hides a system's complexity behind a simpler contract. A well-designed class usually does both.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 440 130" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of a broken inheritance tree where a rubber duck subclass must override a fly method it can't honestly implement, next to a composed alternative where each duck holds a swappable fly-behavior object instead."><rect class="box" x="20" y="15" width="90" height="26" rx="5"></rect><text x="65" y="32" class="boxText" style="font-size:7px">Duck.fly()</text><line class="flowMuted" x1="65" y1="41" x2="65" y2="65"></line><rect class="boxWarn" x="20" y="70" width="90" height="30" rx="5"></rect><text x="65" y="88" class="boxText" style="font-size:6.5px">RubberDuck</text><text x="65" y="112" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:6.5px">overrides fly() to do nothing</text><line class="divider" x1="220" y1="10" x2="220" y2="120"></line><rect class="box" x="250" y="30" width="90" height="26" rx="5"></rect><text x="295" y="47" class="boxText" style="font-size:7px">Duck</text><line class="flow" x1="340" y1="43" x2="380" y2="43"></line><rect class="boxAccent" x="385" y="15" width="55" height="24" rx="4"></rect><text x="412" y="30" class="boxText" style="font-size:6.5px">FlyWithWings</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="385" y="55" width="55" height="24" rx="4"></rect><text x="412" y="70" class="boxText" style="font-size:6.5px">CannotFly</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Inheritance forces every duck through the same fly() method; composition lets each duck hold whichever fly-behavior actually fits.

frames.title: The idea
frames.text: Inheritance models “is-a” and gives you polymorphism for free, but it can quietly lock a class into behavior it can’t escape as requirements change — which is exactly why “favor composition over inheritance” is one of the most repeated pieces of design advice.

frames.title: The mechanism
frames.text: Inheritance couples a subclass tightly to its superclass’s implementation, and deep hierarchies become fragile as new cases appear that don’t cleanly fit the existing tree. Composition builds behavior by holding a reference to another object instead — it’s more flexible because the referenced piece can be swapped at runtime, not fixed at compile time by which class you extended.

frames.title: In practice
frames.text: A classic failure: a Duck base class with a fly() method, extended by RubberDuck. Every duck subclass now inherits fly() whether it makes sense or not — a rubber duck can’t fly, so the method has to be awkwardly overridden to do nothing, or the hierarchy has to be restructured every time a new kind of duck breaks the assumption. The fix is composition: give Duck a FlyBehavior field instead of a fixed fly() method — a real duck is composed with a FlyWithWings behavior, a rubber duck with a CannotFly behavior, and new duck types just get assigned whichever behavior actually fits, with no restructuring required.

frames.title: Remember
frames.text: Reach for inheritance only for a genuine, stable is-a relationship; reach for composition when behavior needs to vary or swap at runtime — which, in practice, is most of the time.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 420 120" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of one overloaded Invoice class handling calculation, printing, and storage, splitting into three focused classes each responsible for one concern."><rect class="boxWarn" x="20" y="35" width="140" height="50" rx="8"></rect><text x="90" y="55" class="boxText" style="font-size:7.5px">Invoice</text><text x="90" y="70" class="figHint" style="font-size:6.5px">calc + print + save</text><line class="flow" x1="160" y1="60" x2="200" y2="60"></line><rect class="boxAccent" x="205" y="15" width="90" height="24" rx="5"></rect><text x="250" y="31" class="boxText" style="font-size:6.5px">Invoice</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="205" y="48" width="90" height="24" rx="5"></rect><text x="250" y="64" class="boxText" style="font-size:6.5px">InvoicePrinter</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="205" y="81" width="90" height="24" rx="5"></rect><text x="250" y="97" class="boxText" style="font-size:6.5px">InvoiceRepository</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: One class with three reasons to change splits into three classes, each with exactly one.

frames.title: The idea
frames.text: A class should have exactly one reason to change — one responsibility, answering to one actor or concern. It's the first SOLID principle because most of the others become easier once this one is respected.

frames.title: The mechanism
frames.text: “One responsibility” doesn’t mean “one method” — a class can have many methods and still answer to a single concern. The test is whether the class would need to change for more than one unrelated reason: if pricing logic, print formatting, and storage format each independently might change, and all three live in the same class, that class has three reasons to change, not one.

frames.title: In practice
frames.text: An Invoice class that calculates totals, formats itself for printing, and saves itself to a database has three separate reasons to change: a new tax rule, a new print layout, a new storage backend — each touches the same class. Splitting it into Invoice (data and calculation), InvoicePrinter, and InvoiceRepository means each class now changes for exactly one of those reasons, and changing the print layout can never accidentally break the tax calculation.

frames.title: Remember
frames.text: Ask whether a class would need to change for more than one unrelated reason — that's the real test for single responsibility, not how many methods it has.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 420 120" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of an if-else chain that grows with every new discount tier, next to a single dispatch point calling a swappable discount interface instead."><rect class="boxWarn" x="20" y="15" width="160" height="90" rx="8"></rect><text x="100" y="35" class="boxText" style="font-size:7.5px">if/else chain</text><text x="35" y="50" class="figHint" style="font-size:6.5px">regular</text><text x="35" y="66" class="figHint" style="font-size:6.5px">premium</text><text x="35" y="82" class="figHint" style="font-size:6.5px">vip</text><text x="35" y="98" class="figHint" style="font-size:6.5px">+ next tier</text><line class="divider" x1="210" y1="10" x2="210" y2="110"></line><rect class="box" x="230" y="45" width="90" height="26" rx="5"></rect><text x="275" y="62" class="boxText" style="font-size:6.5px">Calculator</text><line class="flow" x1="320" y1="58" x2="360" y2="58"></line><rect class="boxAccent" x="365" y="15" width="50" height="22" rx="4"></rect><text x="390" y="29" class="boxText" style="font-size:6px">Regular</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="365" y="45" width="50" height="22" rx="4"></rect><text x="390" y="59" class="boxText" style="font-size:6px">Premium</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="365" y="75" width="50" height="22" rx="4"></rect><text x="390" y="89" class="boxText" style="font-size:6px">+ new</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: A growing if/else chain versus one dispatch point to swappable, independently addable implementations.

frames.title: The idea
frames.text: A class should be open for extension but closed for modification — you should be able to add new behavior without editing and re-testing code that already works.

frames.title: The mechanism
frames.text: The usual violation is an if/else or switch chain that branches on type, growing by one more branch every time a new case appears. The usual fix is polymorphism: define an interface for the varying behavior, put each case behind its own implementation, and have the calling code depend only on the interface — adding a case means adding a new class, never touching the ones that already shipped.

frames.title: In practice
frames.text: A DiscountCalculator with an if/else chain checking customer.type against “regular”, “premium”, and “vip” means adding a new tier requires editing that method and re-testing every existing branch alongside it. Replacing it with a Discount interface — one implementation per tier — lets the calculator just call discount.apply(order) polymorphically; a new tier is a new class that implements the interface, and the calculator's code never changes again.

frames.title: Remember
frames.text: When a branch keeps growing with every new case, that's the signal to close it off behind an interface — not a reason to abstract everything else in anticipation.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 420 110" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of code written against Rectangle that assumes setWidth leaves height unchanged, breaking silently when a Square instance is substituted in."><rect class="box" x="20" y="20" width="160" height="30" rx="6"></rect><text x="100" y="39" class="boxText" style="font-size:7px">caller: setWidth(5), expects height unchanged</text><line class="flow" x1="180" y1="35" x2="220" y2="35"></line><rect class="boxAccent" x="225" y="10" width="90" height="26" rx="5"></rect><text x="270" y="27" class="boxText" style="font-size:7px">Rectangle</text><text x="270" y="50" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:6.5px">works as expected</text><line class="flowMuted" x1="180" y1="70" x2="220" y2="70"></line><rect class="boxWarn" x="225" y="60" width="90" height="26" rx="5"></rect><text x="270" y="77" class="boxText" style="font-size:7px">Square</text><text x="270" y="100" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:6.5px">height silently changes too</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Square honors Rectangle's method signatures but not its behavioral contract, breaking the caller's assumption silently.

frames.title: The idea
frames.text: A subclass must be usable anywhere its superclass is expected, without breaking the caller's assumptions — a subtype has to honor the parent's contract, not just match its method signatures.

frames.title: The mechanism
frames.text: Matching method names and signatures is necessary but not sufficient. LSP is about behavior: if code written against the superclass would break when handed a specific subclass instead, that subclass isn’t a valid substitute — regardless of whether it compiles cleanly and looks like a reasonable “is-a” in English.

frames.title: In practice
frames.text: The classic case: Square extends Rectangle. Rectangle has independent setWidth() and setHeight() methods, and any caller of Rectangle reasonably assumes setting one leaves the other unchanged. A Square, to stay a valid square, must override both setters to keep width and height equal — which means code that calls setWidth(5) expecting only the width to change silently gets the height changed too when handed a Square. Squares genuinely are rectangles geometrically, but Square is not a valid substitute for Rectangle in code.

frames.title: Remember
frames.text: A valid subtype honors its parent's behavioral contract, not just its method signatures — an "is-a" relationship in English doesn't guarantee that on its own.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 420 110" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of a fat Worker interface forcing a Robot to implement an eat method it can't honestly support, versus two thin interfaces letting Robot implement only the one it needs."><rect class="boxWarn" x="20" y="15" width="140" height="30" rx="6"></rect><text x="90" y="34" class="boxText" style="font-size:7px">Worker: work(), eat()</text><line class="flowMuted" x1="90" y1="45" x2="90" y2="70"></line><text x="105" y="58" class="figHint" style="font-size:6.5px">eat() no-op</text><rect class="box" x="35" y="75" width="110" height="26" rx="5"></rect><text x="90" y="92" class="boxText" style="font-size:7px">Robot</text><line class="divider" x1="200" y1="10" x2="200" y2="105"></line><rect class="boxAccent" x="220" y="15" width="90" height="24" rx="5"></rect><text x="265" y="31" class="boxText" style="font-size:6.5px">Workable</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="320" y="15" width="90" height="24" rx="5"></rect><text x="365" y="31" class="boxText" style="font-size:6.5px">Eatable</text><line class="flow" x1="265" y1="39" x2="265" y2="70"></line><rect class="box" x="220" y="75" width="90" height="26" rx="5"></rect><text x="265" y="92" class="boxText" style="font-size:7px">Robot</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: A fat interface forces an implementer to fake support for methods it doesn't need; thin interfaces let it depend on only what applies.

frames.title: The idea
frames.text: No client should be forced to depend on methods it doesn't use — several small, focused interfaces beat one broad interface that tries to serve every implementer at once.

frames.title: The mechanism
frames.text: A “fat” interface bundles methods that make sense for some implementers but not others, forcing the ones that don’t need a method to implement it anyway — usually as a no-op or a thrown exception, both of which are warning signs that the interface is doing too much. Splitting it by which clients actually need which methods keeps every implementer honest about what it really supports.

frames.title: In practice
frames.text: A Worker interface with both work() and eat() forces a Robot implementing it to also implement eat(), which means nothing for a robot — it either does nothing or throws an exception, and either way it's lying about what a Robot can actually do. Splitting into Workable (just work() ) and Eatable (just eat() ) lets Robot implement only Workable, while a HumanWorker implements both.

frames.title: Remember
frames.text: If an implementer has to fake, ignore, or throw on part of an interface, that interface is bundling more than one client actually needs — split it along those lines.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 420 110" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of OrderService directly instantiating MySQLDatabase, a rigid direct dependency, versus both OrderService and MySQLDatabase depending on a shared Database interface in between."><rect class="box" x="20" y="40" width="120" height="28" rx="6"></rect><text x="80" y="58" class="boxText" style="font-size:7px">OrderService</text><line class="flowMuted" x1="140" y1="54" x2="185" y2="54"></line><text x="162" y="44" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:6.5px">new</text><rect class="boxWarn" x="190" y="40" width="120" height="28" rx="6"></rect><text x="250" y="58" class="boxText" style="font-size:7px">MySQLDatabase</text><line class="divider" x1="330" y1="10" x2="330" y2="105"></line><rect class="box" x="345" y="15" width="60" height="24" rx="5"></rect><text x="375" y="31" class="boxText" style="font-size:6.5px">Order</text><text x="375" y="8" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:6px">Service</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: OrderService constructing MySQLDatabase directly is a rigid dependency; both depending on a shared interface removes it.

frames.title: The idea
frames.text: High-level modules shouldn't depend on low-level modules directly — both should depend on an abstraction in between, so a change to one detail never has to ripple up into business logic that shouldn't care about it.

frames.title: The mechanism
frames.text: “High-level” here means the code that expresses policy — what the application actually does; “low-level” means the specific mechanism — which database, which HTTP client. DIP says the high-level code should depend on an interface it defines in its own terms, and the low-level mechanism should implement that interface — not the other way around, where high-level logic is written against a specific low-level class's API.

frames.title: In practice
frames.text: An OrderService that directly writes new MySQLDatabase() inside its own constructor is coupled to that one concrete class — swapping storage, or testing OrderService without a real database, means editing OrderService itself. Once OrderService instead depends on a Database interface it defines (with methods like save(order) ), and MySQLDatabase is just one implementation of that interface supplied from outside, OrderService never needs to change to support a different database or a fake one in tests.

frames.title: Remember
frames.text: Depend on an interface your own code defines, not on a specific low-level class — the mechanism for wiring it together is a separate, later decision.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 130" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of two three-compartment UML class boxes, Book and Library, connected by an aggregation relationship, each box showing its name, attributes, and methods in separate sections."><rect class="box" x="30" y="15" width="130" height="95" rx="4"></rect><line class="divider" x1="30" y1="42" x2="160" y2="42"></line><line class="divider" x1="30" y1="78" x2="160" y2="78"></line><text x="95" y="31" class="boxText" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:8px">Book</text><text x="40" y="56" class="figHint" style="font-size:6.5px">title</text><text x="40" y="70" class="figHint" style="font-size:6.5px">author</text><text x="240" y="31" class="boxText" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:8px">Library</text><rect class="box" x="175" y="15" width="130" height="95" rx="4"></rect><line class="divider" x1="175" y1="42" x2="305" y2="42"></line><line class="divider" x1="175" y1="78" x2="305" y2="78"></line><text x="185" y="56" class="figHint" style="font-size:6.5px">books: Book[]</text><text x="185" y="93" class="figHint" style="font-size:6.5px">addBook()</text><line class="flowMuted" x1="160" y1="60" x2="175" y2="60"></line></svg>
diagrams.caption: Each box's three compartments show a class's name, attributes, and methods; the line between them shows how they relate.

frames.title: The idea
frames.text: A class diagram shows a design's static structure — the classes that exist, their attributes and methods, and the relationships between them — giving visual notation to the vocabulary this course already built up in words.

frames.title: The mechanism
frames.text: Each class is drawn as a box with three compartments: the class name on top, its attributes in the middle, its methods at the bottom. Relationships between classes are drawn as lines, distinguished by the same vocabulary covered earlier — association, aggregation, composition, dependency — so the diagram communicates not just which classes exist, but exactly how they're coupled.

frames.title: In practice
frames.text: A two-class diagram for a tiny library slice: a Book box listing title and author as attributes and no methods of its own, and a Library box listing a books collection as an attribute and addBook() as a method, connected to Book by an aggregation line — the library holds books, but a book's existence doesn't depend on any one library holding it.

frames.title: Remember
frames.text: A class diagram earns its keep by showing attributes, methods, and relationships together — a box with just a name is barely more useful than a bullet list.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 420 150" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of a sequence with four vertical lifelines for Customer, OrderService, Inventory, and PaymentService, with horizontal arrows stepping downward in call order and dashed arrows showing responses."><g><line x1="40" y1="20" x2="40" y2="140" stroke="currentColor" stroke-opacity="0.35" stroke-dasharray="3,3"></line><text x="40" y="14" class="figLabel" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:7px">Customer</text></g><g><line x1="150" y1="20" x2="150" y2="140" stroke="currentColor" stroke-opacity="0.35" stroke-dasharray="3,3"></line><text x="150" y="14" class="figLabel" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:7px">OrderService</text></g><g><line x1="260" y1="20" x2="260" y2="140" stroke="currentColor" stroke-opacity="0.35" stroke-dasharray="3,3"></line><text x="260" y="14" class="figLabel" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:7px">Inventory</text></g><g><line x1="370" y1="20" x2="370" y2="140" stroke="currentColor" stroke-opacity="0.35" stroke-dasharray="3,3"></line><text x="370" y="14" class="figLabel" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:7px">Payment</text></g><line class="flow" x1="40" y1="35" x2="150" y2="35"></line><text x="95" y="30" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:6px">placeOrder()</text><line class="flow" x1="150" y1="55" x2="260" y2="55"></line><text x="205" y="50" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:6px">reserve()</text><line class="flowMuted" x1="260" y1="72" x2="150" y2="72"></line><line class="flow" x1="150" y1="90" x2="370" y2="90"></line><text x="260" y="85" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:6px">charge()</text><line class="flowMuted" x1="370" y1="107" x2="150" y2="107"></line><line class="flowMuted" x1="150" y1="125" x2="40" y2="125"></line><text x="95" y="120" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:6px">confirmation</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Each arrow's order and direction shows exactly which call waits on which, for one specific scenario.

frames.title: The idea
frames.text: Where a class diagram shows static structure, a sequence diagram shows dynamic behavior — the order that messages pass between specific objects for one concrete scenario, over time.

frames.title: The mechanism
frames.text: Each participating object gets a vertical lifeline; time runs top to bottom. A horizontal arrow from one lifeline to another represents a call, labeled with the method being invoked; a dashed return arrow represents the response coming back. A sequence diagram only ever describes one scenario at a time — it complements the class diagram rather than replacing it.

frames.title: In practice
frames.text: For a “place an order” scenario: Customer calls OrderService.placeOrder(), which calls Inventory.reserve(), waits for its response, then calls PaymentService.charge(), waits for that response, and finally returns a confirmation back to the Customer. The diagram makes the order of these calls — and which call is waiting on which — explicit in a way a class diagram never could.

frames.title: Remember
frames.text: A class diagram tells you the pieces exist; a sequence diagram tells you the order they actually talk in for one specific scenario.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 440 130" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of an order moving through Placed, Paid, Shipped, and Delivered states in sequence, with a Cancelled state reachable only from Placed or Paid, not from Shipped or Delivered."><rect class="box" x="20" y="20" width="80" height="30" rx="15"></rect><rect class="box" x="120" y="20" width="80" height="30" rx="15"></rect><rect class="box" x="220" y="20" width="80" height="30" rx="15"></rect><rect class="boxAccent" x="320" y="20" width="80" height="30" rx="15"></rect><text x="60" y="39" class="boxText" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:7px">Placed</text><text x="160" y="39" class="boxText" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:7px">Paid</text><text x="260" y="39" class="boxText" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:7px">Shipped</text><text x="360" y="39" class="boxText" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:7px">Delivered</text><line class="flow" x1="100" y1="35" x2="120" y2="35"></line><line class="flow" x1="200" y1="35" x2="220" y2="35"></line><line class="flow" x1="300" y1="35" x2="320" y2="35"></line><rect class="boxWarn" x="120" y="85" width="90" height="30" rx="15"></rect><text x="165" y="104" class="boxText" style="font-size:7px">Cancelled</text><line class="flowMuted" x1="60" y1="50" x2="140" y2="88"></line><line class="flowMuted" x1="160" y1="50" x2="165" y2="82"></line></svg>
diagrams.caption: The diagram makes clear that cancellation is only reachable from Placed or Paid, never from Shipped or Delivered.

frames.title: The idea
frames.text: A state diagram is worth drawing for objects whose behavior genuinely depends on “what mode am I in right now” — an order, a traffic light, a media player — showing every state it can be in and exactly which events move it between them.

frames.title: The mechanism
frames.text: States are drawn as boxes or rounded shapes; transitions are labeled arrows showing which event moves the object from one state to another. The diagram's real value is often in what it deliberately leaves out — a transition that isn't drawn is a transition that isn't allowed, which is exactly the kind of rule that's easy to forget when the same logic is buried in scattered if-statements instead.

frames.title: In practice
frames.text: An order's states: Placed → Paid → Shipped → Delivered, with a Cancelled state reachable from Placed or Paid — but deliberately not from Shipped or Delivered, since a shipped order can't simply be cancelled without a separate returns process. Drawing the diagram makes that missing arrow — Shipped to Cancelled — an explicit design decision instead of an accident.

frames.title: Remember
frames.text: A missing arrow in a state diagram is a design decision, not an oversight — it's often the most important information the diagram carries.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 420 140" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of two actors, Member and Librarian, connected to labeled use-case ovals for borrowing, returning, paying a fine, and adding a book."><circle class="ringNode" cx="30" cy="40" r="10"></circle><text x="30" y="62" class="figLabel" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:7px">Member</text><circle class="ringNode" cx="30" cy="100" r="10"></circle><text x="30" y="122" class="figLabel" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:7px">Librarian</text><ellipse class="boxAccent" cx="180" cy="20" rx="70" ry="16"></ellipse><text x="180" y="24" class="boxText" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:6.5px">Borrow Book</text><ellipse class="boxAccent" cx="180" cy="55" rx="70" ry="16"></ellipse><text x="180" y="59" class="boxText" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:6.5px">Return Book</text><ellipse class="boxAccent" cx="180" cy="90" rx="70" ry="16"></ellipse><text x="180" y="94" class="boxText" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:6.5px">Pay Fine</text><ellipse class="box" cx="330" cy="115" rx="70" ry="16"></ellipse><text x="330" y="119" class="boxText" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:6.5px">Add Book</text><line class="flowMuted" x1="40" y1="35" x2="115" y2="22"></line><line class="flowMuted" x1="40" y1="42" x2="115" y2="53"></line><line class="flowMuted" x1="40" y1="48" x2="115" y2="86"></line><line class="flowMuted" x1="40" y1="95" x2="260" y2="112"></line><line class="flowMuted" x1="40" y1="105" x2="115" y2="60"></line></svg>
diagrams.caption: Actors connect to the goals they can accomplish; the diagram deliberately says nothing about how any of it is implemented.

frames.title: The idea
frames.text: A use case diagram shows who can do what with a system, at the highest level of abstraction UML offers — closer to a scoping tool than a design tool, and usually the very first diagram drawn, before any class exists.

frames.title: The mechanism
frames.text: Actors (the people or external systems interacting with it) connect to use cases (goals the system helps them accomplish), drawn as labeled ovals. A use case diagram deliberately says nothing about how the system achieves any of it — that's what class and sequence diagrams are for, once scope is agreed on.

frames.title: In practice
frames.text: A library system has two actors: Member and Librarian. Member connects to “Borrow Book,” “Return Book,” and “Pay Fine.” Librarian connects to “Add Book” and can also perform “Borrow Book” and “Return Book” on a member's behalf at the front desk. None of this says whether Book is a class, or how a fine gets calculated — it only establishes what the system needs to support before any of that is decided.

frames.title: Remember
frames.text: A use case diagram fixes scope — who needs to do what — before any class or sequence diagram gets to decide how.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 120" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of three different callers across an application all calling Logger.getInstance() and receiving a reference to the same single shared Logger object."><rect class="box" x="20" y="15" width="90" height="24" rx="5"></rect><rect class="box" x="20" y="47" width="90" height="24" rx="5"></rect><rect class="box" x="20" y="79" width="90" height="24" rx="5"></rect><text x="65" y="31" class="boxText" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:7px">Module A</text><text x="65" y="63" class="boxText" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:7px">Module B</text><text x="65" y="95" class="boxText" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:7px">Module C</text><line class="flow" x1="110" y1="27" x2="240" y2="60"></line><line class="flow" x1="110" y1="59" x2="240" y2="60"></line><line class="flow" x1="110" y1="91" x2="240" y2="60"></line><rect class="boxAccent" x="250" y="42" width="120" height="36" rx="6"></rect><text x="310" y="64" class="boxText" style="font-size:8px">Logger (one instance)</text></svg>
