diagrams.caption: Every caller's getInstance() call resolves to the same single object, regardless of where in the app it's called from.

frames.title: The idea
frames.text: Singleton ensures a class has exactly one instance and gives every caller the same shared access point to it — the right tool for a genuinely shared, expensive resource, and an easy pattern to reach for too often.

frames.title: The mechanism
frames.text: The mechanics are simple: a private constructor prevents anyone from creating a second instance directly, and a static getInstance() method returns the one shared instance, creating it the first time it's needed. It fits things like a configuration manager or a connection pool, where having two separate instances would mean two different, inconsistent views of the same resource.

frames.title: In practice
frames.text: A Logger class with a private constructor and a static getInstance() method: the first call constructs the one instance and every later call — from any part of the application — returns that same object, so all log output goes through one consistently-configured logger rather than several independently-configured ones.

frames.title: Remember
frames.text: Singleton is right for a genuinely shared resource, not a convenient way to avoid passing a dependency through a constructor — and it needs real thought about concurrent first-time creation.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 420 120" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of a parallel hierarchy: an abstract Creator and Product at the top, with EmailNotificationFactory and SmsNotificationFactory each producing their own matching Notification subtype."><rect class="box" x="30" y="15" width="150" height="24" rx="5"></rect><text x="105" y="31" class="boxText" style="font-size:7px">NotificationFactory</text><rect class="box" x="240" y="15" width="150" height="24" rx="5"></rect><text x="315" y="31" class="boxText" style="font-size:7px">Notification</text><line class="flow" x1="180" y1="27" x2="235" y2="27"></line><line class="flowMuted" x1="70" y1="39" x2="70" y2="60"></line><line class="flowMuted" x1="140" y1="39" x2="140" y2="60"></line><rect class="boxAccent" x="30" y="65" width="90" height="26" rx="5"></rect><text x="75" y="82" class="boxText" style="font-size:6.5px">EmailFactory</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="130" y="65" width="90" height="26" rx="5"></rect><text x="175" y="82" class="boxText" style="font-size:6.5px">SmsFactory</text><line class="flowMuted" x1="290" y1="39" x2="290" y2="60"></line><line class="flowMuted" x1="360" y1="39" x2="360" y2="60"></line><rect class="boxAccent" x="245" y="65" width="90" height="26" rx="5"></rect><text x="290" y="82" class="boxText" style="font-size:6.5px">Email</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="345" y="65" width="90" height="26" rx="5"></rect><text x="390" y="82" class="boxText" style="font-size:6.5px">Sms</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Each concrete factory produces its own matching product subtype — the parallel-hierarchy signature of Factory Method.

frames.title: The idea
frames.text: Factory Method defines an interface for creating an object, but lets subclasses decide which concrete class actually gets instantiated — calling code depends on an abstract product type, never a specific class.

frames.title: The mechanism
frames.text: An abstract Creator class declares a factory method that returns some abstract Product type; each concrete Creator subclass overrides that method to return its own matching concrete Product subclass. The result is a parallel hierarchy — one Creator subclass per Product subclass — which is the pattern's most recognizable visual signature.

frames.title: In practice
frames.text: A NotificationFactory with EmailNotificationFactory and SmsNotificationFactory subclasses, each overriding createNotification() to return an EmailNotification or SmsNotification respectively. Calling code just asks whichever factory it was handed for “a notification” and calls send() on it — no if/else on notification type anywhere in that calling code.

frames.title: Remember
frames.text: Factory Method lets subclasses choose which concrete product gets built — useful only when that choice genuinely varies by subclass, not as a default way to construct objects.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 420 120" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of one DarkUIFactory producing a matched set of a dark button and a dark checkbox, contrasted with Factory Method's single product per creator."><rect class="boxAccent" x="30" y="45" width="120" height="30" rx="6"></rect><text x="90" y="64" class="boxText" style="font-size:7.5px">DarkUIFactory</text><line class="flow" x1="150" y1="52" x2="200" y2="30"></line><line class="flow" x1="150" y1="68" x2="200" y2="90"></line><rect class="box" x="205" y="15" width="90" height="26" rx="5"></rect><text x="250" y="32" class="boxText" style="font-size:7px">Dark Button</text><rect class="box" x="205" y="80" width="90" height="26" rx="5"></rect><text x="250" y="97" class="boxText" style="font-size:7px">Dark Checkbox</text><text x="360" y="60" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:6.5px">always a matched family</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: One factory call produces a guaranteed-matching family of related products, never a mismatched combination.

frames.title: The idea
frames.text: Abstract Factory produces a whole family of related objects through one interface, without specifying their concrete classes — one call gets you a matched set, not just one product.

frames.title: The mechanism
frames.text: Where Factory Method returns one product via subclassing, Abstract Factory returns several related products via composition — a single factory object exposes methods like createButton() and createCheckbox(), and a concrete factory implementation guarantees every product it returns belongs to the same family, so they're never accidentally mismatched.

frames.title: In practice
frames.text: A UIFactory interface with DarkUIFactory and LightUIFactory implementations. Calling createButton() and createCheckbox() on a DarkUIFactory always returns a matching dark button and dark checkbox — there's no code path where a dark button ends up paired with a light checkbox, because both came from the same factory instance.

frames.title: Remember
frames.text: Reach for Abstract Factory when you need a guaranteed-matching family of products, not just one product whose exact type varies.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 420 110" role="img" aria-label="Diagram contrasting a constructor call with eight unlabeled positional arguments against a chained builder call where every value is explicitly named."><rect class="boxWarn" x="20" y="20" width="180" height="30" rx="6"></rect><text x="110" y="39" class="boxText" style="font-size:6.5px">new Pizza(12, true, false, "thin"...)</text><text x="110" y="65" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:6.5px">which argument is which?</text><line class="divider" x1="230" y1="10" x2="230" y2="100"></line><rect class="boxAccent" x="250" y="15" width="150" height="24" rx="5"></rect><text x="325" y="31" class="boxText" style="font-size:6px">.setSize("large")</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="250" y="42" width="150" height="24" rx="5"></rect><text x="325" y="58" class="boxText" style="font-size:6px">.setCrust("thin")</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="250" y="69" width="150" height="24" rx="5"></rect><text x="325" y="85" class="boxText" style="font-size:6px">.addTopping("cheese").build()</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: A telescoping constructor call versus a chained builder where every field is named at the point it's set.

frames.title: The idea
frames.text: Builder separates constructing a complex object from what that object ultimately looks like, letting you build it up step by step instead of via one unreadable constructor call.

frames.title: The mechanism
frames.text: It fits objects with many optional fields, where a single constructor accepting every combination becomes an unreadable list of positional arguments (or worse, a family of overloaded constructors for every combination). A builder exposes one chained method per field, ending in a build() call that assembles the final object once every desired field has been set.

frames.title: In practice
frames.text: A Pizza with size, crust, and a variable list of toppings: a constructor taking eight positional arguments (several of them optional booleans) is easy to call with the wrong value in the wrong position. A PizzaBuilder instead reads as new PizzaBuilder().setSize("large").setCrust("thin").addTopping("cheese").build() — every value is explicitly named at the call site, and optional fields can simply be left out.

frames.title: Remember
frames.text: Builder earns its place once a constructor's argument list becomes hard to read or remember the order of — not before.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 420 110" role="img" aria-label="Diagram contrasting building 100 enemies from scratch, each repeating expensive setup, against cloning one pre-configured prototype 100 times instead."><rect class="boxWarn" x="20" y="20" width="170" height="28" rx="6"></rect><text x="105" y="39" class="boxText" style="font-size:7px">new Enemy() × 100</text><text x="105" y="65" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:6.5px">expensive setup repeated 100 times</text><line class="divider" x1="220" y1="10" x2="220" y2="95"></line><rect class="boxAccent" x="245" y="15" width="150" height="26" rx="5"></rect><text x="320" y="32" class="boxText" style="font-size:7px">Enemy prototype (loaded once)</text><line class="flow" x1="320" y1="41" x2="320" y2="60"></line><text x="320" y="75" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:6.5px">clone() × 100 (cheap)</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Expensive setup happens once on the prototype; every additional instance is a cheap clone of it.

frames.title: The idea
frames.text: Prototype creates new objects by cloning an existing instance rather than building from scratch — valuable when construction is expensive but a similar object already exists to copy.

frames.title: The mechanism
frames.text: A prototype object implements a clone() method that returns a copy of itself; instead of running the same expensive setup logic every time a similar object is needed, that setup runs once, and every subsequent instance comes from copying the already-configured prototype.

frames.title: In practice
frames.text: A GameCharacter template pre-loaded with textures and animation data that took real time to set up. Spawning 100 enemies of the same type by constructing each one from scratch would repeat that expensive load 100 times; cloning the one already-loaded prototype 100 times instead skips the repeated setup entirely, at the cost of a much cheaper copy operation each time.

frames.title: Remember
frames.text: Prototype trades expensive construction for a cheap clone — but only pays off once you've also gotten shallow-versus-deep copying right.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 420 110" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of a client calling a PaymentProcessor interface, which an adapter implements by translating calls into the incompatible LegacyBillingSdk's own method signature."><rect class="box" x="20" y="40" width="90" height="26" rx="5"></rect><text x="65" y="57" class="boxText" style="font-size:7px">Client</text><line class="flow" x1="110" y1="53" x2="150" y2="53"></line><text x="130" y="43" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:6px">charge()</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="155" y="40" width="100" height="26" rx="5"></rect><text x="205" y="57" class="boxText" style="font-size:6.5px">Adapter</text><line class="flow" x1="255" y1="53" x2="300" y2="53"></line><text x="278" y="43" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:6px">bill()</text><rect class="box" x="305" y="40" width="100" height="26" rx="5"></rect><text x="355" y="57" class="boxText" style="font-size:6px">LegacyBillingSdk</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: The adapter is the only new piece; the client and the wrapped class each keep their own interface unchanged.

frames.title: The idea
frames.text: Adapter converts one class's interface into another interface a client expects, letting two incompatible interfaces work together without modifying either one.

frames.title: The mechanism
frames.text: An adapter implements the interface the client already depends on, and internally holds a reference to the incompatible class, translating each call into whatever that class actually expects. Neither the client nor the wrapped class needs to change — the adapter is the only new piece.

frames.title: In practice
frames.text: An application's PaymentProcessor interface expects charge(amountInCents), but a newly integrated third-party LegacyBillingSdk only exposes bill(amountInDollars, currency). A LegacyBillingAdapter implements PaymentProcessor, and inside charge() converts cents to dollars and calls legacyBillingSdk.bill(dollars, "USD") — the rest of the application never learns the legacy SDK's shape.

frames.title: Remember
frames.text: Adapter's whole job is translation between two interfaces that were never designed to match — keep it to just that, and fix interfaces you own instead of adapting around them.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 130" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of a SimpleCoffee object wrapped first in a MilkDecorator and then in a MochaDecorator, each layer adding its own cost on top of the one inside it."><rect class="box" x="140" y="70" width="120" height="40" rx="8"></rect><text x="200" y="94" class="boxText" style="font-size:7.5px">SimpleCoffee</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="110" y="45" width="180" height="70" rx="10" style="fill:none"></rect><text x="200" y="55" class="figLabel" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:7px">MilkDecorator</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="80" y="20" width="240" height="95" rx="12" style="fill:none"></rect><text x="200" y="32" class="figLabel" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:7px">MochaDecorator</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Each decorator wraps the layer inside it, adding its own cost without a hardcoded class for every combination.

frames.title: The idea
frames.text: Decorator attaches additional responsibilities to an object dynamically by wrapping it in another object that implements the same interface — an alternative to subclassing that lets behaviors stack and combine at runtime.

frames.title: The mechanism
frames.text: Each decorator implements the same interface as the object it wraps, and forwards calls to the wrapped object while adding its own behavior before or after. Because a decorator is itself the same interface, decorators can be layered on top of each other, each one adding its own piece.

frames.title: In practice
frames.text: A Coffee interface with a cost() method: a MilkDecorator wraps any Coffee and adds milk's price on top of whatever the wrapped coffee already costs; a MochaDecorator can then wrap that combination and add mocha's price on top of that. Building new MochaDecorator(new MilkDecorator(new SimpleCoffee())) avoids needing a separate hardcoded class for every possible combination of add-ons.

frames.title: Remember
frames.text: Decorator trades a combinatorial explosion of subclasses for a small set of composable wrappers — each one focused on adding exactly one behavior.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 420 120" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of a client calling one Facade method, which internally coordinates calls to a Projector, SoundSystem, and StreamingDevice in the correct order."><rect class="box" x="20" y="45" width="90" height="26" rx="5"></rect><text x="65" y="62" class="boxText" style="font-size:7px">Client</text><line class="flow" x1="110" y1="58" x2="150" y2="58"></line><text x="130" y="48" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:6px">watchMovie()</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="155" y="45" width="110" height="26" rx="5"></rect><text x="210" y="62" class="boxText" style="font-size:7px">HomeTheaterFacade</text><line class="flowMuted" x1="265" y1="58" x2="310" y2="20"></line><line class="flowMuted" x1="265" y1="58" x2="310" y2="55"></line><line class="flowMuted" x1="265" y1="58" x2="310" y2="90"></line><rect class="box" x="315" y="8" width="90" height="24" rx="5"></rect><rect class="box" x="315" y="43" width="90" height="24" rx="5"></rect><rect class="box" x="315" y="78" width="90" height="24" rx="5"></rect><text x="360" y="24" class="boxText" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:6.5px">Projector</text><text x="360" y="59" class="boxText" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:6.5px">SoundSystem</text><text x="360" y="94" class="boxText" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:6.5px">Streaming</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: The client makes one call; the facade knows the correct order to coordinate the subsystem underneath.

frames.title: The idea
frames.text: Facade provides one simplified interface in front of a complex subsystem of many interacting classes — without hiding that subsystem entirely from callers who genuinely need finer control.

frames.title: The mechanism
frames.text: The facade itself contains little logic of its own — its job is to know the right order to call the subsystem's existing classes in, so most callers never have to learn that order themselves. Callers who need something the facade doesn't expose can usually still reach the underlying subsystem classes directly.

frames.title: In practice
frames.text: A HomeTheaterFacade.watchMovie() method internally calls projector.on(), soundSystem.setVolume(), and streamingDevice.play() in the specific order that actually works. A caller just calls watchMovie() once, without needing to know that turning on the sound system before the projector warms up causes a distracting pop.

frames.title: Remember
frames.text: A facade's value is in knowing the right order to call an existing subsystem — not in replacing that subsystem or being the only path to it.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 130" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of a folder tree where a top folder contains two files and a subfolder, and every node responds to the same getSize call regardless of whether it's a file or a folder."><rect class="boxAccent" x="150" y="15" width="100" height="26" rx="5"></rect><text x="200" y="32" class="boxText" style="font-size:7px">Folder</text><line class="flowMuted" x1="200" y1="41" x2="90" y2="70"></line><line class="flowMuted" x1="200" y1="41" x2="200" y2="70"></line><line class="flowMuted" x1="200" y1="41" x2="310" y2="70"></line><rect class="box" x="50" y="75" width="80" height="24" rx="5"></rect><text x="90" y="91" class="boxText" style="font-size:6.5px">File.txt</text><rect class="box" x="160" y="75" width="80" height="24" rx="5"></rect><text x="200" y="91" class="boxText" style="font-size:6.5px">File2.txt</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="270" y="75" width="80" height="24" rx="5"></rect><text x="310" y="91" class="boxText" style="font-size:6.5px">Subfolder</text><line class="flowMuted" x1="310" y1="99" x2="310" y2="115"></line><rect class="box" x="270" y="115" width="80" height="20" rx="4"></rect><text x="310" y="129" class="boxText" style="font-size:6px">File3.txt</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Files and folders alike respond to getSize(); a folder just delegates to whatever its children happen to be.

frames.title: The idea
frames.text: Composite arranges objects into tree structures representing part-whole hierarchies, so a single object and a group of objects can be treated through the exact same interface.

frames.title: The mechanism
frames.text: A shared interface defines an operation that makes sense for both an individual “leaf” and a “composite” that holds children of that same interface. The composite's implementation typically delegates to each of its children — calling code never needs to check whether it's holding a leaf or a composite before calling the shared operation.

frames.title: In practice
frames.text: A file system: File and Folder both implement a FileSystemNode interface with getSize(). File.getSize() just returns its own size; Folder.getSize() recursively sums getSize() across every child, whether each child happens to be a File or another Folder. Calling code asking “how big is this?” never needs to special-case which kind of node it's holding.

frames.title: Remember
frames.text: Composite's payoff is treating one object and a whole subtree of objects identically — the calling code stops needing to know which one it's holding.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 420 110" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of a client calling display() on an ImageProxy, which only loads the real, expensive RealImage the first time display is actually called."><rect class="box" x="20" y="40" width="90" height="26" rx="5"></rect><text x="65" y="57" class="boxText" style="font-size:7px">Client</text><line class="flow" x1="110" y1="53" x2="150" y2="53"></line><text x="130" y="43" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:6px">display()</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="155" y="40" width="100" height="26" rx="5"></rect><text x="205" y="57" class="boxText" style="font-size:7px">ImageProxy</text><line class="flowMuted" x1="255" y1="53" x2="300" y2="53"></line><text x="278" y="43" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:6px">loads once</text><rect class="box" x="305" y="40" width="100" height="26" rx="5"></rect><text x="355" y="57" class="boxText" style="font-size:6.5px">RealImage</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: The proxy stands in for the real object cheaply, deferring the expensive load until it's genuinely needed.

frames.title: The idea
frames.text: Proxy provides a stand-in object that controls access to another object — implementing the same interface, but able to add behavior like lazy loading, access control, or caching before forwarding the call along.

frames.title: The mechanism
frames.text: A proxy implements the same interface as the real object it stands in for, so callers can't tell the difference at the call site. What the proxy adds is control: it might defer creating the real object until it's actually needed, check permissions before allowing a call through, or cache a result instead of forwarding every call.

frames.title: In practice
frames.text: An ImageProxy implements the same Image interface as a RealImage, but doesn't actually load the (expensive) image file from disk until display() is called on it for the first time. Every earlier reference to the proxy — holding it in a list, passing it around — stays cheap, and the real loading cost only happens if and when the image is actually displayed.

frames.title: Remember
frames.text: A proxy looks exactly like the real object to its callers, but controls when — or whether — the real, often expensive object actually gets involved.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 120" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of a ShoppingCart holding a reference to a swappable PaymentStrategy interface, with three concrete strategies underneath it that can each be substituted in."><rect class="box" x="30" y="40" width="110" height="30" rx="6"></rect><text x="85" y="59" class="boxText" style="font-size:7px">ShoppingCart</text><line class="flow" x1="140" y1="55" x2="185" y2="55"></line><rect class="boxAccent" x="190" y="40" width="120" height="30" rx="6"></rect><text x="250" y="59" class="boxText" style="font-size:7px">PaymentStrategy</text><rect class="box" x="330" y="5" width="60" height="24" rx="5"></rect><rect class="box" x="330" y="40" width="60" height="24" rx="5"></rect><rect class="box" x="330" y="75" width="60" height="24" rx="5"></rect><text x="360" y="21" class="boxText" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:6px">CreditCard</text><text x="360" y="56" class="boxText" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:6px">PayPal</text><text x="360" y="91" class="boxText" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:6px">Crypto</text><line class="flowMuted" x1="310" y1="55" x2="330" y2="17"></line><line class="flowMuted" x1="310" y1="55" x2="330" y2="52"></line><line class="flowMuted" x1="310" y1="55" x2="330" y2="87"></line></svg>
diagrams.caption: ShoppingCart delegates to whichever concrete strategy it currently holds, never checking payment type itself.

frames.title: The idea
frames.text: Strategy encapsulates a family of interchangeable algorithms behind a common interface, so the algorithm a class uses can be swapped at runtime — this is the exact fix the earlier duck example reached for, now named and generalized.

frames.title: The mechanism
frames.text: A context object holds a reference to a strategy interface rather than a hardcoded algorithm, and delegates to whichever concrete strategy it currently holds. Swapping behavior means swapping which strategy instance the context holds — not editing the context's own code.

frames.title: In practice
frames.text: A PaymentStrategy interface with CreditCardStrategy, PayPalStrategy, and CryptoStrategy implementations. A ShoppingCart holds whichever strategy the shopper selected at checkout and calls strategy.pay(amount) — there's no if/else on payment type anywhere inside ShoppingCart itself.

frames.title: Remember
frames.text: Strategy turns "which algorithm" into an object you hand in, rather than a branch you edit — the same fix composition offered the duck example, now with a name.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 120" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of a WeatherStation subject notifying three registered observers directly whenever its temperature changes."><rect class="boxAccent" x="30" y="45" width="120" height="30" rx="6"></rect><text x="90" y="64" class="boxText" style="font-size:7.5px">WeatherStation</text><line class="flow" x1="150" y1="60" x2="260" y2="15"></line><line class="flow" x1="150" y1="60" x2="260" y2="50"></line><line class="flow" x1="150" y1="60" x2="260" y2="85"></line><rect class="box" x="265" y="3" width="90" height="24" rx="5"></rect><rect class="box" x="265" y="38" width="90" height="24" rx="5"></rect><rect class="box" x="265" y="73" width="90" height="24" rx="5"></rect><text x="310" y="19" class="boxText" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:6.5px">PhoneDisplay</text><text x="310" y="54" class="boxText" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:6.5px">WebDisplay</text><text x="310" y="89" class="boxText" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:6.5px">WatchDisplay</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: The subject notifies every registered observer directly; it never needs to know what each one does with the update.

frames.title: The idea
frames.text: Observer defines a one-to-many dependency so that when one object changes state, every registered dependent is notified automatically — without the object doing the notifying ever needing to know what its observers actually do with that notification.

frames.title: The mechanism
frames.text: A subject keeps a list of registered observers and calls a shared update() (or similar) method on each of them whenever its own state changes. Adding a new kind of observer means implementing that shared interface and registering an instance — the subject's own code never has to change to support it.

frames.title: In practice
frames.text: A WeatherStation (the subject) calls notify() on every registered display whenever the temperature changes; PhoneDisplay and WebDisplay both implement an Observer interface and register themselves with the station. Adding a SmartWatchDisplay later means writing one new class and registering it — WeatherStation itself is untouched.

frames.title: Remember
frames.text: Observer decouples the subject from its dependents entirely — it just notifies; what each observer does with that notification is never its concern.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 110" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of a remote button, the invoker, holding a Command reference whose execute call acts on the actual receiver object, such as a TV."><rect class="box" x="20" y="40" width="90" height="26" rx="5"></rect><text x="65" y="57" class="boxText" style="font-size:7px">Button (invoker)</text><line class="flow" x1="110" y1="53" x2="150" y2="53"></line><text x="130" y="43" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:6px">execute()</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="155" y="40" width="100" height="26" rx="5"></rect><text x="205" y="57" class="boxText" style="font-size:6.5px">TurnOnCommand</text><line class="flow" x1="255" y1="53" x2="300" y2="53"></line><rect class="box" x="305" y="40" width="80" height="26" rx="5"></rect><text x="345" y="57" class="boxText" style="font-size:7px">TV</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: The invoker never knows what the command does or what it acts on — it just calls execute().

frames.title: The idea
frames.text: Command turns a request into an object, so callers can parameterize behavior with different requests, queue them, log them, or undo them — the action itself becomes a first-class value instead of a direct method call.

frames.title: The mechanism
frames.text: Each command implements a shared interface with an execute() method (and usually undo() ), wrapping everything needed to perform — and reverse — one specific action. An invoker holds a command reference and calls execute() without needing to know what the command actually does or which object it acts on.

frames.title: In practice
frames.text: A TV remote's buttons are each bound to a Command object — TurnOnCommand, VolumeUpCommand — rather than hardcoded logic per button. Because every command also implements undo(), the remote can offer one generic “undo last action” button that calls lastCommand.undo() without needing to know what that last action actually was.

frames.title: Remember
frames.text: Command's real payoff is treating an action as data — something you can queue, log, or reverse — not just a slightly indirect way to call a method.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 120" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of a MediaPlayer context delegating every call to whichever state object is current, with transitions moving the current-state reference between Playing, Paused, and Stopped."><rect class="box" x="30" y="45" width="110" height="30" rx="6"></rect><text x="85" y="64" class="boxText" style="font-size:7px">MediaPlayer</text><line class="flow" x1="140" y1="60" x2="185" y2="60"></line><text x="162" y="50" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:6px">delegates to</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="190" y="10" width="90" height="24" rx="5"></rect><rect class="box" x="190" y="45" width="90" height="24" rx="5"></rect><rect class="box" x="190" y="80" width="90" height="24" rx="5"></rect><text x="235" y="26" class="boxText" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:6.5px">PlayingState</text><text x="235" y="61" class="boxText" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:6.5px">PausedState</text><text x="235" y="96" class="boxText" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:6.5px">StoppedState</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: The player delegates to its current state object; which object that is changes as the player transitions between states.

frames.title: The idea
frames.text: State lets an object change its behavior when its internal state changes, by delegating state-specific logic to separate state objects — the direct code counterpart to the state diagrams drawn earlier in this course.

frames.title: The mechanism
frames.text: Instead of one class checking a status flag with if/else inside every method, each state gets its own class implementing a shared interface, and the context object simply delegates each call to whichever state object is current. The object appears to change its class as it moves between states, without any single method growing a branch per state.

frames.title: In practice
frames.text: A MediaPlayer 's play() button behaves differently depending on whether it's Playing, Paused, or Stopped. Rather than an if/else on a status field inside every method, each state ( PlayingState, PausedState, StoppedState ) implements its own play() / pause() / stop(), and the player just forwards each call to whichever state object it currently holds.

frames.title: Remember
frames.text: State turns "what mode am I in" from a flag checked everywhere into an object the context simply delegates to — the same idea the state diagrams drew, now expressed in code.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 110" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of a fixed process sequence, read then transform then save, defined once in a base class, with only the read and transform steps overridden differently by CSV and JSON subclasses."><rect class="box" x="20" y="15" width="360" height="26" rx="5"></rect><text x="200" y="32" class="boxText" style="font-size:7.5px">process(): readData() → transformData() → saveData()</text><line class="flowMuted" x1="120" y1="41" x2="120" y2="65"></line><line class="flowMuted" x1="280" y1="41" x2="280" y2="65"></line><rect class="boxAccent" x="60" y="70" width="120" height="26" rx="5"></rect><text x="120" y="87" class="boxText" style="font-size:6.5px">CsvProcessor overrides</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="220" y="70" width="120" height="26" rx="5"></rect><text x="280" y="87" class="boxText" style="font-size:6.5px">JsonProcessor overrides</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: The base class owns the sequence; subclasses only ever change what specific steps do, never the order.

frames.title: The idea
frames.text: Template Method defines the skeleton of an algorithm in a base class, deferring specific steps to subclasses — the overall sequence stays fixed and protected, while individual steps remain overridable.

frames.title: The mechanism
frames.text: A base class method calls a fixed sequence of steps, some of which are implemented directly and some of which are left abstract for subclasses to fill in. Subclasses can change what individual steps do, but they can't change the order the base class calls them in — the algorithm's shape is owned in exactly one place.

frames.title: In practice
frames.text: A DataProcessor.process() template method calls readData(), then transformData(), then saveData(), always in that order. CsvProcessor and JsonProcessor subclasses only override readData() and transformData() for their own format — neither one ever touches the overall sequence, or needs to.

frames.title: Remember
frames.text: Template Method fixes the algorithm's shape in one place and lets subclasses vary only its individual steps — never the sequence itself.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 420 100" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of an expense request entering a chain of TeamLead, Manager, and Director handlers, passed along until one handler's approval limit covers it."><rect class="box" x="20" y="35" width="90" height="30" rx="6"></rect><text x="65" y="54" class="boxText" style="font-size:7px">Request: $2,000</text><line class="flow" x1="110" y1="50" x2="150" y2="50"></line><rect class="box" x="155" y="35" width="80" height="30" rx="6"></rect><text x="195" y="54" class="boxText" style="font-size:7px">TeamLead</text><line class="flowMuted" x1="235" y1="50" x2="265" y2="50"></line><text x="250" y="40" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:6px">passes on</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="270" y="35" width="80" height="30" rx="6"></rect><text x="310" y="54" class="boxText" style="font-size:7px">Manager</text><text x="310" y="80" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:6.5px">approves here</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: The request moves along the chain until a handler's limit covers it; the sender never picks which one.

frames.title: The idea
frames.text: Chain of Responsibility passes a request along a chain of handler objects until one of them handles it, decoupling the sender from ever needing to know which specific handler will actually deal with it.

frames.title: The mechanism
frames.text: Each handler in the chain either handles the request itself or passes it to the next handler in line. The sender only ever talks to the first handler — it never knows, or needs to know, how many handlers exist or which one will ultimately act.

frames.title: In practice
frames.text: An expense-approval chain: a TeamLead can approve requests up to $500, a Manager up to $5,000, a Director anything above that. A request for $2,000 enters at TeamLead, which passes it along since it's over its own limit, and Manager approves it — the person submitting the expense never had to know which specific approver's limit would actually cover it.

frames.title: Remember
frames.text: Chain of Responsibility lets the sender hand off a request without knowing — or caring — which handler down the line will end up dealing with it.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 420 110" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of two failure paths: a thrown exception unwinding the call stack for a truly exceptional failure, versus a Result return value the caller must explicitly check for a routine, expected failure."><rect class="box" x="20" y="15" width="170" height="26" rx="5"></rect><text x="105" y="32" class="boxText" style="font-size:7px">withdrawFunds(): DB connection drops</text><line class="flowMuted" x1="105" y1="41" x2="105" y2="65"></line><text x="120" y="55" class="figHint" style="font-size:6.5px">throws</text><rect class="boxWarn" x="45" y="70" width="120" height="24" rx="5"></rect><text x="105" y="86" class="boxText" style="font-size:6.5px">unwinds the stack</text><line class="divider" x1="220" y1="10" x2="220" y2="100"></line><rect class="box" x="240" y="15" width="160" height="26" rx="5"></rect><text x="320" y="32" class="boxText" style="font-size:7px">withdrawFunds(): insufficient balance</text><line class="flow" x1="320" y1="41" x2="320" y2="65"></line><text x="345" y="55" class="figHint" style="font-size:6.5px">returns Result</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="255" y="70" width="130" height="24" rx="5"></rect><text x="320" y="86" class="boxText" style="font-size:6.5px">caller checks explicitly</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: A truly exceptional failure unwinds the stack; a routine, expected failure is a value the caller must actively check.

frames.title: The idea
frames.text: How a class handles failure is a design decision, not an afterthought — deciding which layer validates input, and whether a failure is an exception or a value the caller checks, is part of the class's contract just as much as its normal-case methods are.

frames.title: The mechanism
frames.text: Exceptions suit failures that are truly exceptional — rare, unexpected, and usually unrecoverable at the point they're thrown. Failures that are routine and expected as part of normal operation are often clearer as an explicit return value (a Result type, or a boolean plus a reason) that the caller must actively check, rather than an exception it might forget to catch.

frames.title: In practice
frames.text: A withdrawFunds(amount) method: insufficient balance happens routinely and is entirely expected, so returning a Result (success or a specific failure reason) forces the caller to explicitly handle the case where the withdrawal didn't go through. A genuinely exceptional failure — the underlying database connection dropping mid-transaction — is a better fit for a thrown exception, since it's not something normal calling code is expected to routinely check for.

frames.title: Remember
frames.text: Reserve exceptions for truly exceptional, rare failures; make routine, expected outcomes an explicit value the caller has to check.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 420 110" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of two threads both racing to create a singleton instance under an unsynchronized check, versus a synchronized creation path that only one thread can pass through at a time."><rect class="boxWarn" x="20" y="15" width="180" height="26" rx="5"></rect><text x="110" y="32" class="boxText" style="font-size:7px">unsynchronized getInstance()</text><text x="30" y="55" class="figHint" style="font-size:6.5px">Thread A: sees null, creates</text><text x="30" y="70" class="figHint" style="font-size:6.5px">Thread B: also sees null, creates</text><text x="30" y="88" class="figHint" style="font-size:6.5px">→ two instances exist</text><line class="divider" x1="220" y1="10" x2="220" y2="100"></line><rect class="boxAccent" x="240" y="15" width="160" height="26" rx="5"></rect><text x="320" y="32" class="boxText" style="font-size:7px">synchronized getInstance()</text><text x="250" y="55" class="figHint" style="font-size:6.5px">Thread A: passes, creates</text><text x="250" y="70" class="figHint" style="font-size:6.5px">Thread B: waits, then reuses it</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Without synchronizing the check-and-create step, two threads racing on first creation can each build a separate instance.

frames.title: The idea
frames.text: An LLD only needs to worry about thread safety where an object's mutable state can genuinely be reached by more than one thread at once — the design decision is recognizing which objects that applies to, not applying it defensively everywhere.

frames.title: The mechanism
frames.text: Immutable objects, and objects confined to a single thread, are automatically safe — there's no shared mutable state for two threads to race over. Shared, mutable state is where synchronization actually needs to be reasoned about, and the goal is synchronizing only the specific section that's actually unsafe, not the whole object.

frames.title: In practice
frames.text: Revisit the earlier Logger.getInstance() singleton: two threads calling it for the first time simultaneously can both see no instance yet and both construct one, defeating the “exactly one instance” guarantee entirely. The fix is synchronizing just the check-and-create step (or constructing the instance eagerly at class load time, sidestepping the race entirely) — not synchronizing every method the Logger exposes afterward, which would serialize all logging unnecessarily.

frames.title: Remember
frames.text: Synchronize the specific section where mutable state is genuinely shared — not the whole object, and not by default everywhere just in case.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 420 110" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of a class constructing its own dependency internally, a tight coupling, versus the same dependency being handed in from outside through the constructor, an injected one."><rect class="boxWarn" x="20" y="35" width="170" height="30" rx="6"></rect><text x="105" y="54" class="boxText" style="font-size:7px">OrderService: new StripeGateway()</text><line class="divider" x1="220" y1="10" x2="220" y2="100"></line><rect class="box" x="240" y="20" width="80" height="26" rx="5"></rect><text x="280" y="37" class="boxText" style="font-size:7px">caller</text><line class="flow" x1="320" y1="33" x2="360" y2="33"></line><text x="340" y="23" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:6px">injects</text><rect class="boxAccent" x="245" y="60" width="150" height="28" rx="5"></rect><text x="320" y="78" class="boxText" style="font-size:6.5px">OrderService(gateway)</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: A dependency built internally versus one handed in from outside, ready to be swapped or faked by whoever constructs the service.

frames.title: The idea
frames.text: Dependency Injection is the practical mechanism most often used to satisfy the Dependency Inversion Principle: instead of a class constructing its own dependencies, they're supplied to it from outside.

frames.title: The mechanism
frames.text: DIP is the principle — depend on abstractions, not concrete details. DI is one common way to satisfy it in real code: constructor injection (passing dependencies as constructor arguments), setter injection, or a DI container that wires an entire application's object graph together at startup. A small codebase can satisfy DIP with a few manual constructor calls; DI containers earn their complexity once an application has enough services depending on each other that wiring them by hand becomes unwieldy.

frames.title: In practice
frames.text: Take the earlier OrderService depending on a PaymentGateway interface. Constructor injection looks like new OrderService(new StripeGateway()) — explicit and simple for a handful of classes. A DI container, in a larger application, instead reads configuration once at startup and automatically constructs and wires every service's dependencies, including OrderService's, without any single line of application code calling new on another service directly.

frames.title: Remember
frames.text: DI is how you actually satisfy DIP in code — start with plain constructor injection, and reach for a framework only once wiring by hand genuinely becomes the bottleneck.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 420 110" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of a test unable to isolate a class from a hardcoded real dependency, versus a test injecting a fake dependency to isolate the class under test."><rect class="box" x="20" y="40" width="70" height="26" rx="5"></rect><text x="55" y="57" class="boxText" style="font-size:7px">Test</text><line class="flow" x1="90" y1="53" x2="130" y2="53"></line><rect class="box" x="135" y="40" width="110" height="26" rx="5"></rect><text x="190" y="57" class="boxText" style="font-size:6.5px">OrderService</text><line class="flowMuted" x1="245" y1="53" x2="280" y2="53"></line><rect class="boxWarn" x="285" y="40" width="110" height="26" rx="5"></rect><text x="340" y="57" class="boxText" style="font-size:6px">real StripeGateway</text><text x="200" y="85" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:6.5px">vs. injecting a FakePaymentGateway instead — same test, isolated</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: A hardcoded real dependency can't be isolated in a test; an injected one can simply be swapped for a fake.

frames.title: The idea
frames.text: A class's design directly determines how easily it can be tested in isolation — testability isn't a separate concern bolted on afterward, it's a genuine signal of whether the design itself is sound.

frames.title: The mechanism
frames.text: A dependency that's injected in (per the previous article) can be swapped for a test double that behaves predictably; a dependency constructed internally can't be swapped at all, forcing tests to either exercise the real thing or skip testing that path entirely. If a class is hard to test, that's usually pointing at a real design issue — not just a testing inconvenience to work around.

frames.title: In practice
frames.text: With OrderService depending on an injected PaymentGateway interface, a test can pass in a FakePaymentGateway that deterministically succeeds or fails on command, letting every branch of OrderService's logic be tested without ever touching a real payment provider. With a hardcoded new StripeGateway() buried inside the constructor, testing OrderService means either actually talking to Stripe in every test run, or not testing that logic at all.

frames.title: Remember
frames.text: If a class is hard to test in isolation, that's usually the design telling you something — not just an inconvenience for the test suite to work around.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 420 100" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of a NotificationSender's growing if-else on channel type being refactored into a dispatch call against a shared channel interface, the same shape as the earlier Strategy fix."><rect class="boxWarn" x="20" y="30" width="170" height="30" rx="6"></rect><text x="105" y="49" class="boxText" style="font-size:7px">if/else on channel type</text><line class="flow" x1="190" y1="45" x2="230" y2="45"></line><rect class="boxAccent" x="235" y="30" width="160" height="30" rx="6"></rect><text x="315" y="49" class="boxText" style="font-size:7px">channel.send() — polymorphic</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: The same fix already seen for payment types, recognized here from a different starting symptom.

frames.title: The idea
frames.text: Good LLD is rarely achieved on the first pass — it's usually recognized in hindsight, when a change request becomes unexpectedly painful, and then deliberately restructured toward one of the patterns this course already covers.

frames.title: The mechanism
frames.text: Specific pain points point to specific fixes: an if/else chain that grows with every new case usually wants Strategy or Factory Method behind it; a class doing three unrelated things every time one of them changes usually wants splitting along Single Responsibility lines; a rigid subclass that breaks under a new requirement usually wants composition instead of inheritance. Recognizing which symptom you're looking at is most of the work.

frames.title: In practice
frames.text: A NotificationSender with an if/else on channel type that's grown a new branch every time a channel was added gets refactored the same way Strategy handled payment types earlier: each channel becomes its own class implementing a shared interface, and NotificationSender just calls channel.send() polymorphically — the exact same shape of fix, recognized from a different starting point.

frames.title: Remember
frames.text: Treat a growing if/else, a class with too many reasons to change, or a fragile subclass as a signal pointing at a specific, already-known fix — not a reason to redesign from scratch.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 420 130" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of ParkingLot coordinating Vehicle, ParkingSpot, and Ticket, with a pluggable spot-assignment strategy deciding which spot a vehicle gets."><rect class="boxAccent" x="160" y="15" width="120" height="28" rx="6"></rect><text x="220" y="34" class="boxText" style="font-size:7.5px">ParkingLot</text><line class="flow" x1="220" y1="43" x2="220" y2="65"></line><text x="255" y="58" class="figHint" style="font-size:6.5px">assignment strategy</text><rect class="box" x="150" y="70" width="140" height="26" rx="5"></rect><text x="220" y="87" class="boxText" style="font-size:7px">SpotAssignmentStrategy</text><line class="flowMuted" x1="160" y1="29" x2="60" y2="60"></line><rect class="box" x="20" y="65" width="80" height="24" rx="5"></rect><text x="60" y="81" class="boxText" style="font-size:6.5px">Vehicle</text><line class="flowMuted" x1="280" y1="29" x2="370" y2="60"></line><rect class="box" x="330" y="65" width="80" height="24" rx="5"></rect><text x="370" y="81" class="boxText" style="font-size:6.5px">Ticket</text><rect class="box" x="175" y="105" width="90" height="22" rx="5"></rect><text x="220" y="120" class="boxText" style="font-size:6.5px">ParkingSpot</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: ParkingLot coordinates Vehicle, ParkingSpot, and Ticket, delegating the assignment decision to a swappable strategy.

frames.title: A vehicle arrives.
frames.text: A vehicle arrives. ParkingLot asks its current spot-assignment strategy to find a free spot matching the vehicle's size.

frames.title: The spot is marked occupied,
frames.text: The spot is marked occupied, and a Ticket is created recording the entry time, the assigned spot, and the vehicle.

frames.title: The vehicle exits.
frames.text: The vehicle exits. ParkingLot asks its fee strategy to calculate a charge from the Ticket's duration and the vehicle's type.

frames.title: The spot is marked free again,
frames.text: The spot is marked free again, available for the next vehicle whose size fits it.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 420 120" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of an ElevatorController dispatching a floor call to one of several elevators, each of which delegates the request to whichever state object it currently holds."><rect class="boxAccent" x="20" y="45" width="130" height="30" rx="6"></rect><text x="85" y="64" class="boxText" style="font-size:7px">ElevatorController</text><line class="flow" x1="150" y1="60" x2="190" y2="60"></line><rect class="box" x="195" y="15" width="100" height="26" rx="5"></rect><rect class="box" x="195" y="65" width="100" height="26" rx="5"></rect><text x="245" y="32" class="boxText" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:6.5px">Elevator A</text><text x="245" y="82" class="boxText" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:6.5px">Elevator B</text><line class="flowMuted" x1="295" y1="28" x2="330" y2="28"></line><line class="flowMuted" x1="295" y1="78" x2="330" y2="78"></line><rect class="box" x="335" y="15" width="70" height="26" rx="5"></rect><text x="370" y="32" class="boxText" style="font-size:6px">MovingUp</text><rect class="box" x="335" y="65" width="70" height="26" rx="5"></rect><text x="370" y="82" class="boxText" style="font-size:6px">Idle</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: The controller only dispatches the call; each elevator's own current state decides what handling it actually means.

frames.title: A rider presses “up” on floor 3.
frames.text: A rider presses “up” on floor 3. ElevatorController picks the best candidate — often the nearest idle elevator, or one already moving up toward that floor.

frames.title: The chosen Elevator's current state object handles the request.
frames.text: The chosen Elevator's current state object handles the request. An idle elevator transitions to MovingUpState; one already moving up just queues the new floor.

frames.title: The elevator reaches floor 3
frames.text: The elevator reaches floor 3 and transitions to DoorsOpenState.

frames.title: After a timeout,
frames.text: After a timeout, it returns to IdleState, or continues to any other floors still queued.

frames.title: A member requests to borrow a title.
frames.text: A member requests to borrow a title. The Library finds an available BookCopy of that Book.

frames.title: It checks the member's current loan count
frames.text: It checks the member's current loan count against their borrow limit before proceeding.

frames.title: A Loan is created
frames.text: A Loan is created linking the Member to that specific BookCopy, with a due date, and the copy is marked unavailable.

frames.title: On return,
frames.text: On return, the Loan closes and that same copy becomes available again for the next member.

diagrams.caption: A stock check at the very first transition decides whether payment is even accepted for the selected slot.

frames.title: A customer selects a product while the machine is Idle.
frames.text: A customer selects a product while the machine is Idle. If the slot has stock, it transitions to AwaitingPaymentState; if not, straight to OutOfStockState.

frames.title: The customer inserts coins
frames.text: The customer inserts coins and the machine tracks the running balance against the selected product's price.

frames.title: Once the balance covers the price,
frames.text: Once the balance covers the price, the machine transitions to DispensingState.

frames.title: It dispenses the product, returns any change,
frames.text: It dispenses the product, returns any change, and resets to IdleState for the next customer.

diagrams.caption: Game coordinates three separate collaborators for one turn instead of owning all their logic itself.

frames.title: Game asks the current Player for a move.
frames.text: Game asks the current Player for a move.

frames.title: Game validates the target cell is empty
frames.text: Game validates the target cell is empty via Board before accepting it.

frames.title: Board records the mark
frames.text: Board records the mark at that cell.

frames.title: Game asks a WinChecker to evaluate the board
frames.text: Game asks a WinChecker to evaluate the board from the perspective of the player who just moved.

frames.title: If there's no winner and the board isn't full,
frames.text: If there's no winner and the board isn't full, turn passes to the other Player; otherwise the game ends and reports the result.

diagrams.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 420 120" role="img" aria-label="Diagram of MeetingScheduler checking every attendee's Calendar for a time conflict before committing one Meeting to all of them together."><rect class="boxAccent" x="160" y="15" width="120" height="28" rx="6"></rect><text x="220" y="34" class="boxText" style="font-size:7px">MeetingScheduler</text><line class="flowMuted" x1="220" y1="43" x2="60" y2="65"></line><line class="flowMuted" x1="220" y1="43" x2="220" y2="65"></line><line class="flowMuted" x1="220" y1="43" x2="380" y2="65"></line><rect class="box" x="20" y="70" width="80" height="26" rx="5"></rect><rect class="box" x="180" y="70" width="80" height="26" rx="5"></rect><rect class="box" x="340" y="70" width="80" height="26" rx="5"></rect><text x="60" y="87" class="boxText" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:6.5px">Alice's Calendar</text><text x="220" y="87" class="boxText" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:6.5px">Bob's Calendar</text><text x="380" y="87" class="boxText" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:6.5px">Carol's Calendar</text><text x="220" y="110" class="figHint" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:6.5px">only commits if every calendar reports free</text></svg>
diagrams.caption: Every attendee's calendar is checked before the meeting is committed to any of them, never one at a time.

frames.title: An organizer requests a meeting
frames.text: An organizer requests a meeting with a set of attendees and a time range.

frames.title: MeetingScheduler asks each attendee's Calendar
frames.text: MeetingScheduler asks each attendee's Calendar whether that range overlaps any of their existing bookings.

frames.title: If every calendar reports free,
frames.text: If every calendar reports free, a Meeting is created and added to every attendee's Calendar in one committed step — never partially, since a partial booking would need an awkward rollback if a later attendee turned out busy.

frames.title: If any attendee conflicts,
frames.text: If any attendee conflicts, the whole request is rejected, naming which attendee or attendees caused it.
